lesson.example: The letter T has one sleeping line and one standing line. The letter V has two slanting lines.
lesson.activity: Line pictures: children draw a house using only standing, sleeping and slanting lines, then add curved lines for clouds.

questions.q: Which letter has only a standing line?
Which lines make the letter X?
Is the letter O made of straight or curved lines?

lesson.homework: Find standing, sleeping and slanting lines in your home and draw them.

topics.title: Decoration for Festival (Addition and Subtraction)
topics.summary: Add ones first, then tens: 24 + 15 = 39.
notes: Add ones first, then tens: 24 + 15 = 39.
If the ones make 10 or more, make a new ten (regroup).
Subtract ones first, then tens: 39 − 15 = 24.
Addition and subtraction are opposites.
Read the story to decide whether to add or subtract.
outcomes: Add and subtract 2-digit numbers
Solve word problems about festival decorations

lesson.hook: For the festival, we made 24 paper flowers and our friends made 15. How many flowers for decoration?
lesson.example: 24 + 15: ones 4 + 5 = 9, tens 2 + 1 = 3, so 39 flowers.
lesson.activity: Decoration shop: children buy and use paper decorations and write the sums and differences on a class chart.

questions.q: Find 36 + 22.
Find 47 + 25.
There were 50 diyas; 18 were used. How many are left?

lesson.homework: Make up one adding story and one subtracting story about a festival.

topics.title: Rani's Gift (Measurement)
topics.summary: We can measure length with hand spans, paper clips or a ruler.
notes: We can measure length with hand spans, paper clips or a ruler.
A ruler measures in centimetres (cm).
Different hand spans give different answers; a ruler gives the same answer for everyone.
We compare weights with a simple balance: the heavier side goes down.
We compare how much containers hold by pouring water.
outcomes: Measure length with non-standard and standard units
Compare weights and capacities

lesson.hook: Rani got a ribbon as a gift. Is it long enough to tie around the gift box? How can we check?
lesson.example: The ribbon is 30 cm long; the box needs 40 cm around it. The ribbon is 10 cm too short.
lesson.activity: Measure the gift: children measure a box, a book and a pencil with a ruler and write the lengths in cm.

questions.q: What does a ruler measure in?
On a balance, which side goes down?
Which holds more water: a bucket or a glass?

lesson.homework: Measure three things at home with a ruler.

topics.title: Grouping and Sharing (Multiplication and Division)
topics.summary: Equal groups can be counted quickly: 3 groups of 4 = 12.
notes: Equal groups can be counted quickly: 3 groups of 4 = 12.
Multiplication is repeated addition: 4 + 4 + 4 = 3 × 4.
Sharing equally means everyone gets the same.
12 shared among 3 is 4 each: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
Grouping and sharing are two sides of the same idea.
outcomes: Understand multiplication as equal groups
Understand division as sharing equally

lesson.hook: 12 bananas are to be shared equally among 3 monkeys. How many does each monkey get?
lesson.example: 12 bananas shared by 3 monkeys: give one to each in turn until none are left — each gets 4.
lesson.activity: Fair share: children share counters equally among 2, 3 and 4 friends and record how many each gets.

questions.q: 4 groups of 5 = ?
Share 10 pencils among 2 children. How many each?
Write 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 as multiplication.

lesson.homework: Share some chappatis or fruits equally at home and write how many each got.

chapters.title: Which Season is it? (Measurement of Time)

topics.title: Which Season is it? (Measurement of Time)
topics.summary: There are 7 days in a week and 12 months in a year.
notes: There are 7 days in a week and 12 months in a year.
The months are January to December.
Seasons change through the year: summer, rainy season, winter.
Festivals and holidays come in certain months.
A calendar helps us know the day and date.
outcomes: Know days of the week and months of the year
Relate months to seasons and events

resources.title: Seasons: the Earth round the Sun

lesson.hook: When is it hot, when does it rain, and when is it cold where you live? Which months?
lesson.example: In most of India, April and May are hot (summer), June to September is the rainy season, and December and January are cold.
lesson.activity: Season wheel: children draw a circle divided into 12 months and colour the months of summer, rains and winter.

questions.q: How many months are in a year?
Which day comes after Friday?
In which season do we use umbrellas?

lesson.homework: Mark your birthday and two festivals on a calendar at home.

topics.title: Fun at the Fair (Money)
topics.summary: We pay with coins and notes: ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100.
notes: We pay with coins and notes: ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100.
The same amount can be made in many ways.
Add prices to find the total cost.
Change = money paid − total cost.
Always check the change you get.
outcomes: Use coins and notes to pay and get change
Add money amounts up to ₹100

lesson.hook: At the fair, a balloon costs ₹15 and a toy costs ₹30. Can you buy both with ₹50?
lesson.activity: Fun fair: set up stalls with price tags; children pay with toy money and calculate change.

questions.q: Make ₹20 using ₹5 coins.
A pen costs ₹12 and a book costs ₹25. What is the total?
You pay ₹50 for a ₹38 toy. How much change?

lesson.homework: Go shopping with an adult and check the change you receive.

topics.title: Data Handling
topics.summary: Data is information we collect by asking or counting.
notes: Data is information we collect by asking or counting.
Tally marks help us count quickly.
We can show data in a table.
A picture graph uses pictures to show how many.
We read the graph to see which is the most and least.
outcomes: Collect data by asking questions
Show data in tables and picture graphs and read them

lesson.hook: What is the favourite fruit in our class? Let's ask everyone and find out!
lesson.example: Mango 8, banana 5, apple 4, guava 3. Mango is the favourite; guava is the least liked.
lesson.activity: Fruit vote: each child sticks a fruit picture on a class chart; then the class counts and reads the graph.

questions.q: Which fruit got the most votes in the example?
How many more votes did banana get than guava?
Show 7 using tally marks.
questions.a: One bundle of 5 and 2 more lines.

lesson.homework: Ask your family their favourite colour and make a picture graph.

topics.title: Colours
topics.summary: The poem is about two children who each have only some crayons.
notes: The poem is about two children who each have only some crayons.
One needs red and the other needs black.
When they share, together they have a full pack.
Sharing helps everyone do more; it also makes friendships stronger.
outcomes: Recite a poem about sharing
Read and say words that begin with blends like 'gr' and 'bl'

lesson.hook: You have red, yellow and blue crayons; your friend has green, purple and black. How can you both draw a full rainbow?
lesson.example: Blends: gr as in green, bl as in blue and black, br as in brown.
lesson.activity: Crayon swap: pairs draw one picture using only crayons they get by asking politely: 'May I have the red one, please?'

questions.q: How many children are there in the poem?
Why did they share crayons?
questions.a: Each had only some colours and needed the others.

questions.q: What do they get when they share?

lesson.homework: Rearrange letters to find colours: LEBU, RENEG, NROBW.

topics.title: Badal and Moti
topics.summary: Badal found a puppy shivering in the cold and brought it home; his mother agreed if he took care of it.
notes: Badal found a puppy shivering in the cold and brought it home; his mother agreed if he took care of it.
They named the puppy Moti; Moti grew up and followed Badal everywhere.
One rainy day Badal slipped into a deep pit and could not climb out.
Moti followed Badal's scent, barked near the pit, and neighbours pulled Badal out with a rope; Badal hugged and thanked Moti.
outcomes: Read a story about friendship between a boy and his dog
Understand how animals can help people

lesson.hook: Can a pet be a best friend? How?
lesson.example: Dogs have a strong sense of smell — Moti found Badal by following his scent.
lesson.activity: Kindness to animals: children list three ways to take care of a pet or a street animal.

questions.q: Where did Badal find the puppy?
questions.a: By the road, shivering in the cold.

questions.q: What did Badal fall into?
How did Moti find Badal?
questions.a: He followed Badal's scent and barked.

lesson.homework: Write about an animal you like and how you would care for it.

topics.title: Best Friends
topics.summary: Four friends — Circle, Square, Triangle and Rectangle — fought over who was the best.
notes: Four friends — Circle, Square, Triangle and Rectangle — fought over who was the best.
Circle has no sharp edges; Square has four equal sides; Triangle has three sides; Rectangle has two long and two short sides.
They asked a wise Star to decide.
The Star told them that together they could make beautiful pictures and patterns, so they stopped fighting.
outcomes: Read a story about shapes and teamwork
Name shapes and their sides

lesson.hook: Which shape is the best: circle, square, triangle or rectangle?
lesson.example: A house drawing uses a square (walls), a triangle (roof), rectangles (door) and a circle (sun).
lesson.activity: Shape picture: groups cut paper shapes and make one picture using all four shapes together.

questions.q: How many sides does a triangle have?
Who helped the friends end their fight?
What lesson did they learn?
questions.a: Working together creates wonders; there is no need to fight.

lesson.homework: Find five things at home in each of the four shapes.

topics.title: Out in the Garden
topics.summary: The poem is about a child who plays in the garden every fine day.
notes: The poem is about a child who plays in the garden every fine day.
With a ball, the child bounces, throws and catches.
With a kite, the child tugs, pulls and flies it.
With friends, they run, skip, jump, slide and swing — playing outdoors keeps us healthy and happy.
outcomes: Recite a poem about outdoor play
Use action words: bounce, throw, catch, fly, swing

lesson.hook: What is your favourite game to play outside?
lesson.example: I bounce my ball. I fly my kite. We swing together.
lesson.activity: Playground verbs: the teacher calls out an action word and children act it out.

questions.q: Where does the child play?
What does the child do with the kite?
What should we be careful about while playing outside?
questions.a: Traffic, falling, sharp things — play safely.

lesson.homework: Draw your favourite outdoor game and write two sentences about it.

topics.title: Talking Toys
topics.summary: On a holiday, the toys in a shop waited to see who would buy them.
notes: On a holiday, the toys in a shop waited to see who would buy them.
A girl chose a Snakes and Ladders game; a boy asked his mother (Aayi) for a Vande Bharat toy train.
The aeroplane and the phone hoped to be chosen; marbles, the aeroplane, the elephant, a spinning top and dancing dolls were bought.
Many Indian toys are traditional, like Channapatna wooden toys from Karnataka and Kondapalli dolls from Andhra Pradesh.
outcomes: Read a story told from the toys' point of view
Name traditional Indian toys

lesson.hook: If toys in a shop could talk, what would they say when a child walks in?
lesson.example: Channapatna toys from Karnataka are made of wood and coloured with natural dyes.
lesson.activity: Talking toys: each child picks a toy and speaks as that toy, saying why a child should choose it.

questions.q: Which game did the girl choose?
What did the little boy want?
What do you call your mother in your language?

lesson.homework: Draw your favourite toy and write three words to describe it.

topics.title: Paper Boats
topics.summary: Meena floated paper boats in a stream near a bamboo bridge.
notes: Meena floated paper boats in a stream near a bamboo bridge.
A boy kept overturning her boats because it was fun for him.
Meena told him to stop; the boy said he also wanted to play but did not know how to make boats.
Meena taught him to fold paper boats, and they both enjoyed sailing them — kindness turned a quarrel into friendship.
outcomes: Read a story about solving a quarrel kindly
Follow steps to make a paper boat

lesson.hook: What would you do if someone kept spoiling your game?
lesson.example: Steps: fold the paper in half → fold the corners down → fold the edges up → open and shape the boat.
lesson.activity: Boat making: children follow the teacher's steps to fold paper boats and float them in a tub.

questions.q: What was Meena playing with?
Why was Meena angry?
questions.a: The boy was overturning her boats.

questions.q: How did the problem end?
questions.a: Meena taught him to make boats and they played together.

lesson.homework: Write the steps to make a paper boat in your own words.

topics.title: The Big Laddoo
topics.summary: The poem imagines all laddoos becoming one big laddoo.
notes: The poem imagines all laddoos becoming one big laddoo.
It also imagines one big child and one big sea.
If the big child threw the big laddoo into the big sea — what a big splish-splash!
Poems can be silly and fun; they help us imagine.
outcomes: Recite a funny poem with 'If all the… were one…'
Name round things and sort them into eatable and not eatable

lesson.hook: Imagine all the laddoos in the world made into one giant laddoo! How big would it be?
lesson.example: Round things we can eat: laddoo, orange, roti. Round things we cannot eat: ball, coin, wheel.
lesson.activity: Big imagination: children make their own lines — 'If all the trees were one tree, what a big tree it would be!'

questions.q: What would all the laddoos make?
Where did the big child throw the laddoo?
Name two round things you can eat.

lesson.homework: Write one 'If all the … were one …' line of your own.

topics.title: Thank God
topics.summary: A farmer grew the best grapes and watermelons and wanted to gift the best fruit to the king.
notes: A farmer grew the best grapes and watermelons and wanted to gift the best fruit to the king.
Since the palace was far and watermelons were heavy, he carried grapes.
The playful king threw grapes at the farmer, and each time the farmer said 'Thank God!'
He explained that he was thankful he had not brought watermelons — a wise way of seeing things.
outcomes: Read a folk tale about gratitude and wisdom
Understand why the farmer said 'Thank God!'

lesson.hook: Is it possible to feel thankful when something bad happens to you?
lesson.example: Being hit by a grape hurts a little; being hit by a watermelon would hurt a lot — so the farmer felt lucky.
lesson.activity: Thankful circle: each child says one thing they are thankful for today.

questions.q: What did the farmer grow?
Why did he take grapes, not watermelons?
questions.a: Watermelons were too heavy for the long journey.

questions.q: Why did he say 'Thank God'?
questions.a: He was glad he had not brought watermelons.

lesson.homework: Write about a time you felt lucky that something small happened instead of something big.

topics.title: Madhu's Wish
topics.summary: Madhu loved food; he shared his lunch with an old man under a banyan tree.
notes: Madhu loved food; he shared his lunch with an old man under a banyan tree.
The man let him wish for anything; Madhu wished for food and nothing else.
Laddoos, fruits and savouries appeared, but when he got hiccups there was no water — even sweet drinks did not help.
He gave up the food and asked for water; his hiccups stopped — nothing can replace water.
outcomes: Read a story about a wish and its lesson
Understand the importance of water

lesson.hook: If a magic tree could give you one thing forever, what would you ask for?
lesson.example: Madhu's wishes: laddoos → fruits → savouries → drinks → finally, water.
lesson.activity: Wish discussion: children say what they would wish for and why, then discuss whether it is truly important.

questions.q: What did Madhu wish for?
questions.a: Different kinds of food and nothing else.

questions.q: What happened when he got hiccups?
questions.a: There was no water, and other drinks did not help.

questions.q: What did Madhu learn?
questions.a: Water is very important; nothing can replace it.

lesson.homework: List five ways we use water every day.

topics.title: Night
topics.summary: The poem wonders where the bright Sun goes at night.
notes: The poem wonders where the bright Sun goes at night.
It seems to sink behind a distant hill, and the world grows dark and still.
The child sleeps until the day begins to peep.
In the morning the Sun is shining again — plants, animals and people need the Sun.
outcomes: Recite a poem about day and night
Talk about the Sun and the sky

lesson.hook: Where does the Sun go at night?
lesson.example: The Sun does not really go anywhere; the Earth turns, so our side faces away from the Sun at night.
lesson.activity: I Spy: children play 'I spy with my little eye something that is…' using colours in the classroom.

questions.q: Where does the Sun seem to go at night?
Name two things that need the Sun.
What colours do we see at sunrise and sunset?

lesson.homework: Draw the sky at night and label what you see.

topics.title: Chanda Mama Counts the Stars
topics.summary: Chanda Mama (the Moon) tried to count the stars but fell asleep before finishing.
notes: Chanda Mama (the Moon) tried to count the stars but fell asleep before finishing.
Each night he forgot where he had stopped and started again.
One night he cried; the Sun told him the number of stars equals the number of lovely children.
Now the Moon happily looks at the stars and the children every night.
outcomes: Read a story about the Moon and the stars
Understand that some things are too many to count

lesson.hook: Have you ever tried to count the stars? How far did you get?
lesson.example: The Moon looks different on different nights — sometimes round, sometimes thin.
lesson.activity: Too many to count: children list things they cannot count, like grains of sand, hair or stars.

questions.q: What did Chanda Mama try to count?
Who helped him?
What did the Sun say?
questions.a: The number of stars is the same as the number of lovely children.

lesson.homework: Watch the Moon tonight and draw its shape.

topics.title: Chandrayaan
topics.summary: Rani was a curious girl who asked many questions, like 'How far is the Moon?'
notes: Rani was a curious girl who asked many questions, like 'How far is the Moon?'
Her brother Pratik saw on TV that India had landed on the Moon.
They visited Nandini Aunty, a scientist, who explained that a rocket carries Chandrayaan to the Moon.
'Chandra' means Moon and 'yaan' means vehicle; Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023 and landed on 23 August 2023.
outcomes: Read a story about India's Chandrayaan mission
Use 'a' and 'an' correctly

lesson.hook: How far is the Moon? Can people send a machine there?
lesson.example: We say 'a rocket', 'a girl' but 'an elephant', 'an apple' — 'an' comes before vowel sounds.
lesson.activity: Moon trip list: children list ten things they would take for a 10-day stay on the Moon and explain one.

questions.q: What does 'Chandrayaan' mean?
Who was Nandini Aunty?
When did Chandrayaan-3 land on the Moon?

lesson.homework: Fill in 'a' or 'an': ___ owl, ___ moon, ___ egg, ___ star.

topics.title: सीखो
topics.summary: कवि कहते हैं कि प्रकृति की हर चीज़ से हम कुछ सीख सकते हैं।
notes: कवि कहते हैं कि प्रकृति की हर चीज़ से हम कुछ सीख सकते हैं।
फूलों से हँसना, भौंरों से गाना और झुकी डालियों से विनम्र होना सीखें।
सूरज की किरणों से जागना-जगाना, दीपक से अँधेरा दूर करना और धरती से सेवा करना सीखें।
जलधारा से आगे बढ़ना और धुएँ से ऊँचे उठना सीखें।
outcomes: कविता से प्रकृति से मिलने वाली सीखें समझना
गुणों को चीज़ों से जोड़ना

lesson.hook: फूल, सूरज और नदी हमें बिना बोले क्या सिखाते हैं?
lesson.example: मिलान: फूल → हँसना; सूरज → जगना-जगाना; दीपक → अँधेरा दूर करना; जलधारा → आगे बढ़ना।
lesson.activity: सीख-कार्ड: हर बच्चा प्रकृति की एक चीज़ चुनकर लिखे कि उससे वह क्या सीखता है और चित्र बनाए।

questions.q: झुकी डालियों से क्या सीखना चाहिए?
दीपक से क्या सीख मिलती है?
धरती से क्या सीखें?

lesson.homework: कविता की सबसे अच्छी लगी पंक्ति लिखिए और बताइए क्यों।

topics.title: चींटी
topics.summary: चींटी हर पल चलती रहती है और मेहनत का गीत सुनाती है।
notes: चींटी हर पल चलती रहती है और मेहनत का गीत सुनाती है।
कड़ी धूप हो या बारिश, वह दाना चुनकर लाती है और घर सजाती है।
उसका शरीर छोटा है पर इरादे बड़े हैं; वह कभी नहीं घबराती।
चींटी सिखाती है कि मेहनत ही सबसे बड़ी पूजा है।
outcomes: कविता में चींटी के परिश्रम को समझना
'छोटा तन, बड़े इरादे' का भाव जानना

lesson.hook: क्या आपने कभी चींटियों को अपने से बड़ा दाना उठाते देखा है?
lesson.example: 'छोटा तन, बड़े इरादे' — छोटा होकर भी बड़ा काम करने की हिम्मत।
lesson.activity: चींटी-अवलोकन: बच्चे चीनी का दाना रखकर देखें कि चींटियाँ कैसे आती हैं और उसे ले जाती हैं।

questions.q: चींटी किस मौसम में दाना लाती है?
questions.a: कड़ी धूप हो या वर्षा, हर मौसम में।

questions.q: चींटी हमें क्या सिखाती है?
'बड़े इरादे' का क्या अर्थ है?
questions.a: बड़ा काम करने का पक्का विचार।

lesson.homework: मेहनत से किया गया अपना कोई काम लिखिए।

topics.title: कितने पैर?
topics.summary: कक्षा में अध्यापिका और बच्चे जीवों के पैरों की संख्या पर बात करते हैं।
notes: कक्षा में अध्यापिका और बच्चे जीवों के पैरों की संख्या पर बात करते हैं।
केंचुए के पैर नहीं होते; वह पेट के बल सरकता है।
मनुष्य और सभी चिड़ियाँ दो पैरों वाले (द्विपाद) हैं; कंगारू तेज़ी से दो पैरों पर कूदता है।
अधिकतर पशुओं के चार पैर (चतुष्पाद) होते हैं; कीड़ों के छह और मकड़ी के आठ पैर होते हैं।
outcomes: जीवों को पैरों की संख्या के आधार पर पहचानना
संवाद पढ़ना और प्रश्न पूछना

lesson.hook: आपके कितने पैर हैं? और मकड़ी के कितने होंगे?

questions.q: किस जीव के पैर नहीं होते?
द्विपाद किसे कहते हैं?
कंगारू की क्या खास बात है?
questions.a: वह दो पैरों पर कूदता है और पेट की थैली में बच्चा रखता है।

lesson.homework: चार पैरों वाले पाँच जानवरों के नाम लिखिए।

topics.title: बया हमारी चिड़िया रानी!
topics.summary: बया तिनके लाकर ऊँची डाली पर अपना 'महल' (घोंसला) लटकाती है।
notes: बया तिनके लाकर ऊँची डाली पर अपना 'महल' (घोंसला) लटकाती है।
वह खेतों से दाना और नदियों से पानी लाती है।
बच्चे कहते हैं कि वे आँगन में दाना और हौज में ठंडा पानी रखेंगे।
अंडों से बच्चे निकलेंगे, बड़े होकर उड़ जाएँगे — पर बच्चे बया के पास रहेंगे।
outcomes: कविता में बया पक्षी के घोंसले और जीवन को समझना
पक्षियों के प्रति प्रेम और देखभाल का भाव जगाना

lesson.hook: क्या आपने बया का लटकता हुआ घोंसला देखा है?
lesson.example: बया का घोंसला घास और तिनकों से बुना होता है और डाली से उल्टा लटकता है।
lesson.activity: पक्षियों के लिए पानी: कक्षा मिलकर स्कूल में एक मिट्टी के बर्तन में पक्षियों के लिए पानी रखे।

questions.q: बया अपना घोंसला किससे बनाती है?
बच्चे बया के लिए क्या करेंगे?
questions.a: आँगन में दाना और हौज में पानी रखेंगे।

questions.q: बच्चे बड़े होकर क्या करेंगे?

lesson.homework: किसी पक्षी का घोंसला बनाते हुए चित्र बनाइए।

topics.title: आम का पेड़
topics.summary: सौरभ को चाचाजी के भेजे मीठे आम बहुत अच्छे लगे।
notes: सौरभ को चाचाजी के भेजे मीठे आम बहुत अच्छे लगे।
उसने बगीचे में गुठली बोई और रोज़ पानी डाला, पर पौधा नहीं निकला तो पानी देना छोड़ दिया।
एक दिन बारिश के बाद लाल कोंपलों वाला नन्हा पौधा दिखा; सौरभ और प्रिया बहुत खुश हुए।
पिताजी ने बताया कि पेड़ बनकर फल देने में चार-पाँच वर्ष लगेंगे; सौरभ ने देखभाल करने का निश्चय किया।
outcomes: कहानी से पेड़ उगने में लगने वाले समय को समझना
धैर्य और देखभाल का महत्त्व जानना

lesson.hook: क्या आम की गुठली से आम का पेड़ उग सकता है? कितना समय लगेगा?
lesson.example: गुठली → पौधा (कुछ हफ़्ते) → पेड़ (4–5 वर्ष) → आम।
lesson.activity: धैर्य का प्रयोग: बच्चे एक बीज बोकर रोज़ की ऊँचाई नापें और तालिका में लिखें।

questions.q: सौरभ ने बगीचे में क्या बोया?
पौधे की कोंपलें किस रंग की थीं?
आम लगने में कितने वर्ष लगेंगे?

lesson.homework: आपके आसपास के किसी फलदार पेड़ का नाम और उसका फल लिखिए।

topics.title: बीरबल की खिचड़ी
topics.summary: एक व्यक्ति ने सारी रात यमुना के ठंडे पानी में खड़े रहकर शर्त जीती।
notes: एक व्यक्ति ने सारी रात यमुना के ठंडे पानी में खड़े रहकर शर्त जीती।
अकबर ने कहा कि उसे महल के दीपक की गरमी मिली, इसलिए इनाम नहीं मिलेगा।
बीरबल ने बाँस के ऊँचे सिरे पर हाँडी लटकाकर नीचे थोड़ी-सी आग जलाई और 'खिचड़ी पकाने' लगे।
बादशाह को बात समझ आ गई और उन्होंने उस व्यक्ति को सम्मान सहित मोहरें दीं।
outcomes: बीरबल की चतुराई की कहानी समझना
अन्याय के विरुद्ध समझदारी से बात रखना

lesson.hook: क्या दूर जल रहे दीपक से सर्दी में गरमी मिल सकती है?
lesson.example: जैसे बहुत दूर की आग से हाँडी नहीं पकती, वैसे ही दूर के दीपक से गरमी नहीं मिलती।
lesson.activity: नाटक: बच्चे अकबर, बीरबल और उस व्यक्ति का अभिनय करें।

questions.q: वह व्यक्ति रात भर कहाँ खड़ा रहा?
बीरबल ने हाँडी कहाँ लटकाई?
questions.a: बहुत लंबे बाँस के ऊपरी सिरे पर।

questions.q: अंत में उस व्यक्ति को क्या मिला?

lesson.homework: बीरबल की चतुराई की कोई और कहानी पता कीजिए।

topics.title: मित्र को पत्र
topics.summary: रूपम ने छुट्टियों में गुवाहाटी से अपने मित्र अभिषेक को पत्र लिखा।
notes: रूपम ने छुट्टियों में गुवाहाटी से अपने मित्र अभिषेक को पत्र लिखा।
गुवाहाटी ब्रह्मपुत्र नदी के तट पर है; इसी नदी में माजुली है, जो नदी में स्थित भारत का सबसे बड़ा द्वीप है।
रूपम ने सत्रिया नृत्य देखा और कामाख्या तथा उमानंद मंदिर गया।
नानी ने बताया कि पढ़ाई के साथ खेलना भी ज़रूरी है — स्वस्थ तन में स्वस्थ मन रहता है।
outcomes: पत्र लिखने का तरीका जानना
पूर्वोत्तर भारत के गुवाहाटी के बारे में जानना

lesson.hook: आप अपने किसी दूर रहने वाले मित्र को पत्र में क्या-क्या लिखेंगे?
lesson.example: पत्र के भाग: संबोधन (प्रिय मित्र) → अभिवादन → मुख्य बात → समापन (तुम्हारा मित्र) → नाम।
lesson.activity: पत्र लिखो: हर बच्चा अपने मित्र को छुट्टियों के बारे में छोटा पत्र लिखे।

questions.q: रूपम छुट्टियों में कहाँ गया था?
माजुली क्या है?
questions.a: ब्रह्मपुत्र नदी में स्थित भारत का सबसे बड़ा द्वीप।

questions.q: नानी ने खेल के बारे में क्या कहा?
questions.a: स्वस्थ रहने के लिए खेलना बहुत आवश्यक है।

lesson.homework: अपने किसी रिश्तेदार को चार-पाँच पंक्तियों का पत्र लिखिए।

topics.title: चतुर गीदड़
topics.summary: तालाब की सारी मछलियाँ खाकर मगरमच्छ भूखा था और गीदड़ को खाना चाहता था।
notes: तालाब की सारी मछलियाँ खाकर मगरमच्छ भूखा था और गीदड़ को खाना चाहता था।
कछुए की सलाह पर मगरमच्छ मरने का नाटक करके पड़ा रहा और कछुआ रोने लगा।
गीदड़ ने चाल समझ ली और कहा कि उसने सुना है — मरे मगरमच्छ की पूँछ हिलती रहती है।
मगरमच्छ ने पूँछ हिला दी और गीदड़ समझ गया कि वह ज़िंदा है — गीदड़ भाग गया।
outcomes: एकांकी (नाटक) पढ़ना और अभिनय करना
चतुराई से खतरे से बचना समझना

lesson.hook: अगर कोई आपको धोखे से पकड़ना चाहे, तो आप कैसे बचेंगे?
lesson.example: मरा हुआ जीव हिलता नहीं — पूँछ हिलाकर मगरमच्छ ने अपना भेद खोल दिया।
lesson.activity: एकांकी-अभिनय: तीन बच्चे मगरमच्छ, कछुआ और गीदड़ बनकर दोनों दृश्य खेलें।

questions.q: मगरमच्छ भूखा क्यों था?
questions.a: तालाब की सारी मछलियाँ खत्म हो गई थीं।

questions.q: गीदड़ ने कैसे परखा कि मगरमच्छ ज़िंदा है?
questions.a: उसने कहा कि मरे मगरमच्छ की पूँछ हिलती है, और मगरमच्छ ने पूँछ हिला दी।

questions.q: कहानी का शीर्षक 'चतुर गीदड़' क्यों है?
questions.a: गीदड़ ने चतुराई से अपनी जान बचाई।

lesson.homework: इस कहानी को कोई और शीर्षक दीजिए।

topics.title: प्रकृति पर्व — फूलदेई
topics.summary: फूलदेई उत्तराखंड का बच्चों का त्योहार है, इसलिए इसे 'बाल पर्व' भी कहते हैं।
notes: फूलदेई उत्तराखंड का बच्चों का त्योहार है, इसलिए इसे 'बाल पर्व' भी कहते हैं।
यह चैत्र महीने की संक्रांति को मनाया जाता है और वसंत के आगमन का प्रतीक है।
बच्चों की टोली ('फुलारी') बुरांस, फ्योंली जैसे फूल चुनकर हर घर की देहली पर डालती और मंगल-गीत गाती है।
बदले में घरों से चावल, गुड़ और भेंट मिलती है — यह प्रकृति और समाज से जुड़ने का पर्व है।
outcomes: उत्तराखंड के फूलदेई पर्व के बारे में जानना
त्योहारों और ऋतुओं के संबंध को समझना

lesson.hook: क्या आपके यहाँ कोई ऐसा त्योहार है जो बच्चे मनाते हैं?
lesson.example: बुरांस का लाल फूल उत्तराखंड के पहाड़ों पर वसंत में खिलता है।
lesson.activity: मेरा त्योहार: बच्चे अपने क्षेत्र के किसी त्योहार का नाम, ऋतु और उसमें होने वाले काम बताएँ।

questions.q: फूलदेई किस राज्य का त्योहार है?
इसे बाल पर्व क्यों कहते हैं?
फुलारी घरों की देहली पर क्या डालते हैं?

lesson.homework: वसंत ऋतु में खिलने वाले तीन फूलों के नाम लिखिए।

topics.title: रस्साकशी
topics.summary: रस्साकशी में दो टीमें रस्सी को दोनों ओर से पकड़कर खींचती हैं।
notes: रस्साकशी में दो टीमें रस्सी को दोनों ओर से पकड़कर खींचती हैं।
गीत में सीना तानकर, पैर गड़ाकर, कमर जकड़कर ज़ोर लगाने को कहा गया है।
'हेई सा!' बोलकर सब एक साथ ज़ोर लगाते हैं ताकि ताकत एक साथ लगे।
रस्सी न फिसले, साथी न डगमगाए और जोश कम न हो — यही जीत का राज़ है।
outcomes: खेल-गीत को जोश के साथ गाना
टीम भावना और मिलकर ज़ोर लगाने का महत्त्व समझना

lesson.hook: रस्साकशी में कौन-सी टीम जीतती है — सबसे ताकतवर या सबसे एकजुट?
lesson.example: जब सब एक ही समय पर 'हेई सा!' बोलकर खींचते हैं तो ताकत जुड़ जाती है।
lesson.activity: रस्साकशी: मैदान में दो टीमें गीत गाते हुए सुरक्षित तरीके से रस्साकशी खेलें।

questions.q: रस्साकशी में कितनी टीमें होती हैं?
सब साथ में क्या बोलते हैं?
जीतने के लिए क्या ज़रूरी है?
questions.a: सब मिलकर एक साथ ज़ोर लगाएँ।

lesson.homework: अपने पसंदीदा टीम-खेल के बारे में तीन वाक्य लिखिए।

topics.title: एक जादुई पिटारा
topics.summary: कविता में एक जादुई पिटारा खुलता है और उसमें से गप्पू गोला निकलता है।
notes: कविता में एक जादुई पिटारा खुलता है और उसमें से गप्पू गोला निकलता है।
गोला कठपुतली बनता है, उससे नौ सौ ऊँट, सुपारी से नौ मन आटा, नारियल से घोड़ा निकलता है।
घोड़ा आसमान ले जाता है, गुब्बारे के छेद पर स्टेशन और इंजन मिलता है, इंजन से भैंसे निकलते हैं।
भैंसों से खेत जोता तो बारह सौ सेर अनाज हुआ — एक चीज़ से दूसरी बनती जाती है।
outcomes: कल्पना और हास्य वाली कविता का आनंद लेना
तुकांत शब्द और गिनती के अंक ढूँढ़ना

lesson.hook: अगर एक पिटारे से ऊँट, घोड़ा और इंजन निकलें, तो कैसा लगेगा?
lesson.example: तुकांत जोड़ियाँ: खोला-गोला, सुतली-कठपुतली, खूँट-ऊँट, सवारी-सुपारी।
lesson.activity: कल्पना-श्रृंखला: बच्चे बारी-बारी से एक चीज़ बोलें जो पिछली चीज़ से 'निकली' हो।

questions.q: पिटारे से सबसे पहले क्या निकला?
सुपारी काटने पर क्या निकला?
कविता में आए गिनती के दो अंक बताइए।
questions.a: नौ सौ, नौ, बारह, बारह सौ (कोई दो)।

lesson.homework: 'खोला' और 'सवारी' से तुक मिलाते दो-दो शब्द लिखिए।

topics.title: अपना-अपना काम
topics.summary: सिमरन पढ़ाई से थककर सोचती है कि उसे पढ़ना न पड़े तो अच्छा हो।
notes: सिमरन पढ़ाई से थककर सोचती है कि उसे पढ़ना न पड़े तो अच्छा हो।
वह मधुमक्खी बनना चाहती है, पर मधुमक्खियाँ बताती हैं कि दिनभर रस इकट्ठा करते उनके पंख थक जाते हैं।
पेड़ बताता है कि उसकी जड़ें पानी खींचती हैं, पत्ते खाना बनाते हैं और फल वह दूसरों को दे देता है।
चिड़िया बताती है कि दाना ढूँढ़ने और घोंसला बनाने में बहुत मेहनत है; सिमरन समझ जाती है और मन लगाकर पढ़ने बैठती है।
outcomes: कहानी से हर जीव के काम का महत्त्व समझना
परिश्रम और पढ़ाई के प्रति रुचि जगाना

lesson.hook: क्या आपको कभी लगा है कि पढ़ना बहुत कठिन है और मधुमक्खी या चिड़िया बनना आसान?
lesson.example: हर किसी का अपना काम है: मधुमक्खी रस इकट्ठा करती है, पेड़ फल देता है, बच्चा पढ़ता है।
lesson.activity: मेरा दिन: बच्चे अपने पूरे दिन के कामों की सूची बनाएँ और सबसे पसंदीदा काम पर घेरा लगाएँ।

questions.q: सिमरन क्यों थक गई थी?
questions.a: बहुत सारा पढ़ने-लिखने का काम था।

questions.q: पेड़ क्या-क्या काम करता है?
questions.a: जड़ें पानी खींचती हैं, पत्ते खाना बनाते हैं, फल देता है।

questions.q: अंत में सिमरन ने क्या किया?
questions.a: उत्साह से स्कूल का काम करने बैठ गई।

lesson.homework: घर के किसी सदस्य के दिनभर के कामों की सूची बनाइए।

topics.title: पेड़ों की अम्मा 'तिमक्का'
topics.summary: सालुमरदा तिमक्का कर्नाटक के तुमकुरु ज़िले में जन्मी; उन्हें 'वृक्षमाता' भी कहते हैं।
notes: सालुमरदा तिमक्का कर्नाटक के तुमकुरु ज़िले में जन्मी; उन्हें 'वृक्षमाता' भी कहते हैं।
कन्नड़ में 'सालुमरदा' का अर्थ है पेड़ों की पंक्ति।
उन्होंने हुलिकल और कुदुर के बीच लगभग 45 किलोमीटर लंबे मार्ग पर लगभग 385 बरगद के पेड़ लगाए; कुल 8000 से अधिक पेड़ लगाए।
उनके पति ने इस काम में साथ दिया; भारत सरकार ने उन्हें 2019 में पद्मश्री से सम्मानित किया।
outcomes: 'वृक्षमाता' सालुमरदा तिमक्का के कार्य के बारे में जानना
पर्यावरण के लिए व्यक्तिगत प्रयास का महत्त्व समझना

lesson.hook: क्या एक अकेला व्यक्ति हज़ारों पेड़ लगा सकता है?
lesson.example: कठिनाइयों और पैसों की कमी के बावजूद तिमक्का ने लगन से पेड़ लगाए — लगन से बड़ा काम होता है।
lesson.activity: पेड़ की देखभाल: कक्षा स्कूल के एक पेड़ को 'गोद' ले और उसकी देखभाल का चार्ट बनाए।

questions.q: तिमक्का किस राज्य की हैं?
'सालुमरदा' का क्या अर्थ है?
उन्हें कौन-सा सम्मान मिला?

lesson.homework: तिमक्का को एक धन्यवाद-पत्र लिखिए।

topics.title: किसान की होशियारी
topics.summary: खेत जोतते किसान पर भालू झपटा; किसान ने कहा कि उपज होने दो, फिर जो कहोगे खिलाऊँगा।
notes: खेत जोतते किसान पर भालू झपटा; किसान ने कहा कि उपज होने दो, फिर जो कहोगे खिलाऊँगा।
भालू ने ज़मीन के ऊपर की उपज माँगी तो किसान ने आलू बोए — भालू को पत्ते मिले।
अगली बार भालू ने नीचे की उपज माँगी तो किसान ने गेहूँ बोया — भालू को जड़ें मिलीं।
फिर भालू ने ऊपर और नीचे दोनों माँगे तो किसान ने गन्ना बोया — भालू को पत्ते और जड़ें मिलीं, रसीला गन्ना किसान को।
outcomes: कहानी में किसान की सूझ-बूझ समझना
फसलों के ज़मीन के ऊपर और नीचे वाले भाग पहचानना

lesson.hook: आलू ज़मीन के ऊपर उगता है या नीचे? गेहूँ?
lesson.example: आलू का खाने वाला भाग ज़मीन के नीचे; गेहूँ का दाना ऊपर; गन्ने का रसीला तना बीच में।
lesson.activity: ऊपर-नीचे: बच्चे सब्ज़ियों और फसलों के चित्रों को 'ज़मीन के ऊपर' और 'ज़मीन के नीचे' में बाँटें।

questions.q: पहली बार किसान ने क्या बोया?
गेहूँ बोने पर भालू को क्या मिला?
तीसरी बार किसान ने क्या बोया?

lesson.homework: ज़मीन के नीचे उगने वाली तीन सब्ज़ियों के नाम लिखिए।

topics.title: भारत
topics.summary: कवि कहते हैं कि भारत हमें प्यारा है और सब देशों से अलग है।
notes: कवि कहते हैं कि भारत हमें प्यारा है और सब देशों से अलग है।
हिमालय भारत का सुंदर मुकुट है और समुद्र इसके चरण धोता है।
गंगा-यमुना की धाराएँ हैं और यहाँ अन्न, फूल, फल, जल की भरमार है।
हम सदा भारत के गुण गाएँ और इसका यश बढ़ाएँ।
outcomes: देशप्रेम की कविता को भाव से गाना
भारत की प्राकृतिक विशेषताएँ जानना

lesson.hook: आपको भारत की कौन-सी बात सबसे प्यारी लगती है?
lesson.example: भारत के उत्तर में हिमालय (मुकुट) और दक्षिण में समुद्र (चरण) है।
lesson.activity: भारत का नक्शा: बच्चे भारत के नक्शे में हिमालय, गंगा-यमुना और समुद्र पहचानें।

questions.q: भारत का मुकुट किसे कहा गया है?
भारत के चरण कौन धोता है?
कविता में किन दो नदियों के नाम हैं?

lesson.homework: भारत के बारे में चार पंक्तियाँ लिखिए।

topics.title: चंद्रयान (संवाद)
topics.summary: कक्षा में अध्यापिका और बच्चे चाँद और चंद्रयान पर बात करते हैं।
notes: कक्षा में अध्यापिका और बच्चे चाँद और चंद्रयान पर बात करते हैं।
भारत ने चंद्रयान-1, 2 और 3 चाँद की ओर भेजे।
चंद्रयान-3 चाँद के दक्षिणी ध्रुव के पास उतरा; ऐसा करने वाला भारत पहला देश है।
वैज्ञानिक चाँद पर यान भेजकर पता लगाते हैं कि वहाँ क्या-क्या है।
outcomes: संवाद के माध्यम से चंद्रयान मिशन के बारे में जानना
वैज्ञानिक जिज्ञासा को बढ़ावा देना

lesson.hook: चाँद कभी दिखता है और कभी नहीं — ऐसा क्यों?
lesson.example: 'चंद्र' = चाँद, 'यान' = वाहन; चंद्रयान = चाँद तक जाने वाला वाहन।
lesson.activity: संवाद-पाठ: बच्चे अध्यापिका और विद्यार्थियों की भूमिका लेकर संवाद पढ़ें।

questions.q: चाँद तक यान किससे भेजा जाता है?
चंद्रयान-3 चाँद के किस भाग में उतरा?
वैज्ञानिक चाँद पर यान क्यों भेजते हैं?
questions.a: यह जानने के लिए कि चाँद पर क्या-क्या है।

lesson.homework: अगर आप चाँद पर जाएँ तो क्या-क्या साथ ले जाएँगे? सूची बनाइए।

topics.title: बोलने वाली माँद
topics.summary: भूखा सिंह खरनखर रात बिताने एक माँद में छिपकर बैठ गया, ताकि उसमें रहने वाला पशु आए तो उसे पकड़ ले।
notes: भूखा सिंह खरनखर रात बिताने एक माँद में छिपकर बैठ गया, ताकि उसमें रहने वाला पशु आए तो उसे पकड़ ले।
माँद का मालिक सियार दधिपुच्छ लौटा तो उसने सिंह के पैरों के निशान अंदर जाते देखे, पर लौटते नहीं।
सियार ने बाहर से पुकारा, 'ऐ मेरी माँद! आज बोलती क्यों नहीं?'
सिंह ने सोचा माँद उत्तर देती होगी और खुद दहाड़ उठा; सियार समझ गया और भाग गया।
outcomes: पंचतंत्र की कहानी से बुद्धि का महत्त्व समझना
पैरों के निशानों से अनुमान लगाना

lesson.hook: अगर आपके घर के बाहर किसी के जाने के निशान हों पर लौटने के नहीं, तो आप क्या सोचेंगे?
lesson.example: निशान अंदर जाते हैं पर बाहर नहीं आते → सिंह अभी अंदर है। यह तर्क से निकाला गया निष्कर्ष है।
lesson.activity: निशान पहचानो: बच्चे मिट्टी या आटे पर उँगलियों से अलग-अलग जानवरों के पैरों के निशान बनाएँ और पहचानें।

questions.q: सियार ने कैसे जाना कि सिंह अंदर है?
questions.a: पैरों के निशान अंदर जाते थे, लौटते नहीं।

questions.q: सियार ने माँद से क्या कहा?
questions.a: ऐ मेरी माँद, आज बोलती क्यों नहीं?

questions.q: सिंह की क्या भूल थी?
questions.a: उसने माँद की जगह खुद उत्तर दे दिया।

lesson.homework: अपनी सूझ-बूझ से हल की गई किसी समस्या के बारे में लिखिए।

topics.title: हम अनेक किंतु एक
topics.summary: कविता कहती है कि भारत में कई प्रदेश हैं, पर देश एक है।
notes: कविता कहती है कि भारत में कई प्रदेश हैं, पर देश एक है।
रूप-रंग, बोलियाँ, टोलियाँ और राग अनेक हैं, पर सब भारत के अंग हैं।
सबका गीत एक है और मातृभूमि एक है।
हम कदम मिलाकर एक लक्ष्य की ओर चलते हैं — हम अनेक किंतु एक।
outcomes: विविधता में एकता का भाव समझना
भारत की भाषाओं और संस्कृतियों का सम्मान करना

lesson.hook: आपकी कक्षा में कितनी भाषाएँ बोली जाती हैं? फिर भी हम एक कैसे हैं?
lesson.example: भारत में हिंदी, कन्नड़, तमिल, बंगला, मराठी जैसी अनेक भाषाएँ हैं, पर राष्ट्रगान एक है।
lesson.activity: भाषा-मेला: बच्चे अपनी या किसी और भाषा में 'नमस्ते' और 'धन्यवाद' बोलकर सुनाएँ।

questions.q: कविता में 'अनेक' क्या हैं?
सबमें 'एक' क्या है?
'हम अनेक किंतु एक' का क्या अर्थ है?
questions.a: हम अलग-अलग होकर भी एक देश के लोग हैं।

lesson.homework: पाँच भारतीय भाषाओं के नाम लिखिए।

topics.title: What's in a Name?
topics.summary: We can check if two groups are equal by matching one to one — one pebble for each cow.
notes: We can check if two groups are equal by matching one to one — one pebble for each cow.
Tally marks help us count: four lines and a fifth line across make a group of 5.
Counting in groups of 2, 5 and 10 is faster than counting one by one.
We can compare groups: which has more, which has fewer, are they equal?
Names and numbers can be counted too — like how many letters are in your name.
outcomes: Count objects by matching and by making tally marks
Count in groups and compare counts

lesson.hook: Long ago, shepherds could not count to big numbers. How could they know if all their cows came home in the evening?
lesson.example: Letters in names: RAVI has 4 letters, SUNITA has 6. SUNITA has 2 more letters than RAVI.
lesson.activity: Name count: each child writes their name, counts its letters, and the class makes a tally chart of names with 3, 4, 5, 6 and more letters.

questions.q: Draw tally marks for 8.
questions.a: One bundle of 5 and 3 more lines.

questions.q: Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, … what comes next?
How many letters are in the word ELEPHANT?

lesson.homework: Count and make tally marks for the number of spoons, plates and glasses in your kitchen.

topics.title: Toy Joy
topics.summary: A cube has 6 equal square faces, like a dice.
notes: A cube has 6 equal square faces, like a dice.
A cuboid has 6 rectangular faces, like a brick or a matchbox.
A cylinder has two round flat faces and a curved face, like a can.
A cone has one round flat face and a pointed top, like an ice-cream cone.
A sphere is round all over, like a ball; it rolls in every direction.
outcomes: Identify 3D shapes: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone and sphere
Describe faces, edges and corners and whether a shape rolls or slides

lesson.hook: Look at a ball, a box and a water bottle. Which ones can roll? Which ones can you stack?
lesson.example: A cylinder can roll when lying down and can be stacked when standing up; a sphere can only roll.
lesson.activity: Toy making: children make animal faces on old boxes, cans and cones and name the shape of each toy.

questions.q: How many faces does a cube have?
Name something shaped like a cylinder.
questions.a: A can, a pipe, a glass, a drum (any one).

questions.q: Which shape can roll in every direction?

lesson.homework: Find two things at home for each shape: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere.

topics.title: Double Century
topics.summary: People first kept count with marks on cave walls and knots in ropes.
notes: People first kept count with marks on cave walls and knots in ropes.
Ancient Indians made a way to write any number with just ten digits, 0 to 9.
10 ones make 1 ten; 10 tens make 1 hundred.
We can count in tens: 10, 20, 30 … 100, 110 … 200.
A number like 145 is 1 hundred, 4 tens and 5 ones.
outcomes: Learn how people began counting and writing numbers
Read, write and count numbers up to 200 using tens and ones

lesson.hook: How would you count all the leaves on a small branch — one by one, or in bundles?
lesson.example: Bundles of sticks: 1 big bundle of 100, 4 bundles of 10 and 5 loose sticks make 145.
lesson.activity: Bundle it: children bundle ice-cream sticks into tens with rubber bands and then make a hundred, and show numbers like 132 and 178.

questions.q: How many tens make one hundred?
Write the number: 1 hundred, 6 tens, 3 ones.
Count in tens from 120: 120, 130, …

lesson.homework: Write the numbers from 150 to 200 in your notebook.

topics.title: Vacation with My Nani Maa
topics.summary: Adding means putting together; subtracting means taking away or finding the difference.
notes: Adding means putting together; subtracting means taking away or finding the difference.
Addition and subtraction are linked: 4 + 6 = 10, so 10 − 4 = 6.
A missing number can be found by subtracting: 4 + ? = 10, so ? = 6.
Making tens helps: 8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3 = 13.
Number patterns can be found in addition tables.
outcomes: Add and subtract using mental strategies
Find a missing number in addition and subtraction

lesson.hook: Nani hides some marbles under a handkerchief. There were 10; now 4 are showing. How many are hidden?
lesson.example: Hidden marbles: 10 − 4 = 6. Check: 4 + 6 = 10 ✓.
lesson.activity: Marble magic: in pairs, one child hides some of 10 counters under a cup; the partner sees the rest and says how many are hidden.

questions.q: 7 + ? = 15. Find the missing number.
Find 9 + 6 by making a ten.
Priya had 18 bangles and gave away 5. How many are left?

lesson.homework: Play the hidden-marble game with a family member using 12 objects.

topics.title: Fun with Shapes
topics.summary: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.
notes: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.
A square has 4 equal sides and 4 corners.
A rectangle has 4 sides; opposite sides are equal.
A circle is round and has no corners or straight sides.
Shapes can be joined to make designs like rangoli and tiles.
outcomes: Identify 2D shapes: triangle, square, rectangle, circle
Draw shapes and patterns on a dot grid

lesson.hook: Look at a rangoli. What shapes can you find hidden in it?
lesson.example: Two triangles placed together can make a square; four small squares can make a bigger square.
lesson.activity: Dot rangoli: children join dots on a dot grid to copy and then design their own rangoli, naming every shape used.

questions.q: How many sides does a triangle have?
Which shape has no corners?
How is a square different from a rectangle?
questions.a: All sides of a square are equal.

lesson.homework: Make a picture using only triangles, squares and circles.

topics.title: House of Hundreds – I
topics.summary: 100 is 10 tens; 200 is 2 hundreds.
notes: 100 is 10 tens; 200 is 2 hundreds.
3-digit numbers have hundreds, tens and ones: 347 = 3 hundreds + 4 tens + 7 ones.
We read 347 as 'three hundred forty-seven'.
We can count in hundreds: 100, 200, 300 … 900.
Grouping helps count large collections quickly.
outcomes: Count, read and write numbers up to 999
Show numbers with hundreds, tens and ones

lesson.hook: At the mela there is a long string of paper flags. Guess — are there more than 100 flags?
lesson.example: The flag string has 2 groups of 100 and 5 groups of 10 and 3 more: 200 + 50 + 3 = 253 flags.
lesson.activity: Place-value mat: children use flats (100), longs (10) and cubes (1) drawn on paper to build numbers the teacher calls out.

questions.q: Write 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 6 ones as a number.
Write 582 in words.
What is the value of 7 in 735?

lesson.homework: Find three 3-digit numbers on packets or in a newspaper and write them in expanded form.

topics.title: Raksha Bandhan
topics.summary: Equal groups can be counted by adding again and again: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.
notes: Equal groups can be counted by adding again and again: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.
Multiplication is a short way of repeated addition: 4 × 3 = 12.
An array arranges objects in equal rows and columns.
4 × 3 and 3 × 4 give the same answer.
Skip counting helps us multiply: 3, 6, 9, 12.
outcomes: Understand multiplication as equal groups
Use repeated addition and arrays to multiply

lesson.hook: On Raksha Bandhan, 4 plates each have 3 sweets. How many sweets altogether? Is there a quick way?
lesson.example: 4 plates with 3 sweets each: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 4 × 3 = 12 sweets.
lesson.activity: Rakhi arrays: children arrange beads or buttons into rows (e.g. 3 rows of 5) and write both the addition and multiplication sentence.

questions.q: Write 5 + 5 + 5 as a multiplication.
There are 6 flowers in each of 2 vases. How many flowers?
Skip count by 4 up to 20.

lesson.homework: Find equal groups at home (eggs in a tray, chairs around a table) and write a multiplication for each.

topics.title: Fair Share
topics.summary: Sharing fairly means everyone gets an equal part.
notes: Sharing fairly means everyone gets an equal part.
When one whole is cut into 2 equal parts, each part is a half (½).
When one whole is cut into 4 equal parts, each part is a quarter (¼).
Two quarters make a half.
We can share a group of objects equally too: 12 bananas among 3 children gives 4 each.
outcomes: Share things equally between friends
Understand halves and quarters of a whole

lesson.hook: Two friends share a paratha. One gets a bigger piece. Is that fair? How can we make it fair?
lesson.example: Fold a paper roti in half: both parts match exactly, so each is ½. Fold again: 4 equal parts, each ¼.
lesson.activity: Paper folding: children fold paper circles and squares into halves and quarters, colour one part, and label it ½ or ¼.

questions.q: How many halves make a whole?
How many quarters make a whole?
Share 10 pencils equally between 2 children. How many each?

lesson.homework: Share some fruit or biscuits equally with family members and draw how you divided them.

topics.title: House of Hundreds – II
topics.summary: A number line shows numbers in order with equal gaps.
notes: A number line shows numbers in order with equal gaps.
To compare two numbers, first compare hundreds, then tens, then ones.
543 > 534 because both have 5 hundreds, and 4 tens is more than 3 tens.
We use > (greater than), < (less than) and = (equal to).
Numbers can be arranged in increasing or decreasing order.
outcomes: Place 3-digit numbers on a number line
Compare and order numbers up to 999

lesson.hook: Birbal said there were 543 crows in the city. How can we tell if 543 is more or less than 534?
lesson.activity: Human number line: children hold cards with 3-digit numbers and arrange themselves in order across the classroom.

questions.q: Which is greater, 689 or 698?
Fill in > or <: 407 __ 470.
What number comes just after 599?

lesson.homework: Write five 3-digit numbers using the digits 2, 5 and 8, then put them in order.

topics.title: Fun at Class Party!
topics.summary: We can measure with hand spans, footsteps and fingers, but these differ from person to person.
notes: We can measure with hand spans, footsteps and fingers, but these differ from person to person.
Standard units give everyone the same answer.
Small lengths are measured in centimetres (cm) with a ruler.
Longer lengths are measured in metres (m); 1 metre = 100 centimetres.
Start measuring from the 0 mark on the ruler.
outcomes: Measure length using hand spans, steps and a ruler
Understand the need for standard units: centimetre and metre

lesson.hook: Leena and Adi both measure the same table with their hand spans but get different answers. Why?
lesson.example: The door is 2 metres tall. A pencil is about 15 centimetres long.
lesson.activity: Measure the classroom: groups measure the table with hand spans and then with a metre scale and compare the results.

questions.q: How many centimetres make 1 metre?
Which unit would you use to measure a pencil?
Why do hand spans give different answers?
questions.a: Everyone's hand is a different size.

lesson.homework: Measure five things at home with a ruler and write their lengths in cm.

topics.title: Filling and Lifting
topics.summary: Capacity is how much a container can hold.
notes: Capacity is how much a container can hold.
We can compare capacity by filling one container and pouring into another.
Capacity is measured in litres (L) and millilitres (mL).
Weight tells how heavy something is; we compare weights with a balance.
Weight is measured in kilograms (kg) and grams (g); big things are not always heavier.
outcomes: Compare how much containers can hold (capacity)
Compare how heavy things are (weight) using a balance

lesson.hook: Is a big glass always better than a small glass if you want more juice?
lesson.example: A bucket holds more water than a mug. A small stone can be heavier than a big balloon.
lesson.activity: Fill and pour: using a jug, a bottle, a glass and a cup, children find how many cups fill each container and order them.

questions.q: Which holds more, a bucket or a cup?
What do we use to compare weights?
In which unit do we buy milk?

lesson.homework: Find three things at home sold by weight and three sold by capacity.

topics.title: Give and Take
topics.summary: To add 3-digit numbers, add ones, then tens, then hundreds.
notes: To add 3-digit numbers, add ones, then tens, then hundreds.
If ones add up to 10 or more, carry 1 ten to the tens place (regrouping).
To subtract, start with ones; if there are not enough, borrow 1 ten.
Box diagrams help show what is known and what we need to find.
Check subtraction by adding: answer + number taken away = starting number.
outcomes: Add and subtract 3-digit numbers with and without regrouping
Solve word problems using box diagrams

lesson.hook: Kishan's nursery had 336 saplings. Villagers took 128. How many are left? How many if he grows 50 more?
lesson.example: 336 − 128: ones 6 − 8 not possible, borrow a ten: 16 − 8 = 8; tens 2 − 2 = 0; hundreds 3 − 1 = 2. Answer 208. Check: 208 + 128 = 336 ✓.
lesson.activity: Nursery shop: children play shopkeeper with sapling cards, adding and subtracting as customers take or return saplings.

questions.q: A school has 312 girls and 289 boys. How many children in all?

lesson.homework: Make up two word problems about a shop and solve them.

topics.title: Time Goes On
topics.summary: A week has 7 days; a year has 12 months.
notes: A week has 7 days; a year has 12 months.
Months have 30 or 31 days; February has 28 (or 29 in a leap year).
A calendar shows dates, days and months.
A clock has an hour hand (short) and a minute hand (long).
When the long hand is at 12 it is 'o'clock'; at 6 it is 'half past'.
outcomes: Read a calendar: days, weeks and months
Tell time on a clock to the hour and half hour

lesson.hook: How many days are left until your birthday? How would you find out?
lesson.example: If today is Monday the 5th, then next Monday is the 12th (5 + 7).
lesson.activity: Class calendar: children mark birthdays and holidays on a big calendar and count the days between two events.

questions.q: How many days are in a week?
Which month is the shortest?
The short hand is at 3 and the long hand is at 12. What time is it?

lesson.homework: Write your daily timetable with times for waking up, school, play and sleep.

topics.title: The Surajkund Fair
topics.summary: A shape is symmetrical if one half is a mirror image of the other.
notes: A shape is symmetrical if one half is a mirror image of the other.
The fold line that splits it into matching halves is the line of symmetry.
Many things in nature are symmetrical: butterflies, leaves, flowers.
Crafts like rangoli, block prints and pottery use symmetry and repeating patterns.
We can make symmetrical designs by folding paper and cutting, or by ink blots.
outcomes: Find designs that look the same on both sides (symmetry)
Make symmetrical patterns by folding and printing

lesson.hook: At a crafts fair, a butterfly painting looks the same on both sides of its body. How can we check?
lesson.example: Fold a paper in half, cut half a heart along the fold, open it — a full symmetrical heart.
lesson.activity: Ink blot butterflies: put paint drops on one half of a paper, fold and press, then open to see a symmetrical design.

questions.q: What is a line of symmetry?
questions.a: A line that divides a shape into two matching halves.

questions.q: Name one symmetrical thing in nature.
Does the letter A have a line of symmetry?

lesson.homework: Find three symmetrical things at home and draw them with their line of symmetry.

topics.title: Family and Friends
topics.summary: A family is a group of people who live together and care for each other.
notes: A family is a group of people who live together and care for each other.
Families can be small or big — some live with grandparents, uncles and aunts.
Everyone in a family helps with work at home.
Friends play, share and help us when we need it.
We should be kind and respectful to elders and to friends.
outcomes: Talk about the members of our family and our friends
Understand how family and friends help and care for each other

lesson.hook: Who is the first person you see when you wake up? Who do you play with after school?
lesson.example: Meena's grandmother tells stories at night, her father cooks breakfast, and Meena waters the plants. Everyone has a job.
lesson.activity: Family tree: each child draws their family members as leaves on a tree and writes one way each person helps at home.

questions.q: Name two people in your family.
How do you help at home?
questions.a: Any helpful job (watering plants, laying the table, tidying toys).

questions.q: What makes a good friend?
questions.a: Someone who shares, helps and is kind.

lesson.homework: Ask an elder in your family about a game they played as a child and draw it.

topics.title: Going to the Mela
topics.summary: A mela is a fair where many people come together to shop, eat and have fun.
notes: A mela is a fair where many people come together to shop, eat and have fun.
At a mela we see stalls of toys, bangles, pots, sweets and clothes.
Many people work at a mela: sellers, cooks, ride operators, artists and cleaners.
Melas are often held during festivals and harvest time.
We should stay close to our family and keep the place clean.
outcomes: Describe what we see, hear and buy at a mela (fair)
Learn about the people who work at a mela

lesson.hook: Have you ever been to a mela? What did you see, eat and ride?
lesson.example: At the village mela, a potter sells clay pots, a woman sells colourful bangles, and a man runs the giant wheel.
lesson.activity: Class mela: children set up pretend stalls (toys, fruits, bangles) with paper money and take turns buying and selling.

questions.q: Name three things you can buy at a mela.
questions.a: Toys, bangles, sweets, pots, balloons (any three).

questions.q: Who works at a mela?
questions.a: Sellers, cooks, ride operators, artists, cleaners.

questions.q: What should you do if you get lost at a mela?
questions.a: Stay calm, stand in one place and ask a police officer or a helper for help.

lesson.homework: Draw your favourite stall at a mela and write two lines about it.

topics.title: Celebrating Festivals
topics.summary: India celebrates many festivals: Diwali, Eid, Christmas, Pongal, Onam, Holi, Baisakhi and many more.
notes: India celebrates many festivals: Diwali, Eid, Christmas, Pongal, Onam, Holi, Baisakhi and many more.
Some festivals celebrate harvest, some celebrate seasons, and some are religious.
On festivals we meet family and friends, wear new clothes, make special food and decorate homes.
People of all religions celebrate festivals together and share sweets.
National festivals like Independence Day and Republic Day are celebrated by everyone.
outcomes: Name festivals celebrated in our country
Understand how festivals bring people together

lesson.hook: Which festival do you like most? What do you eat and wear on that day?
lesson.example: At Pongal, families in Tamil Nadu cook rice with jaggery in a new pot and thank the Sun for a good harvest.
lesson.activity: Festival calendar: children put pictures of festivals on a big class calendar in the right month and share one thing they do on each.

questions.q: Name two harvest festivals.
questions.a: Pongal, Baisakhi, Onam, Makar Sankranti, Bihu (any two).

questions.q: Name two national festivals.
questions.a: Independence Day and Republic Day (also Gandhi Jayanti).

questions.q: What do people do on festivals?
questions.a: Meet family, wear new clothes, make special food, decorate homes.

lesson.homework: Make a greeting card for a festival of a friend from a different religion.

topics.title: Getting to Know Plants
topics.summary: A plant has roots, a stem, leaves, flowers and fruits.
notes: A plant has roots, a stem, leaves, flowers and fruits.
Roots hold the plant in the soil and take up water.
The stem holds the plant up; leaves make food using sunlight.
Plants can be big trees, small shrubs, herbs, climbers or creepers.
Leaves have different shapes, sizes and colours.
outcomes: Name the parts of a plant
Notice differences in leaves, stems and flowers of plants around us

lesson.hook: Look out of the window. How many different plants can you see? Are they all the same?
lesson.example: A mango tree is tall with a thick, hard trunk. A tulsi plant is small with a soft stem. A money plant climbs up a stick.
lesson.activity: Leaf collection: children collect five fallen leaves, stick them in a notebook, and compare shape, size, edges and colour.

questions.q: Which part of a plant holds it in the soil?
Name a plant that climbs.
questions.a: Money plant, pea plant, grape vine, bitter gourd (any one).

questions.q: What do leaves need to make food?

lesson.homework: Draw a plant from your home and label its parts.

topics.title: Plants and Animals Live Together
topics.summary: Many animals live on or near plants: birds make nests, squirrels live in holes, ants live near roots.
notes: Many animals live on or near plants: birds make nests, squirrels live in holes, ants live near roots.
Animals get food from plants: fruits, leaves, seeds and nectar.
Some animals help plants: bees carry pollen, birds spread seeds.
Animals live in different homes — nests, burrows, holes, water and trees.
Plants and animals living together make our surroundings healthy.
outcomes: Understand how plants and animals depend on each other
Observe animals around us and their homes

lesson.hook: A tree in the school garden — who lives on it? Who visits it?
lesson.example: A bee drinks nectar from a flower and carries pollen to the next flower, helping the plant make seeds.
lesson.activity: Tree watch: in groups, children observe one tree for 10 minutes and list all the animals they see on it or near it.

questions.q: Name two animals that live on trees.
How do bees help plants?
questions.a: They carry pollen from flower to flower.

questions.q: What do animals get from plants?

lesson.homework: Draw an animal's home you have seen and write who lives there.

topics.title: Living in Harmony
topics.summary: People, animals and plants all share the Earth.
notes: People, animals and plants all share the Earth.
We should not harm animals or break plants.
We can keep water for birds in summer and feed stray animals safely.
Many people in India protect trees and animals, like the Bishnoi community.
Living in harmony means caring for everyone around us.
outcomes: Understand that all living things share the Earth
Learn ways to be kind to animals and plants

lesson.hook: If a bird built a nest on your window, what would you do?
lesson.example: In summer, Arjun keeps a bowl of water on his terrace. Sparrows and crows come to drink every day.
lesson.activity: Kindness pledge: children make a poster listing three ways they will care for animals and plants, and sign it.

questions.q: How can you help birds in summer?
questions.a: Keep a bowl of water and some grains for them.

questions.q: Should we pluck leaves and flowers for fun?
What does 'living in harmony' mean?
questions.a: Living peacefully and caring for people, animals and plants.

lesson.homework: Do one kind act for an animal or plant this week and draw it.

topics.title: Water— A Precious Gift
topics.summary: We get water from rain, rivers, lakes, ponds, wells and taps.
notes: We get water from rain, rivers, lakes, ponds, wells and taps.
We use water for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing and watering plants.
Animals and plants also need water to live.
Clean water is precious; some places have very little of it.
We can save water by closing taps, fixing leaks and reusing water for plants.
outcomes: Know where we get water from and how we use it
Learn ways to save water

lesson.hook: How many times did you use water today, from the moment you woke up?
lesson.example: Water used to wash vegetables can be poured on plants instead of down the drain.
lesson.activity: Drip test: leave a leaking tap dripping into a cup for 10 minutes and measure the water. How much would be wasted in a day?

questions.q: Name three sources of water.
questions.a: Rain, river, well, pond, lake, tap (any three).

questions.q: Name two ways to save water.
questions.a: Close the tap while brushing, fix leaks, reuse water for plants (any two).

questions.q: Why is water precious?
questions.a: All living things need it, and clean water is limited.

lesson.homework: Make a chart: 'How my family uses water' with pictures.

topics.title: Food We Eat
topics.summary: We get food from plants (rice, wheat, dal, vegetables, fruits) and animals (milk, eggs, fish, meat).
notes: We get food from plants (rice, wheat, dal, vegetables, fruits) and animals (milk, eggs, fish, meat).
People in different places eat different foods: idli in the south, roti in the north, rice and fish in the east.
Some foods are eaten raw, some are cooked.
We need different foods to grow strong and stay healthy.
We should not waste food; many people work hard to grow it.
outcomes: Know different foods we eat and where they come from
Understand why we need different kinds of food

lesson.hook: What did you eat for lunch today? Where did each item come from?
lesson.example: A plate of rice, dal, vegetables and curd has food from plants (rice, dal, vegetables) and from animals (curd).
lesson.activity: Food sorting: children bring pictures of foods and sort them into 'from plants' and 'from animals', then 'raw' and 'cooked'.

questions.q: Name two foods we get from animals.
questions.a: Milk, eggs, fish, meat, honey (any two).

questions.q: Name two foods we eat raw.
Why should we not waste food?
questions.a: Farmers work hard to grow it and many people do not have enough.

lesson.homework: Ask your family about a special dish from your region and write how it is made.

topics.title: Staying Healthy and Happy
topics.summary: Healthy food, clean water, exercise and sleep keep our body healthy.
notes: Healthy food, clean water, exercise and sleep keep our body healthy.
Washing hands before eating and after using the toilet stops germs.
Brushing teeth twice a day and bathing daily keep us clean.
Playing outdoors makes us strong and happy.
Talking about our feelings with family and friends helps us stay happy.
outcomes: Learn good habits for staying healthy
Understand that play, rest and feelings are part of good health

lesson.hook: What makes you feel happy and full of energy? What makes you feel tired?
lesson.example: Ria washes her hands with soap for 20 seconds before lunch — as long as singing a short rhyme twice.
lesson.activity: Handwashing steps: children practise the six steps of washing hands with soap and make a poster for the classroom sink.

questions.q: When should we wash our hands?
questions.a: Before eating and after using the toilet (also after playing).

questions.q: How many times should we brush our teeth?
Name one thing that helps you stay happy.
questions.a: Playing, talking to friends and family, enough sleep (any one).

lesson.homework: Keep a 'healthy habits' chart for one week and tick what you do every day.

topics.title: This World of Things
topics.summary: Things around us are made of materials like wood, metal, plastic, glass, cloth, clay and paper.
notes: Things around us are made of materials like wood, metal, plastic, glass, cloth, clay and paper.
Materials have properties: hard or soft, rough or smooth, heavy or light.
Some things float in water and some sink.
We choose materials based on what the thing is used for — glass for windows so light can pass.
Many materials can be reused or recycled.
outcomes: Identify materials that things are made of
Sort things by properties such as hard, soft, rough and smooth

lesson.hook: Look at your school bag. What is it made of? What about your water bottle?
lesson.example: A spoon can be steel (hard, shiny), wood (light) or plastic (cheap). A cloth towel is soft so it can soak up water.
lesson.activity: Float or sink: children test a pencil, eraser, coin, leaf, key and paper boat in a tub of water and record the results.

questions.q: Name two things made of wood.
Why are windows made of glass?
Does a steel key float or sink?

lesson.homework: Find five things at home and write what each is made of.

topics.title: Making Things
topics.summary: Many things we use are made by skilled people: potters, weavers, carpenters, basket makers.
notes: Many things we use are made by skilled people: potters, weavers, carpenters, basket makers.
A potter shapes wet clay on a wheel and bakes it to make pots.
A weaver makes cloth from threads on a loom.
Things can be made by hand or by machines in factories.
We can also make useful things from waste, such as pen stands from old bottles.
outcomes: Learn how some things are made by people
Appreciate the skills of craftspeople

lesson.hook: Who made the clay pot, the basket or the cloth in your home? How do you think they made it?
lesson.example: Channapatna in Karnataka is famous for colourful wooden toys made on a lathe and coloured with natural dyes.
lesson.activity: Clay craft: children make a small pot or animal with clay or play-dough and describe each step.

questions.q: Who makes clay pots?
What does a weaver use to make cloth?
Name one useful thing you can make from waste.
questions.a: Pen stand, flower pot, bird feeder (any one).

lesson.homework: Make something useful from waste material at home and bring it to class.

topics.title: Taking Charge of Waste
topics.summary: Waste is what we throw away: vegetable peels, paper, plastic, bottles, broken things.
notes: Waste is what we throw away: vegetable peels, paper, plastic, bottles, broken things.
Wet waste (peels, leftover food) can become compost for plants.
Dry waste (paper, plastic, metal, glass) can often be recycled.
We should use separate bins for wet and dry waste.
Reduce, reuse and recycle: carry a cloth bag, reuse bottles and give old books to others.
outcomes: Understand where waste comes from
Learn to sort waste and reduce, reuse and recycle

lesson.hook: How much waste does your family throw away in one day? Where does it go?
lesson.example: Green bin for wet waste like banana peels; blue bin for dry waste like newspaper and plastic bottles.
lesson.activity: Sort it out: children sort a pile of clean waste pictures into green (wet) and blue (dry) bins drawn on the floor.

questions.q: Is a banana peel wet or dry waste?
What can wet waste be turned into?
Name one way to reduce waste.
questions.a: Carry a cloth bag, use a steel bottle, avoid plastic (any one).

lesson.homework: Help sort wet and dry waste at home for a week.

topics.title: Together We Can
topics.summary: The poem says that when we stand together and help each other, we do not fall.
notes: The poem says that when we stand together and help each other, we do not fall.
Teamwork can overcome any difficulty.
A good team shares, whether it wins or loses, and trusts each other.
Team spirit brings joy and brings the goal closer.
outcomes: Recite a poem about teamwork
Explain why helping each other makes a team strong

lesson.hook: Can one person win a tug of war alone? What about a whole team?
lesson.example: Rhyming pairs in the poem: tall–fall, sing–anything, share–there, near–cheer.
lesson.activity: Human knot: groups hold hands in a tangle and must untangle without letting go — possible only by working together.

questions.q: What happens when we help each other?
questions.a: We never fall; we become strong.

questions.q: What can teamwork overcome?
What does a good team do whether it wins or loses?
questions.a: It shares and keeps its bond of trust.

lesson.homework: Write about a time your team or group achieved something together.

topics.title: The Tinkling Bells
topics.summary: Chinna wanted to buy tinkling bells for his pet goat kid, Tara, but found his money was missing.
notes: Chinna wanted to buy tinkling bells for his pet goat kid, Tara, but found his money was missing.
His mother Kamala comforted him and took him to the market.
The fruit seller gave ten rupees extra by mistake; Chinna wanted to keep it for the bells and chocolates.
His mother asked how he felt when he lost money; Chinna understood and returned it. Then she bought him the bells, and he tied them on Tara.
outcomes: Read a story about honesty
Understand how others feel when they lose something

lesson.hook: If a shopkeeper gave you ten rupees too much by mistake, what would you do?
lesson.example: Kamala gave ₹100 for two pineapples at ₹45 each. Change = ₹100 − ₹90 = ₹10, but Chinna got ₹20 — ₹10 extra.
lesson.activity: Honesty role play: pairs act out a shop scene where the customer gets extra change and returns it.

questions.q: What did Chinna want to buy?
What mistake did the fruit seller make?
questions.a: He gave ten rupees extra change.

questions.q: Why did Chinna return the money?
questions.a: His mother helped him see the seller would feel sad and it was wrong to keep it.

lesson.homework: Write what you would say to a shopkeeper when returning extra change.

topics.title: Be Smart, Be Safe
topics.summary: The traffic police wrote a letter to children with road safety tips.
notes: The traffic police wrote a letter to children with road safety tips.
Cross at the zebra crossing: look right, then left, then right again.
Follow traffic lights and the pedestrian signal; walk calmly, never run across.
Walk on footpaths, hold an adult's hand near roads, wear reflective stickers at night, and do not use headphones or phones near traffic.
outcomes: Read and follow road safety rules
Understand signs and signals for pedestrians

lesson.hook: What colour of the traffic light tells you it is safe to walk?
lesson.example: Before crossing: stop at the zebra crossing → look right → look left → look right again → cross when clear.
lesson.activity: Classroom crossing: tape a zebra crossing on the floor and practise crossing with a child acting as the traffic light.

questions.q: Where should you cross the road?
Why should you not use headphones near roads?
questions.a: They distract you from traffic sounds.

questions.q: Why wear reflective stickers in the evening?
questions.a: So drivers can see you clearly.

lesson.homework: Make a poster of three road safety rules.

topics.title: One Thing at a Time
topics.summary: The poem says we should work while we work and play while we play.
notes: The poem says we should work while we work and play while we play.
Whatever we do, we should do it with all our might.
Things done by halves are never done right.
Doing one thing at a time, and doing it well, is a good rule; we should not waste time.
outcomes: Recite a poem about focus and doing things well
Find rhyming words in the poem

lesson.hook: Can you do your homework well while watching TV? Why or why not?
lesson.example: Rhyming words: play–way, might–right, well–tell, away–play.
lesson.activity: Focus challenge: children do a short task (copy five lines neatly) once with distractions and once without, and compare.

questions.q: What happens to things done by halves?
What is 'a very good rule' in the poem?
questions.a: Do one thing at a time and do it well.

questions.q: Write two rhyming words from the poem.

lesson.homework: Make a timetable for your evening with separate times for work and play.

topics.title: The Old Stag
topics.summary: A kind old stag lived on a hillock covered with tender grass and was loved by all.
notes: A kind old stag lived on a hillock covered with tender grass and was loved by all.
When he fell ill, his friends visited him, but each visitor also ate the grass on the hillock.
Soon there was little grass left and the stag became weaker.
The animals felt ashamed, found food elsewhere and brought him leaves; the grass grew back and he recovered. Nature has enough for all if we use it wisely.
outcomes: Read a fable about greed and sharing
Understand the wise use of nature's resources

lesson.hook: If you visit a sick friend, should you eat their food?
lesson.example: If every visitor takes a little, nothing is left — small greed adds up.
lesson.activity: Resource game: groups share a bowl of counters as 'grass'; if each takes too many, it runs out. Discuss fair use.

questions.q: Where did the old stag live?
questions.a: On a hillock with tender grass.

questions.q: Why did the stag become weaker?
questions.a: His visitors ate up the grass he needed.

questions.q: What lesson did the animals learn?
questions.a: Nature has enough for everyone, but we must use it wisely.

lesson.homework: Write two ways your family can use water or electricity wisely.

topics.title: Braille
topics.summary: Louis Braille was born in France; at the age of three, an accident with a tool made him blind.
notes: Louis Braille was born in France; at the age of three, an accident with a tool made him blind.
At ten, he joined a school for blind children in Paris, where letters were taught with wood, cloth or pins.
An army captain had invented 'Night Writing' with raised dots and dashes, but it was too hard; Louis simplified it into the Braille alphabet.
Braille is read by touch; each letter is a pattern of raised dots, so Braille books are thicker.
outcomes: Learn about Louis Braille and the Braille script
Understand how people who cannot see read and write

lesson.hook: Close your eyes and touch a coin. Can you tell which side is which?
lesson.example: In Braille, 'a' is one raised dot; letters are made from patterns in a cell of six dots.
lesson.activity: Dot letters: children press a pencil tip into thick paper from behind to make raised dots for their initials, then feel them.

questions.q: How did Louis Braille become blind?
questions.a: A sharp tool pierced his eye when he was three.

questions.q: Why was Night Writing not a success?
Why are Braille books thicker?

lesson.homework: Write three ways we can help classmates who cannot see.

chapters.title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation

topics.title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
topics.summary: The poem introduces children and what they love to do.
notes: The poem introduces children and what they love to do.
Anant plays hockey, Geeta skates and learns from mistakes, Lhamo plays the guitar, Shabana wins a cycle race.
Meena, the speaker, sings in rhythm.
Playing and hobbies keep our body fit and our mind happy — a fit nation needs fit children.
outcomes: Read a poem about children and their hobbies
Describe people with alliterative adjectives

lesson.hook: What do you love doing more than anything — a sport, music, dance or something else?
lesson.example: Alliteration: Active Anant, Graceful Geeta, Swift Shabana, Musical Meena.
lesson.activity: Name poem: each child describes themselves with a quality starting with the same letter as their name (e.g. Happy Harini).

questions.q: Which game does Anant play?
Which instruments are mentioned?
Who learns every day from mistakes?

lesson.homework: Write two lines about your favourite hobby.

topics.title: The Lagori Champions
topics.summary: Prakash visits his cousin Ravi and does not know the game Lagori.
notes: Prakash visits his cousin Ravi and does not know the game Lagori.
Lagori is played with seven flat stones stacked up; one team knocks them down with a ball and tries to rebuild the stack while the other team tries to hit them with the ball.
The same game is called Satoliya in Rajasthan.
In the match, the Sundarpur Tigers rebuild the stack by dodging the ball, and Prakash sets the last stone — they win.
outcomes: Read a play about a traditional game
Learn the rules of Lagori (seven stones)

lesson.hook: Have you ever played a game with seven stones and a ball?
lesson.example: Many Indian games have different names in different places — Lagori, Satoliya, Pithoo.
lesson.activity: Play Lagori: in the playground, two teams play with seven flat stones and a soft ball, following safety rules.

questions.q: How many stones are used in Lagori?
What is Lagori called in Rajasthan?
Who placed the seventh stone?

lesson.homework: Find out what Lagori is called in your language or area.

topics.title: Hekko
topics.summary: 'Hekko' means 'challenging the tiger'; it comes from a Naga folk story of the Man (Aami) and the Tiger (Aakho).
notes: 'Hekko' means 'challenging the tiger'; it comes from a Naga folk story of the Man (Aami) and the Tiger (Aakho).
It is played in Mokokchung district, Nagaland, between two teams of 11 players.
The Aami team forms a human chain inside a circle; Aakho players try to push them out, and Aami tries to catch Aakho players until they say 'Joko' (surrender).
The game ends when a team is all out or time runs out; titles are given to the fastest and strongest players.
outcomes: Read about a traditional game of Nagaland
Understand rules, teams and fair play

lesson.hook: Can a game be based on a folk story? Let's find out!
lesson.example: Two teams × 11 players = 22 players in a Hekko match.
lesson.activity: Circle game: children play a gentle version where one team holds hands in a circle and the other tries to tag them.

questions.q: What does 'Hekko' mean?
What are the two teams called?
What does 'Joko' mean?

lesson.homework: Write the rules of a game you play with friends.

topics.title: The Swing
topics.summary: The poet thinks going up in a swing is the most pleasant thing a child can do.
notes: The poet thinks going up in a swing is the most pleasant thing a child can do.
Swinging high over the wall, the poet can see far and wide.
The poet sees rivers, trees, cattle and the countryside.
Looking down, the poet sees the green garden and the brown roof, then swings up again.
outcomes: Recite a classic poem about swinging
Imagine and describe a view from above

lesson.hook: What can you see when you swing really high?
lesson.example: Up in the air, 'the air so blue' — the poet sees the blue sky all around while swinging.
lesson.activity: Bird's-eye drawing: children draw what they would see from a very high swing.

questions.q: What does the poet see over the wall?
questions.a: Rivers, trees, cattle and the countryside.

questions.q: Does the poet enjoy swings? How do you know?
questions.a: Yes; the poet calls it the pleasantest thing a child can do.

questions.q: What colour is the roof?

lesson.homework: Describe in three sentences how you feel on a swing.

chapters.title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains

topics.title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
topics.summary: Minam lived in a village at the foot of the Himalayas; her grandfather was once a Sherpa.
notes: Minam lived in a village at the foot of the Himalayas; her grandfather was once a Sherpa.
They walked up the mountains, ate lunch by a clear river and saw yaks.
Yaks give milk and wool and carry heavy loads for mountain people.
