Co-prime numbers have only 1 as a common factor (8 and 15).
Every number greater than 1 can be written as a product of primes in only one way (prime factorisation).
Divisibility tests: by 2 (last digit even), 3 (digit sum divisible by 3), 4 (last two digits), 5 (ends in 0 or 5), 8 (last three digits), 9 (digit sum), 10 (ends in 0).
outcomes: Find common factors and common multiples
Identify prime, composite and co-prime numbers
Find prime factorisations and use divisibility tests

lesson.hook: Two friends play a game: one claps every 4 seconds and the other every 6 seconds. If they start together, when will they next clap together?
lesson.example: Prime factorisation of 84: 84 = 2 × 42 = 2 × 2 × 21 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. The claps meet at common multiples of 4 and 6: 12, 24… so after 12 seconds.
lesson.activity: Sieve of Eratosthenes: on a 1-100 grid, pupils cross out multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7 (not the numbers themselves) and circle what remains — the primes up to 100.

questions.q: Is 91 prime?
Are 9 and 16 co-prime?
questions.a: Yes — their only common factor is 1.

questions.q: Is 4536 divisible by 9?
questions.a: Yes — its digit sum is 18, which is divisible by 9.

questions.q: Write the prime factorisation of 60.

lesson.homework: Find all the prime numbers between 100 and 130.

topics.title: Perimeter and Area
topics.summary: Perimeter is the total length of the boundary of a figure.
notes: Perimeter is the total length of the boundary of a figure.
Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 × (length + width); of a square = 4 × side.
Area is the amount of surface enclosed, measured in square units (cm², m²).
Area of a rectangle = length × width; of a square = side × side.
A triangle is half of a rectangle drawn around it, so its area is half of base × height.
Shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas, and the other way round.
outcomes: Find the perimeter of polygons, rectangles and squares
Find the area of rectangles, squares and triangles using square units
Tell perimeter and area apart in real problems

lesson.hook: You have 24 metres of fencing. What shape of garden gives your plants the most room?
lesson.example: Using 24 m of fencing: a 10 m × 2 m garden has area 20 m², a 8 m × 4 m garden has 32 m², and a 6 m × 6 m square has 36 m² — the square gives the most room.
lesson.activity: On squared paper, pupils draw as many rectangles as they can with perimeter 20 cm and record the area of each. Which has the largest area?

questions.q: Find the perimeter of a rectangle 7 cm by 4 cm.
A square has perimeter 36 cm. Find its area.
Find the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm.

lesson.homework: Measure your classroom or a room at home and find its perimeter and floor area.

topics.title: Fractions
topics.summary: A fraction shows equal shares: 1/4 means one of four equal parts of a whole.
notes: A fraction shows equal shares: 1/4 means one of four equal parts of a whole.
Fractions like 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 are fractional units; 3/4 means three units of 1/4.
Fractions are numbers and have places on the number line.
A fraction greater than 1 can be written as a mixed fraction: 7/4 = 1¾.
Equivalent fractions name the same amount: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6; multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number.
To compare, add or subtract fractions with different denominators, first make the denominators the same; Indian mathematicians such as Brahmagupta described these methods long ago.
outcomes: Understand fractions as equal shares and as parts of a whole
Place fractions on the number line and write mixed fractions
Find equivalent fractions, compare fractions, and add and subtract them

lesson.hook: Three friends share two rotis equally. How much does each get? Show it with a drawing.
lesson.example: 2/3 + 1/4: common denominator 12. 2/3 = 8/12 and 1/4 = 3/12, so the sum is 11/12.
lesson.activity: Fraction strips: pupils fold paper strips into halves, quarters and eighths, then line them up to find equivalent fractions and compare 3/4 with 5/8.

questions.q: Write two fractions equivalent to 3/5.
Which is bigger, 3/4 or 5/8?
Write 11/3 as a mixed fraction.

lesson.homework: Find three examples of fractions used in recipes or on packets at home and write each as a fraction.

topics.title: Playing with Constructions
topics.summary: All points on a circle are the same distance (the radius) from the centre; a compass draws circles and arcs.
notes: All points on a circle are the same distance (the radius) from the centre; a compass draws circles and arcs.
A rough sketch helps plan the steps of a construction.
A rectangle can be constructed from its two side lengths, or from one side and a diagonal.
In a rectangle the diagonals are equal and bisect each other; in a square they are also perpendicular.
Points equidistant from two points A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB, found with two intersecting arcs.
Constructions combine circles and lines to make art such as rangoli-like designs.
outcomes: Use a compass and ruler to construct circles, squares and rectangles
Plan constructions with a rough sketch
Explore diagonals and points equidistant from two given points

lesson.hook: Can you draw a perfect square using only a ruler and a compass — without a protractor or set square?
lesson.example: To find points equidistant from A and B, draw arcs of the same radius (more than half of AB) from A and from B; the line through the two crossing points is the perpendicular bisector.
lesson.activity: Construct a rectangle 6 cm × 4 cm with ruler and compass only, then measure both diagonals and check they are equal.

questions.q: What is the radius of a circle?
questions.a: The distance from the centre to any point on the circle.

questions.q: Are the diagonals of a rectangle equal?
Where are all points equidistant from two points A and B?
questions.a: On the perpendicular bisector of AB.

lesson.homework: Design a pattern using only circles and arcs made with a compass and colour it.

topics.title: Symmetry
topics.summary: A figure has symmetry when its parts repeat in a definite pattern.
notes: A figure has symmetry when its parts repeat in a definite pattern.
A line of symmetry divides a figure into two halves that overlap exactly when folded.
A figure can have many lines of symmetry: a square has 4, an equilateral triangle 3, a circle infinitely many.
Rotational symmetry: a figure looks the same after turning by less than a full turn about its centre.
The smallest such turn is the angle of symmetry; the number of times it matches in one full turn is the order.
Symmetry is used in art, architecture, rangoli and nature.
outcomes: Identify lines of symmetry in figures
Recognise rotational symmetry and find the angle and order of rotation
Create symmetrical designs

lesson.hook: Fold a paper butterfly along its middle. Why do both halves match exactly?
lesson.example: A square looks the same after a 90° turn, so its angle of symmetry is 90° and its order is 360° ÷ 90° = 4.
lesson.activity: Ink blots and paper cutting: pupils fold paper and cut designs to make patterns with one, two and four lines of symmetry. Then turn a pinwheel design to find its order of rotation.

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle (not a square) have?
What is the order of rotational symmetry of an equilateral triangle?
Which capital letters of the English alphabet have a vertical line of symmetry? Name three.
questions.a: A, H, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y (any three).

lesson.homework: Draw a rangoli design with at least four lines of symmetry.

topics.title: The Other Side of Zero
topics.summary: Numbers less than zero are negative numbers, written with a − sign: −2, −5.
notes: Numbers less than zero are negative numbers, written with a − sign: −2, −5.
Integers are …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …; negatives lie to the left of 0 on the number line.
On the number line, a number on the right is greater: −1 > −5.
Token model: a positive token (+) and a negative token (−) cancel to make zero.
Adding a negative is like moving left; subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive: 4 − (−3) = 7.
Integers describe temperatures below zero, floors below ground, and money owed; Brahmagupta described rules for negative numbers in the 7th century.
outcomes: Understand negative numbers and integers on the number line
Add and subtract integers using a token model and the number line
Use integers in real situations such as temperatures, floors and money

lesson.hook: A lift is on the ground floor (0). It goes 3 floors down to the parking level, then 5 floors up. Which floor is it on now?
lesson.example: Lift: 0 − 3 + 5 = +2, the second floor. Temperature: at night −4 °C, by noon it rises 9 °C, so −4 + 9 = 5 °C.
lesson.activity: Human number line: pupils hold cards −5 to 5 standing in a row. Others give moves ('start at 2, add −6') and a volunteer walks it.

questions.q: Which is greater, −7 or −2?
Find −6 + 4.
A diver is 12 m below sea level and rises 5 m. Where is he now?
questions.a: −7 m, i.e. 7 m below sea level.

lesson.homework: Find the lowest and highest temperatures of five cities in the news this week and arrange them from coldest to hottest.

topics.title: The Wonderful World of Science
topics.summary: Science is a way of thinking: we observe the world, ask questions and look for answers we can check.
notes: Science is a way of thinking: we observe the world, ask questions and look for answers we can check.
Scientists make a guess (a hypothesis), test it with an experiment, look at the results and draw a conclusion.
If the test does not support the guess, we change the guess and test again — mistakes are part of learning.
Science is everywhere: in the kitchen, the farm, the playground, our body and the sky.
Good observers use all their senses carefully and record what they see, often with drawings and tables.
outcomes: Understand science as a way of asking questions and finding out
Name the steps scientists use: observe, ask, guess, test, conclude
Connect science with things in daily life

lesson.hook: Why does a steel spoon feel colder than a wooden one in the same room? Before anyone tells you the answer, what could you do to find out yourself?
lesson.example: Question: do seeds need water to sprout? Guess: yes. Test: keep some gram seeds on dry cotton and some on wet cotton for three days. Result: only the seeds on wet cotton sprout. Conclusion: seeds need water to germinate.
lesson.activity: Mystery box: put a common object in a closed box. Groups shake, weigh and listen, write down their observations and guesses, then open it. Discuss how scientists work without seeing everything directly.

questions.q: What is a hypothesis?
questions.a: A sensible guess that can be tested.

questions.q: What should you do if an experiment does not support your guess?
questions.a: Think again, change the guess and test it again.

questions.q: Name two senses you use to observe a fruit.
questions.a: Any two of sight, smell, touch, taste, hearing.

lesson.homework: Write down three questions about things you see at home and how you could test one of them.

topics.title: Diversity in the Living World
topics.summary: The huge variety of plants and animals around us is called biodiversity.
notes: The huge variety of plants and animals around us is called biodiversity.
Grouping means arranging things by their common features; it helps us study living things.
By height and stem, plants are herbs (small, soft green stem), shrubs (bushy, hard stem near the base) and trees (tall, thick woody trunk).
Leaves with a net of veins (reticulate venation) usually go with a taproot; leaves with parallel veins go with fibrous roots.
Seeds with two cotyledons (dicots, like gram) or one cotyledon (monocots, like maize) give another way to group plants.
Animals can be grouped by how they move and where they live; the place where a living thing lives is its habitat, and features that help it live there are adaptations.
Sacred groves and traditions of protecting forests help conserve biodiversity.
outcomes: Appreciate the variety (biodiversity) of plants and animals around us
Group plants by height and stem, by leaf venation and roots, and by seeds
Relate plants and animals to their habitats and adaptations

lesson.hook: On the way to school today, how many different kinds of plants and animals did you see? Were any two exactly the same?
lesson.example: A tulsi plant is a shrub; a grass blade shows parallel veins and has fibrous roots; a mango leaf shows a net of veins and the tree has a taproot.
lesson.activity: Leaf and root walk: groups collect fallen leaves and uproot two small weeds (with permission). They sort the leaves by venation and match them with the kind of root, then record in a table on the board.

questions.q: Is a rose plant a herb, a shrub or a tree?
What kind of roots does a plant with parallel venation usually have?
What is a habitat?
questions.a: The place where a plant or animal lives and gets food, water and shelter.

questions.q: Give one adaptation of a camel to the desert.
questions.a: Long legs, humps that store fat, thick eyelashes, or being able to go long without water (any one).

lesson.homework: Collect five leaves from different plants, stick them in your notebook and label the type of venation of each.

chapters.title: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body

topics.title: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
topics.summary: Food gives energy, helps us grow, repairs the body and protects us from disease.
notes: Food gives energy, helps us grow, repairs the body and protects us from disease.
Components: carbohydrates and fats (energy), proteins (growth and repair), vitamins and minerals (protection), dietary fibre (roughage) and water.
Tests: starch turns blue-black with iodine; fat leaves an oily patch on paper; protein turns violet with copper sulphate and caustic soda.
A balanced diet has all the components in the right amounts; lack of a nutrient for a long time causes deficiency diseases, such as scurvy (vitamin C), rickets (vitamin D) and goitre (iodine).
Millets such as ragi, jowar and bajra are rich in nutrients and grow with little water.
Food miles: the distance food travels from farm to plate; local, seasonal food saves fuel and stays fresh.
outcomes: Name the components of food and what each does for the body
Test foods for starch, fats and proteins
Explain a balanced diet, deficiency diseases, millets and food miles

lesson.hook: What did you eat yesterday? Does food from Kerala, Punjab and Assam look different? Why does our body need so many kinds of food?
lesson.example: Iodine test: put two drops of dilute iodine on a slice of potato. It turns blue-black, so the potato contains starch. On a piece of cucumber it does not, so cucumber has little starch.
lesson.activity: Food detectives: groups test boiled potato, rice water, groundnut, boiled egg white and a slice of cucumber for starch, fat and protein and fill a class table.

questions.q: Which nutrient gives the body most of its energy?
Which disease is caused by lack of vitamin C?
How do you test for fat in groundnut?
questions.a: Rub it on paper; an oily, see-through patch shows fat.

questions.q: Why are millets called nutri-cereals?
questions.a: They are rich in nutrients like fibre, minerals and proteins, and grow with little water.

lesson.homework: Write your meals for one day and mark which components each food gives. Is your day's diet balanced?

topics.title: Exploring Magnets
topics.summary: Materials attracted by a magnet (iron, nickel, cobalt) are magnetic; others (wood, plastic, paper, copper) are non-magnetic.
notes: Materials attracted by a magnet (iron, nickel, cobalt) are magnetic; others (wood, plastic, paper, copper) are non-magnetic.
Every magnet has a North pole and a South pole; they always come in pairs, even if the magnet is broken.
Iron filings cling most at the poles, where the magnet's pull is strongest.
A freely hanging magnet rests in the north–south direction; a compass uses this to show directions.
Like poles repel (N–N, S–S) and unlike poles attract (N–S).
Magnets are used in doors of fridges, toys, pencil boxes, speakers and to pick up iron scrap.
outcomes: Sort materials into magnetic and non-magnetic
Find the poles of a magnet and use a magnet to find directions
Show that like poles repel and unlike poles attract

resources.title: Magnetic field of a bar magnet

lesson.hook: How did sailors cross oceans without seeing land for weeks? A small magnetic needle showed them the way. How?
lesson.example: Tie a bar magnet with a thread at its middle and let it hang freely. However you turn it, it settles pointing north–south; the end pointing north is its North pole.
lesson.activity: Open the 3D bar magnet and show the field lines and compass needles. Then groups use a magnet to test 10 objects, sort them into magnetic and non-magnetic, and make a compass by stroking a needle and floating it on a leaf in water.

questions.q: Name two magnetic materials.
What happens when the North poles of two magnets are brought close?
In which direction does a freely hanging magnet rest?
If a magnet is broken into two pieces, how many poles does each piece have?
questions.a: Two: a North and a South pole.

lesson.homework: Find five things at home that use a magnet and write what the magnet does in each.

topics.title: Measurement of Length and Motion
topics.summary: Measuring means comparing with a unit; hand-spans and footsteps differ from person to person, so we use standard units.
notes: Measuring means comparing with a unit; hand-spans and footsteps differ from person to person, so we use standard units.
The SI unit of length is the metre (m): 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm.
Place the scale along the object, start from a clear mark and look straight down at the reading.
A curved line is measured with a thread laid along it, then straightened on a scale.
Position is stated from a reference point; an object is moving if its position changes with time.
Motion can be linear (a car on a straight road), circular (a merry-go-round) or oscillatory (a swing, a pendulum).
outcomes: Measure length correctly with standard units
Measure curved lines
Describe position with a reference point and identify linear, circular and oscillatory motion

lesson.hook: If you measure the classroom with your hand-spans and your teacher does too, will you get the same number? Why do we need standard units?
lesson.example: To measure the length of a curved line on a map, lay a thread along it, mark the end, straighten the thread along a ruler and read the length.
lesson.activity: Measure the length of the desk with hand-spans (each pupil), then with a metre scale; compare the results on the board. Then run the pendulum simulation to see oscillatory motion.

questions.q: How many centimetres are there in 2.5 metres?
What is the SI unit of length?
What type of motion does a swing show?
Why should you look straight down at the scale when reading?
questions.a: Looking from an angle gives a wrong reading.

lesson.homework: Measure the length of three curved things at home (a bangle, a leaf edge, a bottle's neck) with a thread and a scale.

topics.title: Materials Around Us
topics.summary: Objects are made of materials; one object may use several materials, and one material may make many objects.
notes: Objects are made of materials; one object may use several materials, and one material may make many objects.
Grouping (classification) by properties helps us choose materials.
Lustrous or non-lustrous; hard or soft; transparent (glass), translucent (butter paper) or opaque (wood).
Some materials dissolve in water (salt, sugar), others do not (sand, chalk); some float and some sink.
Anything that has mass and occupies space is matter; the space it occupies is its volume.
outcomes: Understand that objects are made of materials
Group materials by lustre, hardness, transparency, solubility and floating
Explain that matter has mass and occupies space

lesson.hook: A spoon can be made of steel, plastic, wood or silver. Why do we choose one material rather than another for each job?
lesson.example: Windows use glass because it is transparent; a frosted bathroom window is translucent, letting light in while blocking the view.
lesson.activity: Property stations: test a spoon of salt, sand, sugar, chalk powder and oil in water for solubility; hold a torch behind glass, oiled paper and cardboard to classify transparent, translucent and opaque.

questions.q: Is butter paper transparent, translucent or opaque?
Name one material that is soluble in water and one that is not.
questions.a: Soluble: salt or sugar. Insoluble: sand or chalk.

questions.q: What is matter?
questions.a: Anything that has mass and occupies space.

questions.q: Why are cooking pots made of metal?
questions.a: Metals are strong and let heat pass through easily.

lesson.homework: List ten objects at home and the material each is made of, and one reason that material was chosen.

topics.title: Temperature and its Measurement
topics.summary: Touch is not a reliable judge of how hot or cold something is; we measure temperature with a thermometer.
notes: Touch is not a reliable judge of how hot or cold something is; we measure temperature with a thermometer.
Temperature tells how hot or cold a body is; scales are Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F) and Kelvin (K, the SI unit).
A clinical thermometer measures body temperature (about 35–42 °C); normal is about 37 °C or 98.6 °F. Digital thermometers are safer than mercury ones.
A laboratory thermometer (about −10 to 110 °C) is used to measure the temperature of other things; keep the bulb in the liquid while reading.
Read at eye level, and shake a clinical thermometer down before use.
outcomes: Understand temperature as a measure of hotness
Use clinical and laboratory thermometers correctly
Know the Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales and normal body temperature

resources.title: Melting point of ice and boiling point of water

lesson.hook: Dip one hand in cold water and the other in warm water for a minute, then put both in lukewarm water. It feels warm to one hand and cold to the other. Can we trust touch to tell temperature?
lesson.example: Normal body temperature, 37 °C, is the same as 98.6 °F. A reading of 39 °C means fever.
lesson.activity: Three-bowl test (cold, lukewarm, warm water) to show touch is unreliable; then groups read the temperature of tap water, warm water and ice water with a laboratory thermometer and record it.

questions.q: What is the normal temperature of a healthy human body?
What is the SI unit of temperature?
Why can't a clinical thermometer measure boiling water?
Why should the laboratory thermometer's bulb stay in the liquid while reading?
questions.a: Otherwise the reading changes as it cools or warms in the air.

lesson.homework: Note the maximum and minimum temperatures of your town from a newspaper or phone for five days and make a table.

chapters.title: A Journey through States of Water

topics.title: A Journey through States of Water
topics.summary: Water exists as solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (water vapour).
notes: Water exists as solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (water vapour).
Heating melts ice into water and turns water into vapour; cooling does the reverse (condensation, freezing).
Evaporation turns water into vapour at any temperature; it is faster with more exposed surface, more heat, more wind and drier air (low humidity).
Evaporation cools: water in an earthen pot stays cool, and sweat cools our body.
Water vapour condenses on cold surfaces, like droplets on a cold glass, and in the sky as clouds.
Tiny droplets join to fall as rain, hail or snow; the circulation of water between Earth and air is the water cycle.
outcomes: Describe water's three states and how heating and cooling change them
Explain evaporation, condensation and the factors affecting evaporation
Explain the cooling effect of evaporation and how clouds give rain (the water cycle)

resources.title: Melting point of ice and boiling point of water

lesson.hook: Wet clothes dry on the line and puddles vanish after rain. Where does the water go, and how does it come back as rain?
lesson.example: A glass of ice-cold water gets droplets on its outside: water vapour in the air condenses on the cold glass — the water did not leak through.
lesson.activity: Drying race: put equal amounts of water in a plate and a narrow glass, one set in the sun and one in shade, one near a fan. Check after an hour and discuss what makes evaporation faster.

questions.q: What is the change of water vapour into liquid called?
Why do clothes dry faster on a windy day?
questions.a: Moving air carries away the vapour, so evaporation is faster.

questions.q: Why does water in an earthen pot stay cool?
questions.a: Water seeps out through the pores and evaporates, cooling the pot.

questions.q: Name the three states of water.

lesson.homework: Draw and label the water cycle, showing evaporation, condensation and rain.

chapters.title: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life

topics.title: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
topics.summary: We separate mixtures to remove unwanted or harmful parts or to get useful ones.
notes: We separate mixtures to remove unwanted or harmful parts or to get useful ones.
Handpicking: remove stones from grains by size, colour and shape. Threshing: beat stalks to free grains. Winnowing: wind blows away light husk from heavy grain.
Sieving separates fine particles from larger ones, like flour from bran.
Sedimentation lets heavy insoluble particles settle; decantation pours off the clear liquid above; filtration removes insoluble solids with a filter.
Evaporation gets a dissolved solid back from its solution, like salt from sea water in salt pans.
Churning separates butter from curd; the lighter butter floats up.
outcomes: Explain why substances in a mixture need separating
Choose methods: handpicking, threshing, winnowing, sieving, evaporation, sedimentation, decantation, filtration, churning
Relate each method to everyday life

lesson.hook: Your grandmother picks stones out of rice, the milkman churns butter out of curd, and farmers throw grain into the wind. Each is separating a mixture. Why so many ways?
lesson.example: Muddy water: let it stand (sedimentation), pour off the clearer water (decantation), then pass it through a cloth or filter paper (filtration) to get clearer water.
lesson.activity: Separation challenge: each group gets a mixture (sand + salt + sawdust + iron filings) and must separate all four, choosing methods — magnet, water, floating, filtration, evaporation — and explaining each step.

questions.q: Which method separates husk from grain?
How is salt obtained from sea water?
questions.a: By evaporation of the water in salt pans.

questions.q: What is decantation?
questions.a: Pouring off the clear liquid after the solid has settled.

questions.q: Which method removes tea leaves from tea?

lesson.homework: Observe your kitchen for a day and list the separation methods used there.

topics.title: Living Creatures: Exploring their Characteristics
topics.summary: Living things move, need food, grow, breathe, excrete, respond to stimuli, reproduce and die.
notes: Living things move, need food, grow, breathe, excrete, respond to stimuli, reproduce and die.
Seeds need water, air and suitable conditions of warmth (and light or dark) to germinate.
When a seed germinates, the root grows down and the shoot grows up.
A plant's life cycle: seed → seedling → young plant → flowering plant → fruits and seeds.
A mosquito's life cycle: egg → larva → pupa → adult; larvae live in stagnant water, so emptying stored water stops mosquitoes breeding.
A frog's life cycle: egg → tadpole → tadpole with legs → froglet → adult frog.
outcomes: List the features that make something living
Find the conditions a seed needs to germinate
Describe the life cycles of a plant, a mosquito and a frog

lesson.hook: A seed sits in a packet for months looking lifeless, yet put it in wet soil and a plant appears. Is a seed living or non-living?
lesson.example: Three bowls of gram seeds: dry, in wet cotton, and fully under water. Only the seeds in wet cotton sprout well: they have both water and air.
lesson.activity: Germination set-up: groups set up the three bowls and record changes daily for a week in a table with drawings; the class compares results on day 5.

questions.q: What three things do seeds need to germinate?
questions.a: Water, air and suitable warmth (light or dark as the seed needs).

questions.q: Name the stages of a mosquito's life cycle.
Why should we not let water collect in coolers and pots?
questions.a: Mosquitoes lay eggs in stagnant water and their larvae grow there.

questions.q: What is a young frog with a tail and gills called?

lesson.homework: Sprout a few seeds at home and draw them on days 1, 3 and 5.

topics.title: Nature’s Treasures
topics.summary: Resources we get from nature are natural resources; things people make from them are human-made resources.
notes: Resources we get from nature are natural resources; things people make from them are human-made resources.
Air, water, sunlight, forests, soil, rocks, minerals and fossil fuels are natural resources.
Renewable resources are replaced by nature in a reasonable time (sunlight, wind, water, forests if not over-cut).
Non-renewable resources are limited and take very long to form (coal, petroleum, minerals).
All living things depend on natural resources, so we must use them judiciously: reduce, reuse, recycle and conserve.
outcomes: Identify natural resources: air, water, sunlight, forests, soil, rocks, minerals, fossil fuels
Classify resources as renewable and non-renewable
Explain why we must use resources wisely

lesson.hook: List everything you used this morning: water, electricity, wooden pencil, cooked food. Where did each one come from in nature?
lesson.example: Coal formed from plants buried millions of years ago; once burnt it is gone. Sunlight falls every day, so solar energy is renewable.
lesson.activity: Resource sort: groups get picture cards (sun, coal, forest, river, petrol, wind, iron ore, soil) and sort them into renewable and non-renewable, then suggest one way to save each non-renewable one.

questions.q: Is petroleum renewable or non-renewable?
Give two examples of renewable resources.
What is a human-made resource? Give an example.
questions.a: Something people make from natural resources, such as a chair from wood or cloth from cotton.

questions.q: Name one way to conserve water at home.
questions.a: Closing taps while brushing, reusing washing water for plants, fixing leaks (any one).

lesson.homework: Make a poster: 'Three things our family will do to save natural resources.'

topics.title: Beyond Earth
topics.summary: Stars appear to form patterns called constellations, such as Saptarishi (Ursa Major) and Orion.
notes: Stars appear to form patterns called constellations, such as Saptarishi (Ursa Major) and Orion.
The Pole Star (Dhruva tara) stays nearly still in the north and helps find the north direction.
The Sun is a star; eight planets orbit it: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
The Earth goes round the Sun in about a year; the Moon, our natural satellite, goes round the Earth in about 27 days.
Asteroids, comets and dwarf planets are also part of the Solar System.
The Solar System is part of the Milky Way galaxy, one of billions of galaxies in the Universe.
outcomes: Recognise stars and constellations and find the Pole Star
Name the members of the Solar System in order
Understand our place in the Milky Way and the Universe

resources.title: Seasons: the Earth round the Sun

lesson.hook: On a clear night away from city lights you can see thousands of stars. Ancient sailors and farmers used them as a map and a calendar. How?
lesson.example: To find the Pole Star, find the Saptarishi and follow the line through its two end stars (the pointers) about five times their distance.
lesson.activity: Open the 3D solar system: turn on 'Planets moving' and have pupils name the planets from the Sun outwards. Then in pairs they make a constellation with a torch and a paper cup punched with holes.

questions.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
Which star helps us find north?
What is the Moon?
What is our galaxy called?

lesson.homework: Look at the night sky for three nights and draw the shape of the Moon each night.

courses.title: Social Science: Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6

topics.title: Locating Places on the Earth
topics.summary: A map is a drawing of a place from above; it uses a scale, directions (N, S, E, W) and symbols with a key.
notes: A map is a drawing of a place from above; it uses a scale, directions (N, S, E, W) and symbols with a key.
A globe is a small model of the Earth; imaginary lines on it help locate places.
Latitudes run east–west; the Equator (0°) divides the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
Longitudes run from pole to pole; the Prime Meridian (0°) passes through Greenwich, near London.
The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so every 15° of longitude is one hour of time difference.
India uses Indian Standard Time, based on 82.5° E (near Mirzapur), 5½ hours ahead of Greenwich.
outcomes: Use maps: scale, directions and symbols
Understand latitudes, longitudes, the Equator and the Prime Meridian
Explain time zones and Indian Standard Time

resources.title: Seasons: the Earth round the Sun

lesson.hook: A friend in London calls you at 7 in the evening your time — but for them it is only 1:30 in the afternoon. How can it be two different times at once?
lesson.example: India's standard meridian is 82.5° E. 82.5 ÷ 15 = 5.5, so IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich: 1:30 p.m. in London is 7:00 p.m. in India.
lesson.activity: Map of the school: groups draw a map of the school campus with a scale, a north arrow and symbols explained in a key.

questions.q: What is the latitude of the Equator?
Which longitude is the Prime Meridian?
How much time does 15° of longitude stand for?
On which meridian is IST based?

lesson.homework: Find the latitude and longitude of your town on an atlas or map app.

topics.title: Oceans and Continents
topics.summary: About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by water, mostly oceans.
notes: About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by water, mostly oceans.
The five oceans: Pacific (largest), Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic.
The seven continents: Asia (largest), Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
Oceans give us food, salt, minerals and sea routes, and they control the climate.
Waves are caused by wind; tides (rise and fall of sea level) are caused mainly by the Moon's pull.
Ocean currents are streams of warm or cold water that move heat around the Earth.
outcomes: Name and locate the continents and oceans
Describe the importance of oceans
Understand waves, tides and ocean currents

lesson.hook: From space the Earth looks blue. Why do astronauts call it the 'blue planet'?
lesson.example: The Indian Ocean is the only ocean named after a country. India's long coastline has helped trade with Africa, Arabia and Southeast Asia for thousands of years.
lesson.activity: Clay map: groups make the continents with clay or paper cut-outs on a blue sheet and label the oceans between them.

questions.q: Which is the largest ocean?
Which is the largest continent?
What mainly causes tides?
Give two uses of oceans.
questions.a: Food (fish), salt, minerals, transport, climate control (any two).

lesson.homework: On an outline world map, colour and label the seven continents and five oceans.

topics.title: Landforms and Life
topics.summary: Mountains are high, steep lands; the Himalayas are among the highest in the world.
notes: Mountains are high, steep lands; the Himalayas are among the highest in the world.
Plateaus are raised flat lands; the Deccan Plateau is rich in minerals.
Plains are flat, low lands formed by rivers; they are fertile and crowded with people.
Deserts are dry lands with little rain; people keep camels and save water carefully.
Life adapts to landforms: terrace farming in mountains, mining on plateaus, dense farming in plains, fishing on coasts.
Landforms also give rivers, forests and places of pilgrimage and tourism.
outcomes: Identify mountains, plateaus, plains, deserts and coasts
Explain how landforms shape the way people live
Appreciate ways people adapt to different landforms

lesson.hook: Why do people in the hills grow crops on steps cut into the slopes, while people in the plains have flat fields?
lesson.example: In Ladakh, a cold desert, people build flat-roofed mud houses and dry vegetables in summer to eat in winter.
lesson.activity: Sand-tray landforms: groups shape a mountain, plateau, plain and valley in a sand tray and pour water to see where rivers flow.

questions.q: What is a plateau?
questions.a: A raised area of flat land.

questions.q: Why do many people live in plains?
questions.a: The land is flat and fertile, and water is easy to get.

questions.q: What is terrace farming?
questions.a: Farming on steps cut into hill slopes.

questions.q: Name one animal useful in deserts.

lesson.homework: Write about the landform your town is on and how it affects people's work.

topics.title: Timeline and Sources of History
topics.summary: History is the study of the past using evidence.
notes: History is the study of the past using evidence.
Timelines show events in order; years before year 1 are BCE (counted backwards) and after are CE.
A decade is 10 years, a century is 100 years and a millennium is 1,000 years.
Sources include archaeological remains (tools, pots, buildings, bones), inscriptions, coins, manuscripts and oral traditions.
Archaeologists dig carefully to find and date remains; historians study all sources to build a picture of the past.
Scientific methods like carbon dating help find the age of remains.
outcomes: Read and make timelines using BCE and CE
Name the sources historians use
Understand how historians and archaeologists find out about the past

lesson.hook: How do we know what people ate or wore 4,000 years ago, when no one alive today was there?
lesson.example: From 300 BCE to 200 CE is 300 + 200 − 1 = 499 years (there is no year 0).
lesson.activity: Personal timeline: each pupil makes a timeline of their life with five important events, then the class builds a timeline of Indian history from 3000 BCE to today.

questions.q: What does BCE mean?
How many years are in a century?
Give two kinds of historical sources.
questions.a: Inscriptions, coins, manuscripts, tools, buildings, oral traditions (any two).

questions.q: Which comes first: 500 BCE or 200 BCE?

lesson.homework: Find an old object at home (coin, photo, utensil) and write what it tells us about the past.

topics.title: India, That Is Bharat
topics.summary: Article 1 of the Constitution says: India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
notes: Article 1 of the Constitution says: India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
Ancient Indian texts use names like Jambudvipa and Bharatavarsha — the land between the Himalayas and the seas.
Persians called the land beyond the Sindhu (Indus) river 'Hindu'; later it became 'Hindustan'.
The Greeks turned 'Sindhu' into 'Indos', which led to the name 'India'.
Travellers and texts from many lands described India's riches and learning.
Many names show a long history and a shared sense of one land.
outcomes: Know the different names of India and their origins
Understand how ancient texts describe the land of Bharat
Link the idea of India to its geography and culture

lesson.hook: Our Constitution says 'India, that is Bharat'. Why does our country have more than one name?
lesson.example: Sindhu → (Persian) Hindu → Hindustan; Sindhu → (Greek) Indos → India.
lesson.activity: Name trail: on a map, pupils trace the Sindhu river and show how travellers from Persia and Greece reached it and named the land.

questions.q: Which article of the Constitution says 'India, that is Bharat'?
From which river does the name 'India' come?
What does 'Bharatavarsha' describe?
questions.a: The land between the Himalayas and the seas.

lesson.homework: Find the names of India in three other languages.

topics.title: The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation
topics.summary: The Harappan civilisation flourished about 2600–1900 BCE in the northwest of the subcontinent.
notes: The Harappan civilisation flourished about 2600–1900 BCE in the northwest of the subcontinent.
Important sites: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi.
Cities were planned with grid streets, baked-brick houses, wells and covered drains; Mohenjo-daro had the Great Bath.
People farmed, made beads, pots and seals, and traded as far as Mesopotamia; Lothal had a dockyard.
Their script, found on seals, has not yet been deciphered.
The cities declined around 1900 BCE, probably due to climate change, drying of the Sarasvati (Ghaggar) river and changes in trade.
outcomes: Describe the Harappan (Indus–Sarasvati) civilisation
Explain the features of Harappan cities
Discuss the causes of its decline

lesson.hook: More than 4,500 years ago, people in our subcontinent built cities with straight streets and covered drains. How did they plan them so well?
lesson.example: Dholavira in Gujarat stored rainwater in huge reservoirs cut into rock — clever water management in a dry area.
lesson.activity: Design a Harappan town: groups draw a town plan with grid streets, drains, a granary, houses and a citadel, and explain their choices.

questions.q: Name two Harappan cities.
questions.a: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi (any two).

questions.q: What was special about Harappan drains?
questions.a: They were covered and connected to houses, showing careful town planning.

questions.q: Why can't we read Harappan writing?
questions.a: The script has not been deciphered.

questions.q: Give one possible reason for the decline of the Harappan cities.
questions.a: Climate change, drying of rivers, or decline of trade.

lesson.homework: Draw a Harappan seal and write what the animal on it might mean.

topics.title: India's Cultural Roots
topics.summary: The Vedas, especially the Rig Veda, are among the oldest texts, passed on orally for centuries.
notes: The Vedas, especially the Rig Veda, are among the oldest texts, passed on orally for centuries.
The Upanishads explored questions like 'Who am I?' and the unity of all life.
Gautama Buddha taught the Middle Path, compassion and freedom from suffering.
Mahavira taught non-violence (ahimsa), truth and not owning more than needed.
Folk and tribal communities have deep traditions of respect for nature, songs, art and healing.
These many roots together shaped India's culture.
outcomes: Describe the Vedas and early Indian philosophy
Explain the teachings of Buddhism and Jainism
Appreciate folk and tribal traditions as cultural roots

lesson.hook: Some ideas from India, like non-violence and 'the world is one family', are thousands of years old. Where did they come from?
lesson.example: Many tribal communities protect sacred groves where no tree may be cut — respect for nature as part of culture.
lesson.activity: Idea wall: groups pick one idea (ahimsa, compassion, unity of life, respect for nature) and make a poster showing it in daily life today.

questions.q: Which is the oldest of the Vedas?
What did the Buddha teach?
questions.a: The Middle Path, compassion and freedom from suffering.

questions.q: What does 'ahimsa' mean?
Give one example of a tribal tradition.
questions.a: Sacred groves, folk songs and dances, traditional healing (any one).

lesson.homework: Ask elders about a tradition in your family or community and write about it.

chapters.title: Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'

topics.title: Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'
topics.summary: India has hundreds of languages, many foods, dresses, dances and festivals.
notes: India has hundreds of languages, many foods, dresses, dances and festivals.
The same idea takes many forms: a harvest festival is Pongal, Lohri, Bihu or Makar Sankranti in different regions.
The Ramayana and Mahabharata are told in many languages and styles across India.
The sari and the dhoti are worn in many different ways in different regions.
Shared values, history and festivals bind people together.
Unity in diversity means respecting differences while feeling one.
outcomes: Identify diversity in India's languages, food, clothing and festivals
Recognise the unity that connects this diversity
Value 'many in the one' in everyday life

lesson.hook: A Kashmiri, a Keralite and a Manipuri meet. Their food, dress and language differ — what might they still share?
lesson.example: Harvest in January: Pongal (Tamil Nadu), Makar Sankranti (Karnataka, Maharashtra), Lohri (Punjab), Bhogali Bihu (Assam) — one idea, many forms.
lesson.activity: Diversity map: groups mark the main language, a dish, a dance and a festival of five states on an outline map of India.

questions.q: Name two harvest festivals from different states.
questions.a: Pongal, Lohri, Bihu, Makar Sankranti, Onam (any two).

questions.q: What does 'unity in diversity' mean?
questions.a: Being united as one people while having many differences.

questions.q: Name one epic told across India in many languages.

lesson.homework: Interview a classmate from another state or community about their festival and food.

topics.title: Family and Community
topics.summary: The family is the oldest and most basic unit of society.
notes: The family is the oldest and most basic unit of society.
Families can be joint (many generations together) or nuclear (parents and children).
Family members care for each other, share work and pass on values and traditions.
A community is a larger group of families living together or sharing interests.
Communities help each other: in festivals, weddings, disasters and shared tasks like cleaning a pond.
Values such as respect, sharing, duty and care hold families and communities together.
outcomes: Understand the family as the basic unit of society
Describe roles and values within families
Explain what a community is and how it supports people

lesson.hook: When someone in your family is ill, who helps? And when a whole village faces a flood, who helps then?
lesson.example: In many villages, people join together in 'shramadaan' (gift of labour) to desilt a tank before the monsoon.
lesson.activity: Family tree and duties: each pupil draws a family tree and notes one way each member contributes.

questions.q: What is a joint family?
questions.a: A family in which several generations live together.

questions.q: What is a community?
questions.a: A group of families or people who live together or share common interests.

questions.q: Give one way communities help each other.
questions.a: Helping in disasters, festivals, cleaning common places (any one).

lesson.homework: Write about one community activity in your area and how people take part.

topics.title: Grassroots Democracy — Part 1: Governance
topics.summary: Government makes rules, keeps order, provides services and protects rights.
notes: Government makes rules, keeps order, provides services and protects rights.
India has three levels of government: national (Union), state and local.
The legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out and the judiciary settles disputes and interprets laws.
Separating these powers prevents misuse of power.
In a democracy, people choose their representatives through elections.
Every adult citizen of 18 years or more has the right to vote.
outcomes: Explain why societies need governments and rules
Name the three levels and three organs of government
Understand what democracy means

lesson.hook: What would happen at a crossroads if there were no traffic rules and no one to make them?
lesson.example: Parliament (legislature) passes a law on road safety, the police (executive) enforce it, and courts (judiciary) decide cases under it.
lesson.activity: Class elections: pupils nominate candidates for class monitor, campaign, vote by secret ballot and count the votes.

questions.q: Name the three levels of government in India.
Which organ of government makes laws?
What is the voting age in India?
Why are powers separated among three organs?

lesson.homework: Find the names of your MP, MLA and local representative.

chapters.title: Grassroots Democracy — Part 2: Local Government in Rural Areas

topics.title: Grassroots Democracy — Part 2: Local Government in Rural Areas
topics.summary: Panchayati Raj is local self-government in villages, made part of the Constitution by the 73rd Amendment (1992).
notes: Panchayati Raj is local self-government in villages, made part of the Constitution by the 73rd Amendment (1992).
It has three tiers: Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti (block) and Zila Parishad (district).
The Gram Sabha — all adult voters of the village — discusses plans and checks the Panchayat's work.
The Gram Panchayat is headed by the Sarpanch (Pradhan) and looks after water, roads, sanitation and local schemes.
One-third of seats are reserved for women; many states reserve half.
Local government lets people solve their own problems.
outcomes: Describe the Panchayati Raj system
Explain the roles of the Gram Sabha, Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti and Zila Parishad
Understand why local government matters

lesson.hook: Who decides where a new hand pump goes in a village — someone in Delhi, or the villagers themselves?
lesson.example: In a Gram Sabha meeting, villagers vote to repair the village tank before the rains; the Panchayat uses government funds to do it.
lesson.activity: Mock Gram Sabha: pupils play villagers, Sarpanch and members, and decide how to spend a small budget on village needs.

questions.q: Who are the members of the Gram Sabha?
questions.a: All adult voters of the village.

questions.q: Who heads the Gram Panchayat?
Name the three tiers of Panchayati Raj.
questions.a: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, Zila Parishad.

questions.q: Which amendment gave Panchayati Raj constitutional status?

lesson.homework: Find out the name of your nearest Gram Panchayat or ward and one work it has done.

chapters.title: Grassroots Democracy — Part 3: Local Government in Urban Areas

topics.title: Grassroots Democracy — Part 3: Local Government in Urban Areas
topics.summary: Towns and cities are run by urban local bodies, given constitutional status by the 74th Amendment (1992).
notes: Towns and cities are run by urban local bodies, given constitutional status by the 74th Amendment (1992).
Big cities have a Municipal Corporation (headed by a Mayor), smaller towns a Municipality, and places changing from rural to urban a Nagar Panchayat.
Cities are divided into wards; each ward elects a councillor.
They provide water, drainage, waste collection, street lights, roads, parks and health services.
They get money from property tax, water charges, fees and state grants.
Citizens help by paying taxes, segregating waste and raising problems with councillors.
outcomes: Describe urban local bodies: Municipal Corporation, Municipality and Nagar Panchayat
Explain their functions and sources of funds
Understand the roles of councillors and citizens

lesson.hook: Who collects the garbage from your street, lights the street lamps and repairs the roads in a town?
lesson.example: Indore has been ranked India's cleanest city many times, thanks to door-to-door collection, waste segregation and citizens' participation.
lesson.activity: Ward survey: groups list three problems in their neighbourhood and write a letter to the ward councillor suggesting solutions.

questions.q: Who heads a Municipal Corporation?
Name two services provided by a municipality.
questions.a: Water supply, waste collection, street lights, roads, parks (any two).

questions.q: What is a ward?
questions.a: A part of a city that elects its own councillor.

questions.q: Name one source of income for urban local bodies.
questions.a: Property tax (also fees, water charges, grants).

lesson.homework: Find out which urban local body governs your town (or the nearest town) and who the councillor is.

topics.title: The Value of Work
topics.summary: Economic activities are done for money or earning: farming, teaching, running a shop.
notes: Economic activities are done for money or earning: farming, teaching, running a shop.
Non-economic activities are done out of love, duty or for society, without payment: cooking at home, caring for elders.
Unpaid work at home is valuable though it is not counted in money.
Volunteers and 'seva' (service) in temples, gurudwaras (langar), disasters and community work help society.
Every kind of honest work deserves respect.
outcomes: Distinguish economic and non-economic activities
Value unpaid work at home and volunteer work
Appreciate the dignity of all work

lesson.hook: A mother cooks for her family all day but is not paid. A cook in a hotel is paid. Are both doing valuable work?
lesson.example: Volunteers at a gurudwara langar cook and serve free meals to thousands every day — non-economic but very valuable.
lesson.activity: Work diary: pupils list all the work done at home in one day, mark which is paid and unpaid, and estimate how long the unpaid work takes.

questions.q: Is a farmer growing crops to sell doing economic or non-economic activity?
Give an example of a non-economic activity.
questions.a: Cooking for family, caring for elders, volunteering (any one).

questions.q: What is seva?

lesson.homework: Help with one household task every day this week and write how it felt.

topics.title: Economic Activities Around Us
topics.summary: Primary activities use natural resources directly: farming, fishing, mining, forestry.
notes: Primary activities use natural resources directly: farming, fishing, mining, forestry.
Secondary activities turn raw materials into goods: factories, weaving, food processing.
Tertiary activities provide services: transport, banking, shops, teaching, health care.
The three sectors depend on each other.
In India, many people still work in agriculture, while the service sector produces the largest share of income.
outcomes: Classify economic activities into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors
Explain how the three sectors depend on each other
Identify economic activities in one's own area

lesson.hook: Follow a cotton shirt backwards: the shop, the tailor, the mill, the farm. How many different kinds of work made it?
lesson.example: Sugarcane is grown (primary), made into sugar at a mill (secondary), then transported and sold in shops (tertiary).
lesson.activity: Sector sort: pupils sort cards of 20 jobs (fisher, doctor, weaver, miner, bus driver, baker …) into three sectors.

questions.q: Which sector does mining belong to?
Which sector does a bank belong to?
Give an example of a secondary activity.
questions.a: Making cloth in a mill, baking bread, making furniture (any one).

questions.q: How do the sectors depend on each other?
questions.a: Primary gives raw materials, secondary makes goods, tertiary transports and sells them.

lesson.homework: List ten jobs in your neighbourhood and sort them into the three sectors.

topics.title: The Day the River Spoke
topics.summary: Jahnavi, nearly ten, looked after her little brothers while her mother worked; she was never sent to school.
notes: Jahnavi, nearly ten, looked after her little brothers while her mother worked; she was never sent to school.
Sitting by the river, she cried, and the River spoke to her, listening to her many questions about the world.
The River told her that girls can do as much as boys and encouraged her to simply go and sit in the school.
She gathered courage, listened at the back of the class; the teacher welcomed her and spoke to her parents, and her mother agreed that girls should learn as much as they want.
outcomes: Read a story about a girl's wish to go to school
Discuss the right of every child to education

lesson.hook: What if you wanted to go to school but everyone said, 'Maybe next year'?
lesson.example: The River's advice — 'It's up to you!' — shows that taking the first step matters.
lesson.activity: Letter to Jahnavi: children write a short letter encouraging Jahnavi on her first day at school.

questions.q: Why was Jahnavi not going to school?
questions.a: She was kept home to look after her younger brothers.

questions.q: What did the River advise her to do?
questions.a: Go and sit in the school, listen, and hope the teacher lets her stay.

questions.q: How did the teacher help?
questions.a: She welcomed Jahnavi and spoke to her father about letting her study.

lesson.homework: Write about why education is important for every girl and boy.

topics.title: Try Again
topics.summary: King Bruce of Scotland had tried and failed to do a great deed and was ready to give up.
notes: King Bruce of Scotland had tried and failed to do a great deed and was ready to give up.
He watched a spider trying to climb its thread to its web on the ceiling.
The spider fell again and again — nine brave attempts — but kept trying.
On the next try it reached its web; inspired, Bruce tried once more and did not fail. (Poem by Eliza Cook.)
outcomes: Recite a narrative poem about perseverance
Relate the spider's effort to one's own goals

lesson.hook: How many times would you try something before giving up?
lesson.example: 'All honour to those who try' — the effort itself is worth respect.
lesson.activity: Never-give-up tower: groups build a paper tower; each time it falls they note what they learned and try again.

questions.q: Why was King Bruce sad?
questions.a: He had tried to do a great deed but failed.

questions.q: How many attempts did the spider make before succeeding?
questions.a: It failed nine times and succeeded on the next try.

questions.q: What did Bruce learn?
questions.a: To try again and not give up.

lesson.homework: Write about a time you succeeded after failing a few times.

topics.title: Three Days to See
topics.summary: Helen Keller, who could not see, enjoyed nature through touch — the symmetry of a leaf, bark, buds and a singing bird's quiver.
notes: Helen Keller, who could not see, enjoyed nature through touch — the symmetry of a leaf, bark, buds and a singing bird's quiver.
If given sight for three days, on the first day she would see the faces of the people whose kindness made her life worth living.
On the second day she would watch the dawn and visit museums to see the history of the earth and mankind.
On the third day she would watch ordinary people in the city; she urges those who can see to use their eyes as if they would lose them tomorrow.
outcomes: Read an essay by Helen Keller
Appreciate the gift of sight and the use of all senses

lesson.hook: If you could see for only three days, what would you want to see first?
lesson.example: She 'sees' a friend's face through her fingertips — touch as a way of seeing.
lesson.activity: Sense walk: children walk around the school noticing five things by sight, touch, sound and smell, then share.

questions.q: How did Helen Keller enjoy nature?
What would she see on the first day?
questions.a: The faces of the people who were kind to her.

questions.q: What is her advice to people who can see?
questions.a: Use your eyes as if you might lose them tomorrow.

lesson.homework: Plan what you would do with 'three days to see'.

topics.title: Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle
topics.summary: The Cat's-food-Man suggested that Doctor Dolittle, who understood animals so well, become an animal doctor.
notes: The Cat's-food-Man suggested that Doctor Dolittle, who understood animals so well, become an animal doctor.
The parrot Polynesia agreed and revealed that animals can talk — parrots even speak two languages.
She taught the Doctor bird language; he wrote down the words in a book.
Polynesia explained that animals talk not only with their mouths but with their ears, feet and tails.
outcomes: Read a humorous extract from 'The Story of Doctor Dolittle'
Understand how animals communicate

lesson.hook: If animals could talk, what would your pet tell you?
lesson.example: A dog wagging its tail or twitching its ears is 'talking' — body language.
lesson.activity: Animal signals: children list signals of a dog or cat (tail, ears, sounds) and what each might mean.

questions.q: Who suggested the Doctor become an animal doctor?
What languages does Polynesia speak?
How else do animals talk?
questions.a: With their ears, feet, tails — with everything.

lesson.homework: Write a short conversation between you and an animal you know.

topics.title: A Funny Man
topics.summary: A funny man comes down the street with a shoe on his head and hats on his feet.
notes: A funny man comes down the street with a shoe on his head and hats on his feet.
He politely presents a 'rose' — but it is a currant bun.
The speaker says the rose has a 'funny looking smell', and the man sings a 'funny feeling sound'.
Asked about the hats, he turns around and hops home on his head — a poem of delightful nonsense.
outcomes: Recite a nonsense poem and enjoy its humour
Identify how the poem mixes up senses and objects

lesson.hook: What would you think if you saw someone wearing a shoe on their head?
lesson.example: Mixed-up senses: 'funny looking smell', 'funny feeling sound' — words describe senses the wrong way for fun.
lesson.activity: Silly lines: children write two nonsense lines that mix up senses, like 'a loud-tasting mango'.

questions.q: What did the man wear on his head?
What did he offer as a rose?
How did he go home?
questions.a: He hopped home on his head.

lesson.homework: Draw the funny man and write a caption.

topics.title: Say the Right Thing
topics.summary: Mrs. Shaw is expecting guests — Mrs. Harding, a wealthy man's wife, and Mrs. Lee, his sister.
notes: Mrs. Shaw is expecting guests — Mrs. Harding, a wealthy man's wife, and Mrs. Lee, his sister.
She advises Mary to be kind, say pleasing things, keep the talk going and ask guests to stay when they leave.
Mary tries, but praises Mrs. Harding's 'children' (she has none), mocks bankers (Mrs. Lee's brother is one) and laughs at blue dresses with red coats (Mrs. Harding wears them).
Each attempt to 'say the right thing' becomes a blunder — the comedy comes from good intentions and bad timing.
outcomes: Read a humorous play and understand its situational comedy
Learn about polite conversation

lesson.hook: Have you ever said something at the wrong time and felt embarrassed?
lesson.example: Mary means well but does not think before she speaks — that is what makes the play funny.
lesson.activity: Role play: groups act a scene of welcoming guests politely, then a funny version with blunders.

questions.q: Who were the guests?
What advice did Mrs. Shaw give Mary?
questions.a: Be kind, say pleasing things, and keep the conversation going.

questions.q: Why did Mary's comment about bankers upset Mrs. Lee?
questions.a: Mrs. Lee's brother was a banker who did exactly what Mary mocked.

lesson.homework: Write three polite sentences to say to guests at home.

topics.title: My Brother's Great Invention
topics.summary: Anita's brother Anand loves tinkering with gadgets; his burglar alarm dropped a water bag on Papa instead of a thief.
notes: Anita's brother Anand loves tinkering with gadgets; his burglar alarm dropped a water bag on Papa instead of a thief.
After watching a film, he built a 'time machine' of wires, springs and bulbs in his room; Papa refused to let him try it.
When their parents were away, a thief (Boppa, the new sweeper) broke in; Anand sent him into his own room.
The thief started the strange machine, crashed and howled, and the children's shouts brought help — the 'failed' invention caught a burglar.
outcomes: Read a humorous story about a young inventor
Understand how curiosity and failure lead to learning

lesson.hook: Have you ever tried to build something that didn't work the way you planned?
lesson.example: Anand's machine never travelled in time, but it did its job when it mattered most.
lesson.activity: Inventor's notebook: children design a simple invention to solve a daily problem and draw its blueprint.

questions.q: What happened with the burglar alarm?
questions.a: A water bag fell on Papa.

questions.q: Who was the thief?
questions.a: Boppa, the man who swept the compounds.

questions.q: How was the thief caught?
questions.a: He started Anand's time machine, crashed, and the children's shouts brought help.

lesson.homework: Write about an invention you would like to make.

topics.title: Paper Boats
topics.summary: A child floats paper boats down a stream every day with their name and village written on them.
notes: A child floats paper boats down a stream every day with their name and village written on them.
The child hopes someone in a strange land will find them and know who they are.
The boats carry shiuli flowers from the garden, and clouds in the sky look like white sails racing the boats.
At night, the child dreams that fairies of sleep sail the boats with baskets full of dreams.
outcomes: Recite a poem by Rabindranath Tagore
Understand the child's dreams and imagination

lesson.hook: If you could send a message in a paper boat, what would you write?
lesson.example: Metaphor: clouds with 'white bulging sails' — clouds are pictured as boats in the sky.
lesson.activity: Message boats: children fold paper boats and write a friendly message on each for a pen-pal display.

questions.q: What does the child write on the boats?
questions.a: Their name and the name of their village.

questions.q: What does the child load on the boats?
Who sails the boats at night in the dream?

lesson.homework: Write four lines about a dream you remember.

topics.title: North, South, East, West
topics.summary: Shaana from Rameswaram travels with her parents and writes postcards to her class.
notes: Shaana from Rameswaram travels with her parents and writes postcards to her class.
In the north she sees the Thajiwas glacier in Kashmir and the quiet mountains of Himachal Pradesh.
In the east she visits the thick forests of Arunachal Pradesh and the Sundarbans wetlands with mangroves in West Bengal.
In the west she reaches the hot, sandy desert of Gujarat with colourful clothes — India's landscapes are very different.
outcomes: Read travel postcards about India's landscapes
Use directions to describe places on a map

lesson.hook: If you could travel from the snow of Kashmir to the desert of Gujarat, what would you pack?
lesson.example: From West Bengal (east) to Gujarat (west), the family travelled for two and a half days.
lesson.activity: Postcard map: children mark Shaana's route on an outline map of India and label directions.

questions.q: Where did Shaana see a glacier?
What grows in seawater in the Sundarbans?
Which state has the desert in the story?

lesson.homework: Write a postcard to your class from a place you would like to visit.

topics.title: The Tunnel
topics.summary: Suraj loved watching the steam engine roar out of a jungle tunnel and walked through the tunnel to see inside.
notes: Suraj loved watching the steam engine roar out of a jungle tunnel and walked through the tunnel to see inside.
He met Sunder Singh, the watchman who inspected the tunnel and warned trains of danger with a red flag or lamp.
That night, waiting for the night mail, they heard a leopard in the tunnel.
They went in with a lamp and shouted together; the leopard ran away, and the train passed safely — both the animal and the train were saved.
outcomes: Read a story by Ruskin Bond about a jungle adventure
Understand respect for wildlife

lesson.hook: Would you walk through a dark railway tunnel in a jungle?
lesson.example: Sunder Singh says the jungle is safer than the town — he nearly got run over by a bus in town.
lesson.activity: Flow chart: groups draw the watchman's daily routine — inspect → danger or no danger → warn or rest.

questions.q: Why did Suraj go to the tunnel?
questions.a: To watch the train come out and to see the inside of a tunnel.

questions.q: What was the watchman's job?
questions.a: To inspect the tunnel and warn trains of danger.

questions.q: How did they save the leopard?
questions.a: They shouted and drove it out before the train came.

lesson.homework: Write the story from the leopard's point of view.

topics.title: Travel
topics.summary: The railroad track is miles away, yet the speaker hears the train whistle all day.
notes: The railroad track is miles away, yet the speaker hears the train whistle all day.
At night, though no train passes, the speaker imagines its red cinders and steaming engine.
The speaker has warm friendships and good friends.
Still, there is no train the speaker would not take, no matter where it goes — a strong desire to travel. (Poem by Edna St. Vincent Millay.)
outcomes: Recite a poem about the longing to travel
Identify the main idea of each stanza

lesson.hook: Does the sound of a train whistle make you want to go somewhere?
lesson.example: Stanza ideas: day — hears the whistle; night — imagines the engine; last — wants to take any train.
lesson.activity: Dream journey: children describe a train journey they would like to take and where it would go.

questions.q: How far is the railroad track?
What does the speaker see at night?
questions.a: Red cinders in the sky and the steaming engine (in imagination).

questions.q: What does the speaker wish in the last stanza?
questions.a: To take any train, no matter where it goes.

lesson.homework: Write about your favourite journey or a journey you dream of.

topics.title: Conquering the Summit
topics.summary: Arunima Sinha, a national-level volleyball player from Uttar Pradesh, lost a leg in a train accident in 2011.
notes: Arunima Sinha, a national-level volleyball player from Uttar Pradesh, lost a leg in a train accident in 2011.
In hospital, she resolved to walk again with a prosthetic leg and climb Mount Everest.
She trained at the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering and was guided by Bachendri Pal, the first Indian woman to climb Everest.
On 21 May 2013 she reached the summit, becoming the first Indian female amputee to do so; she received the Padma Shri in 2015.
outcomes: Read the true story of Arunima Sinha
Understand courage and determination after a setback

lesson.hook: Can a person who has lost a leg climb Mount Everest?
lesson.example: Bachendri Pal told her she had already conquered the Everest within herself.
lesson.activity: Courage timeline: children make a timeline of Arunima's journey from 2011 to 2015.

questions.q: What happened to Arunima in 2011?
questions.a: She lost a leg in a train accident.

questions.q: Who guided her?
When did she reach the summit of Everest?

lesson.homework: Write about someone who inspires you and why.

chapters.title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers

topics.title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
topics.summary: Two friends exchange letters; one describes a school trip to the National War Memorial in New Delhi.
notes: Two friends exchange letters; one describes a school trip to the National War Memorial in New Delhi.
The memorial, near India Gate, spread over 40 acres, was built in 2018–19 and inaugurated in February 2019.
Each brick, called a tablet, bears the names of soldiers who died defending India in wars since 1947.
The memorial reminds us of the cost of freedom and our gratitude to the armed forces.
outcomes: Read letters about the National War Memorial
Understand the sacrifice of soldiers after Independence

lesson.hook: Why should we remember soldiers whose names we may never hear?
lesson.example: Wars remembered include the 1962 conflict, the 1965 and 1971 wars and the Kargil war.
lesson.activity: Letter of thanks: children write a letter of gratitude to the armed forces.

questions.q: Where is the National War Memorial?
What is written on each tablet?
questions.a: The names of soldiers who gave their lives.

questions.q: Why are such memorials important?
questions.a: So we never forget the cost of our freedom.

lesson.homework: Write a letter to a friend about a monument you visited.

topics.title: My Dear Soldiers
topics.summary: The poem addresses soldiers as defenders of the borders and great sons (and daughters) of the land.
notes: The poem addresses soldiers as defenders of the borders and great sons (and daughters) of the land.
They stay awake while we sleep, in wind, snow and scorching sun.
They guard mountains, valleys, deserts, marshes, seas and the sky, like yogis walking lonely expanses.
They give the best years of their youth to the nation; the poet prays for them.
outcomes: Recite a poem by Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam
Appreciate soldiers who guard the nation

lesson.hook: Who keeps watch over our borders while we sleep?
lesson.example: Simile: soldiers tread lonely expanses 'as yogis' — calm and devoted.
lesson.activity: Guardian map: children mark on a map of India where soldiers guard mountains, deserts and seas.

questions.q: Who wrote the poem?
questions.a: Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam.

questions.q: What do soldiers do while we sleep?
questions.a: They stay awake and guard the nation.

questions.q: What have soldiers given to the nation?

lesson.homework: Write a short prayer or poem for soldiers.

topics.title: Rani Abbakka
topics.summary: Rani Abbakka ruled Ullal in coastal Karnataka in the 16th century.
notes: Rani Abbakka ruled Ullal in coastal Karnataka in the 16th century.
The Portuguese wanted Ullal to pay tribute and accept their control, but she refused.
Even when others felt they were no match for the Portuguese army, she stood firm and gathered support.
She fought the Portuguese bravely and attacked their fort; she is remembered as a fearless (dauntless) queen.
outcomes: Read the story of Rani Abbakka, an unsung heroine
Understand resistance to colonial rule

lesson.hook: Have you heard of a queen from coastal Karnataka who fought the Portuguese?
lesson.example: A vassal state pays money to a more powerful state; a sovereign country governs itself fully.
lesson.activity: Cause and effect: groups complete a cause–effect table of events in Rani Abbakka's story.

questions.q: Where did Rani Abbakka rule?
Whom did she fight?
Why did she refuse to pay tribute?
questions.a: She wanted Ullal to remain free and sovereign.

lesson.homework: Find out about another unsung hero of India's freedom.

topics.title: माँ, कह एक कहानी
topics.summary: कविता माँ यशोधरा और बेटे राहुल का संवाद है; राहुल माँ से कहानी सुनाने की ज़िद करता है।
notes: कविता माँ यशोधरा और बेटे राहुल का संवाद है; राहुल माँ से कहानी सुनाने की ज़िद करता है।
माँ बताती हैं कि सवेरे उपवन में राहुल के पिता (सिद्धार्थ) घूम रहे थे; तभी तीर से घायल एक हंस गिरा और उन्होंने उसे बचाया।
शिकारी ने अपना शिकार माँगा, पर पिता रक्षक थे; विवाद न्यायालय तक गया।
माँ पूछती हैं कि न्याय किसका पक्ष लेगा; राहुल कहता है — निरपराध को बचाने वाले का; न्याय दया का दानी है।
outcomes: संवाद-शैली की कविता में न्याय और दया के भाव को समझना
मैथिलीशरण गुप्त के काव्य 'यशोधरा' से परिचित होना

lesson.hook: अगर कोई घायल पक्षी आपकी गोद में आ गिरे और शिकारी उसे माँगे, तो न्याय किसके पक्ष में होगा?
lesson.example: 'न्याय दया का दानी' — सच्चा न्याय वही है जिसमें दया हो।
lesson.activity: न्याय-सभा: बच्चे हंस वाले विवाद पर कक्षा में दोनों पक्षों को सुनकर निर्णय दें।

questions.q: यह कविता किन दो पात्रों का संवाद है?
questions.a: माँ यशोधरा और बेटे राहुल का।

questions.q: हंस को किसने बचाया?
राहुल ने क्या निर्णय दिया?
questions.a: न्याय निरपराध को बचाने वाले के पक्ष में है; न्याय दया का दानी है।

lesson.homework: 'दया ही सच्चा न्याय है' पर चार पंक्तियाँ लिखिए।

topics.title: तीन बुद्धिमान
topics.summary: एक गरीब पिता ने तीन बेटों को सिखाया कि धन की जगह पैनी दृष्टि और तीव्र बुद्धि जमा करो।
notes: एक गरीब पिता ने तीन बेटों को सिखाया कि धन की जगह पैनी दृष्टि और तीव्र बुद्धि जमा करो।
यात्रा में बड़े भाई ने बताया कि यहाँ से एक बड़ा ऊँट गया है, मँझले ने कहा वह एक आँख से नहीं देखता, छोटे ने कहा उस पर महिला और बच्चा सवार थे।
ऊँट का मालिक उन्हें चोर समझकर राजा के पास ले गया।
भाइयों ने कहा कि वे चोर नहीं, बल्कि ध्यान से देखने और सोचने के आदी हैं; राजा ने एक बंद पेटी से उनकी बुद्धि की परीक्षा ली और वे सफल हुए।
outcomes: लोककथा में अवलोकन और तर्क-शक्ति के महत्त्व को समझना
सुराग़ों से निष्कर्ष निकालना सीखना

lesson.hook: क्या बिना देखे भी किसी चीज़ के बारे में सही-सही बताया जा सकता है?
lesson.example: सुराग़ से निष्कर्ष: सड़क के एक ही ओर की घास चरी हुई → ऊँट एक आँख से देखता होगा।
lesson.activity: जासूस-खेल: शिक्षक कक्षा में कुछ बदलाव करें; बच्चे ध्यान से देखकर बताएँ कि क्या बदला और कैसे जाना।

questions.q: पिता ने बेटों को कौन-सा धन जमा करने को कहा?
ऊँट का मालिक भाइयों को चोर क्यों समझा?
questions.a: उन्होंने बिना देखे ऊँट के बारे में सब सही बता दिया।

questions.q: भाइयों ने सब कैसे जाना?
questions.a: ध्यान से देखकर और तर्क से सोचकर।

lesson.homework: अपने घर के आसपास के किसी सुराग़ से कोई निष्कर्ष निकालकर लिखिए।

topics.title: फूल और काँटा
topics.summary: फूल और काँटा एक ही पौधे पर, एक-सी चाँदनी, बारिश और हवा में पलते हैं।
notes: फूल और काँटा एक ही पौधे पर, एक-सी चाँदनी, बारिश और हवा में पलते हैं।
फिर भी उनके ढंग एक-से नहीं होते।
काँटा उँगलियाँ छेदता, कपड़े फाड़ता और तितलियों-भौंरों को घायल करता है।
फूल तितलियों को गोद में लेता, भौंरे को रस पिलाता और सुगंध देता है — इसलिए वह देवताओं के सिर पर शोभता है; बड़प्पन कुल से नहीं, कर्म से आता है।
outcomes: कविता में फूल और काँटे के स्वभाव की तुलना समझना
कुल से नहीं, कर्म से बड़प्पन का भाव जानना

lesson.hook: एक ही पौधे पर उगने वाले फूल और काँटा इतने अलग क्यों होते हैं?
lesson.example: एक ही परिवार में पले दो लोग भी अपने कामों से अलग पहचाने जाते हैं।
lesson.activity: तुलना-तालिका: बच्चे फूल और काँटे के कामों की दो कॉलम वाली तालिका बनाएँ।

questions.q: फूल और काँटे में क्या समानता है?
questions.a: दोनों एक ही पौधे पर एक-से वातावरण में पलते हैं।

questions.q: काँटा क्या करता है?
questions.a: उँगलियाँ छेदता, कपड़े फाड़ता, तितली-भौंरे को घायल करता है।

questions.q: कविता की मुख्य सीख क्या है?
questions.a: बड़प्पन कुल से नहीं, अच्छे कामों से मिलता है।

lesson.homework: 'हम फूल जैसे बनें' पर चार वाक्य लिखिए।

topics.title: पानी रे पानी
topics.summary: किताबी जल-चक्र के अलावा आज पानी का अजीब चक्कर है — गर्मी में नल सूखते हैं, बारिश में बस्तियाँ डूबती हैं।
notes: किताबी जल-चक्र के अलावा आज पानी का अजीब चक्कर है — गर्मी में नल सूखते हैं, बारिश में बस्तियाँ डूबती हैं।
अकाल और बाढ़ एक ही सिक्के के दो पहलू हैं।
धरती एक बड़ी गुल्लक है; तालाब और झीलें वर्षा-जल को ज़मीन के नीचे भूजल-भंडार तक पहुँचाते हैं।
लालच में तालाबों को पाटकर उन पर इमारतें बना दी गईं; हमें फिर से वर्षा-जल को जमा करना होगा।
outcomes: जल-संकट और बाढ़ के कारणों को समझना
धरती को 'गुल्लक' मानकर जल-संरक्षण का महत्त्व जानना

lesson.hook: क्या आपके यहाँ कभी नल में पानी नहीं आया? और कभी बारिश में गलियाँ डूब गईं?
lesson.example: जैसे गुल्लक में जमा पैसे ज़रूरत पर काम आते हैं, वैसे ही धरती में जमा वर्षा-जल साल भर काम आता है।
lesson.activity: जल-सर्वेक्षण: बच्चे अपने मोहल्ले के तालाब, कुएँ या झील की स्थिति पता करके रिपोर्ट बनाएँ।

questions.q: अकाल और बाढ़ को किसके दो पहलू कहा गया है?
धरती की गुल्लक में पानी कौन भरता है?
तालाबों के खत्म होने से क्या हुआ?
questions.a: गर्मी में पानी की कमी और बारिश में बाढ़।

lesson.homework: अपने घर में वर्षा-जल बचाने के तीन उपाय लिखिए।

topics.title: नहीं होना बीमार
topics.summary: अस्पताल में सुधाकर काका को आराम से खीर खाते देखकर बच्चे को लगा कि बीमार होना मज़ेदार है।
notes: अस्पताल में सुधाकर काका को आराम से खीर खाते देखकर बच्चे को लगा कि बीमार होना मज़ेदार है।
एक दिन होमवर्क न करने के कारण उसने सिरदर्द, पेटदर्द और बुखार का बहाना बनाया।
नानाजी ने कड़वी पुड़िया और काढ़ा पिलाया और कहा कि आज इसे कुछ खाने को न दें।
