दिनभर लेटे-लेटे ऊबकर और भूख से परेशान होकर उसे लगा कि इससे अच्छा तो स्कूल जाकर सज़ा ले लेता — बहाना महँगा पड़ा।
outcomes: हास्यपूर्ण कहानी से बहानेबाज़ी के परिणाम को समझना
स्वास्थ्य और ईमानदारी का महत्त्व जानना

lesson.hook: क्या आपने कभी स्कूल न जाने के लिए बीमार होने का बहाना बनाया है?
lesson.example: बहाने का परिणाम: खीर की जगह कड़वी पुड़िया, खेल की जगह ऊब, और भूखे रहना।
lesson.activity: सच या बहाना: बच्चे समूह में चर्चा करें कि होमवर्क न होने पर सच बोलना बेहतर क्यों है।

questions.q: बच्चे को बीमार होना क्यों अच्छा लगा?
questions.a: अस्पताल में काका को आराम और खीर मिलते देखकर।

questions.q: उसने बीमारी का बहाना क्यों बनाया?
नानाजी ने क्या कहा?
questions.a: उसे कुछ खाने को न दें, आराम करने दें।

lesson.homework: इस कहानी का शीर्षक 'नहीं होना बीमार' क्यों है? लिखिए।

topics.title: गिरिधर कविराय की कुंडलिया
topics.summary: पहली कुंडलिया: बिना सोचे-विचारे काम करने वाला बाद में पछताता है, अपना काम बिगाड़ता है और जग में हँसी का पात्र बनता है।
notes: पहली कुंडलिया: बिना सोचे-विचारे काम करने वाला बाद में पछताता है, अपना काम बिगाड़ता है और जग में हँसी का पात्र बनता है।
ऐसे व्यक्ति के मन को चैन नहीं मिलता; खाना-पीना, सम्मान, राग-रंग कुछ अच्छा नहीं लगता।
दूसरी कुंडलिया: जो बीत गया उसे भूल जाओ और आगे की सुध लो।
जो काम सहज हो सके उसी में मन लगाओ — इससे आगे सुख मिलेगा।
outcomes: गिरिधर कविराय की कुंडलियों का अर्थ समझना
नीति-वचनों को जीवन से जोड़ना

lesson.hook: क्या कभी जल्दबाज़ी में कोई काम करके आपको पछताना पड़ा है?
lesson.example: प्रसिद्ध कहावत बनी पंक्तियाँ: 'बिना बिचारे जो करै सो पाछे पछिताय' और 'बीती ताहि बिसारि दे आगे की सुधि लेइ'।
lesson.activity: कहावत-खोज: बच्चे अपने घर में बोली जाने वाली ऐसी कहावतें लिखकर लाएँ जो कुंडलियों से मिलती हों।

questions.q: बिना विचारे काम करने का क्या परिणाम होता है?
questions.a: बाद में पछताना पड़ता है और हँसी होती है।

questions.q: 'बीती ताहि बिसारि दे' का अर्थ क्या है?
questions.a: जो बीत गया उसे भूल जाओ।

questions.q: गिरिधर कविराय किस सदी में जन्मे?

lesson.homework: एक कुंडलिया याद करके उसका अर्थ अपने शब्दों में लिखिए।

topics.title: वर्षा-बहार
topics.summary: वर्षा-बहार सबका मन लुभा रही है; आकाश में घनघोर घटा छाई है।
notes: वर्षा-बहार सबका मन लुभा रही है; आकाश में घनघोर घटा छाई है।
बिजली चमकती है, बादल गरजते हैं, पानी बरसता है और झरने बहते हैं।
ठंडी हवा में डालियाँ हिलती हैं, मालिनें गीत गाती हैं, मोर नाचते और मेंढक गाते हैं।
गुलाब खिलते हैं, हंस कतार में चलते हैं, किसान गीत गाते हैं — संसार की शोभा वर्षा पर निर्भर है।
outcomes: वर्षा ऋतु के सौंदर्य-वर्णन को समझना
कविता में प्रकृति के चित्र पहचानना

lesson.hook: बारिश में आपको कौन-सी आवाज़ें और दृश्य सबसे अच्छे लगते हैं?
lesson.example: ध्वनि-चित्र: 'बिजली चमक रही है, बादल गरज रहे हैं' — आँख और कान दोनों के चित्र।
lesson.activity: वर्षा-कोलाज: बच्चे कविता में आए जीवों और दृश्यों के चित्र काटकर कोलाज बनाएँ।

questions.q: वर्षा में वन में कौन नाचता है?
कविता में कौन-सा फूल खिलता है?
कवि के अनुसार जगत की शोभा किस पर निर्भर है?

lesson.homework: वर्षा के किसी एक दिन का वर्णन लिखिए।

topics.title: बिरजू महाराज से साक्षात्कार
topics.summary: बिरजू महाराज कथक नृत्य के प्रसिद्ध कलाकार थे; उन्हें यह कला विरासत में मिली थी और वे पद्मविभूषण से सम्मानित थे।
notes: बिरजू महाराज कथक नृत्य के प्रसिद्ध कलाकार थे; उन्हें यह कला विरासत में मिली थी और वे पद्मविभूषण से सम्मानित थे।
बच्चों ने उनसे साक्षात्कार में उनके बचपन के बारे में पूछा।
पिता के देहांत के बाद परिवार पर आर्थिक संकट आया; कभी कर्ज़ लेते, कभी पुरानी ज़री की साड़ियों के तार बेचकर गुज़ारा करते।
इस संघर्ष में माँ उनकी सबसे बड़ी सहयोगी थीं; कठिन साधना से वे महान कलाकार बने।
outcomes: साक्षात्कार विधा को समझना
कथक सम्राट बिरजू महाराज के जीवन-संघर्ष को जानना

lesson.hook: अगर आपको किसी प्रसिद्ध कलाकार से मिलने का मौका मिले, तो आप क्या पूछेंगे?
lesson.example: साक्षात्कार में प्रश्न पूछने वाला और उत्तर देने वाला बारी-बारी से बोलते हैं।
lesson.activity: साक्षात्कार-अभ्यास: बच्चे अपने स्कूल के किसी कर्मचारी या कलाकार का साक्षात्कार लेने के लिए पाँच प्रश्न बनाएँ।

questions.q: बिरजू महाराज किस नृत्य के कलाकार थे?
कठिन समय में उनकी सबसे बड़ी सहयोगी कौन थीं?
उन्हें कौन-सा सम्मान मिला?

lesson.homework: किसी बड़े का साक्षात्कार लेकर उसे लिखिए।

topics.title: चिड़िया
topics.summary: पीपल की ऊँची डाली पर बैठी चिड़िया गाकर प्रेम-प्रीति की रीति सिखाती है।
notes: पीपल की ऊँची डाली पर बैठी चिड़िया गाकर प्रेम-प्रीति की रीति सिखाती है।
वन के सब पक्षी — खंजन, कपोत, कोयल, हंस, तोता — मिल-जुलकर रहते और खाते हैं; आसमान उनका घर है।
उनके मन में लोभ नहीं; वे अपने श्रम से जितना मिलता है उतना लेते हैं और बचा हुआ दूसरों के लिए छोड़ देते हैं।
चिड़िया मनुष्य से कहती है कि लोभ की सोने की कड़ियाँ तोड़ो और मानवता से द्रोह छोड़ो।
outcomes: कविता में चिड़िया के संदेश को समझना
लोभ-रहित, स्वतंत्र और मिल-जुलकर जीने का भाव जानना

lesson.hook: चिड़िया के गीत में क्या कोई संदेश छिपा हो सकता है?
lesson.example: 'सोने की कड़ियाँ' — धन का लोभ, जो मनुष्य को बाँध लेता है।
lesson.activity: पक्षियों से सीख: बच्चे पक्षियों के तीन गुण लिखें जो मनुष्य को अपनाने चाहिए।

questions.q: चिड़िया क्या सिखाती है?
questions.a: प्रेम-प्रीति की रीति और मुक्ति का मंत्र।

questions.q: पक्षी बचा हुआ भोजन क्या करते हैं?
questions.a: दूसरों के लिए छोड़ देते हैं।

questions.q: चिड़िया मनुष्य से क्या तोड़ने को कहती है?

lesson.homework: चिड़िया के संदेश पर चार पंक्तियाँ लिखिए।

topics.title: मीरा के पद
topics.summary: मीरा कृष्ण-भक्त संत कवयित्री थीं; राजकुमारी होकर भी उन्होंने संतों का जीवन चुना।
notes: मीरा कृष्ण-भक्त संत कवयित्री थीं; राजकुमारी होकर भी उन्होंने संतों का जीवन चुना।
पहले पद में मीरा चाहती हैं कि नंदलाल (कृष्ण) उनकी आँखों में बस जाएँ — मोहिनी मूरत, साँवली सूरत, मुरली, वैजयंती माला।
दूसरे पद में सावन की बदरिया बरसती है; हरि के आने की आहट से मीरा का मन उमंग से भर जाता है।
नन्ही बूँदें, बिजली और शीतल पवन के बीच मीरा आनंद-मंगल गाती हैं।
outcomes: मीरा के पदों में भक्ति-भाव को समझना
पदों के शब्दों और चित्रों की सराहना करना

lesson.hook: किसी को बहुत याद करने पर मन कैसा हो जाता है?
lesson.example: 'बसो मेरे नैनन में नंदलाल' — भक्त चाहता है कि प्रिय की छवि सदा आँखों में रहे।
lesson.activity: पद-गायन: कक्षा मिलकर मीरा का एक पद गाए और उसके चित्र बनाए।

questions.q: मीरा किसकी भक्त थीं?
पहले पद में मीरा क्या चाहती हैं?
questions.a: नंदलाल उनकी आँखों में बस जाएँ।

questions.q: सावन में मीरा का मन क्यों उमंग से भर गया?
questions.a: हरि के आने की आहट सुनकर।

lesson.homework: मीरा के किसी एक पद का सरल अर्थ लिखिए।

topics.title: वन्दे भारतमातरम्
topics.summary: बच्चे माँ से 'वन्दे मातरम्' का अर्थ और लेखक के बारे में पूछते हैं।
notes: बच्चे माँ से 'वन्दे मातरम्' का अर्थ और लेखक के बारे में पूछते हैं।
बङ्किमचन्द्र चट्टोपाध्याय ने 1882 में 'आनन्दमठ' उपन्यास लिखा, उसी में यह गीत है।
'वन्दे मातरम्' का अर्थ है — 'मैं माता की वंदना करता हूँ'; यहाँ माता भारत-भूमि है।
गीत में भारत को शुद्ध जल, मीठे फल, शीतल वायु और हरी फसलों वाली (सुजलां, सुफलां, मलयजशीतलां, शस्यश्यामलां) बताया गया है।
outcomes: 'वन्दे मातरम्' गीत का अर्थ और इतिहास जानना
मातृभूमि के प्रति श्रद्धा का भाव समझना

lesson.hook: हम 'वन्दे मातरम्' अक्सर गाते हैं — क्या आप इसका अर्थ जानते हैं?
lesson.example: सुजलाम् = अच्छे जल वाली; सुफलाम् = अच्छे फलों वाली; शस्यश्यामलाम् = फसलों से हरी-भरी।
lesson.activity: सस्वर गायन: कक्षा मिलकर 'वन्दे मातरम्' गाए और हर विशेषण का अर्थ बताए।

questions.q: 'वन्दे मातरम्' गीत किसने लिखा?
यह गीत किस उपन्यास में है?
'वन्दे मातरम्' का अर्थ क्या है?
questions.a: मैं माता (मातृभूमि) की वंदना करता हूँ।

lesson.homework: गीत के चार विशेषण और उनके अर्थ लिखिए।

topics.title: नित्यं पिबामः सुभाषितरसम्
topics.summary: 'अयोग्यः पुरुषो नास्ति योजकस्तत्र दुर्लभः' — संसार में कोई अयोग्य नहीं; कमी सही मार्गदर्शक (योजक) की है।
notes: 'अयोग्यः पुरुषो नास्ति योजकस्तत्र दुर्लभः' — संसार में कोई अयोग्य नहीं; कमी सही मार्गदर्शक (योजक) की है।
सुभाषित श्रेष्ठ जनों के सुवचन हैं, जो नैतिक और सामाजिक विकास करते हैं।
'वस्त्रेण वपुषा वाचा विद्यया विनयेन च' — पाँच 'व' (वस्त्र, वपु, वाणी, विद्या, विनय) से युक्त व्यक्ति पूजित होता है।
सुभाषित बताते हैं कि क्या करना चाहिए और क्या नहीं।
outcomes: सुभाषितों का अर्थ, पदच्छेद और अन्वय समझना
सुभाषितों से नैतिक मूल्यों को जानना

lesson.hook: क्या कोई ऐसा व्यक्ति है जिसमें कोई भी योग्यता न हो?
lesson.example: पाँच 'व': वस्त्र (उचित वस्त्र), वपु (स्वस्थ शरीर), वाक् (मधुर वाणी), विद्या (ज्ञान), विनय (नम्रता)।
lesson.activity: सुभाषित-पट्टिका: बच्चे एक सुभाषित सुंदर अक्षरों में लिखकर विद्यालय की दीवार के लिए पट्टिका बनाएँ।

questions.q: 'योजकस्तत्र दुर्लभः' का भाव क्या है?
questions.a: योग्य व्यक्ति को सही काम में लगाने वाला मार्गदर्शक कम मिलता है।

questions.q: पाँच 'व' कौन-से हैं?
सुभाषित पढ़ने से क्या लाभ है?
questions.a: नैतिक और सामाजिक विकास होता है।

lesson.homework: एक सुभाषित का पदच्छेद और भावार्थ लिखिए।

topics.title: मित्राय नमः
topics.summary: योगिता प्रतिदिन पिता के साथ उद्यान जाती है, जहाँ लोग व्यायाम और योगासन करते हैं।
notes: योगिता प्रतिदिन पिता के साथ उद्यान जाती है, जहाँ लोग व्यायाम और योगासन करते हैं।
सब बच्चे योग-शिक्षिका के पास जाकर सूर्य-नमस्कार सीखते हैं।
सूर्य-नमस्कार के मंत्र: ॐ मित्राय नमः, ॐ रवये नमः, ॐ सूर्याय नमः, ॐ भानवे नमः, ॐ खगाय नमः, ॐ पूष्णे नमः…
सूर्य-नमस्कार से शरीर लचीला, मन शांत और स्वास्थ्य उत्तम होता है।
outcomes: सूर्य-नमस्कार के मंत्र और योग का महत्त्व जानना
संवाद के माध्यम से संस्कृत में दिनचर्या बोलना

lesson.hook: सुबह सूर्य को नमस्कार करने से शरीर और मन पर क्या असर होता है?
lesson.example: 'मित्राय नमः' — सूर्य को 'मित्र' (सबका मित्र) कहकर प्रणाम किया जाता है।
lesson.activity: योग-अभ्यास: कक्षा मंत्रों के साथ सूर्य-नमस्कार के कुछ चरण धीरे-धीरे करे।

questions.q: योगिता सुबह कहाँ जाती है?
सूर्य-नमस्कार का पहला मंत्र कौन-सा है?
सूर्य-नमस्कार से क्या लाभ है?
questions.a: शरीर स्वस्थ और लचीला, मन शांत होता है।

lesson.homework: सूर्य के पाँच नाम मंत्रों से ढूँढ़कर लिखिए।

topics.title: न लभ्यते चेत् आम्लं द्राक्षाफलम्
topics.summary: एक भूखा सियार (शृगालः) जंगल में घूम रहा था और उसने ऊँची बेल पर अंगूर देखे।
notes: एक भूखा सियार (शृगालः) जंगल में घूम रहा था और उसने ऊँची बेल पर अंगूर देखे।
उसने बार-बार कूदकर अंगूर पाने की कोशिश की, पर पहुँच न सका।
थककर वह बोला — ये अंगूर तो खट्टे (आम्ल) हैं।
सीख: जो न मिले उसे बुरा बताकर अपनी असफलता नहीं छिपानी चाहिए ('न लभ्यते चेत् आम्लं द्राक्षाफलम्')।
outcomes: 'खट्टे अंगूर' की कथा को संस्कृत गीत के रूप में समझना
कथा की सीख पहचानना

lesson.hook: जो चीज़ न मिले, क्या हम उसे बुरा कहने लगते हैं?
lesson.example: शृगालः द्राक्षाफलानि खादितुम् इच्छति, किन्तु न शक्नोति।
lesson.activity: गीत-अभिनय: बच्चे कथा को संस्कृत गीत के रूप में गाते हुए सियार का अभिनय करें।

questions.q: सियार क्या खाना चाहता था?
अंगूर न मिलने पर उसने क्या कहा?
'आम्लम्' का अर्थ क्या है?

lesson.homework: इस कथा से मिलने वाली सीख अपने जीवन के उदाहरण के साथ लिखिए।

topics.title: सेवा हि परमो धर्मः
topics.summary: जीवन में सफलता के लिए विद्या, धन और पद के साथ सत्य, करुणा, सेवा, परोपकार जैसे मानवीय गुण भी आवश्यक हैं।
notes: जीवन में सफलता के लिए विद्या, धन और पद के साथ सत्य, करुणा, सेवा, परोपकार जैसे मानवीय गुण भी आवश्यक हैं।
प्रसिद्ध रसायनशास्त्री-चिकित्सक नागार्जुन ने सहायक चुनने के लिए दो युवकों को दो दिन में एक रसायन बनाने को कहा।
पहले युवक ने माता-पिता की बीमारी छोड़कर भी रसायन बना दिया; दूसरा रास्ते में मिले एक रोगी की दो दिन सेवा करता रहा और रसायन नहीं बना सका।
नागार्जुन ने दूसरे युवक को चुना — क्योंकि चिकित्सक का पहला धर्म रोगी की सेवा है: 'सेवा हि परमो धर्मः'।
outcomes: कथा से सेवा के महत्त्व को समझना
मानवीय गुणों — करुणा, सेवा, परोपकार — को पहचानना

lesson.hook: परीक्षा में पास होना ज़रूरी है या किसी बीमार की मदद करना?
lesson.example: सिद्धार्थ के पास विद्या, धन, पद सब था, पर मानवीय गुणों से ही वे महात्मा बुद्ध बने।
lesson.activity: सेवा-सूची: बच्चे सप्ताह में किए जा सकने वाले तीन सेवा-कार्य लिखें और करें।

questions.q: नागार्जुन कौन थे?
दूसरा युवक रसायन क्यों नहीं बना सका?
questions.a: वह रास्ते में मिले रोगी की सेवा कर रहा था।

questions.q: नागार्जुन ने किसे चुना और क्यों?
questions.a: दूसरे युवक को, क्योंकि सेवा सबसे बड़ा धर्म है।

lesson.homework: किसी की सेवा करने के अपने अनुभव के बारे में लिखिए।

topics.title: क्रीडाम वयं श्लोकान्त्याक्षरीम्
topics.summary: बारिश के कारण बाहर न जा सकने पर सहेलियाँ घर में 'श्लोकान्त्याक्षरी' खेलती हैं।
notes: बारिश के कारण बाहर न जा सकने पर सहेलियाँ घर में 'श्लोकान्त्याक्षरी' खेलती हैं।
दो दल बनते हैं — 'ज्ञानमाला' और 'रत्नमाला'।
एक दल जिस श्लोक को बोलता है, उसका अंतिम अक्षर जहाँ खत्म होता है, दूसरा दल उसी अक्षर से शुरू होने वाला श्लोक बोलता है।
इस खेल से श्लोक याद होते हैं, उच्चारण सुधरता है और आनंद भी आता है।
outcomes: श्लोक-अंत्याक्षरी खेल के नियम समझना
संस्कृत श्लोकों का शुद्ध उच्चारण और स्मरण

lesson.hook: क्या आपने गानों की अंत्याक्षरी खेली है? संस्कृत श्लोकों से खेलें तो?
lesson.example: यदि श्लोक 'च' पर समाप्त हो, तो अगला श्लोक 'च' से शुरू होना चाहिए।
lesson.activity: कक्षा-अंत्याक्षरी: दो दल बनाकर पाठ और पिछली कक्षाओं के श्लोकों से अंत्याक्षरी खेलें।

questions.q: अंत्याक्षरी के दो दलों के नाम क्या थे?
अगला श्लोक किस अक्षर से शुरू होता है?
questions.a: पिछले श्लोक के अंतिम अक्षर से।

questions.q: इस खेल से क्या लाभ है?
questions.a: श्लोक याद होते हैं और उच्चारण सुधरता है।

lesson.homework: पाँच ऐसे श्लोक याद कीजिए जिनसे आप अंत्याक्षरी खेल सकें।

topics.title: ईशावास्यम् इदं सर्वम्
topics.summary: 'ईशावास्यम् इदं सर्वम्' — यह सारा जगत ईश्वर से व्याप्त है; ईश्वर सर्वत्र है।
notes: 'ईशावास्यम् इदं सर्वम्' — यह सारा जगत ईश्वर से व्याप्त है; ईश्वर सर्वत्र है।
दैत्यराज हिरण्यकशिपु स्वयं को सर्वशक्तिमान और अमर मानता था।
उसका पुत्र प्रह्लाद दिन-रात हरि का गुणगान करता था; हाथी के पैरों तले, पर्वत से गिराने और समुद्र में फेंकने पर भी वह बच गया।
बालक प्रह्लाद ने दिखाया कि ईश्वर सर्वत्र है — यह प्रसंग नाटक के रूप में प्रस्तुत है।
outcomes: 'ईशावास्यम् इदं सर्वम्' का भाव समझना
प्रह्लाद की कथा को नाटक रूप में पढ़ना

lesson.hook: ईश्वर केवल मंदिर में है या हर जगह?
lesson.example: ईशावास्यम् = ईश + आवास्यम् — ईश्वर के रहने योग्य (ईश्वर से व्याप्त)।
lesson.activity: नाटक-मंचन: बच्चे हिरण्यकशिपु की सभा का दृश्य संस्कृत संवादों के साथ प्रस्तुत करें।

questions.q: 'ईशावास्यम् इदं सर्वम्' का अर्थ क्या है?
questions.a: यह सब जगत ईश्वर से व्याप्त है।

questions.q: हिरण्यकशिपु स्वयं को क्या मानता था?
प्रह्लाद किसका गुणगान करता था?

lesson.homework: 'ईश्वर सर्वत्र है' पर अपने विचार पाँच वाक्यों में लिखिए।

topics.title: हितं मनोहारि च दुर्लभं वचः
topics.summary: सूक्ति का अर्थ है सुंदर वचन; सूक्तियों में जीवन-मूल्य छिपे होते हैं।
notes: सूक्ति का अर्थ है सुंदर वचन; सूक्तियों में जीवन-मूल्य छिपे होते हैं।
'माता भूमिः पुत्रोऽहं पृथिव्याः' — पृथ्वी माता है, हम उसकी संतान हैं।
'न रत्नमन्विष्यति, मृग्यते हि तत्' — रत्न किसी को नहीं ढूँढ़ता, लोग रत्न को ढूँढ़ते हैं; गुणी व्यक्ति को गुणज्ञ स्वयं खोज लेते हैं।
'शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्' — शरीर ही सब कर्तव्यों का पहला साधन है, इसलिए उसे स्वस्थ रखें।
outcomes: संस्कृत सूक्तियों का अर्थ और जीवन-मूल्य जानना
सूक्तियों को जीवन में अपनाने की प्रेरणा लेना

lesson.hook: 'सत्यं वद, धर्मं चर' — क्या आपने यह सूक्ति सुनी है?
lesson.example: 'हितं मनोहारि च दुर्लभं वचः' — ऐसी बात जो हितकारी भी हो और मन को भी अच्छी लगे, दुर्लभ होती है।
lesson.activity: सूक्ति-डायरी: बच्चे हर दिन एक सूक्ति लिखें और उस दिन उसे अपनाने का प्रयास करें।

questions.q: 'सूक्ति' का अर्थ क्या है?
'शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्' का भाव क्या है?
questions.a: स्वस्थ शरीर ही सब कर्तव्यों का पहला साधन है।

questions.q: 'न रत्नमन्विष्यति' से क्या सीख मिलती है?
questions.a: गुण हों तो लोग स्वयं हमें खोजते हैं।

lesson.homework: दो सूक्तियाँ लिखकर उनका अर्थ लिखिए।

topics.title: अन्नाद् भवन्ति भूतानि
topics.summary: भारत के प्राचीन ऋषि, गणितज्ञ, खगोलविद, वैद्य और शिल्पी संस्कृत ग्रंथों में अपना ज्ञान छोड़ गए हैं।
notes: भारत के प्राचीन ऋषि, गणितज्ञ, खगोलविद, वैद्य और शिल्पी संस्कृत ग्रंथों में अपना ज्ञान छोड़ गए हैं।
माँ-बेटी के संवाद में उपनिषदों के अनुसार सृष्टि-क्रम बताया गया है: ब्रह्म से आकाश, आकाश से वायु, वायु से अग्नि, अग्नि से जल, जल से पृथ्वी।
पृथ्वी से वनस्पतियाँ, वनस्पतियों से अन्न और अन्न से प्राणी उत्पन्न होते हैं।
'अन्नाद् भवन्ति भूतानि' — सभी प्राणी अन्न से उत्पन्न और पोषित होते हैं; इसलिए अन्न का आदर करें।
outcomes: भारतीय चिंतन में सृष्टि-क्रम की अवधारणा जानना
'अन्नाद् भवन्ति भूतानि' का अर्थ समझना

lesson.hook: मनुष्य, पशु, पेड़ — ये सब धरती पर कैसे आए होंगे?
lesson.example: क्रम: आकाश → वायु → अग्नि → जल → पृथ्वी → वनस्पति → अन्न → प्राणी।
lesson.activity: सृष्टि-चक्र: बच्चे सृष्टि-क्रम का चित्र-चार्ट बनाकर संस्कृत नाम लिखें।

questions.q: आकाश से क्या उत्पन्न हुआ?
जल से क्या उत्पन्न हुई?
'अन्नाद् भवन्ति भूतानि' का अर्थ क्या है?
questions.a: सभी प्राणी अन्न से उत्पन्न होते हैं।

lesson.homework: अन्न का सम्मान करने के तीन उपाय लिखिए।

topics.title: दशमः कः?
topics.summary: दस बालक नदी में स्नान करके पार गए; नायक ने पूछा कि क्या सब पार आ गए।
notes: दस बालक नदी में स्नान करके पार गए; नायक ने पूछा कि क्या सब पार आ गए।
एक बालक ने सबको गिना पर खुद को नहीं गिना — केवल नौ निकले; दूसरे ने भी यही किया।
सबने सोचा कि दसवाँ नदी में डूब गया और वे दुखी हो गए।
एक पथिक ने गिनती कराई और कहा — 'दशमः त्वम् असि' (दसवें तुम हो); सब प्रसन्न होकर घर गए।
outcomes: 'दशमः कः?' कथा का हास्य और सीख समझना
संस्कृत में क्रमसूचक संख्याएँ (प्रथमः, द्वितीयः…) सीखना

lesson.hook: गिनती करते समय क्या आप कभी खुद को गिनना भूल गए हैं?
lesson.example: क्रमसूचक: प्रथमः, द्वितीयः, तृतीयः, चतुर्थः, पञ्चमः… दशमः।
lesson.activity: गिनती-खेल: दस बच्चे पंक्ति में खड़े होकर संस्कृत में क्रमसूचक संख्याएँ बोलें — 'अहं प्रथमः/प्रथमा…'।

questions.q: दस बालक कहाँ गए थे?
केवल नौ क्यों गिने गए?
questions.a: गिनने वाला स्वयं को नहीं गिनता था।

questions.q: पथिक ने क्या कहा?
questions.a: दशमः त्वम् असि — दसवें तुम हो।

lesson.homework: संस्कृत में प्रथम से दशम तक क्रमसूचक संख्याएँ लिखिए।

topics.title: द्वीपेषु रम्यः द्वीपोऽण्डमानः
topics.summary: अंडमान-निकोबार द्वीपसमूह भारत के आठ केंद्रशासित प्रदेशों में से एक है।
notes: अंडमान-निकोबार द्वीपसमूह भारत के आठ केंद्रशासित प्रदेशों में से एक है।
इसकी राजधानी 'श्रीविजयपुरम्' है; अंग्रेज़ी शासन ने इसका नाम 'पोर्ट ब्लेयर' रखा था।
सूर्यांश ने बताया कि रामायण काल में इसे 'हण्डुकमान्' कहते थे, जो 'हनूमान्' से बना माना जाता है।
भारत के स्वतंत्रता-संग्राम में इस द्वीप की बड़ी भूमिका है; यह सुंदर तटों और वनों वाला रमणीय द्वीप है।
outcomes: अंडमान-निकोबार द्वीपसमूह के बारे में जानना
संवाद से इतिहास और भूगोल को जोड़ना

lesson.hook: भारत के मानचित्र में बंगाल की खाड़ी में दूर स्थित वे द्वीप कौन-से हैं?
lesson.example: द्वीपेषु रम्यः द्वीपोऽण्डमानः = द्वीपों में अंडमान रमणीय द्वीप है।
lesson.activity: मानचित्र-कार्य: बच्चे भारत के मानचित्र पर अंडमान-निकोबार और उसकी राजधानी चिह्नित करें।

questions.q: अंडमान-निकोबार की राजधानी का वर्तमान नाम क्या है?
अंग्रेज़ी शासन में राजधानी का नाम क्या था?
रामायण काल में इसे क्या कहते थे?

lesson.homework: अंडमान-निकोबार के बारे में पाँच तथ्य संस्कृत या हिंदी में लिखिए।

topics.title: वीराङ्गना पन्नाधाया
topics.summary: सोलहवीं सदी में मेवाड़ के महाराणा संग्रामसिंह के दो पुत्र थे — विक्रमादित्य और उदयसिंह।
notes: सोलहवीं सदी में मेवाड़ के महाराणा संग्रामसिंह के दो पुत्र थे — विक्रमादित्य और उदयसिंह।
बनवीर ने छल से विक्रमादित्य को मारकर मेवाड़ पर अधिकार किया और उदयसिंह को भी मारने की योजना बनाई।
यह जानकर पन्ना धाय ने उदयसिंह के बिस्तर पर अपने पुत्र चंदन को सुला दिया; बनवीर ने चंदन को उदयसिंह समझकर मार दिया।
पन्ना ने 'व्यक्तिहित नहीं, राष्ट्रहित श्रेष्ठ है' मानकर मेवाड़ की रक्षा की; बाद में उदयसिंह ने बनवीर को हराकर राज्य पाया।
outcomes: वीरांगना पन्ना धाय के त्याग की कथा जानना
राष्ट्रहित को व्यक्तिगत हित से ऊपर रखने का भाव समझना

lesson.hook: क्या कोई माँ देश के भविष्य के लिए अपने ही बच्चे का बलिदान कर सकती है?
lesson.example: 'माता भूमिः पुत्रोऽहं पृथिव्याः' (अथर्ववेद) — पन्ना धाय के त्याग में मातृभूमि-प्रेम की पराकाष्ठा दिखती है।
lesson.activity: वीरांगना-परिचय: बच्चे भारत की किसी अन्य वीरांगना पर संक्षिप्त प्रस्तुति दें।

questions.q: पन्ना धाय किस राज्य से संबंधित थीं?
पन्ना ने उदयसिंह को कैसे बचाया?
questions.a: उसके बिस्तर पर अपने पुत्र चंदन को सुलाकर।

questions.q: बाद में मेवाड़ का राजा कौन बना?

lesson.homework: पन्ना धाय के त्याग पर पाँच वाक्य लिखिए।

topics.title: Large Numbers Around Us
topics.summary: Indian system: thousand, lakh (1,00,000), crore (1,00,00,000), arab (100 crore); commas after the first three digits, then every two digits.
notes: Indian system: thousand, lakh (1,00,000), crore (1,00,00,000), arab (100 crore); commas after the first three digits, then every two digits.
International system: thousand, million (1,000,000), billion (1,000,000,000); commas every three digits.
1 lakh = 100 thousand; 10 lakh = 1 million; 1 crore = 10 million; 100 crore = 1 billion.
Our number system is based on tens: each place is 10 times the place to its right.
Exact values are not always needed; we round to the nearest thousand, lakh or crore to estimate.
Patterns in products (like 25 × 4 = 100) help calculate large numbers mentally.
outcomes: Read and write large numbers in the Indian and international systems
Convert between lakhs/crores and millions/billions
Estimate and round large numbers sensibly

lesson.hook: India's population is about 140 crore. How would a newspaper in London write the same number?
lesson.example: 140 crore = 1,40,00,00,000 (Indian) = 1,400,000,000 (international) = 1.4 billion.
lesson.activity: Newspaper hunt: pupils find five large numbers in a newspaper, write each in both systems, and round each to the nearest lakh.

questions.q: Write 5,00,00,000 in words (Indian system).
How many lakhs make one million?
Write 3,256,789 in the Indian system.
Round 7,48,650 to the nearest lakh.

lesson.homework: Find the populations of five Indian states and write them in both systems.

topics.title: Arithmetic Expressions
topics.summary: An expression is a combination of numbers and operations; its value is the number it stands for.
notes: An expression is a combination of numbers and operations; its value is the number it stands for.
Brackets show which part to work out first.
Multiplication and division are done before addition and subtraction; otherwise work from left to right.
Subtraction can be seen as adding a negative: 30 − 10 + 5 = 30 + (−10) + 5 = 25.
Terms of an expression can be swapped and grouped when they are added (commutative and associative properties).
We can compare expressions like 47 + 38 and 48 + 37 by reasoning without calculating.
outcomes: Read and evaluate arithmetic expressions correctly
Use brackets and the order of operations
Compare expressions by reasoning instead of calculating

lesson.hook: Is 30 − 10 + 5 equal to 15 or 25? Two pupils got different answers. Who is right, and why?
lesson.example: 5 × (8 + 4) = 5 × 12 = 60, and also 5 × 8 + 5 × 4 = 40 + 20 = 60 (distributive property).
lesson.activity: Shopping expressions: pupils write an expression for a bill (3 pens at ₹12, 2 notebooks at ₹35, minus a ₹10 discount) and evaluate it, then compare with partners.

questions.q: Evaluate 18 − 3 × 4.
Evaluate (18 − 3) × 4.
Without calculating, which is bigger: 63 − 27 or 64 − 26?
Write an expression: 'five less than three times twelve'.

lesson.homework: Write three expressions for money you spent this week and evaluate each.

topics.title: A Peek Beyond the Point
topics.summary: To measure more exactly, we split a unit into 10 equal parts (tenths), each tenth into 10 (hundredths), and so on.
notes: To measure more exactly, we split a unit into 10 equal parts (tenths), each tenth into 10 (hundredths), and so on.
The decimal point separates whole units from parts: 3.47 = 3 units + 4 tenths + 7 hundredths.
Place value continues to the right: 1 = 10 tenths = 100 hundredths.
Decimals appear in measurement: 1.25 m = 1 m 25 cm; ₹12.50 = 12 rupees 50 paise.
To compare decimals, compare place by place from the left: 6.45 > 6.405.
Add or subtract decimals by lining up the decimal points.
outcomes: Understand tenths, hundredths and thousandths as smaller units
Read, write, locate and compare decimals using place value
Add and subtract decimals, and use decimals in measurement

lesson.hook: Your height is between 1 m and 2 m. How can you say it more exactly without using centimetres?
lesson.activity: Measure and record: pupils measure the length of their desk, book and pencil in metres using decimals (e.g. 0.18 m) and arrange them in order.

questions.q: Write 5 tenths and 3 hundredths as a decimal.
Which is greater, 0.7 or 0.65?
Write 2 kg 350 g in kilograms.

lesson.homework: Collect three bills or packets showing decimal numbers and add the amounts.

topics.title: Expressions using Letter-Numbers
topics.summary: Letter-numbers (variables) like n or x stand for any number.
notes: Letter-numbers (variables) like n or x stand for any number.
Algebraic expressions use numbers and letters: 3n + 1, 2(l + b).
Formulas are expressions for patterns: perimeter of a square = 4s.
The rules of arithmetic apply to letters too: a + b = b + a, and 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6.
Like terms have the same letter part (4x and 7x) and can be added: 4x + 7x = 11x.
Algebra helps us see a relationship once and use it for every case.
outcomes: Use letters to stand for numbers in formulas and patterns
Write and evaluate algebraic expressions
Simplify expressions by combining like terms

lesson.hook: A matchstick pattern makes squares in a row: 1 square uses 4 sticks, 2 squares use 7, 3 squares use 10. How many sticks for 50 squares?
lesson.example: Matchsticks: each new square adds 3 sticks, so n squares need 3n + 1 sticks. For 50 squares: 3 × 50 + 1 = 151.
lesson.activity: Pupils build matchstick (or toothpick) triangles in a row, record sticks used for 1-5 triangles, and write an expression for n triangles.

questions.q: Simplify 5a + 3b − 2a + b.
Find the value of 4x − 3 when x = 5.
Write an expression: 'Ravi's age 6 years from now' if he is r years old now.
Expand 2(3p + 4).

lesson.homework: Make up your own matchstick pattern, draw four stages, and write an expression for stage n.

topics.title: Parallel and Intersecting Lines
topics.summary: Two intersecting lines make four angles; vertically opposite angles are equal, and angles in a linear pair add up to 180°.
notes: Two intersecting lines make four angles; vertically opposite angles are equal, and angles in a linear pair add up to 180°.
Lines meeting at 90° are perpendicular.
Parallel lines lie in the same plane and never meet; the distance between them stays the same.
A transversal cuts two or more lines, making corresponding, alternate and interior angles.
If the lines are parallel, corresponding angles are equal and alternate angles are equal; interior angles on the same side add up to 180°.
We can draw a parallel line through a point using equal corresponding angles (set square or paper folding).
outcomes: Identify angles formed by intersecting lines: vertically opposite angles and linear pairs
Recognise parallel and perpendicular lines
Use corresponding and alternate angles formed by a transversal

lesson.hook: Railway tracks never meet, but a road crossing them makes angles. Why are some of these angles always equal?
lesson.example: A transversal cuts two parallel lines and one angle is 65°. Its corresponding angle is 65°, its alternate angle is 65°, and the angle forming a linear pair with it is 115°.
lesson.activity: On a ruled notebook page, pupils draw a slanting line across the ruled lines, measure all eight angles at two crossings and colour equal angles the same.

questions.q: Two lines intersect and one angle is 40°. Find the other three.
What are the corresponding angles when the lines are parallel?
Interior angles on the same side of a transversal to parallel lines add to?

lesson.homework: Find three examples of parallel and perpendicular lines around your home and draw them.

topics.title: Number Play
topics.summary: Numbers can describe how things are arranged even without knowing the actual values.
notes: Numbers can describe how things are arranged even without knowing the actual values.
Parity: even numbers can be arranged in pairs, odd numbers leave one out.
Even + even = even, odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd; the sum of five odd numbers is always odd.
Grid puzzles and magic squares can be solved using sums and parity.
Virahāṅka–Fibonacci numbers (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13…) count the ways to make a rhythm with short and long beats, and appear in nature.
Letter puzzles ('digits in disguise') can be solved by logical reasoning about place value.
outcomes: Use numbers to describe arrangements and sequences
Understand parity (odd and even) and use it to reason
Explore grids, the Virahāṅka–Fibonacci sequence and digit puzzles

lesson.hook: Can you make a total of 20 by adding exactly five odd numbers? Try before you decide.
lesson.example: Five odd numbers can never add up to 20: odd + odd is even, so four odd numbers make an even sum and one more odd number makes the total odd.
lesson.activity: Magic square: pupils fill a 3 × 3 grid with 1 to 9 so every row, column and diagonal adds to 15. What must go in the centre, and why?

questions.q: Is the sum of 7 odd numbers odd or even?
What number goes in the centre of a 1-9 magic square?

lesson.homework: Find how many ways you can climb 6 stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Compare with the Virahāṅka sequence.

chapters.title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines

topics.title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
topics.summary: A compass makes it easy to construct a triangle when its three sides are given.
notes: A compass makes it easy to construct a triangle when its three sides are given.
Triangle inequality: each side must be shorter than the sum of the other two.
An equilateral triangle has all sides and angles equal (60° each).
The angles of every triangle add up to 180°.
An altitude is a perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension).
Triangles are classified by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse).
outcomes: Construct triangles with given side lengths using a compass
Use the triangle inequality to decide if a triangle is possible
Draw altitudes and classify triangles by sides and angles

lesson.hook: Can you make a triangle with sticks of length 3 cm, 4 cm and 9 cm? Try it and explain what happens.
lesson.example: 3, 4, 9: 3 + 4 = 7, which is less than 9, so no triangle is possible. 5, 6, 8: every pair sums to more than the third side, so the triangle exists.
lesson.activity: Straw triangles: pupils cut straws into lengths (3, 4, 5, 7, 9 cm) and test which sets of three make a triangle, recording the results in a table.

questions.q: Can 4 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm form a triangle?
Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 70°. Find the third.
What is an altitude of a triangle?
questions.a: A perpendicular line from a vertex to the opposite side.

lesson.homework: Construct a triangle with sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm and draw its three altitudes.

topics.title: Working with Fractions
topics.summary: Multiplying fractions: multiply numerators and multiply denominators — Brahmagupta's rule.
notes: Multiplying fractions: multiply numerators and multiply denominators — Brahmagupta's rule.
'Of' means multiply: 1/2 of 3/4 = 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8.
Cancel common factors before multiplying to keep numbers small.
Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 gives a smaller answer.
Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal: 3 ÷ 1/4 = 3 × 4 = 12.
Fractions solve real problems of sharing, measuring and recipes.
outcomes: Multiply fractions and understand 'of' as multiplication
Divide fractions using reciprocals
Solve word problems involving fractions

lesson.hook: A recipe needs 3/4 cup of rice. You want to make half the recipe. How much rice do you need?
lesson.example: Half of 3/4 cup = 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8 cup. How many 1/4-litre glasses can be filled from 3 litres? 3 ÷ 1/4 = 12 glasses.
lesson.activity: Paper folding: pupils fold a paper in quarters, shade 3/4, then fold in half the other way and find 1/2 of 3/4 by counting parts.

questions.q: What is the reciprocal of 7/3?
A ribbon of 6 m is cut into pieces of 3/4 m. How many pieces?

lesson.homework: Take a recipe from home and rewrite the quantities for half and for one and a half times the amount.

topics.title: Geometric Twins
topics.summary: Congruent figures have the same shape and size; one fits exactly over the other (it may need to be turned or flipped).
notes: Congruent figures have the same shape and size; one fits exactly over the other (it may need to be turned or flipped).
SSS: if three sides of one triangle equal three sides of another, the triangles are congruent.
SAS: two sides and the angle between them are equal.
ASA: two angles and the side between them are equal; RHS: in right triangles, the hypotenuse and one side are equal.
Matching parts of congruent triangles are equal (corresponding sides and angles).
In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal; in an equilateral triangle each angle is 60°.
outcomes: Understand congruent figures as having the same shape and size
Use SSS, SAS, ASA and RHS conditions to decide congruence of triangles
Find angles in isosceles and equilateral triangles

lesson.hook: Two roti makers claim their rotis are exactly the same. How could you prove it without measuring every point?
lesson.example: An isosceles triangle has a top angle of 40°. The two base angles are equal, so each = (180° − 40°) ÷ 2 = 70°.
lesson.activity: Straw triangles: pupils make triangles with the same three straw lengths and check that they always fit on top of each other (SSS). Then try two sides and different angles to see why SSA fails.

questions.q: What does 'congruent' mean?
questions.a: Having exactly the same shape and size.

questions.q: Which condition applies: two sides and the angle between them equal?
The base angles of an isosceles triangle are 65° each. Find the third angle.
Why is each angle of an equilateral triangle 60°?
questions.a: All three angles are equal and add up to 180°.

lesson.homework: Find five pairs of congruent objects at home (tiles, coins, bangles) and describe why they are congruent.

topics.title: Operations with Integers
topics.summary: Integers include positive numbers, negative numbers and zero.
notes: Integers include positive numbers, negative numbers and zero.
Multiplication can be seen as repeated addition: 3 × (−2) = (−2) + (−2) + (−2) = −6.
Patterns in multiplication tables show why the product of two negatives is positive.
The same sign rules apply to division: (−12) ÷ (−3) = 4 and (−12) ÷ 3 = −4.
Multiplying by −1 gives the opposite number; division by zero is not defined.
outcomes: Revise integers and their addition and subtraction
Multiply and divide integers using sign rules
Use patterns and the number line to justify the rules

lesson.activity: Multiplication grid: pupils fill in a grid from −3 to 3 on both axes, colour positive products one colour and negative ones another, and describe the pattern of colours.

questions.q: A submarine descends 12 m every minute. How far below the surface is it after 5 minutes, as an integer?

lesson.homework: Make your own pattern that shows why (−2) × (−4) = 8.

topics.title: Finding Common Ground
topics.summary: Prime factorisation writes a number as a product of primes: 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.
notes: Prime factorisation writes a number as a product of primes: 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.
All factors of a number can be built from its prime factors.
HCF (highest common factor) is the largest number dividing all the given numbers — take the common prime factors.
LCM (lowest common multiple) is the smallest number that all the given numbers divide — take every prime factor the greatest number of times it appears.
For two numbers, HCF × LCM = product of the numbers.
Euclid's method finds the HCF by repeated division (or subtraction).
outcomes: Find the HCF and LCM of numbers using prime factorisation
Use HCF and LCM to solve real problems
Explore the relationship between HCF, LCM and the product of two numbers

lesson.hook: You have 24 laddoos and 36 jalebis. What is the largest number of identical plates you can make with no sweets left over?
lesson.example: 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3². HCF = 2² × 3 = 12 plates (2 laddoos and 3 jalebis each). LCM = 2³ × 3² = 72. Check: 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36.
lesson.activity: Bell problem: two bells ring every 8 and 12 minutes. Pupils list the times each rings in the first hour and circle when both ring together, then check with the LCM.

questions.q: Find the HCF of 18 and 30.
Find the LCM of 6 and 10.
The HCF of two numbers is 4 and their product is 96. Find their LCM.
What is the HCF of two co-prime numbers?

lesson.homework: Find two real situations at home where you need HCF and two where you need LCM; solve one of each.

topics.title: Another Peek Beyond the Point
topics.summary: To multiply decimals, multiply as whole numbers, then count the total decimal places in both numbers for the product.
notes: To multiply decimals, multiply as whole numbers, then count the total decimal places in both numbers for the product.
Multiplying by 10, 100, 1000 moves the decimal point 1, 2, 3 places to the right; dividing moves it left.
To divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by a power of 10 to make the divisor a whole number.
Multiplying by a decimal less than 1 makes a number smaller; dividing by it makes a number larger.
Estimating first ('look before you leap') helps catch misplaced decimal points.
outcomes: Multiply decimals using place value
Divide decimals, including by decimals
Estimate before calculating to check answers

lesson.hook: Petrol costs ₹104.50 per litre. How much for 2.5 litres? Estimate first, then calculate.
lesson.activity: Market maths: pupils use real prices from a shop receipt (₹/kg) to calculate the cost of 0.5 kg, 1.25 kg and 2.75 kg of different items, estimating first.

questions.q: Is 4.8 × 0.5 more or less than 4.8? Why?
questions.a: Less — multiplying by a number less than 1 makes it smaller (answer 2.4).

lesson.homework: Write a shopping list with decimal quantities and prices and calculate the total bill.

topics.title: Connecting the Dots...
topics.summary: A statistical question expects variety in the answers ('How long do pupils in our class sleep?').
notes: A statistical question expects variety in the answers ('How long do pupils in our class sleep?').
Representative values summarise data: the arithmetic mean (average) and the median.
Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values.
Median = middle value of sorted data; with an even number of values, the average of the middle two.
Range = maximum − minimum; dot plots show where data cluster and how spread out they are.
Outliers (very large or small values) affect the mean more than the median.
outcomes: Frame statistical questions and collect data
Find the mean, median and range of data
Represent data with dot plots and interpret the spread

lesson.hook: Who is the 'typical' pupil in our class — in height, in hours of sleep, in travel time to school? How do we decide?
lesson.example: Sleep hours of 7 pupils: 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 12. Mean = 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Median = 8. Range = 12 − 6 = 6. Without the 12, the mean drops to 7.33 but the median is 7.5.
lesson.activity: Class data detective: pupils record their travel time to school on sticky notes, build a dot plot on the board, and find the mean, median and range.

questions.q: Find the mean of 4, 8, 6, 10, 2.
Find the median of 3, 9, 5, 7, 1, 11.
What is the range of 15, 22, 9, 30?
Why might the median be a better 'typical value' than the mean?
questions.a: It is not pulled by a few very large or small values (outliers).

lesson.homework: Record the daily maximum temperature for a week and find its mean, median and range.

topics.title: Constructions and Tilings
topics.summary: Bisection divides a segment or angle into two equal parts.
notes: Bisection divides a segment or angle into two equal parts.
Points equidistant from the ends of a segment lie on its perpendicular bisector, which can be drawn with two arcs.
The same method gives a 90° angle; bisecting it gives 45°. An equilateral triangle gives 60°, and bisecting it gives 30°.
A tiling covers a flat surface with shapes that leave no gaps and do not overlap.
Regular polygons tile a plane only if their angles fit exactly around a point (add to 360°): equilateral triangles (6 × 60°), squares (4 × 90°) and regular hexagons (3 × 120°).
Tilings appear in floors, rangoli and Islamic and Indian architecture.
outcomes: Bisect a line segment and construct perpendiculars with ruler and compass
Construct angles of 90°, 60°, 45° and 30°
Explore which regular shapes tile a plane

lesson.hook: Floor tiles are usually squares or hexagons, never regular pentagons. Why?
lesson.example: Why not pentagons? Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°; 3 × 108° = 324° leaves a gap and 4 × 108° = 432° overlaps.
lesson.activity: Pupils cut out 10 copies each of equilateral triangles, squares, regular pentagons and hexagons and try to tile a sheet without gaps.

questions.q: What is a perpendicular bisector?
questions.a: A line that cuts a segment into two equal parts at 90°.

questions.q: How do you construct a 30° angle?
questions.a: Construct 60° (from an equilateral triangle) and bisect it.

questions.q: Which three regular polygons can tile a plane on their own?
questions.a: Equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons.

lesson.homework: Photograph or draw a tiling pattern from your home or a temple, mosque or monument, and name the shapes in it.

topics.title: Finding the Unknown
topics.summary: An equation says two expressions are equal: 3x + 7 = 31.
notes: An equation says two expressions are equal: 3x + 7 = 31.
A solution is a value of the unknown that makes the left side equal the right side.
Doing the same operation on both sides keeps the equation balanced.
Undo operations in reverse order: subtract 7, then divide by 3.
Always check the answer by substituting it back.
Indian mathematicians like Brahmagupta and Bhaskara solved such equations centuries ago.
outcomes: Write equations for word problems
Solve simple linear equations by doing the same operation on both sides
Check solutions and spot common mistakes

lesson.hook: I think of a number, multiply it by 3 and add 7. I get 31. What was my number?
lesson.example: 3x + 7 = 31. Subtract 7: 3x = 24. Divide by 3: x = 8. Check: 3 × 8 + 7 = 31 ✓.
lesson.activity: Balance puzzles: draw a see-saw with bags of unknown weight and known weights on both sides; pupils remove the same weights from both sides to find the unknown.

questions.q: Solve x + 12 = 30.
Solve 5y − 4 = 21.
Ravi's father is 3 times as old as Ravi. Their ages add up to 48. How old is Ravi?
A pupil solved 2x + 5 = 13 as x = 9. What was the mistake?
questions.a: They added 5 instead of subtracting; correctly 2x = 8, x = 4.

lesson.homework: Make up three 'think of a number' puzzles for your family and write the equation for each.

topics.title: The Ever-Evolving World of Science
topics.summary: Science grows: new observations and better tools can change what we think.
notes: Science grows: new observations and better tools can change what we think.
A good scientific question can be tested by observing or experimenting.
Science links with daily life — cooking, health, electricity, weather and the sky.
Careful recording, repeating experiments and sharing results make science reliable.
Curiosity and asking 'why?' and 'what if?' are the starting point.
outcomes: See science as a process that keeps changing with new evidence
Connect the topics of the year: substances, electricity, life processes, light, Earth and sky
Practise asking testable questions

lesson.hook: People once believed the Sun went round the Earth. What made them change their minds? Can a scientific idea ever be proved wrong?
lesson.example: Ancient Indian astronomers like Aryabhata said the Earth spins on its axis, which explains why the stars seem to move across the sky each night — an idea based on careful observation.
lesson.activity: Question sort: each pupil writes a question about nature on a slip. The class sorts them into 'can test in school', 'can test with help', and 'cannot test yet', and picks one to test this week.

questions.q: Why can scientific ideas change?
questions.a: Because new observations and evidence can show a better explanation.

questions.q: Give an example of a question you could test in class.
questions.a: Does sugar dissolve faster in hot water than in cold water? (or similar)

questions.q: Why do scientists repeat experiments?
questions.a: To make sure the result is reliable and not a one-time accident.

lesson.homework: Ask an elder about a belief they once had that changed when they learned something new; write it in three lines.

chapters.title: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral

topics.title: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral
topics.summary: Substances can be acidic (lemon juice, vinegar), basic (soap, baking soda solution) or neutral (sugar solution, pure water).
notes: Substances can be acidic (lemon juice, vinegar), basic (soap, baking soda solution) or neutral (sugar solution, pure water).
Indicators change colour with acids and bases: blue litmus turns red in acids; red litmus turns blue in bases.
Red rose extract turns red in acids and green in bases; turmeric turns red in bases but stays yellow in acids and neutral solutions.
Litmus comes from lichens; red cabbage and hibiscus make good home indicators.
An acid and a base cancel each other's effect: neutralisation, which gives a salt and water and releases heat.
Daily uses: antacids for acidity, baking soda on ant bites, lime for acidic soil, treating factory wastes.
outcomes: Classify substances as acidic, basic or neutral
Use natural indicators such as litmus, red rose, turmeric and hibiscus
Explain neutralisation and its uses in daily life

lesson.hook: Why does a red rose petal turn green when rubbed with soap? Nature gives us its own colour-changing detectives.
lesson.example: Add a few drops of turmeric solution to soap water: it turns red, so soap is basic. In lemon juice it stays yellow.
lesson.activity: Make a red cabbage (or hibiscus) indicator by soaking leaves in warm water. Groups test lemon, vinegar, soap, baking soda, salt water and sugar water, and sort them into acidic, basic and neutral.

questions.q: What colour does blue litmus turn in an acid?
What does turmeric show in a basic solution?
What is formed when an acid reacts with a base?
Why is an antacid taken for acidity?
questions.a: It is basic and neutralises the extra acid in the stomach.

lesson.homework: Test five things at home with turmeric paper and record the results.

topics.title: Electricity: Circuits and their Components
topics.summary: An electric cell is a portable source of electricity with a positive (+) and a negative (−) terminal; cells joined together make a battery.
notes: An electric cell is a portable source of electricity with a positive (+) and a negative (−) terminal; cells joined together make a battery.
In an incandescent bulb a thin filament gets hot and glows; an LED glows only when its longer lead goes to the positive side.
Current flows only in a closed (complete) circuit: cell → switch → lamp → back to the cell.
A switch opens (off) or closes (on) the circuit.
Circuit diagrams use standard symbols for the cell, battery, switch, lamp and wires.
Materials that let current pass are conductors (metals); those that do not are insulators (plastic, rubber, wood).
outcomes: Identify the parts of a torch, a cell, a lamp and an LED
Build a simple circuit and draw it with symbols
Separate conductors from insulators

lesson.hook: A torch has only a few parts, yet one switch makes it glow. What path does electricity take inside it?
lesson.example: An LED does not glow when connected one way but glows when turned around: current passes through it in one direction only.
lesson.activity: Make a conductor tester with a cell, a bulb and wires with a gap. Groups test a key, eraser, coin, pencil lead, paper clip and plastic scale, and sort them into conductors and insulators.

questions.q: What happens to the bulb when the switch is open?
questions.a: It does not glow: the circuit is broken.

questions.q: Why are electric wires covered with plastic?
questions.a: Plastic is an insulator, protecting us from shocks.

questions.q: Which lead of an LED connects to the positive terminal?
Name one conductor and one insulator.
questions.a: Conductor: copper, iron, aluminium. Insulator: plastic, rubber, wood.

lesson.homework: Draw a circuit diagram of a torch using the correct symbols.

chapters.title: The World of Metals and Non-metals

topics.title: The World of Metals and Non-metals
topics.summary: Metals are usually lustrous, malleable (beaten into sheets), ductile (drawn into wires), sonorous (ring when struck), and good conductors of heat and electricity.
notes: Metals are usually lustrous, malleable (beaten into sheets), ductile (drawn into wires), sonorous (ring when struck), and good conductors of heat and electricity.
Non-metals are usually dull, brittle, not sonorous, and poor conductors.
Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are basic; non-metals form oxides that are acidic.
Iron rusts when exposed to both air and moisture; painting, oiling and galvanising prevent rusting.
Some substances are exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal; graphite conducts electricity.
Non-metals are essential: oxygen for breathing, carbon in all living things, nitrogen and phosphorus in fertilisers.
outcomes: Compare metals and non-metals by lustre, malleability, ductility, sonority and conduction
Describe how metals react with air and water, including rusting
Explain the importance of non-metals

lesson.hook: Why does a temple bell ring but a wooden block just thuds? Why are wires made of copper and not of sulphur?
lesson.example: Rusting needs both air and water: an iron nail in dry air (with a drying agent) and one in boiled water under oil do not rust, while one in tap water with air does.
lesson.activity: Metal or non-metal: groups test samples (iron nail, aluminium foil, copper wire, coal, sulphur) for lustre, beating, ringing and conduction and fill a comparison table.

questions.q: What does 'ductile' mean?
questions.a: Able to be drawn into thin wires.

questions.q: What two things are needed for iron to rust?
Are metal oxides acidic or basic?
Why is aluminium used to make cooking pans?
questions.a: It conducts heat well and does not rust.

lesson.homework: Find three iron objects at home: which are rusted, and how could each be protected?

chapters.title: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

topics.title: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical
topics.summary: A physical change alters shape, size or state, but no new substance forms (melting ice, tearing paper, dissolving sugar).
notes: A physical change alters shape, size or state, but no new substance forms (melting ice, tearing paper, dissolving sugar).
A chemical change forms one or more new substances and can be written as a chemical equation (burning, cooking, rusting).
Combustion is burning with heat and light; the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire is its ignition temperature.
Some changes are reversible (melting, freezing), others irreversible (cooking an egg).
Some changes are desirable (ripening fruit), others undesirable (rusting, spoiling food).
Slow natural changes shape the land: weathering breaks rocks, erosion carries the pieces away.
outcomes: Distinguish physical changes from chemical changes
Describe rusting and combustion as chemical changes
Explain reversible and irreversible, desirable and undesirable, and slow natural changes

lesson.hook: Ice melting and paper burning are both changes. One you can undo, the other you cannot. What is the real difference?
lesson.example: Burning a candle shows both: the wax melting is a physical change; the wax vapour burning to form carbon dioxide and water is a chemical change.
lesson.activity: Change stations: melt ice, dissolve salt, burn a bit of paper (teacher), mix baking soda with vinegar, cut an apple and leave it. Groups decide physical or chemical and whether each can be reversed.

questions.q: Is rusting a physical or a chemical change?
questions.a: A chemical change: a new substance (rust) forms.

questions.q: What is ignition temperature?
questions.a: The lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire.

questions.q: Give one reversible change.
questions.a: Melting of ice, freezing of water, dissolving salt (any one).

questions.q: What is weathering?
questions.a: The slow breaking down of rocks by heat, water, wind and living things.

lesson.homework: List five changes in your home in a day and classify each as physical or chemical.

chapters.title: Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change

topics.title: Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change
topics.summary: Adolescence is the change from childhood to adulthood, roughly from 10 to 19 years.
notes: Adolescence is the change from childhood to adulthood, roughly from 10 to 19 years.
Puberty brings growth spurts and the development of the reproductive system; the timing differs from person to person, and that is normal.
Secondary sexual characteristics help distinguish males and females (voice change, facial hair, breast development).
Girls begin menstrual cycles; menstrual hygiene and support are important and nothing to be ashamed of.
Emotional changes — mood swings, wanting independence — are part of growing up.
Stay healthy with a balanced diet rich in iron and protein, personal hygiene, exercise, enough sleep, trusted adults to talk to, and avoiding harmful substances.
outcomes: Understand adolescence and puberty as natural stages of growth
Describe physical, emotional and behavioural changes
Know how to stay healthy through nutrition, hygiene, exercise and a balanced social life

lesson.hook: Between ages 10 and 19 your body and feelings change more than at almost any other time. Why does this happen, and how can you take care of yourself through it?
lesson.example: Iron-rich foods like green leafy vegetables, jaggery, dates and pulses help adolescents, especially girls, avoid anaemia.
lesson.activity: Anonymous question box: pupils write questions about growing up; the teacher answers them in class the next day. Groups also plan a week's balanced diet for an adolescent.

questions.q: At about what age does adolescence begin?
Why do adolescents need iron-rich food?
questions.a: For healthy blood and growth; lack of iron causes anaemia.

questions.q: Give one example of a secondary sexual characteristic.
questions.a: Deepening of the voice, facial hair, breast development (any one).

questions.q: Name two habits of personal hygiene.
questions.a: Bathing daily, washing hands, clean clothes, menstrual hygiene (any two).

lesson.homework: Write down one habit you will start this week to take care of your health.

topics.title: Heat Transfer in Nature
topics.summary: Heat flows from hotter to colder places in three ways: conduction, convection and radiation.
notes: Heat flows from hotter to colder places in three ways: conduction, convection and radiation.
Conduction passes heat through a solid without the particles moving from place to place; metals are good conductors, wood and plastic are insulators.
Convection moves heat in liquids and gases as warm fluid rises and cooler fluid sinks.
During the day land heats faster than the sea, warm air rises over land and a cool sea breeze blows in; at night the land breeze blows out to sea.
Radiation carries heat without any medium, as the Sun's heat reaches Earth; dark surfaces absorb more heat.
In the water cycle, evaporation, condensation and rain move water; some rainwater seeps into the ground and fills groundwater.
outcomes: Explain conduction, convection and radiation
Relate land and sea breezes to convection
Describe the water cycle and seepage of water into the ground

resources.title: Melting point of ice and boiling point of water

lesson.hook: Why does the handle of a steel spoon in hot tea get hot, why does a cool breeze blow from the sea during the day, and how does the Sun's heat reach us through empty space?
lesson.example: Pour warm water and cold water in two identical steel cups: touch them from outside — heat has reached the outer surface of the hot one by conduction.
lesson.activity: Convection in a beaker: heat water with a few potassium permanganate crystals at one side (teacher demonstration) and watch the coloured water rise and sink in a loop.

questions.q: How does heat reach us from the Sun?
Why does a sea breeze blow during the day?
questions.a: Land heats faster, warm air over it rises, and cooler air from the sea moves in.

questions.q: Why are cooking pan handles made of plastic or wood?
questions.a: They are poor conductors, so they do not get hot.

questions.q: In which way is heat mainly transferred in liquids?

lesson.homework: Find one example each of conduction, convection and radiation in your home.

topics.title: Measurement of Time and Motion
topics.summary: People measured time with the sun's shadow, water clocks and sand clocks; a simple pendulum swings with a regular time period.
notes: People measured time with the sun's shadow, water clocks and sand clocks; a simple pendulum swings with a regular time period.
The time period of a simple pendulum of a given length stays the same at a place.
The SI unit of time is the second (s); 60 s = 1 min, 60 min = 1 h.
Speed = distance covered / time taken; its SI unit is metre per second (m/s); km/h is also common.
Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time.
Uniform linear motion has constant speed in a straight line; non-uniform motion has changing speed.
outcomes: Measure time with a simple pendulum and know the SI unit of time
Compare slow and fast motion using speed
Calculate speed = distance / time and distinguish uniform and non-uniform motion

lesson.hook: Before clocks, how did people measure time? And how can we say for sure who is faster: a cyclist who goes 10 km in 30 minutes or a runner who goes 3 km in 12 minutes?
lesson.example: Cyclist: 10 km in 0.5 h → 20 km/h. Runner: 3 km in 0.2 h → 15 km/h. The cyclist is faster.
lesson.activity: Pendulum timing: groups hang a stone on a thread, time 20 oscillations, and find the time period. Then open the pendulum simulation and change the length to see how the period changes.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of time?
A bus goes 120 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?
What is one oscillation of a pendulum?
questions.a: One complete swing from one end to the other and back.

questions.q: A car's speed keeps changing in traffic. What kind of motion is this?

lesson.homework: Time how long you take to walk 100 steps and to run 100 steps; work out your speed each time.

topics.title: Life Processes in Animals
topics.summary: Life processes include nutrition, respiration, circulation, excretion and reproduction.
notes: Life processes include nutrition, respiration, circulation, excretion and reproduction.
The alimentary canal: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus, helped by the liver and pancreas.
Digestion breaks food into simple substances; digested food is absorbed through the walls of the small intestine into the blood.
Animals digest differently: grass-eating animals like cows chew the cud; amoeba digests food inside a food vacuole.
Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration releases energy from food inside cells, using oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide.
Other animals breathe through gills (fish), skin (earthworm, frog) or tiny holes called spiracles (insects).
outcomes: Describe the human digestive system and how food is digested and absorbed
Compare digestion in different animals
Explain breathing and respiration in humans and other animals

resources.title: Starch test: light and chlorophyll for photosynthesis

lesson.hook: A roti you eat at lunch becomes energy for playing in the evening. What happens to it on the way, and why do you breathe faster when you run?
lesson.example: Chew a piece of plain roti for two minutes: it starts to taste sweet, because saliva begins to break its starch into sugar.
lesson.activity: Open the 3D digestive system and run 'The journey of food'; pupils call out each organ. Then count breaths per minute sitting and after 20 jumps, and discuss why the rate rises.

questions.q: Where is most digested food absorbed?
Which gas do we breathe out more of than we breathe in?
How do fish breathe?
questions.a: Through gills, taking oxygen dissolved in water.

questions.q: What happens to food in the mouth?
questions.a: It is chewed and mixed with saliva, which starts digesting starch.

lesson.homework: Draw the human digestive system and label its parts.

topics.title: Life Processes in Plants
topics.summary: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water, with sunlight and chlorophyll, give glucose and oxygen.
notes: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water, with sunlight and chlorophyll, give glucose and oxygen.
Leaves are the food factories of the plant; the green pigment chlorophyll traps sunlight.
Tiny pores called stomata on leaves let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out.
Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots; phloem carries food from the leaves to all parts.
Plants also respire day and night, breaking down glucose to release energy.
The iodine test shows starch in a leaf that has been in sunlight.
outcomes: Explain photosynthesis and the role of leaves, chlorophyll, sunlight, air and water
Describe stomata and gas exchange
Explain transport in plants (xylem and phloem) and plant respiration

resources.title: Starch test: light and chlorophyll for photosynthesis

lesson.hook: A plant has no mouth and eats no food, yet it grows into a huge tree. Where does all that material come from?
lesson.example: Cover part of a potted plant's leaf with black paper for two days, then test it with iodine: only the uncovered part turns blue-black, showing that starch is made only where light falls.
lesson.activity: Coloured water: put a white flower or a celery stalk in water with red ink. Over a day pupils see the colour travel up — the path of the xylem.

questions.q: What are the raw materials of photosynthesis?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide and water (with sunlight and chlorophyll).

questions.q: What are stomata?
questions.a: Tiny pores on leaves through which gases pass in and out.

questions.q: Which tissue carries food in plants?
Do plants respire only at night?
questions.a: No, they respire all the time, day and night.

lesson.homework: Set up the covered-leaf experiment at home or in school and draw the result.

topics.title: Light: Shadows and Reflections
topics.summary: Luminous objects give out their own light (the Sun, a lamp); non-luminous ones are seen by the light they reflect.
notes: Luminous objects give out their own light (the Sun, a lamp); non-luminous ones are seen by the light they reflect.
Light travels in straight lines.
Transparent materials let almost all light pass, translucent materials some, opaque ones none.
A shadow forms when an opaque (or translucent) object blocks light; opaque objects cast darker shadows.
Reflection is light bouncing off a surface; a plane mirror forms an image that is erect, the same size, laterally inverted, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
A pinhole camera forms an upside-down image; a periscope uses two mirrors; a kaleidoscope uses mirrors to make patterns.
outcomes: Identify luminous and non-luminous objects
Show that light travels in a straight line and explain shadows
Describe reflection and images in a plane mirror, and make a pinhole camera and periscope

lesson.hook: Why can you not see around a corner, but a submarine captain can see above the water from deep below? Light takes a path you can predict.
lesson.example: Write AMBULANCE backwards on the front of an ambulance: drivers ahead see it the right way round in their mirrors because of lateral inversion.
lesson.activity: Build a pinhole camera from a box, butter paper and a pinhole; view a window or a candle and draw the inverted image. Then make a periscope with two mirrors in a cardboard tube.

questions.q: Is the Moon luminous?
What kind of image does a pinhole camera form?
What is lateral inversion?
questions.a: Left and right appear swapped in a mirror image.

questions.q: What does a periscope use to see above obstacles?

lesson.homework: Watch your shadow at 8 am, noon and 4 pm and describe how its length and direction change.

topics.title: Earth, Moon, and the Sun
topics.summary: The Earth rotates on its axis from west to east in about 24 hours, causing day and night and the apparent motion of the Sun, Moon and stars.
notes: The Earth rotates on its axis from west to east in about 24 hours, causing day and night and the apparent motion of the Sun, Moon and stars.
The Earth revolves around the Sun in about a year; the night sky changes through the year.
The Earth's axis is tilted; as the Earth goes round the Sun, first one hemisphere and then the other leans towards the Sun, causing seasons.
A solar eclipse happens when the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth and blocks the sunlight; never look at it directly.
A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon and the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon (full Moon night).
outcomes: Explain day and night by the Earth's rotation
Explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth's axis and its revolution
Explain solar and lunar eclipses

resources.title: Seasons: the Earth round the Sun

lesson.hook: Why is it summer in India when it is winter in Australia? And why does the Moon sometimes turn a coppery red?
lesson.example: In June the northern half of the Earth leans towards the Sun: India has long hot days (summer) while Australia, in the southern half, has winter.
lesson.activity: Open the 3D Seasons model and step through 'A year round the Sun'. Then with a torch (Sun), a ball (Earth) and a smaller ball (Moon), groups act out a solar and a lunar eclipse.

questions.q: What causes day and night?
questions.a: The rotation of the Earth on its axis.

questions.q: Why do we have seasons?
questions.a: The tilt of the Earth's axis as it revolves round the Sun.

questions.q: On which night can a lunar eclipse happen?
Why must we never look directly at a solar eclipse?
questions.a: The Sun's rays can permanently damage our eyes.

lesson.homework: Note the time of sunrise and sunset for a week from a calendar or phone and see how day length changes.

courses.title: Social Science: Exploring Society: India and Beyond (Parts 1 and 2), Class 7

topics.title: Geographical Diversity of India
topics.summary: The Himalayas in the north are young, high mountains that block cold winds and feed great rivers.
notes: The Himalayas in the north are young, high mountains that block cold winds and feed great rivers.
The Northern (Indo-Gangetic) Plains are flat and fertile, made by rivers like the Ganga, Yamuna and Brahmaputra.
The Thar Desert in the northwest is hot and dry.
The Peninsular (Deccan) Plateau is old and rocky, rich in minerals; it is edged by the Western and Eastern Ghats.
Coastal plains lie along the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal.
The islands: Andaman and Nicobar (Bay of Bengal) and Lakshadweep (Arabian Sea).
outcomes: Describe India's major physical divisions
Locate the Himalayas, plains, deserts, plateaus, coasts and islands
Explain how geography shapes life in each region

lesson.hook: In one country you can find snow-covered peaks, sand dunes, rainforests, and coral islands. Where are they in India?
lesson.example: The Western Ghats catch monsoon winds, giving heavy rain on the western slopes (Kodagu, Konkan) and less on the eastern side.
lesson.activity: Relief map: groups make a relief map of India with clay or paper-mâché, colouring mountains, plains, plateau, desert and coasts.

questions.q: Name India's two groups of islands.
Why are the northern plains fertile?
Which mountains edge the Deccan Plateau on the west?
How do the Himalayas help India?
questions.a: They block cold winds, bring rain and feed rivers.

lesson.homework: On an outline map of India, mark and colour the physical divisions.

topics.title: Understanding the Weather
topics.summary: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a place for a short time.
notes: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a place for a short time.
Its elements are temperature, rainfall, humidity, air pressure, wind speed and wind direction.
Instruments: thermometer (temperature), rain gauge (rainfall), hygrometer (humidity), barometer (air pressure), anemometer (wind speed) and wind vane (direction).
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) records weather and makes forecasts using satellites and weather stations.
Climate is the average weather of a place over many years.
outcomes: Name the elements of weather
Measure weather with simple instruments
Distinguish weather from climate

lesson.hook: Morning was sunny, afternoon was cloudy and by evening it poured. How can weather change so fast, and how do we measure it?
lesson.example: A rain gauge collects rain in a measuring jar; 10 mm of rain means a layer of water 10 mm deep would cover flat ground.
lesson.activity: School weather station: make a rain gauge from a bottle and a wind vane from card and a straw; record weather daily for two weeks.

questions.q: Which instrument measures wind speed?
What is humidity?
questions.a: The amount of water vapour in the air.

questions.q: How is climate different from weather?
questions.a: Climate is the average weather over many years; weather is short-term.

questions.q: Which organisation forecasts weather in India?

lesson.homework: Record the maximum and minimum temperature from a newspaper or app for a week and draw a graph.

topics.title: Climates of India
topics.summary: India has a tropical monsoon climate with four seasons: winter, summer, the southwest monsoon and the retreating monsoon.
notes: India has a tropical monsoon climate with four seasons: winter, summer, the southwest monsoon and the retreating monsoon.
In summer, land heats up and moist winds blow from the sea — the southwest monsoon — bringing most of India's rain from June to September.
Tamil Nadu gets much of its rain from the retreating (northeast) monsoon in October–December.
Climate varies with latitude, altitude, distance from the sea and mountains: Mawsynram is one of the wettest places on Earth; Jaisalmer is very dry.
Farming, water supply and festivals follow the monsoon.
Climate change is making rains less regular and heatwaves and floods more common.
outcomes: Describe India's seasons and the monsoon
Explain factors that make India's climate diverse
Understand the importance of the monsoon and the threat of climate change

resources.title: Seasons: the Earth round the Sun

lesson.hook: Why do farmers across India watch the sky in June and pray for the rains to arrive on time?
lesson.example: Shimla is cool in summer though it is far south of many hot places, because it is high up (altitude).
lesson.activity: Rainfall map: pupils colour an outline map of India by rainfall (very high, high, medium, low) and match it with crops grown.

questions.q: Which months bring the southwest monsoon?
Why is Shimla cool in summer?
questions.a: It is at a high altitude.

questions.q: Which state gets rain from the retreating monsoon?
Give one effect of climate change on India.
questions.a: Irregular rain, more heatwaves, floods or droughts (any one).

lesson.homework: Ask a farmer or elder how the monsoon has changed over the years.

topics.title: New Beginnings: Cities and States
topics.summary: After the Vedic period, groups settled into territories called janapadas.
notes: After the Vedic period, groups settled into territories called janapadas.
By the 6th century BCE, sixteen big states, the mahajanapadas, had formed, such as Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti.
Iron tools helped clear forests and grow more food, supporting towns — India's 'second urbanisation'.
Punch-marked coins made trade easier; cities had walls, moats and markets.
Some states were kingdoms ruled by kings; others, like the Vajji (Vaishali), were gana-sanghas where assemblies took decisions.
Magadha, with fertile land, iron and able rulers, grew to be the most powerful.
outcomes: Describe the growth of janapadas and mahajanapadas
Explain the second urbanisation in the Ganga plains
Compare kingdoms and republics (gana-sanghas)

lesson.hook: About 2,500 years ago, new cities with walls, markets and coins rose along the Ganga. What made them grow?
lesson.example: Vaishali, capital of the Vajji sangha, took decisions in an assembly — an early example of shared rule.
lesson.activity: Map the mahajanapadas: pupils mark the sixteen mahajanapadas on a map and discuss why most were in the Ganga plains.

questions.q: What were mahajanapadas?
questions.a: Sixteen large states in the 6th century BCE.

questions.q: Which mahajanapada became the most powerful?
How was a gana-sangha different from a kingdom?
questions.a: Decisions were taken by an assembly, not by one king.

questions.q: What helped towns to grow?
questions.a: Iron tools, surplus food, trade and coins.

lesson.homework: Write a short description of a day in a city 2,500 years ago.

topics.title: The Rise of Empires
topics.summary: An empire is a large state ruling over many regions and peoples.
notes: An empire is a large state ruling over many regions and peoples.
Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya empire (c. 321 BCE) with guidance from Chanakya (Kautilya), author of the Arthashastra.
The empire had a strong army, officials, spies and a capital at Pataliputra, described by the Greek envoy Megasthenes.
Ashoka was shaken by the Kalinga war and turned to dhamma — non-violence, tolerance and care for all living beings.
His edicts on rocks and pillars spread his message; the Lion Capital of Sarnath is India's national emblem.
Roads, trade and a common administration linked distant regions.
outcomes: Define an empire
Describe the rise of the Maurya empire and its administration
Explain Ashoka's dhamma and its importance

lesson.hook: A king wins a great war but is so upset by the suffering that he gives up war forever. Who was he?
lesson.example: The Ashoka Chakra on our national flag comes from Ashoka's pillar at Sarnath.
lesson.activity: Edict writing: pupils write a short 'edict' for their school on kindness and fairness, as Ashoka did for his empire.

questions.q: Who founded the Maurya empire?
Who wrote the Arthashastra?
Which war changed Ashoka's life?
What was Ashoka's dhamma?
questions.a: A way of life based on non-violence, tolerance and care for all.

lesson.homework: Find where Ashoka's edicts have been found in your state or near it.

topics.title: The Age of Reorganisation
topics.summary: After the Mauryas (c. 185 BCE), many kingdoms rose: the Shungas, Satavahanas in the Deccan, Kushanas in the northwest and Kharavela in Kalinga.
notes: After the Mauryas (c. 185 BCE), many kingdoms rose: the Shungas, Satavahanas in the Deccan, Kushanas in the northwest and Kharavela in Kalinga.
In the far south, the Chera, Chola and Pandya kingdoms flourished; Sangam poems describe life there.
Trade grew by land (the Silk Route) and sea (with Rome and Southeast Asia); Roman coins are found in south India.
Buddhism spread widely; stupas like Sanchi and Amaravati were built and decorated.
Gandhara and Mathura schools of art made early images of the Buddha.
It is called an age of reorganisation because society, trade and culture adapted and grew in new ways.
outcomes: Describe the kingdoms that followed the Mauryas
Explain growth in trade, art and religion in this period
Understand why it is called an age of reorganisation

lesson.hook: After a huge empire breaks up, does life fall apart — or do new things grow? Let's look at the centuries after the Mauryas.
lesson.example: Hoards of Roman gold coins found near Coimbatore show busy trade in pepper and cloth with the Roman empire.
lesson.activity: Trade routes: pupils draw the land and sea trade routes linking India to Rome, China and Southeast Asia, marking goods traded.

questions.q: Name one dynasty that ruled the Deccan after the Mauryas.
What are Sangam texts?
questions.a: Early Tamil poems describing life in south India.

questions.q: Which two schools of art made early Buddha images?
Why are Roman coins found in south India?

lesson.homework: Find a picture of the Sanchi stupa gateway and describe one carving.

chapters.title: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity

topics.title: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
topics.summary: The Gupta empire (c. 320–550 CE) was built by Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and Chandragupta II.
notes: The Gupta empire (c. 320–550 CE) was built by Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and Chandragupta II.
Samudragupta's victories are recorded on the Allahabad (Prayagraj) pillar by his poet Harishena.
Aryabhata explained that the Earth rotates, calculated π closely and used place value; Varahamihira wrote on astronomy.
Kalidasa wrote great works like Abhijnanashakuntalam and Meghaduta.
Art flourished: Ajanta paintings, temples, and the rust-free Iron Pillar at Delhi.
The Chinese pilgrim Faxian (Fa-Hien) described peaceful towns and charitable hospitals.
outcomes: Describe the Gupta rulers and their empire
Explain achievements in science, mathematics, literature and art
Assess why the period is called an age of creativity

lesson.hook: The idea of zero as a number and our place-value system took shape in India. Who were some of the great minds of this age?
lesson.example: The Iron Pillar at Mehrauli, Delhi, has stood for over 1,600 years with almost no rust — a marvel of ancient metallurgy.
lesson.activity: Gupta gallery: groups prepare a poster on one achiever (Aryabhata, Kalidasa, Varahamihira, the Ajanta painters) and present it.

questions.q: Who recorded Samudragupta's victories?
questions.a: His court poet Harishena, on the Allahabad pillar.

questions.q: Name one contribution of Aryabhata.
questions.a: Earth's rotation, value of π, place value (any one).

questions.q: Name a work by Kalidasa.
What is special about the Iron Pillar?
questions.a: It has not rusted for over 1,600 years.

lesson.homework: Write five sentences on why the Gupta age is called an age of creativity.

topics.title: How the Land Becomes Sacred
topics.summary: A sacred place is one people treat with special respect because of faith, stories or history.
notes: A sacred place is one people treat with special respect because of faith, stories or history.
Rivers such as the Ganga, Yamuna, Kaveri and Narmada are honoured as mothers.
Mountains like Kailash and hills like Tirumala and Sabarimala are pilgrimage sites.
Pilgrimage circuits (Char Dham, jyotirlingas, Shakti peethas) link all corners of India.
Places sacred to many faiths: Bodh Gaya (Buddhists), Sammed Shikharji (Jains), Amritsar (Sikhs), Ajmer Sharif (Sufi shrine), Velankanni (Christians).
Sacred groves protected by communities save forests and wildlife.
outcomes: Explain what makes a place sacred
Describe India's sacred geography — rivers, mountains, groves and pilgrimage sites
Understand how sacredness helps protect nature and bring people together

lesson.hook: Millions walk hundreds of kilometres to bathe in a river or reach a mountain shrine. Why do people feel some places are holy?
lesson.example: Sacred groves called 'devara kaadu' in Karnataka and 'kavu' in Kerala have protected rare trees for centuries.
lesson.activity: Pilgrimage map: pupils mark ten sacred places of different faiths on a map of India and note what each is known for.

questions.q: What is a sacred grove?
questions.a: A patch of forest protected by a community for religious reasons.

questions.q: Name a place sacred to Buddhists.
How do pilgrimages connect India?
questions.a: People travel across regions, sharing culture and trade.

questions.q: Give one river honoured as sacred.

lesson.homework: Find out about a sacred place near your home and why people visit it.

chapters.title: From the Rulers to the Ruled: Types of Governments

topics.title: From the Rulers to the Ruled: Types of Governments
