topics.summary: Maps use scales such as 1 : 50,000 — 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm (0.5 km) on the ground.
notes: Maps use scales such as 1 : 50,000 — 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm (0.5 km) on the ground.
Ratios can have more than two terms: cement : sand : gravel = 1 : 2 : 4.
To divide x in the ratio p : q : r, each part is x times its term divided by (p + q + r).
Pie charts show parts of a whole as angles out of 360°.
Direct proportion: both quantities increase together at the same rate.
Inverse proportion: as one increases the other decreases so that their product stays the same (workers × days = constant).
outcomes: Use ratios in maps and scale drawings
Work with ratios of more than two terms and divide a whole in a given ratio
Recognise and solve inverse proportion problems

lesson.hook: If 4 workers build a wall in 6 days, how long would 8 workers take? Is it 12 days or 3 days?
lesson.example: Workers × days = 4 × 6 = 24 worker-days. With 8 workers: 24 ÷ 8 = 3 days — inverse proportion.
lesson.activity: Map work: using a district map with a scale, pupils measure the distance between two towns in cm and convert it to real km.

questions.q: On a 1 : 100,000 map, two towns are 4.5 cm apart. How far apart are they?
Divide ₹1400 in the ratio 1 : 2 : 4.
A car at 60 km/h takes 3 hours. How long at 90 km/h?
Is 'number of pens and total cost' direct or inverse proportion?

lesson.homework: Draw a pie chart of how you spend a school day (sleep, school, study, play, others).

topics.title: Exploring Some Geometric Themes
topics.summary: Fractals are self-similar shapes: small parts look like the whole, as in ferns, cauliflower and coastlines.
notes: Fractals are self-similar shapes: small parts look like the whole, as in ferns, cauliflower and coastlines.
The Sierpinski gasket is made by repeatedly removing the middle triangle from each triangle.
The Koch snowflake grows by adding a small triangle on the middle third of each side, again and again.
Solids such as cuboids, prisms, pyramids, cylinders and cones can be drawn from different views (top, front, side) and made from nets.
For polyhedra, Euler's formula links faces, vertices and edges: F + V − E = 2.
outcomes: Explore self-similar fractals like the Sierpinski triangle and Koch snowflake
Visualise 3D solids from their nets and views
Relate faces, edges and vertices of polyhedra

lesson.hook: Look closely at a fern leaf: each small leaflet looks like a copy of the whole leaf. How can a shape contain copies of itself?
lesson.example: A cube has 6 faces, 8 vertices and 12 edges: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2. A square pyramid has 5 faces, 5 vertices and 8 edges: 5 + 5 − 8 = 2.
lesson.activity: Pupils draw the first three stages of the Sierpinski triangle on dot paper and count the shaded triangles at each stage (1, 3, 9 …).

questions.q: What is a fractal?
questions.a: A shape whose small parts look like the whole (self-similar).

questions.q: How many shaded triangles are there at stage 4 of the Sierpinski gasket (starting with 1)?
Check Euler's formula for a triangular prism.

lesson.homework: Make a net of a cube and a square pyramid from card and fold them.

topics.title: Tales by Dots and Lines
topics.summary: The mean is the balance point: the total distance of values above it equals the total distance of values below it.
notes: The mean is the balance point: the total distance of values above it equals the total distance of values below it.
Adding a value greater than the mean raises it; adding a smaller one lowers it.
The median changes less when an extreme value is added.
Line graphs show how a quantity changes over time, such as temperature through a day.
Reading graphs carefully means checking scales, labels and whether the axis starts at zero; misleading graphs can exaggerate change.
outcomes: Understand the mean as a balance point of data
See how adding values changes the mean and median
Read and draw line graphs and interpret data displays

lesson.hook: If a cricketer scores 0 in one match, how much does it pull down his average? Much more than one bad match should?
lesson.example: Scores 40, 50, 60: mean 50. Add a 0: mean = 150 ÷ 4 = 37.5, while the median goes from 50 to 45.
lesson.activity: Balance the ruler: pupils place coins at marks 2, 5 and 8 on a ruler and find the point where it balances on a pencil — the mean position (5).

questions.q: Find the mean of 12, 15, 18, 21, 24.
If 50 is added to the data above, does the mean go up or down?
What kind of graph best shows temperature over a day?
Why can a graph whose axis does not start at zero mislead?
questions.a: It makes small differences look large.

lesson.homework: Record your study time every day for a week and draw a line graph; write two observations.

topics.title: Algebra Play
topics.summary: Algebra lets us reason about all numbers at once, not just one example.
notes: Algebra lets us reason about all numbers at once, not just one example.
Think-of-a-number tricks work because the unknown cancels: (2n + 10) ÷ 2 − n = 5.
In number pyramids, each block is the sum of the two below; algebra finds missing blocks.
Grid puzzles and the largest-product problem can be explained using expressions.
A two-digit number with digits a and b is 10a + b; this explains why (10a + b) − (10b + a) is always a multiple of 9.
outcomes: Use algebra to explain number tricks and patterns
Solve number pyramids and grid puzzles with algebra
Justify divisibility rules using algebraic expressions

lesson.hook: Think of a number. Double it, add 10, halve it, then subtract the number you first thought of. Your answer is 5! How did I know?
lesson.example: Reverse and subtract: 72 − 27 = 45 = 9 × 5. In general (10a + b) − (10b + a) = 9(a − b), always a multiple of 9.
lesson.activity: Pupils invent their own think-of-a-number trick, test it on a partner, and prove it with algebra.

questions.q: Show that the sum of three consecutive numbers is always divisible by 3.
Write the two-digit number with tens digit x and units digit y.
In a number pyramid, the bottom blocks are a, 3 and 5, and the top is 20. Find a.
questions.a: Middle blocks: a + 3 and 8; top = a + 11 = 20, so a = 9.

lesson.homework: Prove that the sum of any two odd numbers is even, using algebra.

topics.title: Area
topics.summary: Area of a rectangle = length × breadth; square = side².
notes: Area of a rectangle = length × breadth; square = side².
Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height.
Area of a parallelogram = base × height (cut and move a triangle to make a rectangle).
Area of a rhombus = ½ × product of its diagonals.
Area of a trapezium = ½ × height × (sum of parallel sides).
Any polygon can be split into triangles, whose areas are added.
outcomes: Find areas of triangles, parallelograms, rhombuses and trapeziums
Find the area of any polygon by splitting it into triangles
Apply area formulas to real problems

lesson.hook: A farmer's field is shaped like a trapezium, not a rectangle. How can he find its area to buy the right amount of seed?
lesson.example: Trapezium field: parallel sides 40 m and 60 m, height 30 m. Area = ½ × 30 × (40 + 60) = 1500 m².
lesson.activity: Cut and rearrange: pupils cut a paper parallelogram and move one triangle to make a rectangle; then join two copies of a trapezium to form a parallelogram and derive its area formula.

questions.q: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 9 cm and height 5 cm.
Find the area of a rhombus with diagonals 10 cm and 16 cm.
Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 8 cm and 12 cm and height 5 cm.

lesson.homework: Draw the floor plan of one room at home, split it into rectangles and triangles, and find its area.

chapters.title: Exploring the Investigative World of Science

topics.title: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
topics.summary: An investigation starts with a question that can be tested.
notes: An investigation starts with a question that can be tested.
The variable you change is the independent variable; what you measure is the dependent variable; everything else must be kept the same (controlled) for a fair test.
A prediction says what you expect and why; the results may agree or disagree with it.
Repeat measurements and take an average to make results reliable.
Record results in a table, show them in a graph, and state a conclusion based on the evidence.
outcomes: Plan a fair investigation: question, variables, prediction, test, conclusion
Change one variable at a time and keep others the same
Record and present results in tables and graphs

lesson.hook: Does a ball bounce higher on a cement floor or on grass? How would you design a test so that nobody could argue with your answer?
lesson.example: Bounce test: drop the same ball from the same height (1 m) on cement, wood and grass; measure the bounce three times on each and average. Only the surface changes, so the test is fair.
lesson.activity: Groups plan and run a fair test on a question of their choice (for example, 'Does sugar dissolve faster in hot water?'), naming the variables, recording three trials and presenting a bar graph.

questions.q: What is a fair test?
questions.a: A test in which only one variable is changed and all others are kept the same.

questions.q: Why do we repeat measurements?
questions.a: To reduce errors and get a reliable average.

questions.q: In the bounce test, what is the dependent variable?

lesson.homework: Write a plan for a fair test to find which cloth dries fastest.

chapters.title: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye

topics.title: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
topics.summary: All living things are made of cells; some organisms are a single cell, others have billions.
notes: All living things are made of cells; some organisms are a single cell, others have billions.
Cells have different shapes for different jobs: long nerve cells carry messages, muscle cells contract, red blood cells carry oxygen.
Levels of organisation: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism.
Microorganisms include bacteria, fungi, protozoa, algae and viruses (which live only inside other cells).
Microbes clean the environment by decomposing waste, make curd, bread and idli, and some cause diseases.
Microalgae in water make much of the oxygen we breathe and are the base of water food chains.
outcomes: Describe the cell as the basic unit of life and how cell shapes suit their jobs
Explain the levels of organisation: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
Describe microorganisms and their roles in the environment, food and health

lesson.hook: A drop of pond water looks clear, but under a microscope it is crowded with living things. What lives in the world too small to see?
lesson.example: Curd is made when Lactobacillus bacteria from a spoonful of old curd multiply in warm milk and turn its sugar into acid, which sets the milk.
lesson.activity: Open the 3D animal and plant cells and compare them. Then set up two bowls of warm milk, one with a spoon of curd and one without, and check the next day.

questions.q: What is the basic unit of life?
Put in order: organ, cell, organism, tissue, organ system.
questions.a: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.

questions.q: Name one useful and one harmful microorganism.
questions.a: Useful: Lactobacillus (curd), yeast (bread). Harmful: the bacteria or viruses that cause diseases.

questions.q: How do microbes help clean the environment?
questions.a: They decompose dead plants, animals and waste into simple substances.

lesson.homework: List five foods made with the help of microorganisms.

topics.title: Health: The Ultimate Treasure
topics.summary: Health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just not being sick.
notes: Health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just not being sick.
A healthy lifestyle: balanced diet, exercise, sleep, hygiene, a clean environment and good relationships.
Signs and symptoms tell us we are unwell; a doctor diagnoses the disease.
Communicable diseases are caused by microbes and spread through air, water, food, contact or carriers such as mosquitoes (malaria, dengue).
Non-communicable diseases such as diabetes, heart disease and some cancers are linked to lifestyle and genes.
Prevention: clean water, handwashing, mosquito control, vaccines that train the body's defences, and treatment when needed.
outcomes: Understand health as physical, mental and social well-being
Distinguish communicable and non-communicable diseases and how they spread
Describe ways to prevent and control diseases, including vaccination

lesson.hook: You have no fever and no cough. Does that mean you are healthy? What else does being healthy include?
lesson.example: Dengue is spread by the Aedes mosquito, which breeds in clean stagnant water in coolers, pots and tyres; removing that water once a week breaks its cycle.
lesson.activity: Disease detectives: groups get cards with a disease (cold, cholera, malaria, diabetes, tuberculosis) and find how it spreads (or develops) and one way to prevent it, then present to the class.

questions.q: Is diabetes communicable or non-communicable?
How does a vaccine protect us?
questions.a: It trains the body's defence system to recognise and fight a disease-causing microbe.

questions.q: Name a disease spread by mosquitoes.
Why is handwashing important?
questions.a: It removes germs that spread diseases through food and touch.

lesson.homework: Check your home for places where water collects and could breed mosquitoes; list them and what you did.

topics.title: Electricity: Magnetic and Heating Effects
topics.summary: An electric current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it: a compass needle near it moves.
notes: An electric current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it: a compass needle near it moves.
A coil of wire around an iron nail becomes an electromagnet when current flows; it loses its magnetism when the current stops.
More turns or more current make a stronger electromagnet; electromagnets are used in cranes, electric bells, motors and speakers.
A wire carrying current gets hot: the heating effect is used in heaters, irons, kettles and fuses.
A voltaic cell produces electricity from a chemical reaction between two different metals and a solution.
Dry cells are used in torches and remotes; rechargeable batteries can be recharged; used batteries must be disposed of safely.
outcomes: Show the magnetic effect of electric current and make an electromagnet
Explain the heating effect of current and its uses
Describe how cells and batteries (voltaic, dry, rechargeable) produce electricity

resources.title: Magnetic field of a bar magnet

lesson.hook: At a scrap yard, a crane lifts a whole car with a magnet and then drops it when switched off. How can a magnet be turned on and off?
lesson.example: Wind 50 turns of insulated wire around an iron nail and connect it to a cell: the nail picks up pins. Disconnect it and the pins drop.
lesson.activity: Build an electromagnet with a nail, wire and cells; count the pins it lifts with 20, 40 and 60 turns. Then show the 3D electric motor running on the same effect.

questions.q: How can you make an electromagnet stronger?
questions.a: Use more turns of wire or more current (more cells).

questions.q: Name two appliances that use the heating effect.
questions.a: Electric iron, heater, kettle, toaster (any two).

questions.q: What happens to an electromagnet when the current is switched off?
Why should used batteries not be thrown in ordinary garbage?
questions.a: They contain harmful chemicals that pollute soil and water.

lesson.homework: Find three things at home that use an electromagnet and three that use the heating effect of current.

topics.title: Exploring Forces
topics.summary: A force is a push or a pull; it can change an object's speed, direction or shape.
notes: A force is a push or a pull; it can change an object's speed, direction or shape.
Contact forces need touching: muscular force and friction, which opposes motion between surfaces.
Non-contact forces act from a distance: gravitational, magnetic and electrostatic forces.
Weight is the force of gravity on an object; it is measured with a spring balance, in newtons (N).
Mass is the amount of matter and does not change from place to place; weight changes (less on the Moon).
An object in water feels an upward push (buoyant force); it floats if this push balances its weight.
outcomes: Understand force as a push or a pull and its effects
Distinguish contact forces (muscular, friction) from non-contact forces (gravity, magnetic, electrostatic)
Understand weight and measure it; explain floating and sinking

resources.title: Magnetic field of a bar magnet

lesson.hook: You push a door, pull a drawer, and an apple falls from a tree with nobody touching it. What is common to all three?
lesson.example: Rub a plastic comb in dry hair and hold it near small bits of paper: they jump to the comb — an electrostatic force acting without contact.
lesson.activity: Force stations: roll a ball on a smooth floor and on a carpet (friction), move a paper clip with a magnet under the table (magnetic), lift bits of paper with a rubbed comb (electrostatic), and weigh objects with a spring balance.

questions.q: Give one example of a non-contact force.
questions.a: Gravity, magnetic force or electrostatic force (any one).

questions.q: In what unit is weight measured?
Why is it easier to walk on a rough road than on ice?
questions.a: The rough road gives more friction, so our feet do not slip.

questions.q: Why does a piece of wood float in water?
questions.a: The upward buoyant force of water balances its weight.

lesson.homework: Find five places at home where friction is useful and two where it is a nuisance.

topics.title: Pressure, Winds, Storms, and Cyclones
topics.summary: Pressure = force / area: the same force on a smaller area gives more pressure (sharp knives, nails).
notes: Pressure = force / area: the same force on a smaller area gives more pressure (sharp knives, nails).
Air exerts pressure in all directions: a suction cup sticks, a drinking straw works.
Air moves from a region of high pressure to low pressure: this is wind.
Uneven heating of land and water, and of the equator and poles, creates pressure differences and winds.
Thunderstorms form from rising warm moist air; lightning is a giant electric spark — stay indoors, avoid tall trees and open fields.
A cyclone is a huge spinning storm around a low-pressure centre; warnings from the weather department and shelters save lives.
outcomes: Define pressure and relate it to force and area
Show that air exerts pressure and explain how differences in pressure make wind
Explain storms, thunderstorms, lightning safety and cyclones

resources.title: Seasons: the Earth round the Sun

lesson.hook: Why does a sharp knife cut better than a blunt one, and why do strong winds blow before a storm?
lesson.example: A school bag with thin straps hurts the shoulders more than one with broad straps: the same weight on a smaller area means more pressure.
lesson.activity: Air pressure tricks: cover a full glass of water with a card and turn it upside down (the card stays); blow between two hanging balloons and watch them move together.

questions.q: Why are the wheels of trucks wide?
questions.a: Wider wheels spread the weight over more area, reducing pressure on the road.

questions.q: In which direction does wind blow: high to low pressure or low to high?
questions.a: From high pressure to low pressure.

questions.q: Where should you not stand during a thunderstorm?
questions.a: Under a tall tree or in an open field.

questions.q: What is the calm centre of a cyclone called?

lesson.homework: Find out which cyclones hit India's coasts in recent years and how people were warned.

topics.title: Particulate Nature of Matter
topics.summary: Matter is made of extremely small particles with spaces between them.
notes: Matter is made of extremely small particles with spaces between them.
Particles are always moving and attract each other.
In solids particles are tightly packed and only vibrate: fixed shape and volume.
In liquids particles are close but can slide past each other: fixed volume, no fixed shape.
In gases particles are far apart and move freely: no fixed shape or volume, easily compressed.
Diffusion is the spreading of particles into each other; it is fastest in gases and faster at higher temperatures.
outcomes: Understand that matter is made of tiny particles with spaces between them
Explain solids, liquids and gases by the arrangement and movement of particles
Explain diffusion and changes of state with the particle model

resources.title: Melting point of ice and boiling point of water

lesson.hook: Open a bottle of perfume in one corner and soon the whole room smells of it. How did the smell travel?
lesson.example: Dissolve a spoon of sugar in a full glass of water: the level hardly rises, because sugar particles fit into the spaces between water particles.
lesson.activity: Act out the states: pupils stand close and vibrate (solid), move around slowly holding hands loosely (liquid), then spread out and move quickly (gas). Then drop ink into cold and hot water to compare diffusion.

questions.q: Why do gases have no fixed shape?
questions.a: Their particles are far apart and move freely.

questions.q: In which state do particles only vibrate in fixed positions?
Why does ink spread faster in hot water?
questions.a: Particles move faster at higher temperature.

questions.q: Why can a gas be compressed easily?
questions.a: There are large spaces between its particles.

lesson.homework: Give three examples of diffusion in daily life.

chapters.title: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures

topics.title: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
topics.summary: A mixture has two or more substances not chemically joined; its parts keep their properties and can be separated by physical methods.
notes: A mixture has two or more substances not chemically joined; its parts keep their properties and can be separated by physical methods.
Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Mixtures can be uniform throughout (homogeneous, like salt solution) or not (heterogeneous, like sand in water).
A pure substance has a fixed composition and fixed properties such as melting and boiling points.
Elements are made of only one kind of atom (iron, oxygen); compounds have two or more elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio (water, salt).
Minerals are naturally occurring solid substances with a definite composition, found in rocks.
outcomes: Distinguish mixtures from pure substances
Classify pure substances as elements and compounds
Describe types of mixtures and minerals as naturally occurring substances

lesson.hook: Air, sea water and a gold ring: which are mixtures and which are pure? How could we tell?
lesson.example: Iron filings and sulphur powder mixed together can be separated with a magnet (a mixture); heated together they form iron sulphide, which a magnet cannot separate (a compound).
lesson.activity: Sorting cards: groups classify air, water, salt, sea water, iron, brass, sugar, milk, oxygen and soil into element, compound and mixture, then check with the 3D atoms and molecules.

questions.q: Is water an element, a compound or a mixture?
Give one example of a homogeneous mixture.
questions.a: Salt solution, sugar solution, air (any one).

questions.q: How is a compound different from a mixture?
questions.a: In a compound elements are chemically joined in a fixed ratio; in a mixture they are not and can be separated physically.

questions.q: What is a mineral?
questions.a: A naturally occurring solid with a definite composition, found in rocks.

lesson.homework: List ten things in your kitchen and classify each as element, compound or mixture.

chapters.title: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions

topics.title: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions
topics.summary: In a solution, the substance that dissolves is the solute and the substance it dissolves in is the solvent; water dissolves so much it is called a universal solvent.
notes: In a solution, the substance that dissolves is the solute and the substance it dissolves in is the solvent; water dissolves so much it is called a universal solvent.
A saturated solution cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature.
More solid usually dissolves in hot water; gases dissolve less as temperature rises (fish struggle in warm water).
Density = mass / volume; it tells how tightly matter is packed.
Objects less dense than water float; denser ones sink.
Density usually decreases with heating (except water between 0 °C and 4 °C) and increases with pressure for gases.
outcomes: Define solute, solvent and solution and saturated solutions
Explain how temperature affects solubility of solids and gases
Explain density and why objects float or sink

lesson.hook: Why does a fresh egg sink in tap water but float when you stir in lots of salt?
lesson.example: An egg sinks in tap water because it is denser than water; adding salt makes the water denser than the egg, so the egg floats.
lesson.activity: Saturation race: add spoonfuls of salt to 100 mL of cold and warm water, stirring, and count spoons until no more dissolves. Then do the floating-egg demonstration.

questions.q: In sugar solution, which is the solute and which the solvent?
questions.a: Sugar is the solute; water is the solvent.

questions.q: What is a saturated solution?
questions.a: One that can dissolve no more solute at that temperature.

questions.q: Why does oil float on water?
questions.a: Oil is less dense than water.

questions.q: A block has a mass of 200 g and a volume of 100 cm³. What is its density? Will it float?
questions.a: 2 g/cm³; it will sink (denser than water).

lesson.homework: Test five objects at home in a bucket of water; predict first, then record which float and sink.

topics.title: Light: Mirrors and Lenses
topics.summary: A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere: concave (curved inward) or convex (curved outward).
notes: A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere: concave (curved inward) or convex (curved outward).
Concave mirrors can form enlarged images of near objects (shaving and dentist's mirrors) or real inverted images; they gather light in torches and solar cookers.
Convex mirrors always form small, erect images and show a wide area (rear-view mirrors, road corners).
Laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; the incident ray, reflected ray and the normal lie in one plane.
A lens is a transparent piece that bends light: convex lenses are thicker in the middle and converge light (magnifying glass); concave lenses are thinner in the middle and diverge light.
Lenses are used in spectacles, microscopes, cameras and our eyes.
outcomes: Identify concave and convex spherical mirrors and their images
State the laws of reflection
Identify convex and concave lenses and their uses

resources.title: Focal length of a convex lens and a concave mirror

lesson.hook: The back of a steel spoon shows a small upright face; the inside shows an upside-down one. Why do curved mirrors play such tricks?
lesson.example: A convex mirror at a hilly road bend lets drivers see vehicles coming round the corner, because it shows a wide area in a small image.
lesson.activity: Spoon mirrors and lens hunt: pupils look at their images in both sides of a spoon at different distances, then use a magnifying glass to focus sunlight or a window onto paper.

questions.q: Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror?
State the first law of reflection.
questions.a: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

questions.q: Which lens is used as a magnifying glass?
Why do dentists use concave mirrors?
questions.a: They give an enlarged, upright image of teeth held close.

lesson.homework: Find three curved mirrors or lenses in your surroundings and say what kind each is.

topics.title: Keeping Time with the Skies
topics.summary: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight; as it orbits the Earth we see different amounts of its lit half: the phases.
notes: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight; as it orbits the Earth we see different amounts of its lit half: the phases.
From new Moon it waxes to full Moon in about 15 days and wanes back; a full cycle is about 29.5 days.
The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day.
A lunar calendar follows the Moon's cycle (about 354 days a year); a solar calendar follows the Sun (365¼ days).
Luni-solar calendars (most Indian festival calendars) add an extra month now and then to stay in step with the seasons.
The Indian National Calendar (Saka calendar) starts on 22 March (21 March in a leap year) with the month Chaitra.
outcomes: Explain the phases of the Moon and predict where it will be seen
Understand lunar, solar and luni-solar calendars
Know the Indian National Calendar

resources.title: Seasons: the Earth round the Sun

lesson.hook: Festivals like Eid, Diwali and Holi fall on different dates of the English calendar every year, but Makar Sankranti hardly moves. Why?
lesson.example: Eid follows the lunar calendar, which is about 11 days shorter than the solar year, so it comes about 11 days earlier each year by the English calendar.
lesson.activity: Moon diary: for two weeks pupils draw the Moon's shape and note the time and direction they saw it. In class, act out the phases with a lamp (Sun), a ball on a stick (Moon) and the pupil's head (Earth).

questions.q: Why does the Moon show phases?
questions.a: We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits the Earth.

questions.q: About how long is one cycle of the Moon's phases?
What is a luni-solar calendar?
questions.a: One that follows the Moon's months but adds extra months to keep in step with the solar year.

questions.q: On which date does the Indian National Calendar year begin?
questions.a: 22 March (21 March in a leap year).

lesson.homework: Find the dates of three festivals this year and next year and see which follow the Moon.

topics.title: How Nature Works in Harmony
topics.summary: An ecosystem is a community of plants, animals and microorganisms living together with their non-living surroundings (soil, water, air, sunlight).
notes: An ecosystem is a community of plants, animals and microorganisms living together with their non-living surroundings (soil, water, air, sunlight).
Producers (green plants) make food; herbivores, carnivores and omnivores are consumers; decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients.
Food chains show who eats whom; many food chains connect into a food web.
Nature recycles waste: dead leaves and dung become soil through decomposers.
A change in one part (losing a predator, pollution, cutting trees) spreads through the whole ecosystem.
Healthy ecosystems give clean air and water, fertile soil, pollinators and pest control for farms; a pond, a garden and a farm are human-made ecosystems.
outcomes: Describe an ecosystem and who lives together in it
Build food chains and food webs and explain decomposers
Explain how one change affects others, and the benefits of healthy ecosystems, including farms

lesson.hook: If all the frogs in a village pond disappeared, what else would change? Nature is a web: pull one thread and others move.
lesson.example: Farmers who protect owls and snakes in their fields have fewer rats eating their grain — predators keep pests in check.
lesson.activity: Pond or garden survey: groups list the living things they find in a small patch of school garden and build food chains from them, then connect them into a web on chart paper.

questions.q: Give an example of a food chain with three links.
What do decomposers do?
questions.a: They break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil.

questions.q: Why are bees important to farmers?
questions.a: They pollinate flowers so crops can form fruits and seeds.

questions.q: What could happen if all the snakes in an area were killed?
questions.a: Rats would increase and damage crops.

lesson.homework: Draw a food web of at least eight living things you can find around your home.

chapters.title: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet

topics.title: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet
topics.summary: The Earth is at the right distance from the Sun: not too hot, not too cold, so water stays liquid.
notes: The Earth is at the right distance from the Sun: not too hot, not too cold, so water stays liquid.
The atmosphere gives oxygen, keeps the temperature steady through the greenhouse effect, and the ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet rays.
Water covers most of the Earth and is continually recycled by the water cycle.
Soil forms slowly from weathered rock and decayed matter and supports plants.
The Earth's magnetic field shields life from harmful particles from the Sun.
Human activities — burning fuels, deforestation, pollution — are changing the climate; we must protect our only home.
outcomes: Explain what makes the Earth suitable for life
Describe the atmosphere, water and soil as life-support systems
Understand human impacts on the Earth and how to protect it

lesson.hook: Of all the planets we know, only one has rivers, forests and people. What does the Earth have that Mars and Venus do not?
lesson.example: Venus is closer to the Sun and has a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat, making it hotter than Mercury; Mars has a thin atmosphere and is freezing. The Earth's atmosphere keeps it just right.
lesson.activity: Open the 3D Earth's layers and the solar system; compare the Earth with its neighbours. Then groups make 'Earth report cards' listing three things that support life and one threat to each.

questions.q: Why can water stay liquid on the Earth?
questions.a: The Earth is at the right distance from the Sun and has an atmosphere that keeps the temperature suitable.

questions.q: What does the ozone layer do?
questions.a: It absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun.

questions.q: Name two human activities that harm the Earth's climate.
questions.a: Burning fossil fuels and cutting forests (or other valid examples).

questions.q: What protects the Earth from harmful particles from the Sun?

lesson.homework: Write a letter to a younger student explaining three things that make the Earth special and one thing we can do to protect it.

courses.title: Social Science: Exploring Society: India and Beyond (Parts 1 and 2), Class 8

topics.title: Natural Resources and Their Use
topics.summary: Natural resources are things from nature that people use: air, water, soil, forests, minerals and energy.
notes: Natural resources are things from nature that people use: air, water, soil, forests, minerals and energy.
Renewable resources (sunlight, wind, water, forests) can be replaced naturally if used wisely.
Non-renewable resources (coal, petroleum, minerals) take millions of years to form and can run out.
Over-use causes problems: falling groundwater, deforestation, soil erosion and pollution.
Sustainable use means meeting today's needs without harming future generations.
Traditional practices — stepwells, sacred groves, crop rotation — and new ones like solar power help conserve resources.
outcomes: Classify natural resources as renewable and non-renewable
Explain how resources are used and over-used
Suggest ways of sustainable use

lesson.hook: A borewell that gave water at 50 feet now needs 500 feet. What happened to the water under our feet?
lesson.example: Rainwater harvesting in Chennai's buildings (made compulsory in 2003) helped raise groundwater levels.
lesson.activity: Resource audit: groups list resources used in school in one day (water, paper, electricity) and propose three savings.

questions.q: Give two examples of non-renewable resources.
questions.a: Coal, petroleum, natural gas, minerals (any two).

questions.q: What is sustainable development?
questions.a: Using resources to meet present needs without harming future generations.

questions.q: Why is groundwater falling in many places?
questions.a: More water is pumped out than rain puts back.

questions.q: Name one traditional way of conserving water.

lesson.homework: Measure how much water your family uses in a day and suggest two ways to save it.

topics.title: Reshaping India's Political Map
topics.summary: From the 13th century, the Delhi Sultanate ruled much of north India under dynasties like the Mamluks, Khaljis and Tughlaqs.
notes: From the 13th century, the Delhi Sultanate ruled much of north India under dynasties like the Mamluks, Khaljis and Tughlaqs.
Invasions, battles and heavy taxes brought hardship; many temples and centres of learning were destroyed.
In the south, the Vijayanagara empire (founded 1336) under rulers like Krishnadevaraya flourished at Hampi.
Babur founded the Mughal empire after the battle of Panipat (1526); Akbar expanded it and built a strong administration.
Rulers like the Rajputs, Ahoms and others resisted; many kingdoms stayed independent.
Society responded with resilience: Bhakti and Sufi movements, regional languages and new art forms grew.
outcomes: Describe the rise of the Delhi Sultanate and the Vijayanagara empire
Explain the coming of the Mughals
Discuss how Indian society responded to these changes

lesson.hook: The Qutub Minar in Delhi and the ruins of Hampi in Karnataka were built by very different rulers in the same centuries. Who were they?
lesson.example: The Ahoms of Assam defeated the Mughal navy at the battle of Saraighat (1671), led by Lachit Borphukan.
lesson.activity: Map of power: pupils shade an outline map to show the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara and other kingdoms around 1400 CE.

questions.q: What was the capital of the Vijayanagara empire?
Which battle founded Mughal rule in India?
Who led the Ahoms at Saraighat?
Name one Delhi Sultanate dynasty.
questions.a: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid or Lodi (any one).

lesson.homework: Write about one monument from this period in your state.

topics.title: The Rise of the Marathas
topics.summary: Chhatrapati Shivaji (1630–1680) built an independent Maratha state (swarajya) in western India.
notes: Chhatrapati Shivaji (1630–1680) built an independent Maratha state (swarajya) in western India.
He used hill forts, guerrilla warfare and a strong navy along the Konkan coast.
He was crowned in 1674 at Raigad and set up a council of eight ministers (Ashta Pradhan).
Revenue systems (chauth and sardeshmukhi) and fair treatment of farmers supported the state.
In the 18th century, under the Peshwas, Maratha power spread across much of India.
The Marathas faced defeat at the third battle of Panipat (1761) but remained a major power until the British wars.
outcomes: Describe how Shivaji founded the Maratha state
Explain Maratha administration and military methods
Trace the expansion of Maratha power in the 18th century

lesson.hook: A young leader captured hill forts, built a navy and challenged a great empire. How did Shivaji do it?
lesson.example: Sindhudurg sea fort, built by Shivaji on an island off the Konkan coast, protected his navy.
lesson.activity: Fort study: groups research one Maratha fort and explain how its location helped defence.

questions.q: Where was Shivaji crowned?
What was the Ashta Pradhan?
Why did Shivaji build a navy?
questions.a: To protect the coast from foreign and rival powers.

questions.q: When was the third battle of Panipat?

lesson.homework: Write a short biography of Shivaji in 100 words.

topics.title: The Colonial Era in India
topics.summary: The Portuguese, Dutch, French and English came to India to trade in spices, cotton and indigo.
notes: The Portuguese, Dutch, French and English came to India to trade in spices, cotton and indigo.
The English East India Company won the battles of Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) and gained the right to collect revenue in Bengal.
Through wars and treaties, the Company controlled most of India by the mid-19th century.
Indian wealth was drained to Britain; high land revenue ruined farmers and caused famines.
Cheap British machine-made cloth destroyed India's handloom industry.
After the revolt of 1857, the British Crown took over direct rule.
outcomes: Explain how European trading companies came to rule India
Describe the economic effects of British rule
Understand the impact on Indian industries, farmers and society

lesson.hook: A company that came to trade spices ended up ruling a whole subcontinent. How did that happen?
lesson.example: Once, Indian textiles made up a large share of world trade; by the 1900s India was importing cloth from Britain.
lesson.activity: Two sides of the ledger: groups list what Britain gained and what India lost from colonial rule, using facts from the lesson.

questions.q: Which battle in 1757 gave the Company power in Bengal?
What is meant by the 'drain of wealth'?
questions.a: India's wealth flowing to Britain without equal return.

questions.q: How did British rule affect Indian weavers?
questions.a: Cheap machine cloth ruined the handloom industry.

questions.q: What happened after the revolt of 1857?
questions.a: The British Crown took direct control of India.

lesson.homework: Find out about a famine during British rule and write what caused it.

chapters.title: Universal Franchise and India's Electoral System

topics.title: Universal Franchise and India's Electoral System
topics.summary: Universal adult franchise means every adult citizen (18+) can vote, regardless of gender, caste, religion, wealth or education.
notes: Universal adult franchise means every adult citizen (18+) can vote, regardless of gender, caste, religion, wealth or education.
India gave this right to all from the start in 1950, when many countries still limited voting.
The Election Commission of India conducts free and fair elections.
The country is divided into constituencies; candidates stand, campaign, and voters choose by secret ballot.
Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and VVPAT slips are used today.
Some seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to ensure representation.
outcomes: Explain universal adult franchise
Describe how elections are conducted in India
Understand the role of the Election Commission

lesson.hook: In 1951–52, India held its first general election with 17 crore voters, most of whom had never voted. How was it done?
lesson.example: A polling booth is set up even for a single voter in a remote forest in Gir, Gujarat — because every vote counts.
lesson.activity: Mock election: pupils run a class election with voter list, nomination, campaign, secret ballot and counting.

questions.q: What is universal adult franchise?
questions.a: Every adult citizen has the right to vote.

questions.q: Who conducts elections in India?
What is a constituency?
questions.a: An area that elects one representative.

questions.q: Why is voting by secret ballot?
questions.a: So people can vote freely without fear.

lesson.homework: Ask an adult in your family about their voting experience.

chapters.title: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive

topics.title: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive
topics.summary: India has a parliamentary system: the executive comes from and answers to the legislature.
notes: India has a parliamentary system: the executive comes from and answers to the legislature.
Parliament has the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha and the President.
A bill is discussed and passed by both Houses and signed by the President to become law.
The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers run the government and must keep a majority in the Lok Sabha.
Question Hour, debates and committees hold the government accountable.
States have a similar system with a Governor, Chief Minister and Legislative Assembly.
outcomes: Describe the parliamentary system in India
Explain how laws are made
Describe the role of the executive and how it is held accountable

lesson.hook: Who actually decides that a new law will be made? And who checks that the government does its job?
lesson.example: In Question Hour, MPs ask ministers questions about their departments, which ministers must answer.
lesson.activity: Mock Parliament: pupils introduce, debate and vote on a bill; include a Question Hour for 'ministers'.

questions.q: What does 'parliamentary system' mean?
questions.a: The executive is formed from and answerable to the legislature.

questions.q: Who signs a bill to make it law?
What is Question Hour?
questions.a: Time in Parliament when members ask ministers questions.

questions.q: Who heads a state government?

lesson.homework: Find one law passed by Parliament recently and what it does.

topics.title: Factors of Production
topics.summary: Production needs land (natural resources), labour (human effort), capital (tools, machines, money) and entrepreneurship.
notes: Production needs land (natural resources), labour (human effort), capital (tools, machines, money) and entrepreneurship.
Land includes soil, water, minerals and space.
Labour includes physical and mental work; skills and education make workers more productive (human capital).
Physical capital: tools, machines, buildings; working capital: raw materials and money.
The entrepreneur brings the factors together, takes risks and innovates.
Using factors efficiently raises output and incomes.
outcomes: Name the factors of production: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship
Explain how they combine to produce goods and services
Understand the importance of human capital

lesson.hook: To make a cup of tea at a roadside stall, what do you need besides tea leaves?
lesson.example: Tea stall: land = the spot and water; labour = the tea-maker; capital = stove, kettle, cups, milk and sugar; entrepreneur = the owner who runs it.
lesson.activity: Business plan: groups plan a small business (a juice stall) and list each factor of production it needs.

questions.q: Name the four factors of production.
What is human capital?
questions.a: The skills, education and health of workers.

questions.q: Is a tractor land, labour or capital?
What does an entrepreneur do?
questions.a: Brings the factors together, takes risks and innovates.

lesson.homework: Interview a shopkeeper about what they needed to start their business.

topics.title: World Geography: Some Glimpses
topics.summary: Great mountain ranges: the Himalayas (Asia), Andes (South America), Rockies (North America), Alps (Europe).
notes: Great mountain ranges: the Himalayas (Asia), Andes (South America), Rockies (North America), Alps (Europe).
Great rivers: the Nile (longest), Amazon (largest by volume), Yangtze, Mississippi.
Deserts: the Sahara (hottest large desert), Arabian, Gobi, Atacama; Antarctica is a cold desert.
Grasslands: prairies, pampas, steppes and savannas support farming and grazing.
Rainforests near the Equator hold enormous biodiversity.
People adapt to each region — and human activity is changing many of them.
outcomes: Describe major physical features of the world
Locate important mountains, rivers, deserts and grasslands
Relate world geography to human life

lesson.hook: The Amazon, the Sahara, the Himalayas, the Nile — what makes each of these wonders unique?
lesson.example: The Amazon rainforest produces much of its own rain and holds about 10% of known species on Earth.
lesson.activity: World wonders map: groups mark ten natural wonders on a world map and prepare one fact card for each.

questions.q: Which is the longest river in the world?
In which continent are the Andes?
Name a cold desert.
What are grasslands in Africa called?

lesson.homework: Choose one world region and write how people live there.

topics.title: India's Long Road to Independence
topics.summary: The revolt of 1857 was the first large uprising against British rule.
notes: The revolt of 1857 was the first large uprising against British rule.
The Indian National Congress (1885) began with moderates who petitioned; later leaders like Tilak demanded Swaraj.
The partition of Bengal (1905) sparked the Swadeshi movement.
Gandhi led mass movements: Non-Cooperation (1920), Civil Disobedience with the Salt March (1930) and Quit India (1942).
Revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh and leaders like Subhas Chandra Bose (Indian National Army) also fought for freedom.
India became independent on 15 August 1947, but partition caused huge violence and displacement.
outcomes: Trace India's freedom struggle from 1857 to 1947
Describe the roles of moderates, extremists, revolutionaries and Gandhi
Explain how independence and partition came in 1947

lesson.hook: It took almost a century of struggle. What different paths did Indians take to win freedom?
lesson.example: In the Salt March (1930), Gandhi walked about 390 km to Dandi to make salt, breaking an unjust law; millions joined the movement.
lesson.activity: Freedom timeline: pupils build a timeline from 1857 to 1947 and add one local freedom fighter from their state.

questions.q: When was the Indian National Congress founded?
What was the Salt March?
questions.a: Gandhi's 1930 march to Dandi to break the salt law.

questions.q: Who led the Indian National Army?
When did India become independent?

lesson.homework: Find out about a freedom fighter from your state.

topics.title: A Journey Through Indian Architecture
topics.summary: Indian architecture ranges from Harappan cities to rock-cut caves, stupas, temples, forts, mosques and modern buildings.
notes: Indian architecture ranges from Harappan cities to rock-cut caves, stupas, temples, forts, mosques and modern buildings.
Stupas (Sanchi) and rock-cut caves (Ajanta, Ellora) show early Buddhist and Jain building.
Temple styles: Nagara (north, curved shikhara), Dravida (south, tall gopurams) and Vesara (Deccan, a blend).
Traditional texts (Vastu and Shilpa Shastras) gave rules for proportion and planning.
Indo-Islamic architecture brought arches, domes and minarets (Qutub Minar, Taj Mahal, Gol Gumbaz).
Stepwells, forts and palaces show engineering for water, defence and climate.
outcomes: Trace the development of Indian architecture
Identify styles such as Nagara, Dravida and Vesara temples, stupas, forts and Indo-Islamic buildings
Appreciate architecture as a knowledge tradition

lesson.hook: How did builders centuries ago, without cranes or computers, raise temples and domes that still stand?
lesson.example: Gol Gumbaz in Vijayapura, Karnataka, has one of the largest domes in the world and a famous whispering gallery.
lesson.activity: Style spotting: pupils sort photos of monuments into stupa, Nagara, Dravida, Vesara and Indo-Islamic styles, noting key features.

questions.q: Name the temple style with tall gateways called gopurams.
Which style blends north and south features in the Deccan?
Give one feature of Indo-Islamic architecture.
Where is Gol Gumbaz?

lesson.homework: Sketch a monument near you and label its architectural features.

chapters.title: The Role of the Judiciary in Our Society

topics.title: The Role of the Judiciary in Our Society
topics.summary: The judiciary settles disputes, interprets laws and protects the Constitution and citizens' rights.
notes: The judiciary settles disputes, interprets laws and protects the Constitution and citizens' rights.
India has an integrated judiciary: the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in states and subordinate (district) courts below.
Judges are independent of the government so they can decide fairly.
Civil cases are about disputes (property, contracts); criminal cases are about offences (theft, assault).
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) lets anyone approach courts on behalf of the public.
Free legal aid and Lok Adalats help poor people get justice.
outcomes: Explain the idea of justice and the role of courts
Describe the structure of India's judiciary
Understand judicial independence, PILs and access to justice

lesson.hook: If the government itself breaks a law, who can stop it?
lesson.example: Through PILs, courts have ordered cleaner air measures in Delhi and mid-day meals in schools.
lesson.activity: Moot court: pupils role-play a simple civil dispute with judge, lawyers and witnesses.

questions.q: Which is the highest court in India?
What is a PIL?
questions.a: A case filed in court for the public interest.

questions.q: Is theft a civil or criminal case?
Why must judges be independent?
questions.a: So they can decide fairly without pressure from the government.

lesson.homework: Find the location of the High Court for your state and one of its benches.

topics.title: Citizenship: Rights and Duties
topics.summary: A citizen is a full member of a country with rights and responsibilities.
notes: A citizen is a full member of a country with rights and responsibilities.
The Constitution guarantees Fundamental Rights: equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies.
The Right to Education gives free, compulsory schooling to children aged 6–14.
Fundamental Duties include respecting the Constitution, protecting the environment, promoting harmony and developing a scientific temper.
Rights and duties go together: my rights are safe when everyone does their duty.
Active citizens vote, follow laws, help others and take part in community life.
outcomes: Explain what citizenship means legally and in everyday life
Describe Fundamental Rights and Fundamental Duties
Understand why rights and duties go together

lesson.hook: You have the right to a clean park. Does anyone have a duty to keep it clean?
lesson.example: The right to freedom of speech comes with the duty not to spread hatred or false news.
lesson.activity: Rights and duties pairs: pupils match each right with a related duty and give an example from school life.

questions.q: Name two Fundamental Rights.
questions.a: Equality, freedom, against exploitation, religion, cultural and educational, constitutional remedies (any two).

questions.q: Which age group does the Right to Education cover?
Name one Fundamental Duty.
questions.a: Respect the Constitution, protect the environment, promote harmony (any one).

questions.q: Why do rights need duties?
questions.a: Rights are protected only when everyone does their duties.

lesson.homework: Do one act of good citizenship this week and write about it.

topics.title: Dynamics of Population
topics.summary: Demography is the study of population: its size, growth and composition.
notes: Demography is the study of population: its size, growth and composition.
Population changes through births, deaths and migration.
Population density is the number of people per square kilometre; it is high in the plains and low in deserts and mountains.
India has a large young population — a 'demographic dividend' if they are educated, healthy and employed.
Many countries (and some Indian states like Kerala) have ageing populations and need care for the elderly.
The sex ratio and literacy rate are important indicators of a healthy society.
outcomes: Understand population size, growth, density and distribution
Explain birth rate, death rate and migration
Discuss the demographic dividend and ageing

lesson.hook: India is the most populous country in the world. Is a large population a burden or a strength?
lesson.example: Population density = population ÷ area. A district of 20 lakh people on 4,000 km² has a density of 500 people per km².
lesson.activity: Class census: pupils collect data on family size, ages and birthplaces and make a population pyramid for the class families.

questions.q: What is population density?
questions.a: Number of people per square kilometre.

questions.q: Name three things that change population.
What is the demographic dividend?
questions.a: The benefit of a large working-age population.

questions.q: Where is population density usually high?

lesson.homework: Find the population and area of your district and calculate its density.

topics.title: India's Urban Landscape
topics.summary: Urbanisation is the growth in the share of people living in towns and cities.
notes: Urbanisation is the growth in the share of people living in towns and cities.
Cities offer jobs, education, health care and services, attracting migrants.
Rapid growth causes traffic jams, slums, pollution, water shortage and waste problems.
Planning, public transport (metros, buses), affordable housing and waste management can help.
Smart and sustainable cities use technology and green spaces.
Citizens' participation is key to good cities.
outcomes: Explain why cities grow and attract economic activity
Describe problems of urbanisation
Suggest ways to make cities liveable and sustainable

lesson.hook: Every day thousands of people move to cities like Bengaluru. What draws them, and what do they face when they arrive?
lesson.example: Namma Metro in Bengaluru carries lakhs of commuters daily, reducing road traffic and pollution.
lesson.activity: City planners: groups design an ideal neighbourhood with housing, transport, parks, schools and waste systems.

questions.q: What is urbanisation?
questions.a: Growth in the share of people living in towns and cities.

questions.q: Why do people migrate to cities?
questions.a: For jobs, education, health care and services.

questions.q: Give two problems of fast-growing cities.
questions.a: Traffic, slums, pollution, water shortage, waste (any two).

questions.q: How does public transport help cities?

lesson.homework: Suggest three changes that would make your town better to live in.

topics.title: Cultural Currents: 13th to 17th Centuries
topics.summary: Bhakti saints taught devotion to God through love, not ritual, and often challenged caste differences.
notes: Bhakti saints taught devotion to God through love, not ritual, and often challenged caste differences.
Saints wrote in people's languages: Basavanna (Kannada vachanas), Kabir, Tulsidas and Mirabai (Hindi dialects), Tukaram (Marathi), the Alvars and Nayanars (Tamil).
Sufi saints like Nizamuddin Auliya taught love, humility and service; dargahs became places for all.
Guru Nanak founded Sikhism, teaching one God, equality and langar (community kitchen).
Music (Hindustani and Carnatic), miniature painting and new architectural styles developed.
Cultures met and blended, enriching Indian life.
outcomes: Describe the Bhakti and Sufi movements
Explain growth of regional languages, literature, music and art (13th–17th centuries)
Understand how cultures interacted and blended

lesson.hook: Kabir, Mirabai, Guru Nanak, Basavanna, Tulsidas — why do their words still move people centuries later?
lesson.example: Purandara Dasa of Karnataka organised early lessons of Carnatic music — he is called the 'father of Carnatic music'.
lesson.activity: Saint and song: groups present the life and one teaching (in their own words) of a Bhakti or Sufi saint from different regions.

questions.q: What did Bhakti saints emphasise?
questions.a: Devotion to God through love; equality.

questions.q: In which language did Basavanna write vachanas?
Who founded Sikhism?
Who is called the father of Carnatic music?

lesson.homework: Find a vachana, doha or abhang and explain its message in your own words.

chapters.title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read

topics.title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
topics.summary: As a twelve-year-old in a north Karnataka village, the author read aloud each week's episode of Triveni's Kannada serial novel 'Kashi Yatre' to her grandmother Krishtakka, who could not read.
notes: As a twelve-year-old in a north Karnataka village, the author read aloud each week's episode of Triveni's Kannada serial novel 'Kashi Yatre' to her grandmother Krishtakka, who could not read.
The grandmother identified with the novel's old lady, who gave up her dream of going to Kashi to help an orphan girl marry.
When the author was away at a wedding for a week, her grandmother could not read the new episode and felt helpless and dependent.
She decided to learn to read; the granddaughter taught her, and by the next Saraswati Puja she could read the novel herself — she even honoured her granddaughter as her teacher.
outcomes: Read a memoir by Sudha Murty about literacy
Understand that it is never too late to learn

lesson.hook: Can a person learn to read at the age of sixty-two?
lesson.example: The grandmother's lesson: not being able to read makes you dependent on others; learning makes you free.
lesson.activity: Literacy drive: children plan how they could help one adult in their family or neighbourhood learn to read or use a phone.

questions.q: Which novel did the author read to her grandmother?
Why did the grandmother decide to learn to read?
questions.a: She felt helpless when she could not read the story herself while her granddaughter was away.

questions.q: How did the grandmother honour her teacher?
questions.a: She treated her granddaughter as her teacher (on Saraswati Puja).

lesson.homework: Write about something you taught an elder or an elder taught you.

topics.title: Bharat Our Land
topics.summary: The poet proudly says the mighty Himavant (Himalaya) is ours, unmatched on earth.
notes: The poet proudly says the mighty Himavant (Himalaya) is ours, unmatched on earth.
The generous Ganga and the sacred Upanishads are ours — no river or scripture can match them.
Gallant warriors lived here, sages sanctified the land, and divine music was heard here.
Brahma-knowledge took root here, the Buddha preached his dhamma here; Bharat is ancient and peerless.
outcomes: Recite a patriotic poem by Subramania Bharati
Appreciate India's natural and spiritual heritage

lesson.hook: What makes Bharat 'peerless' in your eyes?
lesson.example: 'Of hoary antiquity is Bharat' — India is very, very old (ancient).
lesson.activity: Heritage map: groups mark on a map of India the mountains, rivers and places mentioned or suggested in the poem.

questions.q: What is said about the Himavant?
questions.a: It is mighty and has no equal on earth.

questions.q: Which scriptures does the poet praise?
Who preached his dhamma in India?

lesson.homework: Write four lines in praise of India.

topics.title: The Pot Maker
topics.summary: Sentila dreamed of becoming a pot maker like her mother and grandmother, but her mother, Arenla, wanted her to be a weaver.
notes: Sentila dreamed of becoming a pot maker like her mother and grandmother, but her mother, Arenla, wanted her to be a weaver.
Arenla said pot making was hard — carrying clay from a riverbank 16 km away, pounding it, firing it — and paid only a few rupees; weaving paid more.
Sentila secretly watched expert potters shaping clay with a spatula and firing pots in a kiln.
The village council reminded the family it was their duty to pass on the craft; her father promised that Sentila would soon make the best pots in the village.
outcomes: Read a story from Nagaland about a traditional craft
Understand the value of passing skills across generations

lesson.hook: Would you follow your passion even if your parents wanted you to do something else?
lesson.example: Pot making steps: fetch clay → pound it → shape on the lump with spatula → dry in sun → fire in kiln.
lesson.activity: Craft interview: children interview a local artisan about how they learned their craft.

questions.q: What did Sentila want to become?
questions.a: A pot maker, like her mother and grandmother.

questions.q: Why did Arenla prefer weaving?
questions.a: It was easier, could be done indoors, and paid better.

questions.q: Why did the village council call Sentila's father?
questions.a: To ask why the pot-making skill was not being passed on to Sentila.

lesson.homework: Write about a traditional craft in your area and who keeps it alive.

chapters.title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations

topics.title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
topics.summary: The poet hears Bharat celebrating its many vocations.
notes: The poet hears Bharat celebrating its many vocations.
Craftspersons, musicians, carpenters, electricians, boatmen, shoemakers, cooks and masons all take pride in their work.
Each worker contributes to society — carpenters with precision, electricians who brighten lives, boatmen singing at sea.
The voice of their vocation is the voice of their identity — all work deserves honour.
outcomes: Recite a poem celebrating different vocations
Respect every kind of work

lesson.hook: Whose work do you depend on every single day?
lesson.example: The poem is modelled on a famous line 'I hear America singing' — here it is Bharat celebrating.
lesson.activity: Riddle round: children write riddles about different vocations for classmates to guess.

questions.q: What do the carpenters create?
questions.a: Anything out of wood with mathematical precision.

questions.q: How do electricians help us?
questions.a: They work with cables and wires to brighten our lives.

questions.q: What is the poem's main message?
questions.a: Every vocation is valuable and gives people their identity.

lesson.homework: Write a thank-you note to a worker who helps your family.

topics.title: Winds of Change
topics.summary: The word 'pankha' comes from 'pankh', meaning a bird's feather; a small plumed fan was called 'pankhi'.
notes: The word 'pankha' comes from 'pankh', meaning a bird's feather; a small plumed fan was called 'pankhi'.
Buddhist wall paintings at Ajanta (around the 2nd century CE) show fans; they were used in temples and royal courts.
Fans were traded along routes and considered stylish; each region developed its own varieties.
They are made of bamboo, cane, palm leaf, silk and other local materials — like Assam's bamboo fans, Kerala's palm-leaf fans and Uttar Pradesh's moonj grass fans.
outcomes: Read an informative text about traditional Indian hand fans
Understand how crafts reflect regional identity

lesson.hook: What is a hand fan called in your language, and what is it made of?
lesson.example: Pankh (feather) → pankhi (small plumed fan) → pankha (all fans).
lesson.activity: Fan craft: children make a simple hand fan from paper or leaves and decorate it with a regional pattern.

questions.q: Where does the word 'pankha' come from?
Where is early evidence of fans found?
questions.a: In Buddhist wall paintings at Ajanta.

questions.q: Name two materials used for fans.
questions.a: Bamboo, cane, palm leaf, silk, moonj grass (any two).

lesson.homework: Write about a traditional object in your home and its history.

topics.title: Canvas of Soil
topics.summary: The earth is a rich palette where gardeners' dreams seep in.
notes: The earth is a rich palette where gardeners' dreams seep in.
Seeds planted are like brushstrokes, waiting for spring's bright colours.
Blossoms bloom like a painted sight, in shades of green, red and blue — nature's ever-new artwork.
Each plot is a canvas where art and life meet; in the hands of those who till, gardens become paintings.
outcomes: Recite a poem comparing a garden to a painting
Identify metaphors in poetry

lesson.hook: How is a gardener like a painter?
lesson.example: Metaphor: 'Palette of earth' — the soil is compared to a painter's palette.
lesson.activity: Garden painting: children paint or draw a garden and label its 'palette', 'hues' and 'canvas'.

questions.q: What is the earth compared to?
What are the seeds compared to?
What do gardens become in the hands of those who till?

lesson.homework: Write four lines comparing a kitchen, a classroom or a field to a work of art.

topics.title: Vitamin-M
topics.summary: Ravi's mother wishes someone would invent 'Vitamin-M', a memory vitamin for old people.
notes: Ravi's mother wishes someone would invent 'Vitamin-M', a memory vitamin for old people.
Ravi's grandfather had come to live with them; he could not hear, see or remember well and once took a double dose of medicine and got lost.
During the holidays, Ravi looks after Grandpa and learns about his life, stories and dignity.
Ravi realises the elderly need love, patience and respect — and spending time with them is the best 'vitamin'.
outcomes: Read a story about caring for the elderly
Understand patience and empathy towards grandparents

lesson.hook: What would you do if your grandparent kept forgetting things?
lesson.example: The 'M' could stand for memory — or for moments of love and company.
lesson.activity: Grandparent's corner: children collect a story, recipe or saying from an elder and share it in class.

questions.q: What did Ravi's mother wish for?
questions.a: A memory vitamin, Vitamin-M, for old people.

questions.q: Why was it a difficult month?
questions.a: Grandpa took a double dose of medicine and once got lost.

questions.q: What does the story teach about the elderly?
questions.a: They need patience, love, respect and company.

lesson.homework: List five ways you can help an elderly person at home.

topics.title: I Cannot Remember My Mother
topics.summary: The poet cannot remember his mother, but a tune she hummed while rocking his cradle seems to hover over his playthings.
notes: The poet cannot remember his mother, but a tune she hummed while rocking his cradle seems to hover over his playthings.
In early autumn, the smell of shiuli flowers and the temple's morning service remind him of her.
Looking out at the blue of the distant sky, he feels the stillness of her gaze spread over it.
Memories live on through sound, smell and sight, even when clear pictures are gone.
outcomes: Recite a poem by Rabindranath Tagore
Identify sensory images in poetry

lesson.hook: Can you remember someone through a smell, a song or a look?
lesson.example: Senses in the poem: hearing (the tune), smell (shiuli, morning service), sight (the sky).
lesson.activity: Sense memory: children write one memory linked to a sound, one to a smell and one to a sight.

questions.q: What seems to hover over the poet's playthings?
questions.a: The tune of a song his mother used to hum.

questions.q: What reminds him of his mother in autumn?
questions.a: The smell of shiuli flowers and the temple's morning service.

questions.q: What does he feel when he looks at the sky?
questions.a: The stillness of his mother's gaze spread over it.

lesson.homework: Write a short poem about a person you love using at least two senses.

topics.title: The World of Limitless Possibilities
topics.summary: The Paralympic Games celebrate athletes with locomotor, sensory or intellectual disabilities and challenge stereotypes.
notes: The Paralympic Games celebrate athletes with locomotor, sensory or intellectual disabilities and challenge stereotypes.
India first took part in 1968 and won its first Paralympic medal (in swimming) in 1972.
Dr Deepa Malik was paralysed waist down at 29 after a spine tumour; she chose to transform her life rather than live in regret.
She became a celebrated para-athlete and received the Khel Ratna, Arjuna Award and Padma Shri; para-archer Sheetal Devi received the Arjuna Award in 2024.
outcomes: Read about the Paralympics and Dr Deepa Malik
Understand resilience and inclusion in sport

lesson.hook: What does 'limitless possibilities' mean to someone told they will never walk again?
lesson.example: Deepa Malik's choice: 'squander my life in remorse or transform it' — she chose transformation.
lesson.activity: Inclusive games: groups design a school game that everyone, including children with disabilities, can play.

questions.q: When did India first take part in the Paralympics?
What happened to Deepa Malik at 29?
questions.a: A spine tumour left her paralysed waist down.

questions.q: Name one award she received.
questions.a: Khel Ratna, Arjuna Award or Padma Shri.

lesson.homework: Write about a para-athlete who inspires you.

topics.title: Nine Gold Medals
topics.summary: Athletes gathered for the final hundred-yard dash at the Special Olympics.
notes: Athletes gathered for the final hundred-yard dash at the Special Olympics.
When the gun fired, the smallest runner stumbled and fell, crying in frustration.
The other eight runners stopped, went back and helped him to his feet.
All nine joined hands and walked to the finish line together — nine gold medals and a standing ovation. (Poem by David Roth.)
outcomes: Recite a narrative poem about kindness in a race
Distinguish empathy, sympathy and compassion

lesson.hook: Would you stop in the middle of a race to help someone who fell?
lesson.example: Empathy: 'I can imagine how you feel' — feeling with someone, not just for them.
lesson.activity: Kindness race: the class discusses when helping others matters more than winning.

questions.q: What happened to the smallest runner?
What did the other runners do?
questions.a: They went back, helped him up and walked together.

questions.q: Why were there nine gold medals?
questions.a: All nine finished together, holding hands.

lesson.homework: Write about a time someone chose kindness over winning.

topics.title: Twin Melodies
topics.summary: Shruti, a young violinist, plays in an Indo-Western fusion group with Iqbal (flute), Avinash (tabla) and Peter (keyboard).
notes: Shruti, a young violinist, plays in an Indo-Western fusion group with Iqbal (flute), Avinash (tabla) and Peter (keyboard).
Her father, Guru Nabin Sharma, principal of a music school, allows only one solo performance every six months and dislikes group concerts.
Shruti struggles to tell him about the group's concert and plans to drop out after one last practice.
Her parents secretly watch the practice; her father is moved by how she keeps to the raga's notes and proudly applauds — tradition and fusion find harmony.
outcomes: Read a play about music, family and harmony
Understand how tradition and new ideas can blend

lesson.hook: Can classical music and modern fusion go together?
lesson.example: Idiom: 'bite the bullet' — to face a difficult situation bravely.
lesson.activity: Fusion corner: groups combine a classical song line with a modern beat and perform it.

questions.q: Which instrument does Shruti play?
What was her father's rule?
How did her father react to the practice?
questions.a: He was moved and proudly praised them.

lesson.homework: Write a dialogue in which you explain your hobby to a parent.

topics.title: A Friend Found in Music
topics.summary: The poet calls music an ocean that pulls her to the shore.
notes: The poet calls music an ocean that pulls her to the shore.
Music is a rhythm that moves her to the core.
Music is therapy when she feels blue and lifts her spirits.
When no one seems to care, music is the needed friend.
outcomes: Recite a poem about music as a friend
Identify metaphors and similes

lesson.hook: Which song do you listen to when you feel low?
lesson.example: Metaphor to simile: 'Music is the ocean' → 'Music is like an ocean'.
lesson.activity: My music: children share a song that comforts them and say why.

questions.q: What is music compared to in the first line?
When does the poet need music as therapy?
What kind of friend is music?
questions.a: The needed friend when no one seems to care.

lesson.homework: Write a short poem about your favourite kind of music.

topics.title: Carrier of Words
topics.summary: Khetaram is the only Gramin Dak Sevak (postman) of the Somarad branch post office in the Thar desert, near the Indo-Pakistan border.
notes: Khetaram is the only Gramin Dak Sevak (postman) of the Somarad branch post office in the Thar desert, near the Indo-Pakistan border.
For 15 years he has carried the mailbag through extreme heat to far-flung hamlets (dhaanis).
Families depend on money orders sent by relatives; the post office is trusted deeply.
He reads letters aloud and writes replies for villagers; he is welcomed with tea or jaggery, and dreads only the letter with a torn corner that brings news of death.
outcomes: Read a true account of a rural postman
Appreciate the role of Gramin Dak Sevaks

lesson.hook: Who carries letters to villages in the middle of a desert?
lesson.example: A money order lets a person send cash through the post office to a remote village.
lesson.activity: Postcard project: children write postcards to someone far away and discuss how letters travel.

questions.q: Who is Khetaram?
questions.a: The Gramin Dak Sevak (postman) of Somarad branch post office.

questions.q: Where does he work?
questions.a: In the Thar desert in Rajasthan, near the Indo-Pakistan border.

questions.q: Why do villagers trust him?
questions.a: He delivers money orders and letters and reads and writes for them.

lesson.homework: Write a letter of appreciation to your local postman.

topics.title: Words
topics.summary: The poet says words, like summer birds, often leave only empty air.
notes: The poet says words, like summer birds, often leave only empty air.
When the heart needs comfort, many words can be as worthless as weeds.
A little said, and truly said, gives deeper joy than a host of words that reach only the head.
Words are like showy plants with blossoms but no fruit — sincerity matters more than quantity. (Poem by Charles Swain.)
outcomes: Recite a poem about the power of few, true words
Understand the difference between many words and meaningful words

lesson.hook: Have a few kind words ever meant more to you than a long speech?
lesson.example: Simile: 'words, like summer birds, depart' — words fly away without leaving anything lasting.
lesson.activity: Few true words: children write a three-word message of comfort for a friend.

questions.q: What are words compared to in the first stanza?
What kind of words give deeper joy?
What does the poet compare empty words to at the end?
questions.a: Showy plants that bear no fruit.

lesson.homework: Write about a time a few words made a big difference to you.

topics.title: Follow That Dream
topics.summary: In a letter dated 19 June 1995, Irene Chua tells her daughter Ming: by all means follow that dream.
notes: In a letter dated 19 June 1995, Irene Chua tells her daughter Ming: by all means follow that dream.
Great people become great because they pursue their dreams with effort and sacrifice.
Reaching world-class standard in any field takes about ten years of intense work; count the cost, and if the passion still burns, plunge.
The road is uphill, but doing what you love keeps you going; successful people also thank the support network behind them.
outcomes: Read a mother's letter to her daughter about following dreams
Understand effort, sacrifice and support behind success

lesson.hook: What is the difference between a wish and a dream you follow?
lesson.example: Dr Kalam: a dream is not what you see in sleep; it is something that does not let you sleep.
lesson.activity: Dream map: children draw a road map from today to their dream with milestones and helpers.

questions.q: Who wrote the letter and to whom?
questions.a: Irene Chua to her daughter Ming.

questions.q: How long does it take to reach world-class standard?
questions.a: About ten years of intense effort.

questions.q: What keeps you going on the uphill road?
questions.a: Knowing you are doing what you love.

lesson.homework: Write a letter to yourself ten years from now about your dream.

topics.title: Believe in Yourself
topics.summary: The poem urges us to step up to the challenge — there is no crowd, just you and your future.
notes: The poem urges us to step up to the challenge — there is no crowd, just you and your future.
As the future comes near, fear can push us back and choices feel difficult.
Staying in comfort (the status quo) is easy, but it is not how we grow.
The first step is the hardest; believe in yourself and your future will be on track. (Poem by Robert Langley.)
outcomes: Recite a motivational poem about self-belief
Identify the central idea of each stanza
