questions.a: सभी जीवों की — मनुष्य, पशु, पक्षी, पेड़।

questions.q: प्रकृति मनुष्य के स्वार्थ का जवाब कैसे देती है?
questions.a: बाढ़, तूफ़ान, भूकंप, अधिक गर्मी जैसे रूपों में।

questions.q: लेखक की माँ का स्वभाव कैसा था?
questions.a: वे पशु-पक्षियों और पेड़ों के प्रति करुणा रखती थीं।

lesson.homework: पर्यावरण बचाने के लिए पाँच उपाय लिखिए जो आप रोज़ अपना सकते हैं।

topics.title: पतझर में टूटी पत्तियाँ
topics.summary: रवींद्र केलेकर के इस पाठ में दो प्रसंग हैं: 'गिन्नी का सोना' और 'झेन की देन'।
notes: रवींद्र केलेकर के इस पाठ में दो प्रसंग हैं: 'गिन्नी का सोना' और 'झेन की देन'।
गिन्नी का सोना: शुद्ध सोने में ताँबा मिलाकर गहने मज़बूत बनाए जाते हैं; वैसे ही व्यवहारवादी लोग आदर्शों में व्यावहारिकता मिलाते हैं।
लेखक कहते हैं कि गांधीजी ने व्यावहारिकता को आदर्श के स्तर पर चढ़ाया, आदर्श को नीचे नहीं गिराया।
झेन की देन: जापान में लोग तनाव से बचने के लिए 'चा-नो-यू' (टी-सेरेमनी) करते हैं, जहाँ शांति से चाय पी जाती है।
इससे लेखक ने सीखा कि बीता कल और आने वाला कल दोनों मिथ्या हैं; सच्चाई केवल वर्तमान है।
outcomes: 'पतझर में टूटी पत्तियाँ' के दोनों प्रसंगों का संदेश समझना
आदर्श और व्यावहारिकता का अंतर जानना
मानसिक शांति के लिए वर्तमान में जीने का महत्व समझना

lesson.hook: आप हमेशा भविष्य की चिंता करते हैं या बीते कल को याद करते हैं? आज के पल में कितना जीते हैं?
lesson.example: गिन्नी का सोना: शुद्ध सोना बहुत नरम होता है, इसलिए उसमें थोड़ा ताँबा मिलाते हैं — यह आदर्श में व्यावहारिकता मिलाने जैसा है।
lesson.activity: कक्षा में दो मिनट की 'शांत बैठक': विद्यार्थी आँखें बंद करके केवल अपनी साँस पर ध्यान दें, फिर बताएँ कि कैसा लगा।

questions.q: 'गिन्नी का सोना' किसे कहते हैं?
questions.a: जिस सोने में ताँबा मिलाया गया हो और जो मज़बूत हो।

questions.q: जापान में चाय पीने की विधि को क्या कहते हैं?
'झेन की देन' से लेखक ने क्या सीखा?
questions.a: केवल वर्तमान ही सत्य है; उसी में जीना चाहिए।

lesson.homework: जीवन में आदर्शों का महत्व — 100 शब्दों में अपने विचार लिखिए।

topics.title: कारतूस
topics.summary: हबीब तनवीर की यह एकांकी अवध के नवाब वज़ीर अली की कहानी पर है।
notes: हबीब तनवीर की यह एकांकी अवध के नवाब वज़ीर अली की कहानी पर है।
अंग्रेज़ों ने वज़ीर अली को गद्दी से हटा दिया था; वह अंग्रेज़ों को भारत से निकालना चाहता था।
कर्नल की सेना वज़ीर अली को पकड़ने के लिए खेमे डाले है; वह बहुत दिनों से पकड़ में नहीं आ रहा।
एक सवार कर्नल के खेमे में आकर कारतूस माँगता है और जाते-जाते अपना नाम बताता है: वही वज़ीर अली था।
यह प्रसंग वज़ीर अली के अद्भुत साहस और अंग्रेज़ों के प्रति उसकी नफ़रत को दिखाता है।
outcomes: एकांकी 'कारतूस' की कथा और पात्रों को समझना
वज़ीर अली के साहस और देशप्रेम को पहचानना
एकांकी की विशेषताएँ जानना

lesson.hook: क्या कोई अकेला व्यक्ति पूरी सेना को चुनौती दे सकता है? किस गुण से?
lesson.example: एकांकी की विशेषता: एक ही अंक, कम पात्र, छोटे संवाद और एक ही मुख्य घटना — यहाँ खेमे का दृश्य।
lesson.activity: विद्यार्थी कर्नल, लेफ़्टिनेंट और सवार बनकर एकांकी का मंचन करें।

questions.q: वज़ीर अली कौन था?
questions.a: अवध का नवाब, जिसे अंग्रेज़ों ने गद्दी से हटा दिया था।

questions.q: सवार कर्नल के पास क्यों आया?
कर्नल क्यों चकित रह गया?
questions.a: जिसे पकड़ने के लिए सेना खड़ी थी, वही वज़ीर अली खुद आकर कारतूस ले गया।

lesson.homework: वज़ीर अली के चरित्र की तीन विशेषताएँ लिखिए।

topics.title: शुचिपर्यावरणम्
topics.summary: यह पाठ आधुनिक संस्कृत कवि हरिदत्त शर्मा के कविता-संग्रह से लिया गया है।
notes: यह पाठ आधुनिक संस्कृत कवि हरिदत्त शर्मा के कविता-संग्रह से लिया गया है।
कवि कहते हैं कि महानगरों में जीवन कठिन हो गया है: वाहनों का शोर, धुआँ और दूषित जल।
'लोहचक्र' (वाहन) और कारखानों से वायु और जल प्रदूषित हो रहे हैं।
कवि कुछ समय के लिए शहर छोड़कर गाँव, नदी, वन और हरियाली की ओर जाना चाहते हैं।
संदेश: शुद्ध पर्यावरण ही स्वस्थ जीवन का आधार है।
outcomes: पाठ 'शुचिपर्यावरणम्' का भाव समझना
नगर के प्रदूषण और प्रकृति की शुद्धता की तुलना करना
पाठ के नए शब्दों और संधि-प्रयोगों को पहचानना

lesson.hook: शहर की सड़क पर और गाँव के खेत में साँस लेने में क्या अंतर लगता है?
lesson.example: शब्द-अर्थ: शुचि = शुद्ध, पर्यावरणम् = वातावरण; 'शुचिपर्यावरणम्' = शुद्ध वातावरण।
lesson.activity: विद्यार्थी संस्कृत में पर्यावरण पर पाँच सरल वाक्य बनाएँ, जैसे 'वृक्षाः अस्माकं मित्राणि सन्ति।'

questions.q: कवि किस कारण से महानगर छोड़ना चाहते हैं?
questions.a: प्रदूषण, शोर और दूषित वातावरण के कारण।

questions.q: 'लोहचक्र' शब्द से क्या अभिप्राय है?
पाठ का मुख्य संदेश क्या है?
questions.a: शुद्ध पर्यावरण स्वस्थ जीवन के लिए आवश्यक है।

lesson.homework: पर्यावरण-संरक्षण पर पाँच संस्कृत वाक्य लिखिए।

topics.title: बुद्धिर्बलवती सदा
topics.summary: यह कथा 'शुकसप्तति' नामक कथा-ग्रंथ से ली गई है।
notes: यह कथा 'शुकसप्तति' नामक कथा-ग्रंथ से ली गई है।
बुद्धिमती नाम की स्त्री अपने दो पुत्रों के साथ पिता के घर जा रही थी, तब वन में एक बाघ सामने आया।
उसने चतुराई से अपने पुत्रों को डाँटते हुए कहा कि एक-एक बाघ खाने के लिए झगड़ा मत करो — बाघ डरकर भाग गया।
एक सियार ने बाघ को फिर लौटाया, पर बुद्धिमती ने फिर अपनी बुद्धि से सियार और बाघ दोनों को भगा दिया।
शिक्षा: बुद्धि सदा बलवान होती है।
outcomes: कथा 'बुद्धिर्बलवती सदा' को समझना
संकट में बुद्धि के प्रयोग का महत्व जानना
पाठ के क्रिया-पदों को पहचानना

lesson.hook: एक शेर या बाघ सामने आ जाए और भागने का रास्ता न हो — तब आप ताकत से बचेंगे या बुद्धि से?
lesson.example: पाठ का शीर्षक ही सूक्ति है: 'बुद्धिर्बलवती सदा' = बुद्धि सदा बलवती (शक्तिशाली) होती है।
lesson.activity: विद्यार्थी कथा का सरल नाट्य-रूपांतरण करें (बुद्धिमती, दो पुत्र, बाघ, सियार) और कुछ संवाद संस्कृत में बोलें।

questions.q: बुद्धिमती कहाँ जा रही थी?
बुद्धिमती ने बाघ को कैसे भगाया?
questions.a: पुत्रों से यह कहकर कि एक-एक बाघ खाने के लिए झगड़ा मत करो।

questions.q: यह कथा किस ग्रंथ से ली गई है?

lesson.homework: कथा का सार हिंदी में 80 शब्दों में लिखिए।

topics.title: शिशुलालनम्
topics.summary: यह नाट्यांश दिङ्नाग रचित 'कुन्दमाला' नाटक के पाँचवें अंक से लिया गया है।
notes: यह नाट्यांश दिङ्नाग रचित 'कुन्दमाला' नाटक के पाँचवें अंक से लिया गया है।
लव और कुश रामायण गान के लिए राम की सभा में आते हैं।
राम उन्हें अपने पास सिंहासन पर बिठाते हैं और उनका परिचय पूछते हैं।
बालकों की बातों से राम को उनमें अपनापन और सीता की छवि दिखती है।
नाटक में वात्सल्य (संतान-प्रेम) की भावना प्रमुख है।
outcomes: नाट्यांश 'शिशुलालनम्' का प्रसंग समझना
राम और लव-कुश के संवाद की भावना जानना
संस्कृत नाटक की शैली पहचानना

lesson.hook: जब आप किसी अनजान व्यक्ति से मिलते हैं और वह बहुत अपना-सा लगता है — ऐसा क्यों होता है?
lesson.example: 'शिशुलालनम्' = बच्चों का लाड़-प्यार; राम लव-कुश को गोद में बिठाकर यही स्नेह दिखाते हैं।
lesson.activity: विद्यार्थी राम, लव, कुश और विदूषक बनकर नाट्यांश के कुछ संवाद संस्कृत में पढ़ें।

questions.q: यह नाट्यांश किस नाटक से लिया गया है?
लव-कुश राम की सभा में क्यों आए?
इस पाठ में कौन-सी भावना प्रमुख है?

lesson.homework: पाठ के पाँच नए शब्दों के अर्थ लिखिए।

topics.title: जननी तुल्यवत्सला
topics.summary: यह कथा महाभारत के वनपर्व से ली गई है।
notes: यह कथा महाभारत के वनपर्व से ली गई है।
एक किसान दो बैलों से खेत जोत रहा था; उनमें एक बैल दुर्बल था और गिर पड़ा, फिर भी किसान उसे पीटता रहा।
यह देखकर सब गायों की माता सुरभि की आँखों में आँसू आ गए।
इन्द्र के पूछने पर सुरभि ने कहा कि माँ के लिए सभी संतान समान हैं, पर दुर्बल संतान पर अधिक करुणा होती है।
इन्द्र ने वर्षा की, जिससे किसान का खेत जोतना रुक गया और बैल को आराम मिला।
outcomes: पाठ 'जननी तुल्यवत्सला' की कथा समझना
माँ के समान-प्रेम और दुर्बल पर विशेष करुणा का भाव जानना
पशुओं के प्रति दया पर चर्चा करना

lesson.hook: अगर घर में दो भाई-बहन हों और एक बीमार हो, तो माँ किसका अधिक ध्यान रखती है? क्यों?
lesson.example: 'जननी तुल्यवत्सला' = माँ सभी संतानों से समान प्रेम करती है।
lesson.activity: विद्यार्थी पशुओं के प्रति दया के तीन उदाहरण अपने आस-पास से बताएँ।

questions.q: सुरभि क्यों रो रही थी?
questions.a: किसान अपने दुर्बल बैल को पीट रहा था।

questions.q: यह कथा किस ग्रंथ से ली गई है?
इन्द्र ने क्या किया?
questions.a: वर्षा की, जिससे बैल को राहत मिली।

lesson.homework: 'पशुओं के प्रति हमारा कर्तव्य' विषय पर पाँच वाक्य लिखिए।

topics.title: सुभाषितानि
topics.summary: सुभाषित = सुंदर और हितकारी वचन; ये श्लोक विभिन्न संस्कृत ग्रंथों से लिए गए हैं।
notes: सुभाषित = सुंदर और हितकारी वचन; ये श्लोक विभिन्न संस्कृत ग्रंथों से लिए गए हैं।
आलस्य मनुष्य का सबसे बड़ा शत्रु है और परिश्रम सबसे अच्छा मित्र।
क्रोध मनुष्य के शरीर में ही रहने वाला शत्रु है, जो उसी को नष्ट करता है।
जो बात कही न गई हो, उसे भी समझ लेना बुद्धिमान का लक्षण है।
सज्जनों की मित्रता, विनम्रता और सही समय पर सही काम जीवन को सफल बनाते हैं।
outcomes: सुभाषितों का अर्थ और जीवन-मूल्य समझना
सुभाषितों को शुद्ध उच्चारण से पढ़ना
आलस्य, क्रोध और मित्रता संबंधी शिक्षाओं को जीवन से जोड़ना

lesson.hook: आपके दादा-दादी कौन-सी कहावतें कहते हैं? उनमें कौन-सी सीख छिपी है?
lesson.example: एक सुभाषित का भाव: परिश्रम के समान कोई मित्र नहीं, और परिश्रम करने वाला कभी दुखी नहीं होता।
lesson.activity: सुभाषित-कार्ड: विद्यार्थी एक-एक सुभाषित सुंदर लिखकर उसके नीचे हिंदी अर्थ लिखें और कक्षा की दीवार पर लगाएँ।

questions.q: 'सुभाषित' का अर्थ क्या है?
मनुष्य का सबसे बड़ा शत्रु किसे बताया गया है?
क्रोध को शरीर में स्थित शत्रु क्यों कहा गया है?
questions.a: क्योंकि वह स्वयं मनुष्य को ही नष्ट करता है।

lesson.homework: दो सुभाषित याद करके उनका अर्थ लिखिए।

topics.title: सौहार्दं प्रकृतेः शोभा
topics.summary: वन में पशु-पक्षी इस बात पर झगड़ते हैं कि उनमें राजा बनने योग्य सबसे श्रेष्ठ कौन है।
notes: वन में पशु-पक्षी इस बात पर झगड़ते हैं कि उनमें राजा बनने योग्य सबसे श्रेष्ठ कौन है।
सिंह, बाघ, हाथी, वानर, बगुला, कोयल, कौआ, उल्लू — सब अपनी-अपनी विशेषताएँ बताते हैं और दूसरों की कमियाँ।
अंत में प्रकृति माता आकर समझाती हैं कि सबका अपना-अपना महत्व है।
सबके मिलकर रहने से ही प्रकृति की शोभा है।
शिक्षा: आपसी सौहार्द (मित्रता और सहयोग) ही सबसे बड़ी शक्ति है।
outcomes: पाठ 'सौहार्दं प्रकृतेः शोभा' का संदेश समझना
पशु-पक्षियों के संवाद से सहयोग का महत्व जानना
संस्कृत संवाद पढ़ना और समझना

lesson.hook: कक्षा का सबसे ज़रूरी व्यक्ति कौन है — मॉनिटर, सबसे होशियार छात्र, या हर कोई? क्यों?
lesson.example: कौआ और कोयल: कोयल अपनी मधुर आवाज़ पर गर्व करती है, पर उसके अंडे कौआ ही पालता है — दोनों का महत्व है।
lesson.activity: विद्यार्थी पशु-पक्षी बनकर संस्कृत में एक-एक वाक्य बोलें, जैसे 'अहं सिंहः अस्मि, अहं वनराजः अस्मि।'

questions.q: पशु-पक्षियों में किस बात पर विवाद हुआ?
questions.a: कौन सबसे श्रेष्ठ है और राजा बनेगा।

questions.q: विवाद किसने सुलझाया?
पाठ की मुख्य शिक्षा क्या है?
questions.a: सबका महत्व है; मिलकर रहना ही प्रकृति की शोभा है।

lesson.homework: 'सहयोगः' (सहयोग) पर पाँच संस्कृत वाक्य लिखिए।

topics.title: विचित्रः साक्षी
topics.summary: यह कथा बंकिमचंद्र चट्टोपाध्याय के एक न्यायाधीश से संबंधित एक घटना पर आधारित है।
notes: यह कथा बंकिमचंद्र चट्टोपाध्याय के एक न्यायाधीश से संबंधित एक घटना पर आधारित है।
एक निर्धन व्यक्ति रात में एक घर में ठहरा; वहाँ एक चोर ने चोरी की और पुलिस ने उल्टा उसी निर्धन व्यक्ति पर आरोप लगाया।
न्यायाधीश ने सत्य जानने के लिए एक विचित्र उपाय किया: एक व्यक्ति को मृत बनाकर लिटाया और आरोपी तथा सिपाही को शव उठाने भेजा।
रास्ते में सिपाही ने आरोपी को डाँटा; 'मृत' व्यक्ति ने उठकर न्यायाधीश को सब बता दिया — वही विचित्र साक्षी था।
सच्चाई सामने आई; निर्दोष छूट गया और दोषी को दंड मिला।
outcomes: कथा 'विचित्रः साक्षी' को समझना
न्यायाधीश की बुद्धिमत्ता को पहचानना
सत्य और न्याय पर चर्चा करना

lesson.hook: अगर किसी अपराध का कोई गवाह न हो, तो सच्चाई कैसे पता की जा सकती है?
lesson.example: 'विचित्रः साक्षी' = अनोखा गवाह — जो मृत समझा गया, वही सच्चाई का गवाह बना।
lesson.activity: विद्यार्थी कथा का मंचन करें: न्यायाधीश, निर्धन व्यक्ति, सिपाही और 'शव' बने पात्र।

questions.q: न्यायाधीश ने सत्य जानने के लिए क्या उपाय किया?
questions.a: एक व्यक्ति को मृत बनाकर लिटाया और उसे साक्षी बनाया।

questions.q: विचित्र साक्षी कौन था?
कथा का संदेश क्या है?
questions.a: बुद्धि से सत्य का पता लगाया जा सकता है और न्याय होता है।

lesson.homework: कथा के पाँच मुख्य वाक्य संस्कृत में लिखिए।

topics.title: सूक्तयः
topics.summary: यह पाठ तमिल भाषा के प्रसिद्ध ग्रंथ 'तिरुक्कुरल' की कुछ सूक्तियों का संस्कृत रूपांतर है।
notes: यह पाठ तमिल भाषा के प्रसिद्ध ग्रंथ 'तिरुक्कुरल' की कुछ सूक्तियों का संस्कृत रूपांतर है।
तिरुक्कुरल के रचयिता तिरुवल्लुवर हैं; इसे तमिल का 'वेद' भी कहा जाता है।
पिता का सबसे बड़ा कर्तव्य पुत्र को विद्वान बनाना है।
मीठी वाणी बोलनी चाहिए; कठोर वाणी का प्रयोग पका फल छोड़कर कच्चा फल खाने जैसा है।
सच्चा मनुष्य दूसरों का भला करता है; ये सूक्तियाँ सब भाषाओं और समय के लिए उपयोगी हैं।
outcomes: 'सूक्तयः' पाठ की नीति-सूक्तियों को समझना
तमिल ग्रंथ 'तिरुक्कुरल' के बारे में जानना
सूक्तियों को दैनिक जीवन से जोड़ना

lesson.hook: क्या अच्छी बातें किसी एक भाषा की होती हैं? क्या तमिल की कोई सीख संस्कृत में भी कही जा सकती है?
lesson.example: कच्चे और पके फल का उदाहरण: मधुर वाणी पके फल जैसी है; मधुर वाणी छोड़कर कठोर बोलना, पका फल छोड़कर कच्चा खाने जैसा मूर्खतापूर्ण है।
lesson.activity: विद्यार्थी अपनी मातृभाषा की कोई एक नीति-वचन या कहावत लाएँ और उसका अर्थ बताएँ — देखें कि अलग भाषाओं में एक-सी सीख है।

questions.q: 'तिरुक्कुरल' किस भाषा का ग्रंथ है?
तिरुक्कुरल के रचयिता कौन हैं?
पिता का पुत्र के प्रति मुख्य कर्तव्य क्या बताया गया है?

lesson.homework: दो सूक्तियाँ याद करके उनका हिंदी अर्थ लिखिए।

topics.title: भूकम्पविभीषिका
topics.summary: यह पाठ 26 जनवरी 2001 को गुजरात (कच्छ क्षेत्र) में आए विनाशकारी भूकंप का वर्णन करता है।
notes: यह पाठ 26 जनवरी 2001 को गुजरात (कच्छ क्षेत्र) में आए विनाशकारी भूकंप का वर्णन करता है।
गणतंत्र दिवस के उत्सव के बीच धरती काँपी; ऊँची इमारतें गिरीं और हज़ारों लोग मारे गए।
पृथ्वी के भीतर की चट्टानों (प्लेटों) की हलचल से भूकंप आते हैं; ज्वालामुखी भी धरती के भीतर की ऊर्जा का रूप है।
प्रकृति पर मनुष्य का पूरा नियंत्रण नहीं, पर भूकंप-रोधी भवन और सावधानी से नुकसान कम किया जा सकता है।
आपदा के समय धैर्य, सहयोग और राहत कार्य बहुत महत्वपूर्ण हैं।
outcomes: पाठ 'भूकम्पविभीषिका' में वर्णित आपदा को समझना
भूकंप के कारण और बचाव के उपाय जानना
प्राकृतिक आपदाओं के समय धैर्य और सहयोग पर चर्चा करना

lesson.hook: अगर कक्षा में बैठे-बैठे धरती हिलने लगे, तो आपको सबसे पहले क्या करना चाहिए?
lesson.example: भूकंप में बचाव: 'झुको, ढको, पकड़ो' — मेज़ के नीचे झुककर सिर ढकें और मेज़ पकड़कर रखें; खिड़कियों और ऊँची अलमारियों से दूर रहें।
lesson.activity: कक्षा में भूकंप अभ्यास (मॉक ड्रिल) करें और फिर संस्कृत-हिंदी में बचाव के पाँच नियम लिखें।

questions.q: पाठ में किस भूकंप का वर्णन है?
भूकंप क्यों आते हैं?
questions.a: पृथ्वी के भीतर की चट्टानों (प्लेटों) की हलचल से।

questions.q: भूकंप से होने वाले नुकसान को कैसे कम किया जा सकता है?
questions.a: भूकंप-रोधी भवन बनाकर और सुरक्षा नियम अपनाकर।

lesson.homework: भूकंप के समय क्या करें और क्या न करें — एक चार्ट बनाइए।

topics.title: अन्योक्तयः
topics.summary: अन्योक्ति का अर्थ है किसी एक को लक्ष्य करके किसी दूसरे के माध्यम से बात कहना।
notes: अन्योक्ति का अर्थ है किसी एक को लक्ष्य करके किसी दूसरे के माध्यम से बात कहना।
इस पाठ के श्लोकों में राजहंस, सरोवर, चातक, मेघ, माली आदि के माध्यम से मनुष्यों को सीख दी गई है।
राजहंस के बिना सरोवर की शोभा नहीं — गुणी व्यक्ति के बिना स्थान की शोभा नहीं।
चातक केवल मेघ से ही जल माँगता है — स्वाभिमानी व्यक्ति हर किसी के सामने हाथ नहीं फैलाता।
सभी मेघ बरसते नहीं, कुछ केवल गरजते हैं — हर व्यक्ति से याचना नहीं करनी चाहिए।
outcomes: 'अन्योक्ति' का अर्थ और शैली समझना
अन्योक्तियों में छिपे संदेश को पहचानना
प्रतीकों के माध्यम से कही गई बात को समझना

lesson.hook: कभी-कभी हम किसी से सीधी बात न कहकर किसी और के बहाने कहते हैं — ऐसा क्यों?
lesson.example: चातक-मेघ की अन्योक्ति: चातक पक्षी केवल वर्षा का जल पीता है; यह स्वाभिमान और एक ही स्थान पर विश्वास का प्रतीक है।
lesson.activity: विद्यार्थी किसी पशु, पक्षी या पेड़ के माध्यम से एक सीख देने वाली अपनी 'अन्योक्ति' हिंदी में लिखें।

questions.q: 'अन्योक्ति' किसे कहते हैं?
questions.a: किसी एक को लक्ष्य करके दूसरे के माध्यम से कही गई बात।

questions.q: चातक किससे जल माँगता है?
राजहंस और सरोवर की अन्योक्ति से क्या सीख मिलती है?
questions.a: गुणी व्यक्ति के बिना किसी स्थान की शोभा नहीं होती।

lesson.homework: दो अन्योक्तियाँ याद करके उनका भावार्थ लिखिए।

topics.title: Real Numbers
topics.summary: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number is a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from the order.
notes: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number is a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from the order.
HCF = product of the smallest powers of the common prime factors; LCM = product of the greatest powers of all the prime factors.
For any two positive integers a and b: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b.
A number is irrational if it cannot be written as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0; √2, √3, √5 and π are irrational.
To prove √2 is irrational, assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms and show that 2 then divides both a and b: a contradiction.
The sum or product of a non-zero rational and an irrational number is irrational: 5 + √3 and 2√7 are irrational.
outcomes: State and use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
Find HCF and LCM by prime factorisation and use HCF × LCM = product of two numbers
Prove that numbers such as √2 and √3 are irrational

lesson.hook: Every whole number bigger than 1 can be built from primes, like a house from bricks, and there is only one way to do it. Try to write 60 as a product of primes in two different ways.
lesson.activity: Factor-tree race: each pair gets two numbers (e.g. 140 and 156). They draw factor trees, find the HCF and LCM, then check that HCF × LCM equals the product. Fastest correct pair explains on the board.

questions.q: Express 3825 as a product of its prime factors.
Find the LCM of 6, 72 and 120.
Can the number 6ⁿ end with the digit 0 for any natural number n? Why?
questions.a: No: its prime factors are only 2 and 3; to end in 0 it would need the prime 5.

questions.q: Is 3 + 2√5 rational or irrational?

lesson.homework: Prove that √5 is irrational, following the steps used in class for √2.

topics.title: Polynomials
topics.summary: The degree of a polynomial is its highest power: linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3).
notes: The degree of a polynomial is its highest power: linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3).
A zero of p(x) is a value k with p(k) = 0; on the graph of y = p(x) the zeroes are where the curve cuts the x-axis.
A linear polynomial has one zero; a quadratic at most two (its graph is a parabola); a cubic at most three.
For ax² + bx + c with zeroes α and β: α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a.
A quadratic with a given sum S and product P of zeroes is k(x² − Sx + P).
For a cubic ax³ + bx² + cx + d with zeroes α, β, γ: α + β + γ = −b/a, αβ + βγ + γα = c/a, αβγ = −d/a.
outcomes: Find the zeroes of a polynomial from its graph and by factorising
Relate the zeroes and coefficients of linear and quadratic polynomials
Form a quadratic polynomial from the sum and product of its zeroes

lesson.hook: A ball thrown in the air follows a curve. Where does it hit the ground? Those points are the zeroes of a polynomial, and we can read them off a graph.
lesson.example: Zeroes of x² + 7x + 10: factorise as (x + 2)(x + 5), so the zeroes are −2 and −5. Check: sum = −7 = −b/a and product = 10 = c/a.
lesson.activity: Open the function grapher and plot y = x² − 2x − 8. Pupils read the zeroes off the graph (−2 and 4), then factorise to confirm, and check the sum and product rules. Change the polynomial and repeat.

questions.q: Find the zeroes of 4s² − 4s + 1.
Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes add to −3 and multiply to 2.
How many zeroes does a graph have that cuts the x-axis at three points?
If one zero of x² − 5x + k is 2, find k.

lesson.homework: Find the zeroes of 6x² − 3 − 7x and verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.

chapters.title: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

topics.title: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
topics.summary: A linear equation in two variables, ax + by + c = 0, is a straight line on a graph.
notes: A linear equation in two variables, ax + by + c = 0, is a straight line on a graph.
Two lines can intersect (one solution: consistent), be parallel (no solution: inconsistent) or coincide (infinitely many solutions).
Compare ratios: a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ gives one solution; a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ gives none; all three equal gives infinitely many.
Substitution: make one variable the subject in one equation and put it into the other.
Elimination: multiply the equations so one variable has equal coefficients, then add or subtract to remove it.
Always check the answer in both original equations.
outcomes: Represent a pair of linear equations graphically and read the kind of solution
Solve pairs of linear equations by substitution and elimination
Form and solve equations from word problems

lesson.hook: Two pens and three notebooks cost ₹46; five pens and one notebook cost ₹37. With two unknowns you need two clues: how do we find both prices?
lesson.example: Let a pen cost ₹x and a notebook ₹y: 2x + 3y = 46 and 5x + y = 37. From the second, y = 37 − 5x. Substitute: 2x + 3(37 − 5x) = 46, so 111 − 13x = 46 and x = 5. Then y = 37 − 25 = 12. A pen costs ₹5 and a notebook ₹12. Check in the first equation: 10 + 36 = 46.
lesson.activity: Plot both lines of a pair on squared paper (or the grapher) and mark where they meet. Groups then each get a pair that is parallel or coincident and must explain what that means for the story problem.

questions.q: Solve: x + y = 14 and x − y = 4.
Do 2x + 3y = 7 and 4x + 6y = 5 have a solution? Why?
The sum of two numbers is 20 and their difference is 4. Find them.
For what k do kx + 2y = 5 and 3x + y = 1 have exactly one solution?

lesson.homework: Frame and solve: half the perimeter of a rectangular garden is 36 m, and its length is 4 m more than its width. Find the dimensions.

topics.title: Quadratic Equations
topics.summary: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.
notes: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.
Factorising: split the middle term so that the two parts multiply to ac and add to b.
Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.
The discriminant D = b² − 4ac decides the roots: D > 0 two distinct real roots, D = 0 two equal roots, D < 0 no real roots.
Word problems: choose the unknown, form the equation, solve, and reject answers that make no sense (negative lengths, speeds).
outcomes: Recognise quadratic equations and write word problems as quadratic equations
Solve quadratic equations by factorising and by the quadratic formula
Use the discriminant to find the nature of the roots

lesson.hook: A rectangular prayer hall has an area of 300 m² and its length is one metre more than twice its breadth. Can you find its size? The answer hides in a quadratic equation.
lesson.example: Prayer hall: breadth x, length 2x + 1. x(2x + 1) = 300 → 2x² + x − 300 = 0 → (x − 12)(2x + 25) = 0 → x = 12 (reject −12.5). The hall is 25 m by 12 m.
lesson.activity: Discriminant sort: groups get ten quadratic equations on cards, compute D for each and sort them into 'two roots', 'equal roots' and 'no real roots'. Then graph one of each kind to see the parabola cross, touch or miss the x-axis.

questions.q: Solve x² − 3x − 10 = 0.
Find the discriminant of 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0 and the nature of its roots.
For what value of k does 2x² + kx + 3 = 0 have equal roots?
The product of two consecutive positive integers is 306. Find them.

lesson.homework: A train travels 360 km at a uniform speed. Had the speed been 5 km/h more, it would have taken one hour less. Find its speed.

topics.title: Arithmetic Progressions
topics.summary: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list in which each term is got by adding the same number d (the common difference) to the one before.
notes: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list in which each term is got by adding the same number d (the common difference) to the one before.
General form: a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, …
The nth term: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d; the nth term from the end of an AP with last term l is l − (n − 1)d.
Sum of n terms: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] = n/2 (a + l).
The sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n + 1)/2 (young Gauss added 1 to 100 as 50 pairs of 101).
outcomes: Recognise arithmetic progressions and find their common difference
Find the nth term aₙ = a + (n − 1)d
Find the sum of n terms Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

lesson.hook: You save ₹50 this month and ₹10 more each month than the month before. How much will you have saved after two years, without adding 24 numbers one by one?
lesson.activity: Staircase of blocks: build (or draw) a staircase of 1, 2, 3, … 10 blocks, copy it, turn the copy upside down and fit them together into a rectangle. Pupils see why 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 and then derive Sₙ.

questions.q: Find the 10th term of 2, 7, 12, …
Which term of 3, 8, 13, … is 78?
Find the sum of the first 20 odd numbers.
Is 0, −4, −8, −12 an AP? If so, what is d?

lesson.homework: How many two-digit numbers are divisible by 3? Find their sum.

topics.title: Triangles
topics.summary: Similar figures have the same shape but not necessarily the same size: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio.
notes: Similar figures have the same shape but not necessarily the same size: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio.
All circles are similar, all squares are similar, all equilateral triangles are similar.
Basic Proportionality Theorem: a line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio. Its converse is also true.
AAA (or AA): if the angles are equal, the triangles are similar.
SSS: if the three pairs of sides are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar. SAS: one equal angle between sides in the same ratio.
Similarity is written in matching order: △ABC ∼ △PQR means A ↔ P, B ↔ Q, C ↔ R.
outcomes: Identify similar figures and similar triangles
Prove and use the Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales)
Use the AAA, SSS and SAS similarity criteria

lesson.hook: How could you find the height of a tall tree using only its shadow, a stick and a measuring tape? Ancient Greek mathematician Thales measured a pyramid this way.
lesson.example: A 1.5 m stick casts a 2 m shadow at the same time a tree casts a 24 m shadow. The sun's rays make equal angles, so the triangles are similar: height/24 = 1.5/2, height = 18 m.
lesson.activity: Shadow day: in the playground, groups measure a metre stick's shadow and the shadow of a flagpole or the school building, then work out its height by similar triangles and compare answers.

questions.q: In △ABC, DE ∥ BC with AD = 3 cm, DB = 2 cm and AE = 6 cm. Find EC.
Are two triangles with angles 50°, 60°, 70° and 60°, 70°, 50° similar? By which criterion?
Are all rectangles similar? Give a reason.
questions.a: No: their angles are equal, but their sides need not be in the same ratio.

questions.q: State the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem.
questions.a: If a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, it is parallel to the third side.

lesson.homework: Prove the Basic Proportionality Theorem in your notebook, drawing the figure and giving a reason for each step.

topics.title: Coordinate Geometry
topics.summary: A point on the plane is (x, y): x is its distance from the y-axis, y its distance from the x-axis.
notes: A point on the plane is (x, y): x is its distance from the y-axis, y its distance from the x-axis.
Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂): √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²] — Pythagoras on the grid.
Section formula: the point dividing the join in ratio m : n is ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)).
Midpoint: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
Three points are collinear if the distance between the outer two equals the sum of the other two distances.
The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so they share a midpoint.
outcomes: Find the distance between two points
Find the point dividing a segment in a given ratio (section formula) and the midpoint
Use these to test shapes such as collinear points and parallelograms

lesson.hook: On a map of your town drawn on a grid, your home is at (2, 3) and school at (8, 11). How far apart are they as the crow flies, and where is the halfway tea stall?
lesson.example: Home (2, 3) to school (8, 11): distance = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 units. The tea stall at the midpoint is ((2 + 8)/2, (3 + 11)/2) = (5, 7).
lesson.activity: Classroom grid: mark axes on the floor with tape (or use the board's graph tool). Pupils stand at given points; the class predicts distances and midpoints, then checks with a tape measure.

questions.q: Find the distance between (−5, 7) and (−1, 3).
Find the midpoint of (2, −3) and (4, 7).
Find the point dividing the join of (−1, 7) and (4, −3) in the ratio 2 : 3.
Are (1, 5), (2, 3) and (−2, −11) collinear?

lesson.homework: Show that the points (1, 7), (4, 2), (−1, −1) and (−4, 4) are the vertices of a square.

topics.title: Introduction to Trigonometry
topics.summary: In a right triangle, for angle A: sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan A = opposite/adjacent.
notes: In a right triangle, for angle A: sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan A = opposite/adjacent.
cosec A, sec A and cot A are the reciprocals of sin A, cos A and tan A; tan A = sin A / cos A.
The ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle (similar triangles).
Standard values: sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = 1/√2, sin 60° = √3/2; cos is the same list backwards; tan 45° = 1.
Identities: sin²A + cos²A = 1; 1 + tan²A = sec²A; 1 + cot²A = cosec²A.
outcomes: Define the trigonometric ratios of an acute angle in a right triangle
Recall the ratios for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°
Use the identity sin²A + cos²A = 1 and its forms

lesson.hook: Surveyors, pilots and satellite engineers all use the same three ratios of a right triangle. If a ladder leans on a wall at 60°, how much of the wall does it reach?
lesson.example: If sin A = 3/5, draw a right triangle with opposite 3 and hypotenuse 5; the adjacent side is √(25 − 9) = 4. So cos A = 4/5 and tan A = 3/4.
lesson.activity: Make a table: groups draw right triangles of different sizes with a 30° angle (using a protractor), measure the sides and compute opposite/hypotenuse. Everyone gets about 0.5: the ratio belongs to the angle.

questions.q: Evaluate sin 60° cos 30° + sin 30° cos 60°.
If tan A = 1, what is A?
Simplify (1 − sin²A) sec²A.
In a right triangle, sin A = 12/13. Find cos A.

lesson.homework: Prove that (sin A + cosec A)² + (cos A + sec A)² = 7 + tan²A + cot²A.

topics.title: Some Applications of Trigonometry
topics.summary: The line of sight goes from the eye to the object.
notes: The line of sight goes from the eye to the object.
Angle of elevation: between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look up at an object.
Angle of depression: between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look down; it equals the angle of elevation from the other point (alternate angles).
Draw the figure, mark the right angle, the known side and angle, then pick the ratio that links the known and unknown sides.
tan is used most often: height = distance × tan(angle of elevation).
outcomes: Understand angles of elevation and depression
Use trigonometric ratios to find heights and distances
Draw a clear figure for word problems

lesson.hook: Standing 30 m from the foot of a temple tower, you look up to its top at 60°. Without climbing, how tall is the tower?
lesson.example: Temple tower: tan 60° = h/30, so h = 30√3 ≈ 51.96 m.
lesson.activity: Make a clinometer from a protractor, a straw and a thread with a weight. Groups measure the angle of elevation of the top of the school building from a measured distance and calculate its height.

questions.q: A kite string 60 m long makes 60° with the ground. How high is the kite?
From the top of a 75 m lighthouse, the angle of depression of a ship is 30°. How far is the ship?
The angle of elevation of the sun is 45°. How long is the shadow of a 10 m pole?
Why does the angle of depression from A to B equal the angle of elevation from B to A?
questions.a: They are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines.

lesson.homework: Measure the height of a tree or building near your home with a home-made clinometer and write your calculation.

topics.title: Circles
topics.summary: A secant cuts a circle at two points; a tangent touches it at exactly one point, the point of contact.
notes: A secant cuts a circle at two points; a tangent touches it at exactly one point, the point of contact.
There is exactly one tangent at any point of a circle, and none from a point inside it.
The tangent at any point is perpendicular to the radius through that point.
From an external point there are exactly two tangents, and their lengths are equal.
The line from the external point to the centre bisects the angle between the two tangents.
outcomes: Understand tangents and secants to a circle
Prove that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
Prove that the tangents from an external point are equal

lesson.hook: A bicycle wheel touches the road at just one point. That road is a tangent to the wheel. What special angle does the spoke to that point make with the road?
lesson.example: From a point 5 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 3 cm, the tangent length is √(5² − 3²) = 4 cm, because the radius meets the tangent at a right angle.
lesson.activity: Draw a circle, mark a point outside it and use a ruler to draw both tangents; measure them to find they are equal. Then join the centre to the points of contact and measure the angles (90°).

questions.q: How many tangents can a circle have?
A tangent from a point 13 cm from the centre is 12 cm long. Find the radius.
Two tangents from P touch the circle at A and B. If PA = 7 cm, what is PB?
What angle does the radius make with the tangent at the point of contact?

lesson.homework: Prove that the tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are parallel.

topics.title: Areas Related to Circles
topics.summary: Circumference = 2πr; area = πr².
notes: Circumference = 2πr; area = πr².
A sector of angle θ is the fraction θ/360 of the circle.
Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr; area of sector = (θ/360) × πr².
Area of a segment = area of the sector − area of the triangle formed by the chord and the radii.
For combinations (a design, a track, a flower bed) split the figure into shapes you know, then add or subtract.
outcomes: Find the length of an arc and the area of a sector
Find the area of a segment of a circle
Solve problems on areas of combinations of shapes with circles

lesson.hook: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. What is the area of one slice, and how long is its crust?
lesson.example: Pizza of radius 14 cm cut into 8: each slice is a 45° sector. Area = (45/360) × (22/7) × 14 × 14 = 77 cm². Crust (arc) = (45/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 14 = 11 cm.
lesson.activity: Paper plates: groups fold paper circles into 2, 4 and 8 equal sectors, measure the radius, and calculate each sector's area and arc length; check the arc with a thread.

questions.q: Find the area of a sector of radius 6 cm and angle 60° (π = 22/7).
The minute hand of a clock is 14 cm long. What area does it sweep in 5 minutes?
What fraction of the circle is a sector of 90°?
How is the area of a segment found?
questions.a: Area of the sector minus the area of the triangle.

lesson.homework: A horse is tied with a 5 m rope to one corner of a square field of side 15 m. Find the area of the field it can graze.

topics.title: Surface Areas and Volumes
topics.summary: Recall: cuboid, cube, cylinder, cone, sphere and hemisphere formulas for curved/total surface area and volume.
notes: Recall: cuboid, cube, cylinder, cone, sphere and hemisphere formulas for curved/total surface area and volume.
The surface area of a combination is the total of only the outside surfaces: faces that are joined are hidden and not counted.
The volume of a combination is the sum of the volumes of its parts.
Cylinder: CSA = 2πrh, volume = πr²h. Cone: CSA = πrl, volume = ⅓πr²h. Sphere: 4πr², ⁴⁄₃πr³. Hemisphere: CSA 2πr², volume ⅔πr³.
Draw the solid and list its parts before calculating.
outcomes: Find surface areas of solids made by combining cubes, cuboids, cylinders, cones and hemispheres
Find volumes of such combined solids
Choose which faces count for the surface area

lesson.hook: A capsule of medicine is a cylinder with two hemispheres at its ends. How much gelatin covers it, and how much medicine fits inside?
lesson.example: Capsule: radius 0.25 cm, cylinder length 1 cm. Volume = πr²h + ⁴⁄₃πr³ (two hemispheres make one sphere) = π(0.0625)(1) + ⁴⁄₃π(0.015625) ≈ 0.196 + 0.065 = 0.261 cm³.
lesson.activity: Open the 3D solids, pick the cylinder and the cone, and unfold them to their nets to see where each surface-area formula comes from. Then groups design a toy from two solids and calculate its surface area and volume.

questions.q: Two cubes of side 5 cm are joined end to end. Find the surface area of the cuboid formed.
Which parts count in the surface area of a cone on a hemisphere (a toy top)?
questions.a: The curved surface of the cone and the curved surface of the hemisphere.

questions.q: Write the volume of a hemisphere of radius r.
A cone and a cylinder have the same base and height. How do their volumes compare?
questions.a: The cone's volume is one-third of the cylinder's.

lesson.homework: A tent is a cylinder of height 2.1 m and diameter 4 m topped by a cone of slant height 2.8 m. Find the canvas needed.

topics.title: Statistics
topics.summary: For grouped data, use the class mark (midpoint) of each class as its representative value.
notes: For grouped data, use the class mark (midpoint) of each class as its representative value.
Mean x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ; the assumed-mean and step-deviation methods make the arithmetic easier.
The modal class has the highest frequency; mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h.
Median = l + [(n/2 − cf)/f] × h, where l is the lower limit of the median class and cf the cumulative frequency before it.
Empirical relation: 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean.
Mean uses every value; median is not affected by extreme values; mode shows the most common value.
outcomes: Find the mean of grouped data by the direct, assumed-mean and step-deviation methods
Find the mode of grouped data
Find the median of grouped data using cumulative frequency

lesson.hook: A cricket coach has the runs scored by 40 players grouped as 0–20, 20–40 and so on. What is the typical score, and which kind of 'typical' should he quote?
lesson.activity: Class survey: each pupil writes the time (in minutes) they took to reach school. Group the data in 10-minute classes on the board and find the mean, median and mode together.

questions.q: What is the class mark of 20–30?
In a grouped table, which class is the modal class?
questions.a: The class with the highest frequency.

questions.q: If the mode is 24 and the mean is 21, find the median by the empirical relation.
Why might the median be a better average than the mean for incomes?
questions.a: A few very high incomes pull the mean up; the median is not affected by them.

lesson.homework: Collect the ages of 30 people in your neighbourhood, group them, and find the mean and the modal class.

topics.title: Probability
topics.summary: P(E) = number of outcomes favourable to E / total number of equally likely outcomes.
notes: P(E) = number of outcomes favourable to E / total number of equally likely outcomes.
0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1: an impossible event has probability 0, a sure event 1.
P(E) + P(not E) = 1, so P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
A coin has 2 outcomes; a die 6; two dice 36; a pack of 52 cards has 4 suits of 13.
An elementary event has one outcome; the probabilities of all elementary events add up to 1.
outcomes: Understand theoretical probability of equally likely outcomes
Find the probability of simple events and complementary events
Solve problems with coins, dice and cards

lesson.hook: Before a match, the referee tosses a coin. Why do both captains accept that as fair, and what does 'a 50% chance' really mean?
lesson.example: Two dice are thrown. P(sum is 8)? Favourable: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) = 5 of 36 outcomes, so P = 5/36.
lesson.activity: Each pair tosses a coin 20 times and rolls a die 30 times and records the results; pool the class results on the board and see the fractions come close to 1/2 and 1/6 as the number of trials grows.

questions.q: A die is thrown once. Find the probability of getting a prime number.
P(E) = 0.05. What is P(not E)?
A card is drawn from a well-shuffled pack. Find the probability of a red king.
Can the probability of an event be 1.5? Why?

lesson.homework: Two coins are tossed together. List all the outcomes and find the probability of at least one head.

topics.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
topics.summary: In a chemical reaction new substances form. Signs: change of state, colour change, a gas given off, a change of temperature.
notes: In a chemical reaction new substances form. Signs: change of state, colour change, a gas given off, a change of temperature.
A chemical equation shows reactants → products with formulae and states (s), (l), (g), (aq).
Mass is neither created nor destroyed, so an equation must be balanced: the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.
Combination: two or more substances make one. Decomposition: one substance breaks into two or more (by heat, light or electricity).
Displacement: a more reactive element pushes a less reactive one out of its compound. Double displacement: two compounds swap ions, often making a precipitate.
Oxidation is gain of oxygen (or loss of hydrogen); reduction is loss of oxygen (or gain of hydrogen). Both happen together in a redox reaction.
Corrosion (rusting) and rancidity (fats going stale) are everyday oxidation; paint, oiling, galvanising, airtight packing and nitrogen-filled packets slow them.
outcomes: Recognise a chemical reaction from what you observe
Write and balance a chemical equation
Tell apart combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and redox reactions

lesson.hook: A bright iron nail left in water turns brown; milk left out turns sour; a matchstick bursts into flame. What do these three changes have in common, and how could you prove that something new has formed?
lesson.example: Balance: Fe + H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂. Oxygen: put 4 in front of H₂O (4 O). Hydrogen: now 8 H on the left, so 4 H₂ on the right. Iron: 3 Fe on the right, so 3 Fe on the left.
lesson.activity: Demonstration: dip a clean iron nail in blue copper sulphate solution for 15 minutes. Pupils predict, then watch the nail turn brown and the blue fade. In pairs they write the word equation, then the balanced equation, and name the type of reaction (displacement).

questions.q: Why is magnesium ribbon cleaned with sandpaper before burning?
questions.a: To remove the layer of magnesium oxide on its surface, so that the metal itself burns.

questions.q: Balance: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
What type of reaction is CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating?
In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, which substance is oxidised and which is reduced?
questions.a: Hydrogen is oxidised (gains oxygen); copper oxide is reduced (loses oxygen).

lesson.homework: Find three chemical reactions in your kitchen. For each write the word equation and say which signs of a reaction you saw.

topics.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
topics.summary: Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red; bases taste bitter, feel soapy and turn red litmus blue.
notes: Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red; bases taste bitter, feel soapy and turn red litmus blue.
Indicators: litmus, turmeric (turns red in bases), phenolphthalein (pink in bases), methyl orange; some smell indicators like onion lose their smell in bases.
Acids give H⁺ ions in water; bases that dissolve in water (alkalis) give OH⁻ ions.
Acid + base → salt + water (neutralisation). Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic. The lower the pH, the stronger the acid.
pH matters in life: the stomach, tooth decay below pH 5.5, soil for crops, acid rain.
Useful salts: common salt (NaCl), washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O), baking soda (NaHCO₃), bleaching powder (CaOCl₂), plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O).
outcomes: Describe acids and bases by their properties and by indicators
Explain neutralisation and the pH scale
Name common salts and their uses

lesson.hook: Why does a bee sting hurt less when you rub baking soda on it, and why does a stomach ache after a heavy meal ease with an antacid tablet?
lesson.example: Hydrochloric acid neutralises sodium hydroxide: the H⁺ and OH⁻ ions join to make water, and sodium chloride is left in solution.
lesson.activity: Kitchen indicators: groups test lemon juice, vinegar, soap water, baking soda solution, tap water and a crushed antacid with turmeric paper and with red cabbage (or hibiscus) water. They sort the results into acidic, neutral and basic on a pH line drawn on the board.

questions.q: A solution turns red litmus blue. What is its pH likely to be: 1, 7 or 10?
Why should curd and sour food not be kept in copper or brass vessels?
questions.a: Their acids react with the metal and make poisonous compounds.

questions.q: What gas is given off when zinc reacts with dilute sulphuric acid, and how is it tested?
questions.a: Hydrogen; it burns with a pop when a burning matchstick is brought near.

questions.q: Name the salt used to make a fractured bone set in a cast.

lesson.homework: Make a chart of ten things at home marked acidic, basic or neutral, and how you could test each with turmeric.

topics.title: Metals and Non-metals
topics.summary: Metals are lustrous, hard (mostly), malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity and sonorous. Non-metals are usually dull, brittle and poor conductors.
notes: Metals are lustrous, hard (mostly), malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity and sonorous. Non-metals are usually dull, brittle and poor conductors.
Exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal; sodium and potassium are soft; graphite (a non-metal) conducts electricity; diamond is the hardest natural substance.
Metals burn to form basic oxides; non-metals form acidic oxides. Aluminium and zinc oxides are amphoteric (react with acids and bases).
Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt.
Metals lose electrons and non-metals gain them to form ionic compounds such as NaCl: high melting points, soluble in water, conduct when molten or dissolved.
Extraction depends on reactivity: electrolysis for the most reactive, reduction with carbon for the middle ones, heating alone for the least reactive.
Corrosion is prevented by painting, oiling, galvanising, chrome plating and alloying; stainless steel is an alloy of iron with nickel and chromium.
outcomes: Compare the physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals
Use the reactivity series to predict reactions
Explain ionic bonding, extraction of metals and corrosion

lesson.hook: Why are cooking pots made of steel or aluminium but their handles of plastic or wood, and why does gold stay shiny for thousands of years when iron rusts in months?
lesson.example: Will copper displace iron from iron sulphate? Copper is below iron in the reactivity series, so no reaction. But iron placed in copper sulphate displaces copper: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.
lesson.activity: Property stations: groups test samples (iron nail, aluminium foil, copper wire, coal, sulphur powder) for lustre, hardness (scratching), malleability (gentle hammering), and conduction using a cell, bulb and wires. They fill a table and decide metal or non-metal.

questions.q: Why is sodium kept in kerosene?
questions.a: It reacts so vigorously with oxygen and water in the air that it could catch fire.

questions.q: Give one non-metal that conducts electricity.
Show the formation of MgCl₂ by transfer of electrons.
questions.a: Mg gives two electrons (Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻); each of two Cl atoms takes one (Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻).

questions.q: Why is galvanised iron protected even if its zinc coating is scratched?
questions.a: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes first and protects the iron.

lesson.homework: List five metal objects at home, the metal or alloy each is made of, and the property that makes it suitable.

topics.title: Carbon and its Compounds
topics.summary: Carbon has four valence electrons and forms four covalent bonds by sharing electrons, not by giving or taking them.
notes: Carbon has four valence electrons and forms four covalent bonds by sharing electrons, not by giving or taking them.
Catenation: carbon atoms link to each other in long chains, branches and rings. Tetravalency lets them bond to many other elements too.
Hydrocarbons: alkanes are saturated (single bonds, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂); alkenes (double bond) and alkynes (triple bond) are unsaturated.
A homologous series has the same functional group and differs by CH₂: alcohol –OH, aldehyde –CHO, ketone –CO–, carboxylic acid –COOH, halo –Cl/–Br.
Reactions: combustion, oxidation (ethanol → ethanoic acid), addition of hydrogen (hydrogenation of oils with a nickel catalyst), substitution (methane with chlorine in sunlight).
Ethanol is used in medicines and as a fuel; ethanoic acid (vinegar is 5–8%) reacts with alcohols to form sweet-smelling esters.
Soap molecules have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail; they form micelles that trap oily dirt so water can wash it away. Detergents work even in hard water.
outcomes: Explain covalent bonding and the special bonding of carbon
Name simple carbon compounds and recognise functional groups
Describe key reactions of carbon compounds, ethanol and ethanoic acid, and how soaps clean

lesson.hook: Your food, clothes, fuel and medicines, and you yourself, are built mostly of carbon compounds. How can one element make millions of different substances?
lesson.example: Methane has one carbon and four hydrogens. Carbon shares one electron pair with each hydrogen, so every atom ends with a full outer shell: four single covalent bonds.
lesson.activity: Model building: with clay balls (black carbon, white hydrogen, red oxygen) and matchsticks, groups build methane, ethane, ethene and ethanol, then show them in the 3D molecule viewer and count bonds on each carbon.

questions.q: Why are carbon compounds poor conductors of electricity?
questions.a: They are covalent: they have no free ions or electrons to carry charge.

questions.q: Write the formula of the next member after propane in the alkane series.
Which gas turns lime water milky when ethanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate?
Why does soap not lather well in hard water?
questions.a: Calcium and magnesium salts in hard water react with soap to form an insoluble scum.

lesson.homework: Draw the electron-dot structures of ethane, ethene and ethyne and label the single, double and triple bonds.

topics.title: Life Processes
topics.summary: Life processes keep an organism alive and repair it: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion.
notes: Life processes keep an organism alive and repair it: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion.
Autotrophs make food by photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water, with sunlight and chlorophyll, give glucose and oxygen. Heterotrophs take in ready-made food.
Human digestion: saliva (amylase) → stomach (pepsin, hydrochloric acid) → small intestine (bile, pancreatic juice, intestinal juice; villi absorb food) → large intestine absorbs water.
Respiration releases energy from glucose: aerobic (with oxygen, much ATP) or anaerobic (in yeast gives ethanol; in muscles gives lactic acid).
The four-chambered heart keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood apart: double circulation. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins bring it back, capillaries exchange materials.
Plants move water through xylem (pulled by transpiration) and food through phloem (translocation).
Kidneys filter blood in nephrons and make urine; dialysis does this artificially when kidneys fail. Plants lose waste through leaves, bark and stored resins.
outcomes: Describe nutrition, respiration, transport and excretion as the life processes
Explain how the human heart, lungs and kidneys work
Compare these processes in plants and animals

resources.title: Starch test: light and chlorophyll for photosynthesis

lesson.hook: Even while you sleep, something inside you is working non-stop. What must a living body keep doing every second just to stay alive, and how do we know?
lesson.example: Follow one drop of blood: body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs (picks up oxygen) → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. It passes through the heart twice in one full circuit.
lesson.activity: Open the 3D heart, run 'Double circulation' step by step, and let a pupil trace the path on the board as the class names each chamber and vessel. Then count pulse rate at rest and after 30 seconds of jumping, and explain the difference.

questions.q: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
questions.a: It pumps blood to the whole body, which needs more force than pumping to the nearby lungs.

questions.q: Name the product of anaerobic respiration in yeast.
What is the function of villi in the small intestine?
questions.a: They increase the surface area for absorbing digested food.

questions.q: What is the basic filtering unit of the kidney called?

lesson.homework: Draw and label the human heart, marking with arrows the path of oxygen-rich (red) and oxygen-poor (blue) blood.

topics.title: Control and Coordination
topics.summary: Receptors pick up stimuli; nerve impulses travel along neurons (dendrite → cell body → axon) and cross a gap called a synapse by chemical messengers.
notes: Receptors pick up stimuli; nerve impulses travel along neurons (dendrite → cell body → axon) and cross a gap called a synapse by chemical messengers.
A reflex action is fast and automatic; its path (reflex arc) goes receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle, without waiting for the brain.
The brain has three main parts: forebrain (thinking, senses, voluntary actions), midbrain, and hindbrain (cerebellum for balance and posture; medulla for breathing, heartbeat, swallowing).
The brain is protected by the skull and fluid; the spinal cord by the backbone.

Plants respond without nerves: touch (mimosa leaves fold), light (phototropism), gravity (geotropism), water and chemicals, using plant hormones such as auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin and abscisic acid.
In animals, endocrine glands release hormones into the blood: adrenaline (fight or flight), thyroxine (needs iodine), insulin (blood sugar), growth hormone, testosterone and oestrogen.
Feedback mechanisms keep hormone levels right: for example, rising blood sugar makes the pancreas release more insulin.
outcomes: Describe how nerves and the brain control and coordinate the body
Explain a reflex arc
Explain coordination in plants and by hormones in animals

lesson.hook: You touch a hot pan and your hand jerks away before you even feel the pain. Who gave the order, and how did it travel so fast?
lesson.example: Reflex arc for touching a hot object: heat receptors in the skin → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay neuron) → motor neuron → arm muscle contracts, hand pulls away. The message reaches the brain a moment later, so you feel pain after moving.
lesson.activity: Ruler-drop test: one pupil drops a ruler, the partner catches it; the distance fallen shows reaction time. Compare catching with eyes open versus when told 'now'. Then open the 3D neuron and brain to show where the signal goes.

questions.q: Which part of the brain keeps your balance when you ride a bicycle?
What is a synapse?
questions.a: The small gap between two neurons, where the impulse passes on by chemicals.

questions.q: A plant on a windowsill bends towards the window. Name this response.
Why is iodised salt recommended?
questions.a: Iodine is needed to make thyroxine; lack of it causes goitre.

lesson.homework: Draw a reflex arc for stepping on a sharp pin and label each part.

topics.title: How do Organisms Reproduce?
topics.summary: Reproduction copies DNA; the copies are never perfect, and these small variations help species survive changing surroundings.
notes: Reproduction copies DNA; the copies are never perfect, and these small variations help species survive changing surroundings.
Asexual reproduction has one parent: fission (amoeba, plasmodium), budding (hydra, yeast), fragmentation (spirogyra), regeneration (planaria), spores (bread mould).
Vegetative propagation grows plants from roots, stems or leaves (potato, bryophyllum, rose cuttings, grafting); tissue culture grows many plants from a few cells.
Sexual reproduction joins two gametes (fertilisation), mixing DNA from two parents.

In flowers, stamens make pollen and the pistil holds ovules in the ovary; pollination carries pollen to the stigma, a pollen tube reaches the ovule, and fertilisation makes a seed while the ovary becomes the fruit.
Human reproductive systems develop at puberty; the fertilised egg implants in the uterus and the embryo is fed through the placenta.
Reproductive health: sexually transmitted infections, safe practices, and methods of preventing pregnancy; sex determination of a child before birth is illegal in India.
outcomes: Explain why living things reproduce and why variation matters
Describe asexual reproduction in single-celled and many-celled organisms
Describe sexual reproduction in flowering plants and humans, and reproductive health

lesson.hook: A potato left in the cupboard sprouts new plants; a mango seed grows into a tree. Two very different ways to make new life: what does each gain and lose?
lesson.example: In a hibiscus flower, the pollen from an anther reaches the stigma; it grows a tube down the style into the ovary, where a male cell joins the egg in an ovule. The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary the fruit.
lesson.activity: Open the 3D flower, cut it lengthwise and run 'Pollination and fertilisation'. Then groups examine a real flower (or the model), take it apart whorl by whorl and stick each part on a sheet with labels.

questions.q: How does an amoeba reproduce?
questions.a: By binary fission: it splits into two.

questions.q: What part of the flower becomes the fruit?
Why is variation useful to a species?
questions.a: Some variants may survive when conditions change, so the species does not die out.

questions.q: What is the role of the placenta?
questions.a: It passes food and oxygen from the mother's blood to the embryo and removes its wastes.

lesson.homework: Grow a money plant or bryophyllum leaf in water for a week and record how new roots or plantlets appear.

topics.title: Heredity
topics.summary: Traits are inherited through genes, which are sections of DNA on chromosomes; each parent gives one copy of each gene.
notes: Traits are inherited through genes, which are sections of DNA on chromosomes; each parent gives one copy of each gene.
Mendel crossed tall and short pea plants: all first-generation (F1) plants were tall; in F2 tall and short appeared in a 3 : 1 ratio.
The trait that shows in F1 is dominant (tall, T); the hidden one is recessive (short, t). A short plant must be tt.
When two traits are followed together (seed shape and colour), they are inherited independently: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 in F2.
Genes control traits by making proteins, such as the enzyme that makes the growth hormone for tallness.
Human sex is decided by the father's sperm: the mother always gives an X chromosome; a sperm carrying X gives a girl (XX), one carrying Y a boy (XY).
Variations that arise during reproduction are the raw material for evolution.
outcomes: Explain how traits are passed from parents to offspring
Use Mendel's experiments to explain dominant and recessive traits
Explain how the sex of a child is determined

lesson.hook: You may have your mother's eyes and your grandfather's curly hair. How does a feature skip a generation and come back?
lesson.example: Cross Tt × Tt. Gametes T or t from each parent. Combinations: TT, Tt, tT, tt → three tall to one short, and one-quarter of the plants are pure tall (TT).
lesson.activity: Coin genetics: each pair tosses two coins (heads = T, tails = t), one per parent, 40 times and tallies the results. Pool the class data on the board and compare with 3 : 1. Use the DNA model's ladder view to show that each strand carries the code.

questions.q: In Mendel's cross of tall (TT) and short (tt) plants, what are all the F1 plants?
Who decides the sex of the child, and why?
questions.a: The father: his sperm may carry X or Y, while the mother's egg always carries X.

questions.q: What are genes made of?
A trait that shows in only one of four F2 plants is called what?

lesson.homework: Draw the checkerboard (Punnett square) for a cross between a round-yellow (RRYY) and a wrinkled-green (rryy) pea plant up to F1.

topics.title: Light – Reflection and Refraction
topics.summary: Reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and both rays and the normal lie in one plane.
notes: Reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and both rays and the normal lie in one plane.
Concave mirrors can form real inverted images or (object inside F) enlarged virtual erect images; convex mirrors always form small virtual erect images and give a wide view (rear-view mirrors).
Mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with the New Cartesian sign convention; f = R/2; magnification m = −v/u.
Refraction: light bends because it changes speed between media; sin i / sin r is constant (Snell's law); the refractive index n = c/v.
Convex lenses converge light and can form real or virtual images; concave lenses diverge light and always form small virtual images.
Lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f; magnification m = v/u; power P = 1/f (f in metres), measured in dioptres (D).
Ray diagrams use three easy rays: one parallel to the axis, one through the focus, one through the centre (optical centre for a lens).
outcomes: State the laws of reflection and refraction
Form images with plane and spherical mirrors and lenses using ray diagrams
Use the mirror and lens formulae, magnification and power

resources.title: Focal length of a convex lens and a concave mirror

lesson.hook: A spoon shows your face upside down on one side and right way up on the other. A pencil in a glass of water looks broken. Light is doing something different each time: what?
lesson.example: An object is 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. With u = −30 cm, f = +20 cm: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so v = +60 cm. The image is real, inverted, 60 cm behind the lens, and m = v/u = −2 (twice the size).
lesson.activity: Focus the image of a window or a distant tree on a sheet of paper with a convex lens (or magnifying glass); measure the distance to estimate f. Groups then draw the ray diagram on the board for an object beyond 2F and compare with what they see.

questions.q: Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles, and why?
questions.a: Convex: it always gives an erect image and a wider field of view.

questions.q: The power of a lens is −2 D. What kind of lens is it and what is its focal length?
Light slows down from 3 × 10⁸ m/s in air to 2 × 10⁸ m/s in glass. What is the refractive index of glass?
Where must an object be placed before a concave mirror to get a virtual, enlarged image?
questions.a: Between the pole and the focus.

lesson.homework: Draw ray diagrams for a concave mirror with the object at C, between C and F, and between F and P, and describe each image.

chapters.title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World

topics.title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
topics.summary: The eye focuses light on the retina with the cornea and lens; the ciliary muscles change the lens's thickness (accommodation) for near and far objects.
notes: The eye focuses light on the retina with the cornea and lens; the ciliary muscles change the lens's thickness (accommodation) for near and far objects.
The iris controls the pupil's size; rods and cones in the retina send signals along the optic nerve to the brain.
Myopia (short sight) is corrected with a concave lens, hypermetropia (long sight) with a convex lens, presbyopia with bifocals; cataract is treated by surgery.
A glass prism splits white light into VIBGYOR (dispersion) because each colour bends by a different amount: violet most, red least.
A rainbow forms when sunlight is refracted, dispersed and reflected inside raindrops; you see it with the Sun behind you.
Atmospheric refraction makes stars twinkle and lets us see the Sun about two minutes before it actually rises and after it sets.
Tiny particles scatter blue light the most, so the sky is blue; at sunrise and sunset light crosses more air, the blue is scattered away and the Sun looks red.
outcomes: Describe the parts of the human eye and how it focuses
Explain defects of vision and how lenses correct them
Explain dispersion, the rainbow, atmospheric refraction and scattering

resources.title: Refraction and dispersion by a prism

lesson.hook: Why is the sky blue at noon and red at sunset, and why does a star twinkle while a planet shines steadily?
lesson.example: A myopic person cannot see beyond 2 m. To see far objects, a concave lens must make distant objects appear to be at 2 m: f = −2 m, so the power needed is P = 1/f = −0.5 D.
lesson.activity: Open the 3D eye, cut it open and trace light through cornea, lens and vitreous humour to the retina. Then use the 3D prism: run 'Splitting white light' and have pupils call out the colours in order. If there is sun, make a rainbow with a glass of water on a white sheet.

questions.q: What is the function of the ciliary muscles?
questions.a: They change the curvature of the eye lens so that it can focus near and far objects (accommodation).

questions.q: Which colour bends the most in a prism?
Why do danger signals use red light?
questions.a: Red is scattered least by fog and smoke, so it can be seen from far away.

questions.q: Name the defect corrected by a convex lens.

lesson.homework: Watch a sunrise or sunset and a clear night sky; write two observations explained by this chapter.

topics.title: Electricity
topics.summary: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q/t, measured in amperes (A) with an ammeter in series.
notes: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q/t, measured in amperes (A) with an ammeter in series.
Potential difference is the work done per unit charge: V = W/Q, measured in volts (V) with a voltmeter in parallel.
Ohm's law: at constant temperature, V = IR. Resistance R depends on length, area and material: R = ρL/A.
In series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …, same current everywhere. In parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …, same voltage across each; homes are wired in parallel.
Heating effect (Joule's law): H = I²Rt; used in heaters, irons, bulbs and fuses.
Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R, in watts; energy used in kWh (1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J) is what the electricity bill counts.
Circuit symbols: cell, battery, key, bulb, resistor, rheostat, ammeter, voltmeter.
outcomes: Define current, potential difference and resistance and use Ohm's law
Solve series and parallel circuit problems
Calculate electrical energy and power and explain the heating effect

lesson.hook: Why can the same wall socket run a tiny phone charger and a heavy electric iron, and why does the iron's cord never glow while its base gets red hot?
lesson.example: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 12 Ω are joined in parallel across 6 V. 1/R = 1/4 + 1/12 = 4/12, so R = 3 Ω; total current I = V/R = 2 A. Across each resistor the voltage is 6 V: 1.5 A through 4 Ω and 0.5 A through 12 Ω.
lesson.activity: With cells, a bulb, a key and an ammeter (or the circuit tool on the board), groups compare the bulb's brightness with one bulb, two in series and two in parallel, and explain what they see using current and resistance.

questions.q: A bulb draws 0.5 A from a 220 V supply. What is its power?
How is a voltmeter connected in a circuit?
questions.a: In parallel with the part whose potential difference is measured.

questions.q: Why are household appliances connected in parallel?
questions.a: Each gets the full mains voltage and can be switched on or off independently.

questions.q: Why is tungsten used for bulb filaments?
questions.a: It has a very high melting point and gives light when white hot.

lesson.homework: Read the power rating of five appliances at home, estimate hours of use per day, and work out the energy in kWh used in a month.

topics.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
topics.summary: Field lines go from the north pole to the south pole outside a magnet; they never cross, and their closeness shows the strength of the field.
notes: Field lines go from the north pole to the south pole outside a magnet; they never cross, and their closeness shows the strength of the field.
A current-carrying straight wire has circular field lines around it; the right-hand thumb rule gives their direction.
A solenoid carrying current behaves like a bar magnet; with a soft iron core it becomes an electromagnet.
A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force; Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger field, second finger current, thumb motion.
The electric motor uses this force to turn a coil; the split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn so it keeps turning.
Homes get AC at 220 V, 50 Hz: live (red/brown), neutral (black/blue) and earth (green) wires.
Fuses and MCBs break the circuit on overloading or a short circuit; earthing protects people from shocks from metal appliance bodies.
outcomes: Describe magnetic fields of magnets and of currents
Use the right-hand thumb rule and Fleming's left-hand rule
Explain the electric motor, domestic circuits and safety devices

resources.title: Magnetic field of a bar magnet

lesson.hook: Place a compass near a wire carrying current and the needle jumps. Electricity and magnetism are two sides of one thing: how does that make a fan spin?
lesson.example: In a motor the magnet's field points from N (left) to S (right). On the coil's left side the current flows back into the page; by Fleming's left-hand rule that side is pushed down while the right side, with current coming out, is pushed up: the coil turns.
lesson.activity: Open the 3D electric motor: switch it on, then step through 'How it works' while pupils hold up their left hands to check Fleming's rule. Then show the bar magnet's field lines and have pupils map them with a compass and a magnet on paper.

questions.q: What happens to the force on a conductor if the current is reversed?
What is the function of the split-ring commutator?
questions.a: To reverse the current in the coil every half turn so that the coil keeps rotating in one direction.

questions.q: Why is an earth wire connected to the metal body of an electric iron?
questions.a: If the live wire touches the body, the current flows to earth and the fuse blows, instead of the user getting a shock.

questions.q: What is the frequency of AC supplied to Indian homes?

lesson.homework: Draw a diagram of household wiring showing live, neutral and earth wires, a fuse and two appliances in parallel.

topics.title: Our Environment
topics.summary: An ecosystem is all the living things (biotic) and their non-living surroundings (abiotic) in an area, working together.
notes: An ecosystem is all the living things (biotic) and their non-living surroundings (abiotic) in an area, working together.
Producers make food; consumers eat it (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores); decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.
Food chains link who eats whom; food webs show many interlinked chains. Each level is a trophic level.
Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level passes on to the next, so food chains rarely have more than four levels.
Some harmful chemicals (pesticides like DDT) are not broken down and build up at each level: biological magnification, highest in top consumers.
The ozone layer high in the atmosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays; CFCs from old refrigerants damage it.
Biodegradable waste is broken down by microbes; non-biodegradable waste (plastics, metals, glass) must be reduced, reused and recycled.
outcomes: Describe an ecosystem and its food chains and webs
Explain the ten per cent law and biological magnification
Discuss the ozone layer and managing garbage

lesson.hook: A plastic bag thrown away today may still be in the soil when your grandchildren go to school, while a banana peel is gone in weeks. Where does our waste go, and who clears it up?
lesson.example: Grass (10,000 J) → grasshopper (1,000 J) → frog (100 J) → snake (10 J) → eagle (1 J). With 10% passed on at each step, the eagle gets only one ten-thousandth of the energy the grass captured.
lesson.activity: Food-web string game: each pupil holds a card (sun, grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle, rabbit, fox, fungi) and a ball of string is passed along 'who eats whom'. Remove one animal and see how many strings go slack.

questions.q: Why are decomposers important in an ecosystem?
questions.a: They break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil for producers.

questions.q: If a snake gets 50 J of energy, about how much did the frogs it ate get?
Which chemicals damage the ozone layer?
Name two non-biodegradable things you used today.
questions.a: For example, a plastic pen and a polythene bag (any two).

lesson.homework: Keep a waste diary for three days: sort everything you throw away into biodegradable and non-biodegradable, and suggest one way to reduce each.

courses.title: Social Science: Contemporary India II (Geography), Class 10

topics.title: Resources and Development
topics.summary: Resources can be classified by origin (biotic, abiotic), exhaustibility (renewable, non-renewable), ownership (individual, community, national, international) and development (potential, developed, stock, reserves).
notes: Resources can be classified by origin (biotic, abiotic), exhaustibility (renewable, non-renewable), ownership (individual, community, national, international) and development (potential, developed, stock, reserves).
Sustainable development means meeting today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs; the Rio Earth Summit (1992) adopted Agenda 21.
Resource planning in India: identify and map resources, make a plan with suitable technology and skill, and match it with national plans.
Land use: net sown area, forests, barren and wasteland, fallow and pasture; overuse leads to land degradation.
Major soils: alluvial (northern plains, very fertile), black or regur (Deccan plateau, good for cotton), red and yellow, laterite, arid and forest soils.
Soil erosion by water (gullies, sheet erosion) and wind is checked by contour ploughing, terrace farming, strip cropping, shelter belts and planting trees.
outcomes: Classify resources and explain why resource planning is needed
Describe the major soil types of India and where they are found
Explain land degradation and ways to conserve soil

lesson.hook: Everything in this room came from the earth: the wooden desk, the cotton in your clothes, the iron in the fan. Which of these can we use forever, and which could run out in your lifetime?
lesson.example: Black soil forms from weathered basalt lava of the Deccan. It holds moisture well, becomes sticky when wet and cracks when dry, so it 'ploughs itself' and suits cotton — which is why Maharashtra and Gujarat grow so much cotton.
lesson.activity: Soil samples: pupils bring a spoonful of soil from home. Compare colour, feel (sandy, clayey) and how much water each holds in a paper cone. Mark on a map of India where each type of soil is found.

questions.q: Give one example each of a renewable and a non-renewable resource.
questions.a: Renewable: solar energy, forests, water. Non-renewable: coal, petroleum, minerals.

questions.q: Which soil is best for cotton and why?
questions.a: Black soil: it retains moisture and is rich in lime, potash and magnesium.

questions.q: What is Agenda 21?
questions.a: A declaration signed at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit for sustainable development worldwide.

questions.q: Name two methods of controlling soil erosion on slopes.

lesson.homework: Find out how the land around your home is used (houses, farms, forest, barren land) and draw a simple land-use map.

topics.title: Forest and Wildlife Resources
topics.summary: Biodiversity is the variety of life; every species plays a part in the ecosystem that supports us.
notes: Biodiversity is the variety of life; every species plays a part in the ecosystem that supports us.
Species are grouped as normal, endangered, vulnerable, rare, endemic and extinct by the IUCN.
Causes of decline: agricultural expansion, large dams and mining, shifting cultivation, grazing, poaching, pollution and forest fires.
The Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 set up protected areas; Project Tiger began in 1973; national parks and sanctuaries protect habitats.
Forests are classified as reserved, protected and unclassed.
Communities conserve too: the Chipko movement, Bishnoi traditions, sacred groves, Joint Forest Management.
outcomes: Explain the importance of biodiversity and forests
Describe the causes of the decline of flora and fauna
Explain government and community efforts to conserve forests and wildlife

lesson.hook: India has about 8% of the world's species on just 2.4% of its land. Name five wild animals you have seen with your own eyes. Why are so many of them becoming rare?
lesson.example: Chipko movement (1970s, Himalayas): village people, many of them women, hugged trees to stop them being cut, showing that local communities can protect forests.
lesson.activity: Species cards: groups are given animals and plants (tiger, Asiatic lion, Nicobar pigeon, blue sheep, red sanders, dodo) to sort into IUCN categories, then discuss what threatens each and one way to save it.

questions.q: In which year was Project Tiger launched?
What is an endemic species? Give an example.
questions.a: One found only in a particular area, such as the Andaman teal or Nicobar pigeon.

questions.q: Name two causes of the loss of forests.
questions.a: Agricultural expansion, mining, large dams, shifting cultivation (any two).

questions.q: What were the Chipko protesters trying to protect?
questions.a: Trees in their forests from being cut down.

lesson.homework: Find out about one national park or wildlife sanctuary nearest to your town: its location, main animals and one threat it faces.

topics.title: Water Resources
topics.summary: Only about 2.5% of the world's water is fresh, and most of that is locked in ice; water is renewable through the water cycle, but usable water is limited.
notes: Only about 2.5% of the world's water is fresh, and most of that is locked in ice; water is renewable through the water cycle, but usable water is limited.
Scarcity is caused by growing population, over-use for irrigation and industry, and pollution, not only by low rainfall.
Multipurpose projects (Bhakra–Nangal, Hirakud) give irrigation, electricity, flood control and water supply; Nehru called dams 'the temples of modern India'.
Dams also displace people, change river flow and sediment, affect aquatic life and can cause conflicts between states; movements such as Narmada Bachao Andolan opposed them.
Traditional rainwater harvesting: guls and kuls in the western Himalayas, rooftop tankas in Rajasthan, bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya, tanks in the south.
Rooftop rainwater harvesting refills groundwater; Tamil Nadu made it compulsory for all houses.
outcomes: Explain why fresh water is scarce even though Earth is covered with water
Discuss the benefits and problems of multipurpose river projects
Describe rainwater harvesting methods

lesson.hook: Three-quarters of the Earth is covered with water, yet many towns get tap water only once a week. Where is all that water, and why can we not use it?
lesson.example: In the dry Thar desert, houses in Phalodi and Barmer collected rainwater from their flat roofs into underground tankas; this 'palar pani' was their main drinking water in summer.
