lesson.activity: Water audit: pupils estimate the water their family uses in a day (bucket counts for bathing, washing, cooking), total it for the class, and suggest three ways to save water.

questions.q: Why is water scarce in areas with good rainfall?
questions.a: Over-use, unequal access, growing demand and pollution of the available water.

questions.q: Give two benefits of multipurpose river projects.
questions.a: Irrigation, electricity, flood control, water supply, fish breeding (any two).

questions.q: Give one problem caused by large dams.
questions.a: Displacement of people, loss of forests, silting, damage to aquatic life (any one).

questions.q: What is a tanka?
questions.a: An underground tank in Rajasthan houses that stores rainwater collected from the roof.

lesson.homework: Design a rooftop rainwater harvesting system for your school: draw it and explain where the water goes.

topics.title: Agriculture
topics.summary: Types of farming: primitive subsistence (slash and burn, called jhumming in the north-east), intensive subsistence, and commercial farming (plantations of tea, coffee, rubber).
notes: Types of farming: primitive subsistence (slash and burn, called jhumming in the north-east), intensive subsistence, and commercial farming (plantations of tea, coffee, rubber).
Cropping seasons: rabi (sown in winter, harvested in spring: wheat, barley, mustard), kharif (sown with the monsoon: rice, maize, cotton), zaid (short summer season: watermelon, cucumber).
Rice needs high temperature and heavy rainfall; wheat a cool growing season and bright sunshine at ripening; millets (jowar, bajra, ragi) grow in dry areas and are very nutritious.
Pulses fix nitrogen and improve the soil; India is the largest producer of pulses.
Reforms: land reforms, the Green Revolution, the White Revolution (Operation Flood), crop insurance, Kisan Credit Cards and minimum support prices.
Farming now faces falling land holdings, costly inputs, and competition from global markets.
outcomes: Describe the types of farming practised in India
Explain the cropping seasons and the major crops with their conditions
Discuss technological and institutional reforms in agriculture

resources.title: Seasons: the Earth round the Sun

lesson.hook: Two-thirds of India's people depend on farming. Where does your rice or roti come from, and in which season was it sown?
lesson.example: Punjab and Haryana grow rice as a commercial crop even with low rainfall, because canals and tube wells supply irrigation; in Odisha rice is a subsistence crop grown for the family.
lesson.activity: Crop calendar: groups make a year-long calendar showing when rice, wheat, mustard, cotton and watermelon are sown and harvested in your state. Ask a farming family to check it.

questions.q: Name two rabi crops and two kharif crops.
questions.a: Rabi: wheat, barley, mustard, gram. Kharif: rice, maize, cotton, jowar.

questions.q: What is slash-and-burn farming called in the north-east?
Why are pulses grown in rotation with other crops?
questions.a: Being legumes, they fix nitrogen and restore soil fertility.

questions.q: What was the Green Revolution?
questions.a: The use of high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation to raise food production, especially of wheat, from the late 1960s.

lesson.homework: Interview a farmer (or a family member who knows farming) about one crop: when it is sown, what it needs and where it is sold.

topics.title: Minerals and Energy Resources
topics.summary: A mineral is a naturally occurring homogeneous substance with a definite composition; ores are rocks from which metals can be extracted profitably.
notes: A mineral is a naturally occurring homogeneous substance with a definite composition; ores are rocks from which metals can be extracted profitably.
Minerals occur in veins and lodes, in beds and layers, in alluvial deposits (placer), and in ocean water.
Ferrous minerals: iron ore (Odisha–Jharkhand, Karnataka's Kudremukh and Bellary), manganese. Non-ferrous: copper, bauxite. Non-metallic: mica, limestone.
Conventional energy: coal (Damodar valley), petroleum (Mumbai High, Assam), natural gas, electricity from thermal and hydel plants, nuclear power.
Non-conventional energy: solar, wind (Tamil Nadu, Gujarat), tidal, geothermal, biogas; they are renewable and cleaner.
Minerals are finite and take millions of years to form, so they must be recycled, used carefully and replaced by alternatives.
outcomes: Distinguish metallic and non-metallic minerals and their modes of occurrence
Locate the major mineral and energy resources of India
Compare conventional and non-conventional energy and explain conservation

lesson.hook: Your phone, the steel spoon and the electricity in this room all come from rocks under the ground. What happens when they are used up?
lesson.example: Kudremukh in Karnataka has one of the world's largest iron ore deposits; the ore was sent as slurry through a pipeline to the port of Mangaluru for export.
lesson.activity: Energy detectives: pupils list every source of energy used in their home (LPG, electricity, firewood, petrol, solar) and mark which are renewable. The class then makes a pie chart.

questions.q: Name two non-metallic minerals.
Which is India's largest offshore oil field?
Give two advantages of solar energy.
questions.a: It is renewable, cheap to run and does not pollute.

questions.q: What is an ore?
questions.a: A rock with enough of a mineral to extract it profitably.

lesson.homework: List five ways your family could save electricity and estimate the units saved in a month.

topics.title: Manufacturing Industries
topics.summary: Manufacturing turns raw materials into more valuable products; it creates jobs, uses agricultural produce and earns foreign exchange.
notes: Manufacturing turns raw materials into more valuable products; it creates jobs, uses agricultural produce and earns foreign exchange.
Industries can be classified by raw material (agro-based, mineral-based), by ownership (public, private, joint, cooperative), by size (small, large), and by main role (basic, consumer).
Location depends on raw materials, power, labour, markets, capital, transport and government policy.
Examples: cotton textiles (Maharashtra, Gujarat), jute (Hugli basin), sugar (Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra), iron and steel (Chota Nagpur plateau), IT (Bengaluru).
Industries pollute air, water, land and create noise; treating waste water, filters on chimneys and using cleaner fuels reduce harm.
outcomes: Explain the importance of manufacturing for development
Classify industries and explain the factors that decide their location
Describe industrial pollution and ways to reduce it

lesson.hook: Raw cotton sells for a few rupees a kilo, but a cotton shirt sells for hundreds. Where does the extra value come from, and who earns it?
lesson.example: The iron and steel industry clusters on the Chota Nagpur plateau because iron ore, coal, manganese and limestone are all close by, with cheap labour and rail links to markets.
lesson.activity: Product journey: each group picks something (a notebook, a biscuit packet, a bicycle) and traces its raw materials, the factory stage and the market, drawing the chain on the board.

questions.q: Give one example of an agro-based industry.
questions.a: Cotton textiles, jute, sugar, vegetable oil (any one).

questions.q: Why is the Chota Nagpur plateau good for iron and steel plants?
questions.a: Iron ore, coal and other raw materials are found nearby, with cheap labour and transport.

questions.q: Name one way to reduce water pollution by factories.
questions.a: Treating waste water before releasing it.

questions.q: What is a cooperative industry?
questions.a: One owned and run by the producers of the raw material, such as sugar mills owned by cane farmers.

lesson.homework: Find one factory near your town: what it makes, where its raw materials come from and how it affects the area.

topics.title: Lifelines of National Economy
topics.summary: Transport, communication and trade are the lifelines of the national economy.
notes: Transport, communication and trade are the lifelines of the national economy.
Roads: Golden Quadrilateral, North–South and East–West corridors, national highways, state highways, district and rural roads, border roads.
Railways are the largest carriers of goods and passengers over long distances; pipelines carry oil and gas.
Waterways: national waterways on the Ganga, Brahmaputra and the west coast canal; major sea ports (Mumbai, Kandla, Kochi, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Kolkata).
Communication: post, telephone, mass media; international trade — exports and imports — and the balance of trade.
Tourism brings foreign exchange and jobs and supports local handicrafts.
outcomes: Describe India's roadways, railways, pipelines, waterways and airways
Explain the role of communication and trade in the economy
Understand tourism as a trade

lesson.hook: The rice you ate yesterday may have travelled a thousand kilometres, and a message to a friend abroad travels in a second. What links make this possible?
lesson.example: The Golden Quadrilateral highway joins Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Mumbai, cutting travel time and costs between India's biggest cities.
lesson.activity: Map race: on an outline map of India, groups mark the four metros of the Golden Quadrilateral, three major ports and one national waterway; the first accurate map wins.

questions.q: Which four cities does the Golden Quadrilateral join?
Why are pipelines useful?
questions.a: They carry oil, gas and even solids in slurry form cheaply and steadily, with few losses.

questions.q: What is a favourable balance of trade?
questions.a: When the value of exports is more than the value of imports.

questions.q: Name one major port on the east coast.
questions.a: Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip or Kolkata (any one).

lesson.homework: Trace how a letter or a parcel reaches your home from another state: which modes of transport and communication it uses.

courses.title: Social Science: Democratic Politics II, Class 10

topics.title: Power-sharing
topics.summary: Belgium accommodated its Dutch- and French-speaking communities with equal ministers, community governments and a special Brussels government, and avoided civil war.
notes: Belgium accommodated its Dutch- and French-speaking communities with equal ministers, community governments and a special Brussels government, and avoided civil war.
Sri Lanka's majoritarian policies (Sinhala only, 1956) alienated the Tamil minority and led to a long civil war.
Prudential reason: sharing power reduces conflict between groups. Moral reason: people have a right to be consulted in a democracy.
Horizontal sharing among legislature, executive and judiciary (checks and balances).
Vertical sharing among levels of government: union, state and local (federalism).
Sharing among social groups (reserved seats) and among political parties, pressure groups and movements (coalitions).
outcomes: Explain why power-sharing is good for democracy
Compare how Belgium and Sri Lanka dealt with social diversity
Describe the different forms of power-sharing

lesson.hook: Imagine your class captain made every decision alone — which games to play, who sits where. Would that be fair? How should power be shared in a class, and in a country?
lesson.example: In Belgium the number of Dutch- and French-speaking ministers in the central government is equal, so no single community can make decisions alone.
lesson.activity: Role-play: split the class into two language groups deciding a school rule. First let the bigger group decide alone; then let both share. Discuss which result felt fair and which would last.

questions.q: Which language was declared the only official language of Sri Lanka in 1956?
Give the prudential reason for power-sharing.
questions.a: It reduces the chance of conflict between social groups and so keeps the country stable.

questions.q: What is horizontal distribution of power?
questions.a: Sharing among the legislature, executive and judiciary at the same level.

questions.q: What is a coalition government?
questions.a: A government formed by two or more parties together.

lesson.homework: Find one example of power-sharing in your town or school (a committee, reserved seats, a council) and describe it.

topics.title: Federalism
topics.summary: Federalism has two or more levels of government, each with its own powers written in the Constitution, over the same citizens.
notes: Federalism has two or more levels of government, each with its own powers written in the Constitution, over the same citizens.
India's Constitution divides powers into the Union List (defence, currency), the State List (police, agriculture) and the Concurrent List (education, forests); residuary subjects go to the Union.
Linguistic states (from 1956), a flexible language policy (Hindi with English and 22 scheduled languages) and centre–state relations keep federalism working.
Changing the basic structure needs the agreement of both levels; courts settle disputes.
Decentralisation: since 1992 the Constitution requires elected panchayats and municipalities, with seats reserved for women, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and a State Election Commission.
outcomes: Explain what federalism is and its key features
Describe how India's federal system works (lists, languages, states)
Explain decentralisation and local self-government

lesson.hook: Who decides the syllabus of your school, who looks after the police in your town, and who issues the rupee notes? Different governments do different jobs: why?
lesson.example: Education is on the Concurrent List: both Parliament and state legislatures can make laws on it, but if they conflict, the Union law prevails.
lesson.activity: Sort the subjects: groups get cards (defence, police, banking, agriculture, education, marriage, trade unions, cyber laws) and place them on Union, State or Concurrent List posters, then check with the teacher.

questions.q: Name one subject from the Union List.
questions.a: Defence, foreign affairs, banking, currency (any one).

questions.q: What are residuary subjects? Who makes laws on them?
questions.a: Subjects not in any list, such as computer software; the Union government.

questions.q: What proportion of seats in local bodies is reserved for women?
Who conducts elections to panchayats and municipalities?

lesson.homework: Find the names of your gram panchayat or ward councillor and one work they did in your area.

topics.title: Gender, Religion and Caste
topics.summary: Gender division assigns roles by sex; women's work at home is often unpaid and unrecognised, and women remain under-represented in legislatures.
notes: Gender division assigns roles by sex; women's work at home is often unpaid and unrecognised, and women remain under-represented in legislatures.
Feminist movements demanded equal rights; the one-third reservation in local bodies has increased women's participation.
Religion in politics becomes communalism when one religion is seen as superior or as the basis of the nation; it can lead to violence.
India is a secular state: no official religion, freedom to follow any faith, and no discrimination on grounds of religion.
Caste inequalities persist; caste can play a role in voting and party choice, but no party wins by caste votes alone, and politics has also given voice to disadvantaged castes.
outcomes: Explain how gender, religion and caste can shape politics
Distinguish secularism from communalism
Discuss how social divisions are expressed in a democracy

lesson.hook: Who does most of the unpaid work in your home, like cooking and caring for children? Should that decide who gets to make laws?
lesson.example: The Constitution makes India secular: there is no state religion, every person may profess any religion, and the state may intervene in religion only to ensure equality (e.g. banning untouchability).
lesson.activity: Time-use survey: pupils note who does which housework at home for a day and total the hours by men and women. Discuss what the figures say about gender division.

questions.q: What is patriarchy?
questions.a: A system that values men more and gives them power over women.

questions.q: Define communalism.
questions.a: Politics based on religious identity that treats one religion as superior or as the only basis of the nation.

questions.q: Give one constitutional provision that makes India secular.
questions.a: No official religion; freedom of religion; ban on religious discrimination (any one).

questions.q: Why can no party win elections on caste votes alone?
questions.a: No constituency has a clear majority of one caste, and voters consider many other issues.

lesson.homework: Collect a news report about women's representation or about a secular value in action, and write three lines on it.

topics.title: Political Parties
topics.summary: A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power, with shared policies.
notes: A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power, with shared policies.
Parties contest elections, put forward policies, make laws, form and run governments, play the role of the opposition and shape public opinion.
Systems: one-party (China), two-party (USA, UK), multi-party (India) with alliances and coalitions.
The Election Commission recognises national and state parties; parties get a reserved symbol.

Challenges: lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, few meaningful choices; reforms include the anti-defection law, affidavits on assets and criminal cases, and internal elections.
outcomes: Explain why democracies need political parties and what parties do
Compare one-party, two-party and multi-party systems
Discuss challenges to parties and ways to reform them

lesson.hook: If there were no political parties, how would you choose among thousands of independent candidates, and who would form the government?
lesson.example: The anti-defection law disqualifies an MLA or MP who changes party after being elected, so representatives cannot be bought after an election.
lesson.activity: Mock party: groups form parties, choose a name, a symbol and three promises for the school, then present them; the class votes and discusses what makes a promise believable.

questions.q: Name one country with a two-party system.
questions.a: The USA or the United Kingdom.

questions.q: What is the role of the opposition party?
questions.a: To question and criticise the government and hold it to account.

questions.q: Who recognises political parties in India?
Give one challenge political parties face.
questions.a: Lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power (any one).

lesson.homework: Choose one national party and find its symbol, its founding year and one of its main promises.

topics.title: Outcomes of Democracy
topics.summary: Democracy produces a government that is accountable, responsive and legitimate — chosen by the people and answerable to them.
notes: Democracy produces a government that is accountable, responsive and legitimate — chosen by the people and answerable to them.
Decisions may be slower, but they are more acceptable because they follow deliberation; transparency lets citizens check decisions.
On economic growth, democracies and dictatorships show mixed records; democracy is not a guarantee of prosperity.
Economic inequality persists in many democracies; poor voters remain large in number but not always heard.
Democracy accommodates social diversity and protects minorities; it promotes the dignity and freedom of individuals, especially women and disadvantaged castes.
Its ability to examine its own weaknesses and correct them makes democracy better than the alternatives.
outcomes: Assess what outcomes we can expect from democracy
Evaluate democracy on accountability, economic growth, inequality, social diversity and dignity
Explain why democracy is better than other forms of government

lesson.hook: Democracy is often slow: debates, elections, protests. Would a strong ruler who decides quickly be better? What should we expect democracy to give us?
lesson.example: The Right to Information Act lets any citizen ask a government office for records, making the government more transparent and accountable.
lesson.activity: Report card: groups grade Indian democracy (A–E) on accountability, economic growth, reducing inequality, accommodating diversity and dignity of citizens, with one piece of evidence for each grade.

questions.q: What makes a government legitimate?
questions.a: It is chosen by the people through free and fair elections.

questions.q: Why are democratic decisions often slower?
questions.a: They involve discussion, consultation and following procedures.

questions.q: Does democracy always reduce economic inequality?
questions.a: No; inequality remains in many democracies.

questions.q: Why is democracy considered better than dictatorship?
questions.a: It is accountable, respects rights and dignity, handles differences peacefully and can correct its own mistakes.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph: 'One thing Indian democracy has achieved and one thing it still must improve.'

courses.title: Social Science: India and the Contemporary World II (History), Class 10

chapters.title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

topics.title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
topics.summary: The French Revolution (1789) transferred sovereignty from the monarch to the people, introducing ideas like la patrie (fatherland) and le citoyen (citizen).
notes: The French Revolution (1789) transferred sovereignty from the monarch to the people, introducing ideas like la patrie (fatherland) and le citoyen (citizen).
Napoleon's Civil Code (1804) ended privileges based on birth, protected property and simplified administration, even as his rule was authoritarian.
After 1815 the Congress of Vienna restored monarchies; liberals and nationalists worked through secret societies and uprisings, as in 1830 and 1848.
Italy was unified (1861) through Mazzini's ideas, Cavour's diplomacy and Garibaldi's volunteers; Germany (1871) through Prussia's army under Bismarck — 'blood and iron'.
Romanticism, folk songs, language and allegories like Marianne and Germania built national feeling.
Later, narrow nationalism and imperial rivalry, especially in the Balkans, led to the First World War.
outcomes: Explain how the idea of the nation-state grew in Europe after the French Revolution
Describe the unification of Italy and Germany
Explain how nationalism was expressed in culture and how it later led to conflict

lesson.hook: What makes a group of people feel they are one nation: a common language, a flag, a song, a shared history? Think of how you feel when the national anthem is played.
lesson.example: Giuseppe Mazzini founded Young Italy in 1831; he believed nations were the natural units of mankind, so Italy could not remain a patchwork of small kingdoms.
lesson.activity: Build a timeline on the board from 1789 to 1871 with pupils placing cards (French Revolution, Napoleonic Code, Congress of Vienna, 1848 revolutions, Italian unification, German unification) in order.

questions.q: What did the Napoleonic Code of 1804 abolish?
Who was the architect of German unification?
questions.a: Otto von Bismarck, the chief minister of Prussia.

questions.q: Name the three leaders linked with Italian unification.
Why did the Balkans become a source of conflict?
questions.a: Rival nationalisms of its peoples and the ambitions of big European powers there.

lesson.homework: Design a symbol (allegory) for India as a nation: draw it and explain what each part stands for.

topics.title: Nationalism in India
topics.summary: The First World War brought taxes, price rises and forced recruitment, adding to discontent.
notes: The First World War brought taxes, price rises and forced recruitment, adding to discontent.
Gandhiji's satyagraha — truth and non-violence — was tried at Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad.
The Rowlatt Act (1919) led to protests and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre at Amritsar.
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) joined with the Khilafat movement: boycott of foreign cloth, schools, courts and councils; withdrawn after Chauri Chaura.
Civil Disobedience began with the Salt March to Dandi (1930); peasants, business groups, women and others joined for different reasons, while some Dalits and Muslims kept apart.
Collective belonging grew through the image of Bharat Mata, folk tales, songs and the national flag.
outcomes: Explain how the First World War and Gandhiji's satyagraha changed the national movement
Describe the Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience movements
Explain how different groups joined and how a sense of collective belonging grew

lesson.hook: Can people win freedom from an empire without weapons? In the 1920s millions of Indians tried — by refusing to cooperate.
lesson.example: In March 1930 Gandhiji walked about 390 km from Sabarmati to Dandi and made salt from sea water, breaking the salt law — a simple act everyone could copy, since everyone uses salt.
lesson.activity: Role-play a village meeting in 1930: a peasant, a merchant, a woman volunteer and a Dalit leader each explain why they will (or will not) join the Civil Disobedience Movement.

questions.q: Why did Gandhiji choose salt for the 1930 movement?
questions.a: Salt was used by everyone, rich and poor, and the tax on it affected all.

questions.q: Why was the Non-Cooperation Movement withdrawn?
questions.a: After the violence at Chauri Chaura in 1922.

questions.q: What did the Rowlatt Act allow?
questions.a: Detention of political prisoners without trial for up to two years.

questions.q: Who painted the famous image of Bharat Mata?

lesson.homework: Find out how the national movement reached your region: a local leader, event or place connected with it.

chapters.title: The Making of a Global World

topics.title: The Making of a Global World
topics.summary: The silk routes linked Asia, Europe and Africa; food crops like potato and maize travelled across the world after 1492.
notes: The silk routes linked Asia, Europe and Africa; food crops like potato and maize travelled across the world after 1492.
The 19th century saw huge flows of goods, labour and capital; railways, steamships and refrigerated ships made trade faster and cheaper.
Colonialism reshaped economies; the rinderpest cattle plague in Africa helped colonisers force people into wage labour; Indian indentured labourers went to the Caribbean, Fiji and Mauritius.
The First World War and the Great Depression (from 1929) caused collapse of prices, trade and jobs; Indian peasants were badly hit.
After 1945, the Bretton Woods system set up the IMF and the World Bank; decolonised countries formed the G-77 to demand a fairer order.
From the 1970s, production moved to low-wage countries and globalisation grew.
outcomes: Trace how the world economy became connected from early trade to the present
Explain the effects of colonialism, the Great Depression and the world wars on the global economy
Describe the post-war international economic order and globalisation

lesson.hook: Potatoes, chillies and tomatoes came to India from the Americas; Indian indigo and cotton went across the seas. Trade has been making one world for centuries: how?
lesson.example: Indentured labourers were hired under contracts to work on plantations abroad for a fixed period; many from Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh went to Trinidad, Guyana and Fiji, and their culture blended into new forms such as chutney music.
lesson.activity: Map the journeys: on a world map pupils draw the silk routes, the voyage of food crops from the Americas, and the routes of indentured labourers from India, using different colours.

questions.q: Name two food items that came to India from the Americas.
questions.a: Potato, chillies, tomato, maize, groundnut (any two).

questions.q: What were the Bretton Woods institutions?
questions.a: The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

questions.q: How did the Great Depression affect Indian farmers?
questions.a: Crop prices fell sharply but land revenue did not, so many fell into debt.

questions.q: What was indentured labour?
questions.a: Bonded labour under a contract to work for an employer for a fixed period, often abroad.

lesson.homework: Pick one food you eat often and find out where it first came from and how it reached India.

topics.title: The Age of Industrialisation
topics.summary: Proto-industrialisation: before factories, merchants supplied raw materials to rural spinners and weavers who worked at home.
notes: Proto-industrialisation: before factories, merchants supplied raw materials to rural spinners and weavers who worked at home.
Factories grew slowly in Britain; cotton and iron led the way, but hand labour remained important for a long time.
The East India Company controlled Indian weavers through gomasthas (paid agents), and Manchester cloth flooded Indian markets, hurting weavers.
Indian entrepreneurs such as Dwarkanath Tagore, Jamsetjee Jeejeebhoy and later the Tatas set up industries; the first cotton mill opened in Bombay in 1854.
The Swadeshi movement and the First World War helped Indian industry grow.
Advertisements, labels and calendars used images of gods and national figures to sell goods and build markets.
outcomes: Understand proto-industrialisation and the coming of factories in Britain
Explain how industrialisation affected Indian weavers and how Indian industries grew
Describe how markets for goods were created through advertising

lesson.hook: For centuries fine Indian cotton was prized across the world. Why, by the 1850s, was cheap British mill cloth being sold in Indian bazaars?
lesson.example: The fly shuttle, used by many Indian weavers in the early 20th century, let a weaver make wider cloth faster, helping handloom production survive against mill cloth.
lesson.activity: Advertisement study: groups bring an old or current advertisement and discuss what it uses to persuade — national pride, religion, beauty, health — and compare it with a 1900s label shown by the teacher.

questions.q: What was proto-industrialisation?
questions.a: Large-scale production for international markets by rural workers at home, before factories, organised by merchants.

questions.q: Who were gomasthas?
questions.a: Paid agents appointed by the East India Company to supervise weavers and collect their cloth.

questions.q: When and where did the first cotton mill in India start?
How did the Swadeshi movement help Indian industry?
questions.a: People boycotted foreign goods and bought Indian-made goods.

lesson.homework: Find a handloom or handicraft still made in your region and describe how it is made and sold today.

chapters.title: Print Culture and the Modern World

topics.title: Print Culture and the Modern World
topics.summary: The earliest printing, by hand on paper with wooden blocks, came from China and spread to Japan and Korea.
notes: The earliest printing, by hand on paper with wooden blocks, came from China and spread to Japan and Korea.
Gutenberg developed the printing press in Germany in the 1430s; the first book he printed was the Bible.
Print created a reading public, spread Martin Luther's ideas (the Protestant Reformation) and later the ideas of the Enlightenment that shaped the French Revolution.
In India, Portuguese missionaries brought the press to Goa in the mid-16th century; newspapers and books in Indian languages grew in the 19th century.
Print spread religious debates, reform ideas (against sati, for widow remarriage), women's writing and lower-caste protest.
The British tried to control the press, as with the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, but newspapers spread nationalist ideas.
outcomes: Trace the history of print from East Asia to Europe
Explain how print changed religion, ideas and politics in Europe
Describe how print spread in India and shaped reform and nationalism

lesson.hook: Before printing, every book was copied by hand, so only a few people could own one. How did the printing press change who could read, think and argue?
lesson.example: Rashsundari Debi, a housewife in East Bengal, secretly learnt to read in the kitchen and wrote her autobiography Amar Jiban (1876) — one of the first by an Indian woman.
lesson.activity: Make a simple print: pupils carve a letter or pattern into a potato or rubber and print it with ink or paint, then discuss how much faster movable type was than copying by hand.

questions.q: Who invented the printing press, and what was the first book he printed?
Where did printing first develop?
What was the Vernacular Press Act (1878)?
questions.a: A British law giving the government power to censor reports and editorials in Indian-language newspapers.

questions.q: How did print help social reform in India?
questions.a: It spread debates on practices like sati and child marriage and gave reformers a wide audience.

lesson.homework: Look at a newspaper at home and list the different kinds of content in it (news, editorial, advertisements, letters). Which ones shape opinion?

courses.title: Social Science: Understanding Economic Development, Class 10

topics.title: Development
topics.summary: Different people have different, sometimes conflicting, development goals; besides income, people want equal treatment, freedom, security and respect.
notes: Different people have different, sometimes conflicting, development goals; besides income, people want equal treatment, freedom, security and respect.
National income and per capita income (average income) are used to compare countries; the World Bank classifies countries by per capita income.
Averages hide inequality, so we also use other indicators: infant mortality rate, literacy rate, net attendance ratio.
The Human Development Index (UNDP) combines income, health (life expectancy) and education.
Kerala has lower per capita income than some states but better health and education indicators, because of public facilities.
Development must be sustainable: groundwater, crude oil and other resources are being over-used.
outcomes: Understand that different people have different development goals
Compare countries and states using income and other indicators
Explain human development and the sustainability of development

lesson.hook: For a farmer, development may mean more rain and fair prices; for a city girl, safety and a good college. Can one country's 'development' mean the same to everyone?
lesson.example: Village A: five families earn ₹9,000, ₹10,000, ₹10,000, ₹10,000 and ₹11,000 a month. Village B: ₹2,000, ₹2,000, ₹3,000, ₹3,000 and ₹40,000. Both have an average income of ₹10,000, but life in the two villages is very different — the average hides it.
lesson.activity: Class survey on development goals: each pupil writes their top three 'development wishes' for their family and village or town; tally them and discuss which need money and which need public services.

questions.q: What is per capita income?
questions.a: The total income of a country divided by its population.

questions.q: What three things does the Human Development Index combine?
Why can averages be misleading?
questions.a: They hide how unequally income is shared.

questions.q: What does sustainable development mean?
questions.a: Development that does not harm the resources future generations will need.

lesson.homework: Find the literacy rate and infant mortality rate of your state and compare them with Kerala's and Bihar's.

topics.title: Sectors of the Indian Economy
topics.summary: Primary sector uses natural resources directly (farming, fishing, mining); secondary sector manufactures (industry); tertiary sector gives services (transport, banking, teaching).
notes: Primary sector uses natural resources directly (farming, fishing, mining); secondary sector manufactures (industry); tertiary sector gives services (transport, banking, teaching).
Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year; counting only final goods avoids double counting.
In India the tertiary sector now produces the largest share of GDP, but the primary sector still employs the largest number of people.
Disguised unemployment: more people work than are needed, as on small family farms.
The MGNREGA 2005 guarantees 100 days of paid work a year to rural households.

Organised sector jobs are regular, with rules and benefits; unorganised sector jobs are low-paid and insecure. Public sector is owned by government (railways), private sector by individuals or companies.
outcomes: Classify economic activities into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors
Explain GDP and how sectors changed over time
Distinguish organised and unorganised, public and private sectors, and explain underemployment and MGNREGA

lesson.hook: A farmer grows wheat, a miller turns it into flour, a baker makes bread and a shopkeeper sells it. Who belongs to which part of the economy?
lesson.example: A cotton farmer sells cotton for ₹100; a mill spins it into yarn worth ₹180; a weaver makes cloth worth ₹300; a tailor sells shirts for ₹600. Only the final value, ₹600, counts in GDP; adding 100 + 180 + 300 + 600 would count the cotton four times.
lesson.activity: Occupations in your street: pupils list the jobs of ten adults they know and classify each into primary, secondary or tertiary, and organised or unorganised. Pool the results on the board.

questions.q: In which sector is a teacher?
What is disguised unemployment?
questions.a: When more people are working than are needed, so some add nothing to output.

questions.q: What does MGNREGA guarantee?
questions.a: 100 days of paid work a year to every rural household that wants it.

questions.q: Why are only final goods counted in GDP?
questions.a: Their value already includes the value of the intermediate goods used, so counting both would double-count.

lesson.homework: Make a chart of the goods and services your family used today and classify each by sector.

topics.title: Money and Credit
topics.summary: Money removes the need for double coincidence of wants that barter requires.
notes: Money removes the need for double coincidence of wants that barter requires.
Modern money: currency (issued by the Reserve Bank of India) and demand deposits in banks, used through cheques and digital payments.
Banks keep a part of deposits as cash and lend the rest; the difference between interest on loans and on deposits is their income.
Terms of credit: interest rate, collateral, documents and mode of repayment.
Formal credit (banks, cooperatives) is regulated by the RBI; informal credit (moneylenders, traders) often charges very high interest and can trap borrowers in a debt trap.
Self-help groups of 15–20 rural women pool savings and give small loans, and can get bank loans without collateral.
outcomes: Explain money as a medium of exchange and its modern forms
Describe how banks and other sources give credit and on what terms
Compare formal and informal credit and explain self-help groups

lesson.hook: Before money, a shoe-maker who wanted wheat had to find a farmer who wanted shoes. How did money solve this, and why do people sometimes borrow at crushing rates of interest?
lesson.example: Suresh, a small farmer, borrows ₹20,000 from a moneylender at 3% a month for seeds and fertiliser. The rains fail, the crop is poor and the interest keeps adding up; to repay he has to sell his pair of bullocks. Credit that should have helped has pushed him into a debt trap.
lesson.activity: Loan comparison: groups compare a ₹10,000 loan for a year at 12% from a bank and at 5% per month from a moneylender. They calculate what each would cost and discuss why poor families still use moneylenders.

questions.q: What is the double coincidence of wants?
questions.a: Both parties in a barter must want what the other has.

questions.q: Who issues currency notes in India?
What is collateral?
questions.a: An asset (land, gold, a house) the borrower pledges as a guarantee until the loan is repaid.

questions.q: Give one benefit of self-help groups.
questions.a: Members get small loans at reasonable interest without collateral, and gain confidence and a voice.

lesson.homework: Ask at home: where has your family borrowed from (bank, relatives, others) and on what terms? Keep the answers private; share only the types of sources.

topics.title: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
topics.summary: A multinational corporation (MNC) owns or controls production in more than one country, often where labour and resources are cheaper.
notes: A multinational corporation (MNC) owns or controls production in more than one country, often where labour and resources are cheaper.
MNCs spread production by setting up factories, joint ventures with local firms, buying local companies, or placing orders with small producers.
Globalisation is the rapid integration of countries through trade, investment, technology and movement of people.
It was driven by cheaper transport and information technology and by liberalisation — removing barriers to foreign trade and investment (India, 1991); the WTO sets trade rules.
Impact: more choice and better products for consumers and new jobs in some sectors, but small producers and workers may face tough competition and insecure jobs.
Fair globalisation needs government policies that protect workers and small producers.
outcomes: Explain how multinational corporations connect production across countries
Understand globalisation and the factors that made it possible
Assess the impact of globalisation and the need for fair globalisation

lesson.hook: Look at your phone, shoes and school bag. Where were they made? Many things you use travelled across the world before reaching you.
lesson.example: Toyota Kirloskar, a joint venture of a Japanese car maker and an Indian company, makes cars at Bidadi near Bengaluru for Indian buyers and exports them to other countries — production, investment and trade linked across borders.
lesson.activity: Label hunt: pupils check where ten things at home or in class were made (look for 'Made in'). Mark the countries on a world map and discuss why so many products come from abroad.

questions.q: What is an MNC?
questions.a: A company that owns or controls production in more than one country.

questions.q: When did India remove many barriers to foreign trade and investment?
Name two factors that helped globalisation.
questions.a: Improvements in technology (transport, IT) and liberalisation of trade and investment.

questions.q: Give one negative effect of globalisation.
questions.a: Small producers face strong competition; workers may lose job security (any one).

lesson.homework: Interview a shopkeeper about which products they sell that are made by foreign companies or imported.

topics.title: Consumer Rights
topics.summary: Consumers are exploited through under-weighing, adulteration, defective goods, high prices and misleading advertisements.
notes: Consumers are exploited through under-weighing, adulteration, defective goods, high prices and misleading advertisements.
Consumer rights: to safety, to be informed, to choose, to be heard, to seek redress, and to consumer education.
Look for the maximum retail price (MRP), the expiry date, the ISI or Agmark and hallmark labels.
The Consumer Protection Act 1986 (updated in 2019) set up consumer commissions at district, state and national levels.
Consumers also have duties: ask for a bill, check quality marks, and complain when cheated; 24 December is National Consumers' Day.
outcomes: Recognise ways in which consumers are exploited
Explain consumer rights and duties
Describe how consumer courts help and how to file a complaint

lesson.hook: You buy a packet of biscuits and find it half empty, or a new fan stops working in a week. What can you do about it?
lesson.example: A family buys a pressure cooker whose safety valve is faulty; it bursts in the first week. With the bill and the warranty card they complain to the district consumer commission, which orders the seller to replace it and pay compensation.
lesson.activity: Label reading: groups examine five packets (biscuits, soap, oil, medicine, milk) and record MRP, date of manufacture and expiry, quality marks and weight. Discuss what each tells the consumer.

questions.q: Name two rights of consumers.
questions.a: Right to safety, to information, to choose, to be heard, to seek redress, to consumer education (any two).

questions.q: Which mark shows the purity of gold jewellery?
When is National Consumers' Day?
What should you always ask for when you buy something expensive?
questions.a: A bill (receipt), and a guarantee or warranty card if there is one.

lesson.homework: Draft a short complaint letter to a consumer commission about a defective product, listing the details you would include.
